He describes a world at rest before any dust settled on it, where every created thing was steady in its obedience and each one was content with its place. Then the ocean of mercy began to move, and a creature was planned who could love God by choice rather than by nature. On his reading the angels were measuring the world they knew, and God was about to make something the universe had no sample of.

Think of a factory where every machine runs at the same speed and the manager announces that a new worker will be hired to run one bench by hand. The staff point out that machines do not make mistakes. The manager knows that the point of the new bench is not speed. It is a pair of hands that can choose.

**THE ANSWER THAT CLOSES THE SUBJECT**

***“Allah responded, “I know what you do not know.””*** Al-Saʿdī explains the ground of the answer. The angels had spoken from what they expected, and God knows the outward and the hidden. He also knows the good that will come out of creating this deputy: the prophets, the truthful, the witnesses who die for what they know, and the righteous who carry the earth for a season. Not one of them would have existed if the appointment had not been made.

Al-Jalālayn lists the same goods in his own words: the benefits of placing Adam on the earth, and the fact that his descendants would include both the obedient and the disobedient, so that justice would have something to work with. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the sentence short and lets it carry: God replied that He knew the deep wisdom behind the creation of these creatures and behind their appointment as guardians, and the angels did not.

The answer has one property that makes it worth carrying into every argument a person has with a difficult decree. It is not a refusal to explain. It is a statement that the explanation is larger than the questioner's current position, and that the One who gave the order is already in possession of the end of the story. A reader who takes that seriously will find that it changes the way he asks his own questions about the world.

---
## Verse 2:31

> He taught Adam the names of all things, then He presented them to the angels and said, “Tell Me the names of these, if what you say is true?”

**THE LESSON ADAM WAS GIVEN**

The verse names the lesson given to the first human being: ***“He taught Adam the names of all things”***, Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the lesson in the plainest terms: God taught Adam the names of everything, living and otherwise, along with their pronunciation and their meanings. Al-Jalālayn says the same and adds that the knowledge was placed into his heart. The verse does not describe a class with a teacher standing at a board. It describes a person receiving the basic equipment of a mind that can speak about the world.

Ibn ʿAbbās, in his commentary, reads the names as the names of the creatures and the descendants who would come after Adam, and he gives an example that makes the list concrete: a cooking pot, a plate, a saucer. tafsir_initial gathers the different positions the early scholars took, since the verse left the list open. Ibn ʿAbbās read the names as the words people use when they talk to one another, such as man, sea, mountain. Mujāhid read them as the names of everything. Others read them as the names of the angels. Al-Ṭabarī preferred the reading that they are the names of Adam's descendants, and he gave a grammatical reason: the pronoun used for the things presented is the masculine plural, which Arabic uses for beings with reason.

Al-Qurṭubī opens his commentary on this verse with a grammar point and then moves to something larger. The verb means to make known, and the teaching here may have come by direct inspiration or through the angel Gabriel. He records the observation of the Sufi teachers, who noted that Adam knew the names by God's instruction and kept them by God's protection, but that he later forgot what he had been told, in the verse about the covenant he broke ((20:115 — **“And indeed, We had taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot”**)). Knowledge given and knowledge kept are two different gifts, and this verse is about the first.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws a conclusion about language itself from this episode. Since the first human being was taught the names rather than inventing them, the position of Imām al-Ashʿarī is supported: language is a creation of God rather than a human convention that appeared by accident. Human beings then developed it into thousands of forms over the centuries, and every one of those forms rests on a capacity that was placed in the first man by his Maker.

Think of a child who walks into a workshop and can already name every tool, its use and its danger, without being told twice. The workman who owns the shop would notice. That is roughly the position Adam holds in this scene, and the angels are the ones who notice it.

**THE DISPLAY BEFORE THE ANGELS**

***“then He presented them to the angels”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the presentation as a display of the named things in front of the angels, and he notes that the names concerned intellectual beings for the most part. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the same act as putting the things before the angels and telling them to give the names.

Ibn Kathīr places the scene in the order of the story as the Qur'an tells it. The discussion in these verses comes before the command to prostrate, and he explains why: the point of the arrangement is to show the rank of Adam and the limits of what the angels knew when they asked their question. The presentation was not a quiz for its own sake. It was the answer to the objection in the previous verse, delivered as evidence rather than as an argument.

Al-Saʿdī keeps the sequence of cause and effect in view. The angels had compared themselves with the creature being appointed, on the basis of what each party did. God answered the comparison with a different measure, and the measure was knowledge. Everything else in this passage follows from that choice: the teacher's seat, the pupils' answer, and the prostration that comes next.

**THE COMMAND THE ANGELS COULD NOT MEET**

***“and said, “Tell Me the names of these”*** ***“if what you say is true?””*** Al-Jalālayn explains the conditional clause and what it refers back to. The angels had said, in effect, that God would not create anything more knowledgeable than they were, or that they were more deserving of the appointment. So the instruction was a reproach: name these things if the claim holds. He notes that the sentence leaves the answer unspoken, because the verse that follows supplies it immediately.

Al-Baghawī records the reasoning behind that claim in the words the commentators transmitted. When the angels heard the announcement, they said among themselves that their Lord would not create a creature more honoured to Him than they were, and that if He did, they were still the more knowledgeable, since they were created first and had seen what the new creature had not. That is a perfectly reasonable argument, and the verse dismantles it with a table of objects standing in front of them.

Al-Mukhtaṣar states the purpose plainly: the display was made to establish the standing of Adam, and the question was asked to show that the angels were not in a position to make the comparison they had made. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws attention to one small difference in wording that carries the meaning. The angels were told to tell God; Adam is later told to tell them. In the first sentence the angels are being questioned. In the second, a human being is given the seat of a teacher and the angels are placed in the seats of students.

A junior clerk who has told the board that the new accountant knows nothing is asked to take the man's ledger and read a page of it aloud. The question in the verse is that ledger. Its whole point is that it is in front of everybody and the reading is short.

---
## Verse 2:32

> They replied, “Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

**THE WORDS THE ANGELS ANSWERED WITH**

The angels answer with a confession: ***“They replied, “Glory be to You!”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the first word as an act of declaring God far above what does not suit Him, and he adds what the angels were clearing away: the idea that anyone could object to God's decision. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds that the sentence carries an admission of their own limits and a recognition that God's judgement and His law cannot be doubted.

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the word as an expression of return, spoken in the sense of turning back from what they had said, and the commentators record that reading alongside the first. Al-Qurṭubī draws the moment out. The angels answered the command to name the things by stating that nobody besides God knows the unseen, and they did not reach for knowledge they did not have. That is the behaviour of a created being who knows where his information comes from.

The verse records the angels answering a question with a confession, and the confession is the correct answer to this particular test. They were not asked what they had read or heard. They were asked to produce knowledge that lives in the hand of God alone, and the honest reply to that demand is the one they gave.

**WHAT THEY ADMITTED ABOUT KNOWLEDGE**

***“We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise.””*** Al-Jalālayn explains the closing words as a statement about God's knowledge and His wisdom together. Nothing escapes His knowledge. His wisdom means that everything He does has a reason, even when the reason has not been shown to the one asking the question. Al-Mukhtaṣar words it as the angels' acceptance: God is the Knowing from whom nothing is hidden, and the Wise in His decrees and His laws.

Al-Qurṭubī builds a rule out of the angels' reply, and it is one of the most useful sentences in the passage. He says that anyone who is asked about a matter he does not know should say: God knows best, and I do not know. The angels did it, the prophets did it, and the leading scholars of the community did it. He then notes the sharp contrast with the ignorant man among us, who fabricates an answer to protect his reputation. The difference between the two positions is not intelligence. It is honesty.

Ibn Kathīr places the same reply inside the larger lesson of the passage, which is the excellence God gave Adam above the angels in knowledge. The angels are not diminished by the scene. They keep their rank and their worship, and they gain something as well: an increase in knowledge, delivered by a human being, since Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that even the knowledge of angels can grow.

Al-Qurṭubī adds a grammatical note that widens the sentence. The phrase about what God has taught can be read as except the things You taught us, or as except Your teaching of us, so that the angels name the act itself as the only thing they possess. Either reading keeps them in the same position, and it is the position every creature holds before the One who knows all things: a borrower, not an owner.

Think of a technician called to fix a machine he has never seen. He could open the casing and guess. Instead he says the engineer who built it knows the design, and he will wait for the manual. A confident man can say that sentence, and the verse records a group of beings whose ranks do not tempt them to pretend otherwise.

---
## Verse 2:33

> Allah said, “O Adam! Inform them of their names.” Then when Adam did, Allah said, “Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?”

**THE NAMES ADAM WAS ASKED TO GIVE**

The verse records: ***“Allah said, “O Adam!”*** ***“Inform them of their names.””*** Al-Jalālayn describes what Adam did with the instruction: he named each thing by its name and mentioned the wisdom behind its creation. The answer went past a list of labels. He could tell the angels what each thing was for, which is the difference between knowing a word and understanding a thing.

Al-Qurṭubī explains the order of the events and the reason for it. God commanded Adam to teach the angels after the things had been shown to them, so that they would know that he understood what they had failed to name. Adam was given precedence, he adds, and the angels were made his students, told to learn from him. He reads the whole exchange as a statement about knowledge and the people who carry it, and he quotes the report the scholars cite on that subject: that the angels lower their wings in pleasure for the one who goes out seeking knowledge.

Al-Baghawī records the report of the angels' private reasoning and shows how this verse puts it to rest. They had said that they were more knowledgeable because they were created first and had seen what Adam had not. The instruction to sit and receive a lesson from him answers that argument in the most direct way available.

**THE QUESTION THAT CLOSED THE ARGUMENT**

The sentence moves on: ***“Then when Adam did, Allah said, “Did I not tell you”*** ***“that I know the secrets of the heavens”*** ***“and the earth, and I know what you reveal”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the question as a reminder aimed at the angels' earlier words. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the phrase about the secrets as the unseen that will take place in the heavens and the earth. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the reminder covers everything hidden in the two creations.

tafsir_initial collects the places where the Book uses this attribute, so that a reader can see how often it appears: (35:38), (49:18), (13:9), (23:92), (64:18). The phrase is one of the names the Qur'an gives its Maker, and the sūrah brings it into the middle of a conversation about who knows the future of the earth's new residents.

Al-Qurṭubī notes that the reminder is exact. Nobody had said anything out loud about Adam's fitness for the appointment in a way that could be answered by a demonstration of knowledge alone, and yet the reminder names secrets. The verse is answering a thought and not just a sentence, and the next clause says so in plain words.

**NOTHING IS HIDDEN FROM HIM**

The verse continues: ***“and what you conceal?””*** Al-Jalālayn explains both halves by matching them to the scene. What the angels revealed was their spoken question about the deputy who would spill blood. What they concealed was the estimate they kept to themselves, that God would not create a thing more knowledgeable than they were. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the same reading of revealed and hidden, and he records a second report about what was concealed, which he ties to Iblīs.

tafsir_initial examines that second possibility with care. If the concealed thing was the pride of Iblīs, the verse speaks to his condition and explains what will happen to him in the next verses. If it was the angels' private belief about their own nobility, then the answer is correct in a different way: the angels had accepted Adam's excellence, and what they concealed was not a fault. That note is a small lesson in reading the Qur'an. The verse is certain and the identification of some of its parts can be a matter of discussion.

Kashānī draws a line under the scene from the side of the inner life. The knowledge given to Adam is the sort that lifts a person, and it belongs to the comprehensiveness of the human being, which is why the command was to tell and not to teach. On his account, the whole passage describes a capacity that other created beings do not carry, and the scene with the angels is the first time the universe is shown it.

The sūrah has now answered the angels' question in three steps, and each step is worth keeping. First the announcement, which named the risk in advance. Then the evidence, which put the names in front of them. Then the reminder, which said that the private thoughts of the objectors had been counted as well. Think of a workshop where the staff have objected to a new machine and the manager answers them twice over. He shows them the machine working, and then he repeats their private doubts back to them word for word. Nobody in that room is in any doubt afterwards about how much the manager knows. That is the position this verse leaves the angels in, and their next words are the prostration that God commanded.

The story will now turn to the prostration, and to the one angel who refused it.

---
## Verse 2:34

> And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,” so they all did—but not Iblîs, who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful

**THE COMMAND GIVEN TO THE ANGELS**

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains why the story reaches this point. The previous verses showed that Adam carried a kind of knowledge the angels did not have. Now God willed to make that superiority visible, so the command went out for the angels to bow before him in his honour. The prostration was a greeting of respect and a public acknowledgment of the rank that had already been established.

The verse has it: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,””*** Al-Jalālayn calls it a bow of salutation, and he is careful with the word. The prostration was directed at Adam as a way of honouring him, and the commentators are agreed that no created being may be worshipped. Al-Baghawī reports the same clarification and adds the disagreement about who received the command. Some said it went to the angels who were resident on the earth. The majority of the scholars read it as a command to all the angels, and he supports that reading with the verse that describes the angels prostrating together, every one of them ((15:30 — **“So the angels prostrated—all of them together”**)).

Al-Qurṭubī notes a detail of the Arabic that a reader of the translation will miss. God says We said in the plural form rather than I said, and he explains that this is the speech of a great King reporting His own action in the majestic plural. The same usage fills the verses about creation in this sūrah. A reader who hears it aloud hears a decree being issued, not a conversation being resumed.

tafsir_initial gathers the places where the story is told in full so that a reader can follow it across the Book: (7:11-27), (15:31-40), (17:61-65), and (18:50). Each telling adds something. The version before us keeps its attention on the honour given to the human being, and on the one creature in the scene who would not accept it.

**THE OBEDIENCE THEY SHOWED**

The wording is: ***“so they all did”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the obedience in a few words: they prostrated to Adam out of recognition and respect, eager to do what they had been told. Ibn Kathīr reads the prostration as the great honour given to Adam, and he notes that the sūrah reminds the children of Adam of it, generation after generation. The man whose ancestors were bowed to by angels is being told what he was made for.

The commentators note that the command was given in a few words and the obedience was complete. No angel is recorded asking whether the command might be reconsidered. This is the same group that asked a careful question two verses earlier about the wisdom of appointing a deputy on the earth. A question was permitted, and it did not turn into a refusal. The difference between an honest question and a rebellion is not in the words. It is in what the questioner does after the answer arrives.

Tazkirul Qur'an treats the scene as a demonstration set up for the human race. In front of Adam stood two possible futures, and both were acted out in the same hour. One group bowed to a command it could not fully explain, and one creature refused to bow, because he had decided that he was the better of the two men in the room. Every person will do one of those two things many times in his life, and the sūrah is showing him the original.

**THE ONE WHO HELD BACK**

The verse puts it: ***“but not Iblîs, who refused”*** Al-Jalālayn identifies Iblīs as the father of the jinn and says that he was counted among the angels at the time. He also supplies the reason Iblīs gave for his refusal, from the sūrah that tells the story in more detail: (7:12 — **“He said, ‘I am better than he: You created me from fire and him from clay’”**). The refusal came with an argument attached, which is what makes it dangerous as a model. Here is a created being who has taken a fact about his own material and turned it into a reason for disobeying a direct order.

Al-Mukhtaṣar fills in the history. Iblīs was originally of the jinn, and because of the excellence of his worship God had placed him in the company of the angels. Then he returned to his own nature. He refused to prostrate, he grew proud toward Adam, and the sentence at the end of the verse followed. That detail matters for the rest of the story, because the reader needs to understand that the enemy of the human race was once a worshipper whose record was good enough to put him among angels. A past record is not a guarantee.

Ibn ʿAbbās records the identification that the earliest commentators gave, that Iblīs was the first disbeliever, and he also preserves the reading in which the verse describes what God already knew about him. The two readings are not in competition. The Book describes an act that happened in time and a knowledge that never had a beginning, and it is comfortable holding both in one sentence.

**REFUSAL AND PRIDE TOGETHER**

The verse carries on: ***“and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful”*** The verse names two things, and the order matters. Iblīs refused, and the reason underneath the refusal was arrogance. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the pride as the cause rather than the companion of the disobedience. He would not follow his Lord's command because the command asked him to bow to someone he considered beneath him. Al-Jalālayn keeps the same sequence: he refused, he drew himself up, and he became one of the disbelievers.

Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the outcome in the plainest terms: his pride toward Adam led to his becoming a disbeliever. The word for the condition at the end of the verse is the same word the sūrah has been using for the open rejecters in its opening passage. The reader has met this word twice already, first in the description of the men whose hearts and hearing were sealed, and now in the account of the being who started the line. The Book is showing the family tree of the attitude it has been warning about since verse six.

Ibn Kathīr adds a useful clarification for anyone who gets stuck on the details of the story. Iblīs was among those ordered to prostrate although he was not an angel. The command went out to everyone present who carried understanding, the angels and the jinn alike, and the Qur'an names the angels because they were the greater of the two groups. The lesson does not depend on the ordering. A creature with understanding received a clear instruction, and he put his own assessment of himself above it.

Think of a servant in a great house who has kept it spotless for years, and who is then told to hold the door for a new gardener. He refuses, on the grounds that he has been polishing silver since before the gardener was born. The house is unchanged by his opinion of himself, and the door stays open in his hand. The verse records what happens to a man when he makes his own standing the measure of every order he receives.

---
## Verse 2:35

> We cautioned, “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.”

**THE WARNING GIVEN IN PARADISE**

The verse has it: ***“We cautioned, “O Adam!”*** Al-Saʿdī opens his commentary on this verse with the completion of the favour. God created Adam, honoured him above the angels, and then made a spouse from him, so that he would have someone to live with and find rest in. The verse that follows in another sūrah states the purpose directly: (7:189 — **“He created from it its mate so that he may find comfort in her”**). The command in this verse is addressed to a man who has just been given a home, a partner, and food with no restriction attached.

The word at the front of the sentence carries a note of warning, and the commentators hear it. This is not a command issued to a stranger. It is the shape of a host explaining the one rule of the house while the table is full, and the reader should feel the difference between a prohibition that arrives as a rule and one that arrives as a caution.

**A HOME FOR TWO**

As the verse says: ***“Live with your wife in Paradise”*** Al-Jalālayn identifies the wife as Eve, and repeats the account the commentators transmitted, that she was created from Adam's left rib. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the command as an instruction to enter the Garden, the two of them together. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the same arrangement: live with your wife in the Garden with nothing to spoil your happiness there.

Al-Saʿdī draws attention to the word for dwelling, which carries the sense of settling down rather than merely being present. The Garden was not a waiting room. It was a home with a companion, and the command to live there is the sound of a door being opened rather than a sentence being served.

The verse also shows the human being as a creature made for company. The angels around him were not a substitute for a wife, and the Qur'an states elsewhere that the pairing of male and female is among the signs of the Creator. Adam is given a house and then given the person to share it with, in that order, in the middle of a passage about blessings a person cannot see.

**FREEDOM TO EAT**

The verse goes on: ***“and eat as freely”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the phrase as permission to eat without restriction, from anywhere in the Garden that Adam and his wife wished. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes delightful food available throughout the Garden. Al-Saʿdī explains the Arabic word for freely as a wide and easy plenty, and he brings in the verse that lists what was guaranteed to Adam inside that home: no hunger, no nakedness, no thirst, and no exposure to the burning sun ((20:118-119)).

That list is worth keeping beside this permission, because it describes a life without any of the four pressures that drive most human decisions. Nobody in that Garden had to steal for food, or work for shade, or beg for water, or hurry indoors before dark. The one prohibition in the middle of all that plenty is what makes the next clause so sharp.

**THE TREE THAT WAS OFF LIMITS**

The verse records: ***“as you please, but do not approach this tree”*** The commentators discussed the tree, and they did not settle on a single identification, because the text does not name it. Al-Jalālayn lists the possibilities the narrations carried: wheat, a vine, or something else. Al-Saʿdī says that God knows which tree it was, and that the tree itself is not the point of the verse. Ibn ʿAbbās, in one report, describes it as a tree of knowledge that included all types.

What the commentators do agree on is the wording of the prohibition. The verse does not say do not eat from it. It says do not come near it. Al-Saʿdī works the difference through: the command was given in the form that removes the occasion of the sin before the sin can happen. A person who keeps a distance from a boundary cannot be caught by it, and the Book's prohibitions are often stated in this shape, which is why the coming verses tell the reader to stay away from the roads that lead to a wrong rather than only from the wrong itself.

Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the practical frame: they were told to eat from anywhere in the Garden except this tree, and they were warned what eating from it would make them.

Think of a mountain road with a cliff along one side. The sign does not say do not fall. It says keep back from the edge, because the distance is what saves the driver, not the warning alone.

**THE WARNING THAT NAMED THE COST**

The verse puts the matter: ***“or else you will be wrongdoers.””*** Al-Saʿdī draws a ruling out of the ending. The warning attaches the word wrongdoers to the act, which shows that the prohibition was binding rather than advisory. A person who breaks his own body by eating what harms him is a wrongdoer in the plain sense of the word: he has crossed a line and damaged something that was placed in his care. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the phrase as a warning that they would harm themselves.

The word for wrongdoing is important in the sūrah, and this is not its last appearance. It will return in the story of the golden calf, in the account of the man who kills and then repents, and in many of the legal passages that follow. Here it appears for the first time in the chapter, attached to a single tree in a garden, and the reader is being taught the vocabulary of guilt with the smallest case in the whole Book: one fruit, one warning, one clear boundary, and two people who already have everything else.

---
## Verse 2:36

> But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in, and We said, “Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.”

**THE SLIP THE ENEMY CAUSED**

The sūrah opens the sentence: ***“But Satan deceived them”*** Al-Jalālayn describes the act as causing them to slip, and he records how the enemy worked. He told them that the tree was the tree of eternity, and he swore to them by God that he was only giving them good advice, and they ate from it. Al-Qurṭubī explains the two readings of the verb here. The common reading describes a stumble, the kind of small slip that follows a loss of footing. A second reading, carried by Ḥamzah, describes a removal, as when a man is moved out of a place. He also records Ibn Kaysān's note that the second reading points to a shift away from the obedience a person was standing in.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān pauses over a question the story raises. Satan had already been expelled from the Garden for refusing to prostrate, so how did he get close enough to deceive Adam and Eve? He sets out the possibilities the scholars discussed. Satan may never have met them at all, since his whisper can reach a heart from a distance, just as a hypnotist moves a person who is sitting in the same room. He may have entered the Garden in the shape of a snake, since the jinn are said to have powers that human beings do not have, and that shapeshifting may explain why Adam did not connect the voice to the warning he had been given. He notes that the Qur'an records Satan swearing an oath to them ((7:21)), which suggests that a conversation did take place.

Before the reader takes the bait for the first time, the sūrah shows the method. The enemy did not claim to be an enemy. He came with a promise of something better, an oath on God's name, and a story about a tree that would not end. The next time that offer appears in a person's life, the shape will be familiar.

**THE STATE THEY LOST**

The verse names it: ***“leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the result: they slipped and fell by eating from the tree God had told them to avoid, and for that they were sent out of the Garden. tafsir_initial notes that the image of stumbling into sin works the same way in Arabic and in English, and that the verse is about a loss of footing rather than a crime planned for years. Adam and Eve did not set out to disobey. They were talked into it, one sentence at a time.

Al-Saʿdī states the sequence in his commentary on the passage: they were deceived by the enemy and they obeyed him, and so they were taken out of the ease and the plenty they were living in and sent down to a house of effort, fatigue and struggle. That word for struggle is the key to everything that follows in the human story. The earth is not being described as a punishment cell. It is being described as a workshop, and the verses that follow in this sūrah will spend many pages explaining how to work in it.

The loss was real without being final, and the sūrah is careful about the difference. Adam and Eve are not called enemies of God in this verse. The next verse will describe a forgiveness that arrives before they have asked for it in words, and the verse after that gives the promise of guidance to the children who will live on the earth.

**THE COMMAND TO DESCEND**

Then the verse says: ***“and We said, “Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺”*** tafsir_initial explains the grammar and what it leaves open. The command to descend is in the plural form, so it may cover Adam and Eve, or Adam and Eve together with Iblīs. The reading that fits the rest of the Qur'an takes the addressees to be Adam and Eve and their descendants, with the two of them standing for the human race as a whole, and some of the commentators include Iblīs and his offspring in the command as well. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report carried by one of the commentaries, reads the addressees as Adam, Eve, and the two creatures the storytellers mention, the peacock and the serpent.

Al-Jalālayn reads the command as a descent to the earth, for Adam and Eve and everyone covered by their descendants. The verse does not describe a fall out of a window. It describes a change of address, ordered by the One who made both addresses, and the next clauses explain what the new house will contain.

**ENMITY THAT WOULD OUTLAST THEM**

The verse records: ***“as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the enmity as one that runs through the generations: some of your descendants will be enemies to others. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same sense and joins it to the command: go down to the earth, some of you enemies to others, and there you will stay. Al-Saʿdī describes the earth as a place of labour and effort, and the enmity between people as the conflict that will fill its history, since the enemy who began the trouble will keep working on the children of the man he brought down.

tafsir_initial examines the word translated as residence and gives the two readings the commentators worked with. It can mean a place to live, and the same root is used elsewhere for the earth as an abode ((40:64 — **“the earth is a place of settlement”**)). It can also refer to graves, which is how some readers took it. The other uses of the word in the Book point to the first reading, and the verse's own shape supports that: the sentence ends with provision, and graves do not provide.

The clause names the two things a person needs in a new country: a place to settle and a way to eat. The sūrah has spent its opening verses on the gifts of earth and sky, and this sentence takes the reader back to the same table with a harder set of conditions attached. The home is still furnished. The warning is that the neighbours include an enemy.

**A STAY THAT WOULD END**

The wording continues: ***“and provision for your appointed stay.””*** Al-Jalālayn reads the last phrase as the enjoyment of the earth's produce for a time, until each person's term ends. Ibn ʿAbbās says the same, and adds that the provision lasts until the moment of death. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the phrase general and includes the whole span: they would live there and enjoy its good things until their lifespans were complete.

tafsir_initial sets out what the time limit may refer to. It can mean earthly death, or the Day of Resurrection when the stay of humanity on the earth comes to an end, or an appointed term, which is the plain sense of the Arabic word. All three readings agree on the main point: the arrangement in the earth has a schedule. Nothing about the new garden is permanent except the accountability.

This is the second time the sūrah has marked how short the human stay is, and the first time it does so while describing the start of the human story rather than the end of a single life. A person reading the verse is standing on the far side of that sentence, somewhere in the middle of the while, and the sūrah will spend the rest of the chapter telling him what to do with the days that are still running.

---
## Verse 2:37

> Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord, so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

**THE WORDS ADAM WAS TAUGHT**

The verse records: ***“Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord”*** The verse turns the story around in one line. Ibn Kathīr gathers the earliest authorities who commented on it — Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, Khālid ibn Maʿdān, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd — and they all identified the words Adam received with the prayer his descendants will use for the rest of human history: (7:23 — **“They said, ‘Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be of the losers’”**).

Ibn ʿAbbās, in the second report carried by al-Suddī, describes a longer conversation, in which Adam appeals to what God had already given him: did You not make me a deputy, did You not breathe Your spirit into me, does Your mercy not outrun Your anger? tafsir_initial records the other accounts the commentators transmitted. Some said the words were a prayer God taught him to recite, in which he declares God's oneness, acknowledges his own wrong and asks to be forgiven. Some said they were the rites of the pilgrimage, taught to Adam as a means of return. The readings differ about the sentence and agree about its shape. The words were given to him. They were not invented by him.

Al-Qurṭubī spends time on the verb at the start of the verse. It can mean that Adam understood, or that he received and took hold of what came, or that he met it as a traveller meets an arriving caravan. He notes the variant reading that makes the words themselves the subject of the sentence, so that they came to Adam rather than being picked up by him. On either reading the grace is coming from the same direction.

Al-Saʿdī draws the two-part lesson out of the moment. Adam acknowledged his sin and asked for God's forgiveness, and that acknowledgement is itself a gift. Then God relented toward him. Al-Saʿdī notes that God's acceptance of repentance works in two stages: first He enables the servant to turn, and then He accepts the turning once its conditions are met. The man who repents is standing inside a favour he did not manufacture, and the verse keeps the whole movement inside one sentence about God's mercy.

Think of a child who breaks a window and is handed the words to say to the neighbour whose glass it was. The sentence is not a trick. It is help given to a person who does not know how to come back.

**THE REPENTANCE THAT WAS ACCEPTED**

The verse names it: ***“so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the phrase as God accepting Adam's turning back and receiving him. Al-Mukhtaṣar states the same and adds the names at the end of the verse: God is always forgiving and merciful to His creation. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the pair of names in the order they stand, the One who overlooks misdeeds and the One who shows mercy to anyone who dies having turned back.

Tazkirul Qur'an draws the practical lesson of the tree and what came after it. The story shows how a person goes astray by trusting a deceiver and crossing the limits God has set. When he eats the forbidden fruit he loses the grace he was standing in. The loss is not the end of the account. He still has the opportunity to turn to his Lord, to put his actions right and to ask forgiveness. When he does that, God relents toward him and wipes the sin away as if it had never been, and this note is one of the most important in the whole story.

The order of the two verses is the mercy. The fall is described first, and the forgiveness arrives in the same passage without anyone having to earn it. The sūrah makes this its most memorable statement about how the human story continues: a mistake is followed by a way back, and the way back is provided by the One who was wronged.

---
## Verse 2:38

> We said, “Descend all of you! Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows it, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**THE SECOND COMMAND TO DESCEND**

The verse names it: ***“We said, “Descend all of you!”*** Al-Qurṭubī asks why the command to descend is repeated after it has already been given, and he offers the reasons the commentators gave. One is emphasis, the way a person says stand up, stand up when he means it. A second is that each command has its own ruling attached: the first carries the enmity that will run between people, and the second carries the promise of guidance. A third reading places the two commands at different stages, the first from the Garden to the lowest heaven and the second from the heaven to the earth, and al-Qurṭubī notes that this reading supports the view that the Garden is in the seventh heaven, as the accounts of the night journey describe.

Al-Baghawī records the same readings in shorter form, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws a conclusion that changes the tone of the whole episode. The descent was not a punishment. The command was not withdrawn even after Adam was forgiven, which means the earth was always going to be the destination. What changed was the manner of the journey. The earlier command came in the tone of authority. This one comes in the tone of wisdom, and it brings with it the honour of the trust Adam was made for.

Kashānī notices a detail in the wording that supports the same reading. The first descent is attributed to the enemy's work, and the second is attributed to God directly, the way another verse says that the Prophet did not throw when he threw, but God threw ((8:17 — **“it was not you ˹O Prophet˺ who threw ˹a handful of sand˺, but Allah”**)). The enemy made them slip. The move to the earth was decided by the hand that made them, and the sentence that follows the command explains what the new address will contain.

**GUIDANCE AND THE FEAR THAT LIFTS**

The wording continues: ***“Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows it, there will be no fear”*** ***“for them, nor will they grieve”*** Al-Jalālayn explains what the guidance is: a Book and a prophet, and whoever follows this guidance by believing and by doing what God has ordered will have nothing to fear later and nothing to grieve over. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the guidance comes through the prophets, and that those who follow it and believe in them have nothing to fear in the world to come.

Al-Saʿdī states the promise in the widest possible terms. Guidance here means a messenger and a book that lead a person to what brings him near to God and to His pleasure, and following it means believing in the messengers and the books, accepting everything they report, doing what they command and avoiding what they forbid. He then separates the two words at the end of the verse with a precision worth keeping. A disliked thing that has already happened produces grief. A disliked thing that is still expected produces fear. When God removes both from a person, what remains is complete security, and that is the condition of the man or woman who follows the guidance.

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the pair in the same way with a slightly different frame: no fear about what is coming toward them, and no grief about what they have left behind. He also records a reading of the phrase that extends the promise beyond this life, into the moment when death itself is dealt with and the Fire is closed for those who were spared it. Ibn Kathīr quotes the verse in another sūrah that states the same promise in different words: (20:123 — **“whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray ˹in this life˺ nor suffer ˹in the next˺”**).

This is the first promise of its kind in the sūrah, and it is given on the day the human being leaves the Garden. A person's history will contain hard ground, enemies, work and loss. The verse answers that future before it arrives, and it answers it with two removals rather than a list of gifts.

---
## Verse 2:39

> But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”

**THE END OF THOSE WHO REJECT**

The text says: ***“But those who disbelieve”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the disbelievers here as those who reject, and al-Mukhtaṣar fills the sentence in: those who disbelieve and deny God's signs are the people of the fire of Hell, and they will live there always. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the denial as the rejection of the scripture and of the messenger who brought it.

The sūrah splits humanity here in the same way it did at the beginning, and a reader who has come this far will recognise the pattern. Verses one to five described the people who accept the guidance. Verses six and seven described the people who refuse it openly. Verses eight to twenty described the people who pretend. The story of Adam ends with the same division in one sentence: those who follow the guidance and those who deny the signs. The Book has told the story of the first man in order to state the terms of the appointment, and the terms have not changed since the beginning.

Al-Qurṭubī pauses over the word translated as residents, and his note is a small treasure for the reader who has heard Muslims speak of the Companions. The word describes people who are attached to something, tied to it in a particular state at a particular time. Where the bond is complete and lasting, it is companionship in the fullest sense. He applies that meaning to the people of the Fire, who are bound to it for good, and then draws the comparison that shows how careful the language of the community is: the same word is used for the companions of the Prophet ﷺ, whose ranks no one claims to have measured. The word describes a bond, not a status. What the bond is worth depends on what a person is bound to.

**A STAY WITH NO EXIT**

The sentence continues: ***“and deny Our signs will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.””*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the ending as a state without exit: they will remain there always, never dying and never released. Al-Jalālayn says the same. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the sentence simple and complete. Kashānī reads the fire in this verse as the fire of being cut off from God, which is the privation that a soul feels when it loses the thing it was made for.

The passage closes with this verse, and the next one opens a new section addressed to a specific people: (2:40 — **“O Children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you”**). The story of Adam has served as the foundation for everything that follows in the sūrah. The human being was made as a deputy on the earth, warned about an enemy, given a way back after he slipped, and handed a promise of guidance with two roads under it. Every passage that follows in this chapter — the law, the history of the earlier communities, the long arguments about faith — stands on that floor.

A reader who wants the sūrah's opening in a handful of sentences can have it here. The Book is guidance, and it is the guidance promised on the day the human story started. The people who follow it are secure. The people who reject it are attached to the fire. Everything between these two sentences is the working out of what follows from believing or denying, done in detail, with examples, over the length of a chapter that is the longest in the Book.

Think of a family leaving an old house for a new country and being handed a single letter at the door, with the terms of the journey inside it. The letter names the road, names the danger and names the reward at the end. Everything else in this sūrah is the inside of that letter, opened slowly and read by generations.

---
## Verse 2:40

> O children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you. Fulfil your covenant and I will fulfil Mine, and stand in awe of Me ˹alone˺

**THE ADDRESS TO THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL**

The sūrah opens the sentence: ***“O children of Israel!”*** Al-Saʿdī explains who is being addressed. Israel is another name for Jacob, and the call goes to the tribes descended from him, the families living in Madinah and the villages around it at the time the verse came down, along with everyone who would come after them. Ibn Kathīr draws out the kindness buried in the address. God is reminding the people of their father, a prophet who obeyed his Lord, as if to say: you are the children of a righteous servant, so be like him.

Al-Qurṭubī opens his commentary with a grammar lesson on the phrase, working through the Arabic construction of the word for children and the reasons the grammarians gave for it. The value of the note is its reminder of something easy to forget: the Book speaks to real people with real family names, in their own language, and it opens this long section by naming a household.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān places the address in the structure of the sūrah. The first thirty-nine verses were universal: the Book, the three kinds of people, the call to worship, the story of Adam. This verse begins a long passage addressed to one community, the descendants of Jacob, because they were the neighbours standing in front of the first Muslims in Madinah and because the history between them went back centuries.

**THE FAVOURS AND THE COVENANT**

Its words are: ***“Remember My favours upon you. Fulfil your covenant”*** tafsir_initial sets out the range of the favours the commentators included. The word is usually read first as the rescue from Pharaoh and the gifts that followed it: the sea splitting, the shade of the clouds, the manna and the quails, and the arrival at a land of their own ((2:49-50)). Some read it as the prophets God placed among them and the books He sent down to them. Others read it as the coming of the final message itself, since the verse addresses the Jews of Madinah. The note settles on the widest reading, that the favour includes everything from the gift of existence onward, which fits the universal commands that follow.

Ibn ʿAbbās lists the favours in concrete terms: the Scripture, the messenger, rescue from Pharaoh, safety from drowning, the manna and the quails. Al-Saʿdī explains what remembering a favour actually means in practice, and his explanation turns a soft word into a discipline. Remembering happens in three places at once. The heart acknowledges that the gift came from God. The tongue praises the Giver for it. The limbs use the gift in the way God loves, and not in some other way. A person who says he has remembered a favour while using it against the One who gave it has done the opposite of what the verse asks.

Al-Jalālayn explains the two covenants and how they fit together. The covenant God asks them to keep is the agreement He took from them to believe in Muḥammad ﷺ, and the covenant He promises to keep is their reward in Paradise. Al-Saʿdī quotes the passage that spells the arrangement out in full: (5:12 — **“Allah made a covenant with the Children of Israel, and We raised up twelve leaders from among them. And Allah said, ‘I am surely with you, if you establish prayer, pay alms-tax, believe in My messengers and support them, and lend Allah a gracious loan’”**). The verse before us states the same deal in two clauses, and each clause is doing work the other cannot do.

Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the keeping of the covenant as faith in God, His prophets and His laws, and the promise as a good life in this world and a fine reward on the Day of Judgement.

**THE PROMISE THAT ANSWERS THEIRS**

The sentence continues: ***“and I will fulfil Mine”*** The symmetry in this sentence is the point of it, and the commentators let it stand. Al-Jalālayn reads the second half as the reward that follows the promise: admission to Paradise. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it the same way. The verse does not present the relationship as a master extracting obedience from servants. It presents a promise answered by a promise.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the whole address is built to make gratitude the engine of obedience. The Israelites are not being told to obey a stranger. They are being told to remember what they were given, and to answer an old agreement with the One who kept His side of it through centuries of their failures. Al-Saʿdī describes the second half of the exchange as the recompense that God promises for the keeping of the first half, and he treats the entire arrangement as evidence of grace rather than of harshness.

Think of two neighbours who shook hands over a shared wall years ago and one of them has kept the path clear ever since. The verse speaks to the household that has been living behind the clean path, and it asks them to check the state of their own side.

**FEAR THAT BELONGS TO HIM ALONE**

The verse carries on: ***“and stand in awe of Me ˹alone˺”*** Al-Jalālayn explains why the sentence is worded so sharply. Fear me and nobody else, he says, at the moment when a person is considering whether to abandon belief in the Prophet. The fear being addressed here is social, and it is the oldest reason a person gives for staying where he is: what will my people say. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same clause as a caution against breaking the agreement, and a reminder that no human being needs to be feared in that decision.

Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the instruction in the plainest form: fear God alone, and do not break His contract. That is a rule for a community whose scholars were watched by their own congregations, whose business interests depended on the good opinion of their neighbours, and whose whole standing rested on being the people of the Book.

The command comes at the end of the verse, after the favours and the agreement. The order is deliberate in the way a good argument is deliberate. A person is reminded what he has been given, shown what he promised in return, and only then asked to fear the opinion of the One whose record is being discussed.

---
## Verse 2:41

> Believe in My revelations which confirm your Scriptures. Do not be the first to deny them or trade them for a fleeting gain. And be mindful of Me

**THE COMMAND TO BELIEVE WHAT CAME**

The sentence reads: ***“Believe in My revelations”*** Ibn Kathīr states the command without softening it: God ordered the Children of Israel to enter Islam and follow Muḥammad ﷺ. Al-Jalālayn identifies the revelation as the Qur'an. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the same and adds the detail that gives the sentence its weight for a people who already had a book: the Qur'an confirms what came to them in the Torah before any of it was changed, on the two matters that matter most, the oneness of God and the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ.

Ibn ʿAbbās lists what the confirmation covers: the oneness of God, the description and traits of the coming Prophet, and some of the rulings that were carried over. The verse is not inviting a community to abandon its heritage. It is asking a community to recognise its own book in the message that has just arrived in their city.

**THE WARNING AGAINST BEING FIRST TO DENY**

The verse declares: ***“which confirm your Scriptures. Do not be the first to deny them”*** Al-Jalālayn explains why being first makes the offence heavier. Those who come after you will depend on you, so you will carry their sins as well as your own. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān works the same principle out loud. Being a disbeliever is a ruinous thing whether a man is first or last. But the one who denies first carries his own denial and the weight of everyone he misled by going first. The same rule runs in the other direction: whoever is a means of somebody else's good work shares in the reward without either of them being diminished.

The scholars of that community were the ones who would be asked, and the verse is aimed at them. Maʿārif notes that love of money and love of position were the two forces that made the message hardest for the Jewish scholars of Madinah to accept, and the next clause names the price directly. A scholar's refusal is not a private opinion when his congregation is watching him. It is a decision with a crowd under it.

Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the instruction as a warning against being the first group to disbelieve, and it names the setting: the community had the earlier books and knew the signs they contained.

**THE PRICE THEY TOOK FOR THE TRUTH**

The Book says: ***“or trade them for a fleeting gain.”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the phrase with a picture of what was being sold. The signs God refers to include the description of the Prophet ﷺ in their Book, and the small price was the income and the standing their position brought them. They were being asked not to suppress a passage of their own scripture because a passage can be expensive. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the price as the means of substance the scholars received, and al-Mukhtaṣar calls it the small price of position or leadership.

Ibn Kathīr reads the phrase in the widest sense the Arabic allows, and the scholars of the community are agreed that it covers every sale of knowledge for a worldly return. A judge who tilts a ruling, a teacher who trims a lesson, a scholar who stays silent about a verse because a sponsor would not like it — all of them are working at the same counter. The verse sets the goods on one side and the price on the other, and it trusts the reader to see the difference in size.

Think of a man who owns the only shop in a village and quietly removes the medicine that his richest customer does not want to see on the shelf. He has not lost anything he can measure this month. He has sold the shelf.

**THE FEAR THAT CLOSES THE VERSE**

The next words are: ***“And be mindful of Me”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the closing instruction as: fear Me and nobody else in this matter. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same. The verse has come full circle from the command at the end of the previous verse and it uses the same remedy for the same disease. Twice in two verses, the Book tells the scholars of a community that the fear of people is the thing that will cost them their own book.

Al-Saʿdī groups the two verses together in his commentary and treats them as one instruction in four movements: keep the agreement, believe in what confirms your scripture, do not lead the denial, and do not sell the signs. Each movement is aimed at the same person, the man who knows the truth and has a reason to keep quiet about it.

---
## Verse 2:42

> Do not mix truth with falsehood or hide the truth knowingly

**TRUTH AND FALSEHOOD MIXED**

The verse names it: ***“Do not mix truth with falsehood”*** Al-Qurṭubī opens his commentary with the root of the verb, which means to mix. He explains that to mix a matter for someone is to blend what is clear in it with what is obscure, its truth with its falsehood, so that the listener can no longer separate them. The Qur'an uses the image of clothing in the same family of words, because a thing that is dressed is covered. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the verse as a prohibition on exactly that mixture, and one of the reports applies it to the description of the coming Prophet, which the scholars of the Book were blurring with another figure.

Al-Qurṭubī also preserves a sentence that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib spoke to al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥawṭ, and it has travelled with this verse ever since: the truth is not known by men, so know the truth and you will know its people. That line is the answer to the mixture the verse forbids. A person who sorts the message by who is carrying it will always be adjustable. A person who sorts it by what is true will be steady.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān tells a story that shows what it looks like when somebody refuses to dress up a truth, and he takes it from the Musnad of al-Dārimī. The caliph Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik visited Madinah and wanted to meet a man who had known a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ. He was told that Abū Ḥāzim was the last such man in the city, and the caliph sent for him. The caliph asked why he had shown such disrespect by staying away while everyone else came to visit. Abū Ḥāzim answered that before that day the caliph had never heard his name and he had never seen the caliph's face, so there had been no relationship to neglect. Then the caliph asked him why he did not want to die. Abū Ḥāzim said the reason was simple: the caliph had built up this world and left the next one as bare ground, and nobody enjoys leaving a flourishing city for a desert. The caliph wept and asked how God would deal with them, and Abū Ḥāzim told him to weigh his deeds against the Book of God. The verse before us is the rule that allows a man to speak that way to a ruler, and the story is what the rule sounds like when it is followed.

Ibn Kathīr reports the explanations of the earliest commentators, including al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatādah, and sums the verse up as a ban on two things: blending truth with falsehood, and hiding the truth. He notes that the two prohibitions belong together, because a community that mixes first has something to hide afterwards.

**KNOWLEDGE HELD BACK**

The verse records: ***“or hide the truth knowingly”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar states both halves of the verse in one line: do not mix what God has revealed with lies and falsehood, and do not hide the truth about the description of Muḥammad which came in His scripture, when you know what the truth is and are certain of it.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws the rule out for a general reader. It is not permitted to blend truth and falsehood in a way that leaves the listener unable to tell which is which, and it is not permitted to conceal the truth out of fear or greed. He notes that the last two words of the verse, knowingly, close the excuse that a man was confused. The verse is addressed to people who know. Their problem was never information.

The order of the two clauses is worth noticing. A person usually imagines that concealing comes first and mixing follows as a defence. The verse puts mixing first and calls hiding what it is: the second act of a man who has already clouded a matter and now needs the cloud to stay in place. Think of a shopkeeper who waters down his oil and then refuses to let anyone read the label on the drum. The refusal is not a separate crime from the watering. It is the same crime being protected.

---
## Verse 2:43

> Establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and bow down with those who bow down

**TWO OBLIGATIONS NAMED TOGETHER**

The wording is: ***“Establish prayer, pay alms-tax”*** Al-Qurṭubī notes that both commands are obligations, and he records that no one disagreed about that. He also works through the vocabulary. The verb for establishing a prayer carries the sense of setting something up so that it stands, which is where the English phrase comes from. The verb for paying the alms-tax is the one that means to give. Al-Mukhtaṣar explains what establishing the prayer involves: performing it properly, with its obligatory parts and its recommended ones. And it explains where the alms come from: the wealth that God has placed in a person's hands.

Al-Jalālayn adds a setting for the verse. It came down about some of the religious scholars of the Children of Israel who used to tell their own relatives among the Muslims to stay firm on the religion of Muḥammad ﷺ because it was the truth, while they themselves stayed where they were. The verse answers that position with two things a person can do with his body and his money rather than with his advice.

tafsir_initial raises a question that has interested readers of this verse for a long time. If the command to pray and give alms were the Islamic form of worship, then the verse would be asking these people to become Muslims, which other verses in the sūrah do more directly. The note points to passages that show prayer and alms as older than the final message: (19:31) and (19:55), where the prophets are described as commanding their people to pray and give alms, and (20:14), where God speaks to Moses about the prayer. The conclusion is that the two duties were part of the religion of the earlier prophets as well, and the verse calls the people of the Book back to the worship their own line of messengers had taught.

**THE BOWING THAT IS SHARED**

Then the verse says: ***“and bow down with those”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the command as an instruction to pray in the congregation of Muḥammad ﷺ and his Companions. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it the same way: perform the five prescribed prayers in the congregation with the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the movement itself as humility before God, performed alongside the humble of the Muslim community.

tafsir_initial gives the other places where bowing appears in commands and descriptions, so a reader can see that the word is used as a general act of worship and reverence in more than one community: (3:43), (5:55), (9:112), (38:24). The note adds that bowing carries a specific technical meaning inside the Islamic prayer, and a wider meaning outside it.

The command has a social shape that is easy to miss in the translation. A person can pray alone in a room and give charity from a distance. The third instruction asks for a shoulder in a row, and it is the clause that would have cost the scholars of Madinah the most. The two duties before it are private between a person and God. This one places a man in a line with the people he had been keeping at arm's length.

The verse puts it: ***“who bow down”*** **WHY THE ENDING REPEATS THE WORD**

The repetition of the word at the end of the verse is a small feature of the Arabic that the translation keeps, and the commentators treat it as emphasis. The command is not to bow in general. It is to bow with the people who are already bowing, which settles the question of where a person stands while he does it.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān connects this verse to the one before it and draws out the practical remedy the passage is offering. The two diseases that kept the scholars of the Book from accepting the message were love of money and love of position. Verses 42 and 43 prescribe the cure: truth spoken without mixture, and then patience with prayer. He explains that the Arabic word for patience covers three things at once — bearing hardship without complaint, holding yourself back from sin, and staying steady in obedience — and that this whole package is what the Book calls patience, and what it recommends to anyone whose comfort is standing between him and the truth.

Think of a man who has been told that the row in front of the congregation will cost him his seat at a table he has held for years. The verse asks him to take the step anyway, and it names him one of the humble when he does.

---
## Verse 2:44

> Do you preach righteousness and fail to practice it yourselves, although you read the Scripture? Do you not understand

**THE REBUKE PUT AS A QUESTION**

The verse has it: ***“Do you preach righteousness”*** Al-Jalālayn explains that the question is a rebuke rather than a request for information, and he explains the word the translation renders as righteousness. It means doing good in the widest sense, and in this verse it is tied to faith in the message that had arrived. Ibn ʿAbbās names the audience: the leaders of the Jews, who were telling people of humble background to accept the oneness of God and to follow Muḥammad ﷺ. Al-Baghawī agrees and describes the same word as obedience.

Al-Qurṭubī reports the setting from Ibn ʿAbbās in more detail. A man among the Jews of Madinah would say to his son-in-law, or to a relative, or to someone connected to him by a wet-nurse's tie. The relative or the son-in-law had become a Muslim, and the advice he received was this: stay firm on the way you are on. Stay firm on what this man tells you, because his matter is true. The reports also say that the learned men among them used to command their followers to hold on to the Torah, and then contradict it themselves and alter the description of the Prophet ﷺ in it.

Tazkirul Qur'an describes why the question was addressed to this group in particular. The Israelites were regarded across the Arab world as the people who carried a revealed book, so anyone asking about the Arab Prophet went to them. They would answer with arguments that turned people away from him, while at the same time preaching that people should follow the truth and live by it. The lesson of the verse reaches past the group it was first spoken to, because the gap between what a man teaches and what he does is available to everyone.

**THE GAP BETWEEN SPEECH AND DEED**

The verse goes on: ***“and fail to practice it yourselves”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the word for forgetting in the way Arabic uses it here: to neglect, to leave something aside. Al-Saʿdī defines the failure precisely. The verse says they left their own selves out of what they commanded. They told others to believe and do good, and they did not include themselves in the instruction.

Al-Saʿdī then draws a rule out of the word for understanding that closes the verse. The faculty of reason was given to a person so he could grasp what benefits him and hold himself back from what harms him. The first thing reason asks of a man is that he be the first to act on what he orders. A man who commands good and does not do it has already shown what his reasoning is worth. The same is true of a man who forbids evil and does not leave it. It is worse for a scholar, because the evidence has been established against him.

He also guards the verse from a misunderstanding that has made sincere people give up a duty. The verse does not say that a person who falls short should stop commanding good. Al-Saʿdī notes that the warning is against the contradiction, not against the calling, and he points to the verse that makes the same warning to the believers: (61:2 — **“O believers! Why do you say what you do not do?”**). The two duties stand side by side: keep calling, and keep climbing.

Think of a signpost that has been knocked crooked in the wind. Travellers still read it, and the ones it sends down the wrong road were sent by that post. The verse asks the post to straighten up before it points anyone else anywhere.

Ibn Kathīr quotes the early commentators on the same point, and his summary of the verse is a sentence worth carrying: how is it that you command people to do every kind of good, and forget your own selves, when you are reading the Book of God and you know what it promises to those who disobey?

**THE BOOK THEY READ**

The verse puts the question: ***“although you read the Scripture?”*** The clause adds the fact that makes the contradiction heavy. These were not men who were ignorant of their own book. They recited it, and the book they recited carried a description of the Prophet who had come, along with warnings to those who knew and stayed silent. Ibn ʿAbbās says the phrase means you are readers of the Scripture. Al-Baghawī adds that the Torah in their hands contained his description.

tafsir_initial notes a small detail in the verb. Reading here can also carry the sense of studying, and some of the commentators read it that way: you study the Book. The difference matters, because study describes a person who has gone over the material repeatedly, which makes the gap between his knowledge and his conduct wider rather than narrower.

The question at the end of the verse is the natural one after that. A person with a text in front of him, a warning inside the text, and a public life that contradicts it is not missing information. He is missing the step that turns information into action.

**THE UNDERSTANDING THEY FAILED TO USE**

The sentence reads: ***“Do you not understand”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the question as an invitation to see the ugliness of what the men were doing, so that they might turn from it. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as a question about plain sense: do you not have the reasoning that ordinary human beings have? Al-Mukhtaṣar words the whole verse as a comparison that needs no explanation: what could be more damaging than telling others to believe and do good, while you read the Torah, turn away from it and forget it, knowing that it orders you to follow God's religion and believe in His prophets?

Al-Saʿdī closes the matter with the sharpest sentence in his commentary on the passage. The man who commands what is good and does not do it, and forbids what is evil and does not leave it, has given evidence against his own mind. That is the whole of the argument, and it needs no further evidence from anywhere else. The next verse supplies the remedy for the man who has recognised himself in the description: seek help through patience and prayer.

---
## Verse 2:45

> And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except for the humble—

**TWO TOOLS FOR THE ONE WHO NEEDS HELP**

The text says: ***“And seek help through patience”*** ***“and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except”*** The verse gives two tools, and the commentators treat them as a pair. Al-Qurṭubī opens with the root of the Arabic word for patience, which means to hold or restrain. A man who is held back until he dies is described with a word from that root; a person who restrains himself is described with it as well. Patience in the language of the Book is not a mood of resignation. It is a hand on the reins.

Al-Saʿdī spreads the word over the whole of a person's life and finds three kinds of it. There is patience in obeying God until the act is done. There is patience against disobeying Him until the desire is left. There is patience with the painful things He has measured out, so that a person does not complain about them. He adds the sentence that gives hope to anyone who finds none of the three easy: whoever disciplines himself to be patient, God gives him patience.

Al-Mukhtaṣar states the purpose of the instruction. Ask for help in matters of religion and in matters of daily life through patience and prayer. The two of them bring a person near to God and let him reach what he is aiming at, and God will help him, protect him and lift his difficulties.

Several of the early commentators read patience in this verse as fasting, and Ibn Kathīr records Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān and Mujāhid among them. Al-Qurṭubī notes that this is why the month of Ramadan is called the month of patience in the books of the scholars. Others read patience as holding back from wrong. All the readings fit inside the meaning al-Saʿdī set out, and each of them gives a reader something he can start doing today.

**THE WEIGHT THAT ONLY THE HUMBLE CARRY**

The wording runs: ***“for the humble”*** The pronouns in this sentence were discussed, and the commentators record the possibilities. tafsir_initial notes that the word translated as it can refer to the prayer itself, which is what most of them chose, or to the whole instruction that has been given. Ibn Kathīr reports Muqātil's reading of the verse as a whole: use patience and the prescribed prayer to seek the Hereafter. Al-Jalālayn explains the burden as weight, and al-Mukhtaṣar says the same: the prayer is a hardship except for the people who are humble before their Lord.

tafsir_initial adds an observation that shows how deep the difference runs. Patience is something a person can practice in small daily doses; every act of deferred gratification is a piece of it, and the training is spread across the hours. Prayer demands something else. It asks for a retreat from the world and for the ego to step back, several times a day, on a schedule that does not consult the person's mood. That is why the Book calls it heavy without apology, and why it names the group for whom it becomes light.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains what the humility in question is. The Arabic word describes a restfulness of heart and a low view of oneself that grows out of awareness of God's greatness. When a person has that, obedience becomes easy and pleasant for him. It also shows on the outside, in the way he carries himself, and the scholars note that a man with outward modesty and no inner humility has the posture without the quality. The verse is looking for the inner version, and it says plainly who finds the prayer light.

Ibn Kathīr mentions the report that the men of the early community used to turn to the prayer in the middle of difficulty. He traces the practice to Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān, who described the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in these words: whenever a matter weighed on him, he would pray. Imām Aḥmad narrated it in his Musnad. Al-Jalālayn records the same practice in his commentary on this verse, which is why the two tools are given together. Patience carries a person through a long road, and prayer puts him back on the road when the load has made him forget where he is going.

Think of a climber working up a long ridge. Patience is the rope that holds him to the face of the mountain. Prayer is the ledge he stops at, several times a day, to check the route and get his breath back. A man with the rope but no ledges will exhaust himself, and a man who stops often without the rope will never be far up the ridge.

---
## Verse 2:46

> those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and to Him they will return

**THE CERTAINTY THAT CHANGES A PERSON**

The verse begins: ***“those who are certain”*** The word in the Arabic here is the one that usually means to think or to suppose, and Al-Qurṭubī opens his discussion by noting the majority position: in this verse it means certainty. He gives the evidence for that reading from the Book. The same word is used for a man who is sure of his reckoning ((69:20 — **“I was certain that I would meet my account”**)). It is used again on the Day of Judgement for the guilty, who know what is coming ((18:53)).

tafsir_initial works through the range of the word with care, since a reader who looks it up will find it used for supposition elsewhere ((6:116)) and for belief in another place ((48:6)). The Arabic language lets this word carry everything from a guess to a settled conviction, and context decides which one is in play. In this verse the context leaves no room for guessing, because the sentence that follows names the two things the humble are sure about.

Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the plain sense: the humble are convinced that they will meet their Lord on the Day of Judgement. That conviction is the last piece in the argument the passage has been making. Patience and prayer are heavy for most people, and light for the men and women who already know that the meeting is coming. A person who is certain about the appointment keeps it on the calendar.

**THE MEETING THEY EXPECT**

As the verse says: ***“that they will meet their Lord”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the meeting as the resurrection, when every person stands before his Lord. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the phrase in the fullest sense his commentary allows: they know that they will have to meet their Lord, and the note he attaches to it describes what the meeting involves.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān connects the certainty to the humility in the previous verse and explains why they belong together. A man who is aware of God's greatness and of his own smallness cannot be indifferent to the meeting. The two things run in one direction. The more a person knows who he is and who is waiting for him, the easier five daily appointments become. It also becomes easier to keep his hands off what he is not allowed to take.

The same promise and the same meeting appear in other verses of the sūrah. tafsir_initial gathers a few. In (2:28) the return to God is stated as the end of the human sequence. In (2:156) the people who receive good news in difficulty are described by what they say about returning to Him. The Book keeps the meeting in view at the end of its instructions, which is a way of telling the reader that the instructions were never about the present moment alone.
