**THE ROAD BACK TO HIM**

Then the verse says: ***“and to Him they will return”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the return as the hereafter, where God will reward each person. Ibn ʿAbbās says simply that they are returning to Him after death. The verse repeats the direction twice, once as a meeting and once as a return, and the commentators let both stand because the two words are doing different jobs. A meeting suggests an appointment a person goes to. A return suggests a place a person belongs to and has been heading away from.

Ibn Kathīr closes his commentary on the passage by tying the two verses together again. God commanded His servants to use patience and prayer to acquire what is good in this life and in the next. The people described at the end of the instruction are the ones who are already certain about the day when the account is settled.

Think of a worker who knows the audit is booked for the end of the quarter. He does not need a manager standing over him to keep his records straight, because the appointment is in his head and it is not moving. The verse says the same thing about a person who is certain of meeting his Lord: the appointment explains his patience and it makes his prayer light. That is the last thing the sūrah says before it turns back to the story of the Israelites and the favours they were given.

---
## Verse 2:47

> O Children of Israel! Remember ˹all˺ the favours I granted you and how I honoured you above the others

**A SECOND ADDRESS TO THE SAME PEOPLE**

The sūrah opens the sentence: ***“O Children of Israel!”*** The address opens exactly as it did in verse 40, and the commentators read the repetition as deliberate. Israel is another name for Jacob. The people being addressed are the Jews living around Madinah in the Prophet's time, and their ancestors are the ones who received the favours being named. Al-Qurṭubī states the rule that governs all these verses: the address goes to the people standing in front of the Prophet ﷺ, while the favours were granted to the fathers who came before them. The generations inherited the story, the land, the book and the name.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains why a later generation is asked to remember a favour given to its ancestors. When a man receives a great gift, his children and grandchildren share in what flows from it: safety, standing, education, the doors the gift opened. The verse asks the descendants to do the arithmetic honestly. Everything they were proud of came from a table they did not set.

**THE FAVOURS THEY WERE TOLD TO COUNT**

The verse declares: ***“Remember ˹all˺ the favours I granted you”*** Ibn ʿAbbās lists the favours the verse has in view: the Scripture, the messenger, and the coming of Islam. tafsir_initial widens the list in the way the address suggests. The word for favour covers the deliverance from Pharaoh ((2:49-50)), the manna and the quails, the promised land, the prophets raised among them, and the books sent down to them. In its widest sense it includes the gift of existence itself, which is why the command in the plural fits every reader of the verse and not only the community being addressed.

Al-Mukhtaṣar divides the favours into two kinds, the ones connected with religion and the ones connected with daily life. The first sort includes the prophecy and the guidance that came to them before the rest of the world had it. The second includes the liberation, the food and the security. Tazkirul Qur'an describes the whole arrangement as a task rather than a prize. The Israelites were chosen to receive God's scriptures and pass His commandments on to the rest of mankind, and the blessings that came with the office were part of the equipment for the job.

**THE HONOUR THEY WERE GIVEN**

The sentence moves on: ***“and how I honoured you above the others”*** Al-Qurṭubī records the two readings the commentators took. One is that they were preferred over the peoples of their own era, since every age has its own world of nations, and theirs was chosen among the nations of the time. The other reading takes the phrase as it stands and says they were preferred over all the worlds, because prophets were raised among them and books were sent down to them, and this distinction was theirs alone. Ibn Kathīr supports the second reading and quotes the verses that state it: (44:32 — **“We chose them knowingly above the nations”**), and (5:20 — **“O my people! Remember Allah's favour upon you, when He appointed prophets among you, made you kings, and gave you what no one else in the worlds was given”**).

tafsir_initial adds a balancing note that keeps the verse in proportion. This preference belongs to the past, since another verse in the Book describes the community of the Prophet ﷺ as the best community brought out for mankind ((3:110)). The same word is used elsewhere for other prophets and their peoples, as in the verse that names Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah and Lot ((6:86)). Preference in the Book is a description of what a people were given and what they did with it, not a title that can be inherited without the work.

Tazkirul Qur'an names the danger that grew out of this verse over the centuries. Later generations of Jews read the election of their ancestors as a guarantee of safety in the next world, as though salvation were a family possession. The verse that follows takes that idea apart in a single sentence, and it does it at the moment when a community feels most secure.

---
## Verse 2:48

> Guard yourselves against the Day on which no soul will be of help to another. No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken, and no help will be given

**THE DAY THE VERSE WARNS ABOUT**

The Book says: ***“Guard yourselves against the Day on”*** ***“which no soul will be of help to another. No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken”*** tafsir_initial explains the verb at the front of the sentence, which is usually translated as reverence or mindfulness but carries the sense of being careful, aware and on guard. The word names a posture, not a feeling. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the command here carries a threat inside it, and that the day being named is the day of resurrection and the terror that comes with it.

The verse then names four things that will not work on that day. Ibn Kathīr opens the list with the first: no person will be of help to another. He brings in the verses that state the same fact from other angles. One of them says that no burdened soul will carry another's load ((35:18 — **“No burdened soul will bear another's burden”**)). Another describes the day when every person will have enough of his own concern to make him careless about anyone else ((80:37 — **“everyone will have enough concern of their own”**)).

Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the reader in the position the verse is describing with a question at the end of its commentary: with no appeal, no ransom and no helper, where will a person turn? The answer is the whole point of the address. He turns now, while the door is open, to the One who does not need the intercession or the gold.

**NO INTERCESSION AND NO RANSOM**

Al-Jalālayn notes two readings of the verb, one where the intercession is accepted and one where it is offered. Either way the sense is the same: no intercessor will be allowed to speak for the person, and nothing of that kind will be taken from him. Al-Mukhtaṣar records the exception the Book states elsewhere, that intercession happens only with God's permission. On the ransom, it says the payment would never be enough anyway, even if a person brought the earth filled with gold.

tafsir_initial goes into the subject of intercession with some care, since readers ask about it. The Arabic word for intercession is related to other ideas in the Book, including the request for forgiveness made on behalf of another person, and the act of praying for someone in the sense of blessing. The angels seek forgiveness for those who believe in one verse, and the Prophet is told to bless the givers of charity in another. None of that turns into a system of favours bought at the door. Intercession in the Book is something that happens with the Lord's permission, and the verse before us is one of the places that says so.

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the sentence in its setting and names what the audience was trusting. He explains that no disbelieving soul will help another, no intercessor will be allowed to intercede, and no compensation will be received from it. A community that thought its ancestors' standing would cover its own account is told that the account is personal, and the next line removes the last two escape routes.

**NO HELP FROM ANY SIDE**

The verse goes on: ***“and no help will be given”*** The list closes with the plainest item of the four. Al-Jalālayn reads the phrase as a statement that nobody will be helped to escape God's punishment. Ibn ʿAbbās says the same. The verse has removed the friend, the intercessor, the payment and finally the rescue party, and it has done so in one short sentence about the last day.

Tazkirul Qur'an draws the conclusion the passage is aiming at. On that day people will be judged one by one, according to what each of them did. Any hope built on something other than good deeds has misunderstood the weight of the occasion. That single line is the answer to the idea of inherited salvation, and it is placed directly after the reminder of the election in the previous verse.

Think of a courtroom where the accused has brought a wealthy friend, a lawyer, a purse and a crowd of supporters. The verse tells him that the friend cannot speak, the lawyer is not heard, the purse is not counted and the crowd will have its own cases. He still has one thing left, which is the time before the hearing to change what the record contains. That is why the verse opens with the command to guard, and not with a description of the fire.

---
## Verse 2:49

> ˹Remember˺ how We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with dreadful torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women. That was a severe test from your Lord

**THE RESCUE THEY WERE TOLD TO REMEMBER**

The verse begins with the words: ***“˹Remember˺ how We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh”*** tafsir_initial explains the little word for when that opens this verse and the ones after it. In Arabic it can carry the sense of remember when, even when no verb of remembering is written. So the sūrah is saying to the people in front of it: call this to mind, and it then tells them the story of their ancestors as if it were their own. Al-Qurṭubī works the same point out in his commentary. The address goes to the living, while the deliverance was granted to the fathers, and the Book treats the generosity as a debt the descendants also owe thanks for.

Al-Saʿdī opens his account of the passage by saying that God is now listing the favours in detail. The sequence is the whole history of a household: rescue from a tyrant, a passage through the sea, an appointment with God for their prophet, a book, a fall into idol worship, and a pardon. He notes that each item is told so that gratitude would have something to work with.

**THE TORMENT THEY LIVED UNDER**

The verse puts the matter: ***“who afflicted you with dreadful torment, slaughtering your sons”*** Al-Jalālayn explains what the torment was: the killing of the newborn sons and the sparing of the women, and the verse makes the two halves a single policy. He records the report about the reason, that some of the priests told Pharaoh a child would be born among the Israelites who would bring his rule to an end, and the campaign followed that warning.

tafsir_initial handles that report carefully, and the care is instructive. The Qur'an does not give a reason for the killing. The note points out that Pharaoh repeats the same threat later, when Moses is a grown man ((7:127) and (40:25)). That repetition suggests the murder was a form of collective control rather than the result of one prophecy. Al-Rāzī and others preferred that reading. The comparison with the book of Exodus has also been noticed by readers of both traditions.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān describes the two hands of the policy. The boys were killed because a grown man among the Israelites could threaten the throne. The girls were spared because they could be useful as servants, and even the leniency was calculating. He adds that this detail is worth noticing in a passage about favour. The community being addressed inherited a story in which the mercy of God stood between them and a plan that had already been signed.

**THE LIFE THEY WERE SPARED**

The sentence continues: ***“and keeping your women.”*** al-Saʿdī describes the life of the Israelites under that arrangement in a way that leaves no room for softening. They were caught between three conditions: the males who had been killed, the ones kept alive for hard labour, and the women whose lives were spared as a favour that the state expected gratitude for. He calls the combination the outer limit of humiliation, and he notes how carefully the humiliation was managed so that the people would feel owned.

The sūrah has already used the word for corruption and the word for wrongdoing in the account of the earlier peoples, and this verse shows what the opposite of a favour looks like when it is dressed in the clothing of law. The next clause tells the reader how God answered it: not with a petition, and not with a treaty, but with a rescue that the people could see with their own eyes.

**A TEST THAT LOOKED LIKE A BURDEN**

The verse puts it: ***“That was a severe test from your Lord”*** The commentators discuss the last word of this verse, because the Arabic term can mean a trial and it can mean a favour. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it here as a tremendous calamity from your Lord, and he also records the second reading, that it means a tremendous blessing. Al-Saʿdī chooses the second reading for this verse: what the sentence points at is the deliverance, and the deliverance is a kindness from their Lord, enormous enough to demand a response.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān shows how both readings work in one passage. If the sentence points at the killing of the sons, then the thing being tested is patience, since a calamity is where patience is measured. If it points at the deliverance, then the thing being tested is gratitude, since a blessing is where thankfulness is measured. Either way the verse puts a question to the reader that the rest of the passage keeps asking: what are you going to do with what you were given?

---
## Verse 2:50

> And ˹remember˺ when We parted the sea, rescued you, and drowned Pharaoh’s people before your very eyes

**THE SEA THAT OPENED**

The verse starts with: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We parted the sea, rescued you”*** Al-Qurṭubī opens his commentary with the root of the verb used here, which means to separate or to split. He notes the picture the Book gives elsewhere of the same event, where each divided part of the water stood like a great mountain. Then he traces the word's family. The parting of hair, the criterion that separates truth from falsehood, and the day of distinction are all built on the same root.

tafsir_initial adds something a careful reader of the Arabic will notice. The phrase is literally We parted the sea by means of you, so the people being rescued are named as the means by which the passage opened. The same note identifies the sea as a body of saltwater, and most authorities identify it as the Red Sea. It then lists the other places where the drowning of the Egyptians is told: (7:136), (8:54), (10:90), (17:103), (20:77-79), (26:65-66).

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān lays out the sequence of the escape. Moses had worked for years among Pharaoh and his people. When they refused everything, God told him to take the Israelites out of Egypt quietly. They reached the water with the army behind them, and the command came for the sea to open. They crossed a dry road, and the army followed them into it.

Al-Ṭabarī explains the small preposition in the Arabic that the translation renders as for you. The phrase is literally We parted the sea by means of you. He then gives the reason, and the reason is worth the whole story. The Israelites were twelve tribes, so the sea was opened into twelve paths, and each tribe walked through on a road of its own. He records the report of al-Suddī: when Moses reached the sea, he called it by a nickname and struck it, and it split, and every division of the water stood like a great mountain, and the Israelites went in. Twelve paths under one sea, one for each family, so that no tribe crossed on the credit of another.

**THE ARMY THAT SANK**

Then come the words: ***“and drowned Pharaoh’s people before your very eyes”*** Al-Jalālayn describes the closing of the water over the army while the Israelites watched. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same focus on the witnesses: the sea opened as a dry path for them, and their enemies were drowned in front of them, as they looked on. Ibn ʿAbbās adds a detail from the reports, that the water covered them and the Israelites saw it happen.

Al-Saʿdī explains why the verse insists on the word watching. God drowned the enemy while His people looked on so that their eyes would be comforted. A rescue that happens out of sight leaves a person wondering whether it happened at all. The Book gives the Israelites a scene they could keep for the rest of their lives, and it wants the reader of the sūrah to notice that the same God is still arranging endings.

Think of a family standing on the far bank of a flooded river, watching the water close behind them over the people who had been chasing them. Nobody in that family would ever again need to be told that God can open a road where there is none, and nobody would have an excuse for forgetting it in the next generation.

---
## Verse 2:51

> And ˹remember˺ when We appointed forty nights for Moses, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully

**THE FORTY NIGHTS SET FOR MOSES**

As the verse says: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We appointed forty nights”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the appointment as the period at the end of which Moses would receive the Torah, and he notes the variant reading that makes the sentence a simple promise rather than a mutual appointment. Al-Qurṭubī reports the discussion among the grammarians about that variant, since the form used for a mutual appointment belongs in ordinary Arabic to dealings between people, while the promise belongs to God alone. He also records the view of Abū ʿUbayd, who preferred the reading without the extra letter.

tafsir_initial points to the other place where the period is described ((7:142)), and Ibn Kathīr fills the details in from there. The appointment was for thirty nights, and God completed it with ten more, which is where the forty comes from. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān tells the story with its small human detail. Moses was told to devote a month to worship before receiving the book. When he broke his fast at the end of the month, he was asked to add ten days, so that the state of fasting would be restored for the meeting.

Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the frame of the address. The forty nights were among the blessings given to this people, since the Torah with its light and guidance was completed in them. The verse is placed in a list of gifts, and the gift that matters most in it is not the mountain or the seclusion. It is the book that was about to arrive.

**THE CALF THAT WAS TAKEN UP**

The verse states: ***“for Moses, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully”*** Al-Jalālayn names the maker of the calf, the man called al-Sāmirī, and explains the phrase about absence: the people worshipped it after Moses had gone up for the appointment. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the last words as the harm the act did to the people themselves. Al-Saʿdī explains the sequence as a fall that happened in the middle of a favour. The book was on its way down the mountain while the people were building something to bow to at the foot of it.

Ibn Kathīr notes the other places in the Book where the calf appears — (7:148-154), (2:92-93), (4:153) and (20:88) — and the last of those names al-Sāmirī as the man who produced it. The sūrah will come back to the story more than once, and each return looks at a different part of it: the crime, the repentance, the command, and the pardon.

Al-Qurṭubī fills in what the calf was made of, and the detail makes the scene more painful rather than less. The people had borrowed jewellery from the Egyptians on the night they left, and the calf was fashioned from that gold ((7:148 — **“They took the calf for worship, and it was nothing but a body that lowed”**)). The ornament of a rescue was melted down into an idol inside six weeks, which is what the verse means by the phrase in his absence. The man who had led them out was still on the mountain, and the people were already spending the plunder of the escape on a god they could see.

Think of a family that has just been carried out of a burning building, and who use the first quiet evening to build a small fire in the middle of the floor and sit around it. The verse is written in the plain language of what people do with freedom when the person who was guiding them steps out of the room.

The order of the clauses deserves a moment. The verse puts the appointment first and the calf second, and the placement does the work of a whole sermon. The thing the people were given was a book that would have told them what to do with their hands. The thing they did with their hands while waiting for it was build a god out of metal. A reader who has ever filled an empty hour with something he would not want to defend knows the scene.

---
## Verse 2:52

> Even then We ˹still˺ forgave you so perhaps you would be grateful

**THE PARDON AFTER THE FALL**

The verse opens with the words: ***“Even then We ˹still˺ forgave you”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the pardon as the erasing of the sin after the worship of the calf. Ibn ʿAbbās explains it in practical terms: God left them alone and did not destroy them. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds that the forgiveness followed the request for forgiveness that the people made, which is told in the verses that come shortly after this one.

Al-Qurṭubī draws a distinction between two words that a reader might treat as synonyms. The word used here carries the sense of wiping a trace away. He notes that it can describe a pardon that comes after a penalty as well as one that comes before it. The other word for forgiveness never carries a punishment with it. He points to the way the word is used for wind wiping out a track in the sand. The verse's choice is the image of a record being cleared, not a sentence being shortened.

Kashānī reads the pardon as a kindness that arrived through the turning back of the people when Moses returned to them. He treats the whole sequence as a description of how mercy behaves in a community that has just done something humiliating. It does not leave the people to carry the shame. It lifts the record and gives them work to do with their hands.

**THE GRATITUDE THE PARDON ASKED FOR**

The verse puts it: ***“so perhaps you would be grateful”*** Maʿārif al-Qurʾān pauses over the word rendered as perhaps, which marks an expectation rather than a doubt. God does not speak with uncertainty. The note explains that in a sentence like this, the expectation belongs to the observers: when a man receives a pardon, everyone watching expects him to be grateful. The verse puts the community being addressed in exactly that position, with the whole record of their history reading out in front of them.

Al-Mukhtaṣar describes what the gratitude was supposed to look like: worshipping God in the best way and doing as He instructed. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the ending as a statement of purpose, that they might give thanks for the pardon they had received. tafsir_initial points to the other place where the pardon is mentioned ((4:153)), and it notes that the verse there presents the mercy and the power of God together, since a pardon of that size is beyond anything a human court would produce.

The sūrah will come back to this same pardon later in the chapter, in the middle of a passage about the covenant, and it will use it as evidence in an argument. A community that was forgiven for worshipping a metal calf in the open has no ground for thinking that its standing was earned. The forgiveness arrived while the record was still fresh, and that is why the word gratitude closes the sentence rather than the word shame.

Think of a teacher who discovers a whole class copying in an examination, and who cancels the punishment on condition that the class sits the paper again honestly. Nobody in that room earned the second chance, and every one of them would remember it on the day of the retake.

The passage has now shown a community being given a rescue, a crossing, a book and a pardon, and it has shown the community failing in the middle of it and being lifted back up. The word gratitude at the end of the verse is not a request for a compliment. It is the name of the only reasonable response to a record that has just been wiped clean, and it is the hinge on which the next verses turn as the story of the Israelites continues.

---
## Verse 2:53

> And ˹remember˺ when We gave Moses the Scripture—the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺ that perhaps you would be ˹rightly˺ guided

**THE BOOK GIVEN TO MOSES**

The verse begins: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We gave Moses the Scripture”*** Al-Qurṭubī opens his commentary by identifying the Scripture, and he reports that the commentators agreed on one point: it is the Torah. Al-Jalālayn says the same. Al-Mukhtaṣar places the gift in the list of favours the passage has been counting: God's giving of the Torah to Moses is one of the blessings the Israelites were asked to remember, because it is the book that told them what to do with everything else they had been given.

Ibn Kathīr puts the verse next to the one before it and reads the pair as a single reminder. The pardon came after the calf, and the book came with the pardon, so the community that had just done the worst thing in its history walked away from the mountain carrying a law and a clean record. The verse asks the readers in Madinah to weigh those two facts together, since the book in their hands was a descendant of that same gift.

**THE STANDARD IT BROUGHT**

The Book says: ***“the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺”*** Al-Jalālayn treats the word translated as standard as an explanatory addition to the Torah itself. It is the thing that separates truth from falsehood, and the permitted from the prohibited. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān gives the term its full weight. In the language of the Qur'an it names whatever separates truth from falsehood and marks one off from the other, and he offers three readings of what it refers to here. It can mean the rulings that are found inside the Torah, since a law is what settles the disputes people have about belief and conduct. It can mean the miracles that settle a claim in a way anyone can see. Or it can mean the Torah itself, which carries both qualities at once, being the Book of God and the instrument that separates truth from error.

tafsir_initial examines the word with the same care and adds a fourth possibility. In one verse the Book mentions that God gave Moses and Aaron the criterion ((21:48)), which suggests that the term can describe a power of discrimination placed in a prophet rather than a physical book. The note supports that reading with the verses where prophets are given the Book and wisdom together ((2:151; 3:164; 4:54)), and it points out that the term is also a name of the Qur'an itself ((25:1)).

Al-Qurṭubī records a disagreement among the early grammarians that is worth keeping because of what it shows about reading the Book carefully. Al-Farrāʾ and Quṭrub read the verse as saying that God gave Moses the Torah and gave Muḥammad the criterion, which would make the second gift belong to a different prophet entirely. Al-Naḥḥās rejected the reading on two grounds. A thing that is joined to another in a sentence should be its like, and the meaning of the sentence should stay inside its own subject. The verse is about one prophet and one gift, and the criterion belongs with the Torah.

**THE GUIDANCE IT WAS MEANT TO SHOW**

The verse names it: ***“that perhaps you would be ˹rightly˺ guided”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the ending as the purpose of the gift: so that you might be guided to the truth through it. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as deliverance from error. Al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense. The word translated as perhaps is the one the sūrah has used before, and the commentators treat it as an expression of expectation rather than doubt.

The verse closes a list of favours that runs from the bullocks of Egypt to a book on a mountain, and the final item is the one that explains all the others. A rescue without instruction leaves a people free but lost. The book was given so that the people who had been carried out of one country would know how to live in the next one, and the sūrah asks them to remember that the gift was aimed at a destination.

Think of a man who is pulled out of a flood and then handed a map and a rulebook at the same time. The rescue answers the question of whether he will live. The map answers the question of where, and the rulebook answers the question of how. The verse is about the second and third gifts, and it treats them as favours of the same size as the first.

---
## Verse 2:54

> And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “O my people! Surely you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf, so turn in repentance to your Creator and execute ˹the calf-worshippers among˺ yourselves. That is best for you in the sight of your Creator.” Then He accepted your repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

**THE WORDS OF MOSES TO HIS PEOPLE**

The wording runs: ***“And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “O my people!”*** Al-Jalālayn identifies the people being addressed as the ones who had worshipped the calf. Ibn ʿAbbās records the exchange that follows the opening words, and it is worth following because it shows how the instruction reached the community. When Moses told the people what they had done, they asked him what they should do. He told them to turn back to their Creator. They asked him how a turning back of that kind would be done, and he told them: let those who did not worship the calf kill those who did.

Ibn Kathīr places the whole episode in its frame and calls this the repentance required from the Israelites for the calf. The verse before us, he notes, is one of the places where the Book asks a later generation to remember a moment its ancestors survived, and the memory is meant to work like a scar that still explains a limp.

**THE WRONG THEY DID TO THEMSELVES**

The verse puts it: ***“Surely you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the phrase as harm done to the people themselves by taking the golden calf as a god. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it the same way. The community had not damaged God by building an idol out of borrowed gold. It had damaged the thing inside itself that was made to worship one Lord, and the verse names the injury with the same word the sūrah used for the first sin in the garden.

Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the accounting in view. Moses told the people that they had wronged themselves by taking the calf as a god and worshipping it, and he then gave them the way out. The Book's pattern is consistent across both stories. The wrong is described without softening, and the road back is opened in the same conversation.

**THE CALL TO TURN BACK**

The verse records: ***“so turn in repentance to your Creator”*** The word for turning in this sentence is the one that gives the sūrah's word for repentance, and al-Jalālayn notes the title it attaches to God here: your Creator, the One who made you and can remake you. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the command as a call to leave the worship of the calf behind and return to the One who had brought the people out of Egypt.

Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the turning as asking for forgiveness and repenting to the Creator, and it notes what the alternative would have been. Persisting in the worship of the calf would have ended in an eternity in the fire, and the command that follows, hard as it sounds, was the road out of that ending rather than the punishment for it.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the same verse as a description of a specific mode of repentance prescribed for a specific crime. He adds that the Islamic law also keeps capital penalties for certain major offences even when the offender repents, as in the case of intentional killing or adultery proven by proper evidence. The point of such penalties is not to close the door on mercy. It is to state what the offence costs in a community that has to live with the consequences.

**THE ORDER THAT CAME WITH IT**

The verse continues: ***“and execute ˹the calf-worshippers among˺ yourselves.”*** Al-Jalālayn explains who was to carry out the command: the innocent among the people were to kill the guilty. He also records the setting the commentators describe, that a dark cloud covered the camp so that no man could see the face of the person standing next to him and hold back his hand out of pity. The reports say that almost seventy thousand were killed.

tafsir_initial examines the phrase with the care it deserves. The wording is literally slay yourselves, and the note explains the two ways the commentators read it. The first is the one the translation follows: the guilty were killed by their fellow Israelites, which makes the severity of the act all the more terrible. On that reading some of the commentators add that the ones killed were counted as martyrs and the ones who did the killing had their repentance accepted, so that the whole community came out of the episode forgiven. The second reading takes the phrase in an inner sense. A person is asked to kill his own ego, meaning that he opposes his own appetites and puts them to death.

The comparison with the book of Exodus has been noticed by readers of both traditions ((Exodus 32:27)), and the sūrah's own version keeps its attention on the outcome rather than the arithmetic. This is the hardest command in the passage, and the Book does not dress it up. A community that had just made a god out of the jewellery of its own rescue was told that the only way back ran through its own ranks, and it went, and the record was cleared.

**THE REASON THE COMMAND WAS GOOD**

Its words are: ***“That is best for you in the sight of your Creator.””*** The sentence explains the command while it is being given. Al-Jalālayn reads it as the statement that the killing would be better for the people in the sight of the One who made them and made the command easy for them to carry out. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it the same. The verse does not present the order as a punishment handed down by an angry authority. It presents it as the better of two roads, spoken by a Creator who knows what the alternative costs.

Think of a surgeon who tells a patient that the limb has to come off, and that the operation is better for him than keeping it. Nobody in the room enjoys the sentence. The patient's hope lies in the fact that the man who speaks it can see what the patient cannot see, and that he has no interest in the pain itself.

**THE REPENTANCE THAT WAS ACCEPTED**

Then the verse says: ***“Then He accepted your repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the last sentence as the acceptance that came before the people had finished turning, and he notes the two names at the end: the One who relents toward the penitent, and the One who shows mercy to anyone who dies having turned back. Ibn ʿAbbās reads both names in the same way.

Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the outcome in plain words: the people did what they were told with God's approval, and He forgave them. The verse has now followed the community through a crime and a command and a consequence, and it ends with the same two names that closed the story of Adam's fall in the earlier passage. The Book keeps saying the same thing about God in the middle of the hardest scenes, which is the reason the stories are told in the order they are.

---
## Verse 2:55

> And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses! We will never believe you until we see Allah with our own eyes,” so a thunderbolt struck you while you were looking on

**THE DEMAND THEY MADE OF MOSES**

The verse declares: ***“And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses!”*** Al-Baghawī lays out the scene from the beginning. God had commanded Moses to come to Him with a group of the Israelites who would apologise for the worship of the calf. Moses chose seventy of the best men of his people. He told them to fast, to purify themselves and to wash their clothes, and they did. Then he took them out to Mount Sinai for the appointment with his Lord.

Al-Qurṭubī records that the commentators identified the speakers in this verse as those same seventy men. They had heard God speak, and then they came to Moses with a demand. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān tells the story with the small step that turns a request into a challenge. When the Torah was brought down and presented to the people as the Book of God, some of them said they would not accept it until God Himself addressed them in words. Moses told them the condition could be met and took them to the mountain, where they heard the words of God with their own ears. Then they changed the test again: hearing was not enough, they said, because they could not be sure who had spoken.

**A REFUSAL TO BE CONVINCED**

The verse records: ***“We will never believe you”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the sentence as a shameless address: they told Moses they would not believe him until they saw God with their own eyes. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same. The verse keeps the words as the people spoke them, and the words are addressed to a prophet who had just brought them a book, with the sea crossing behind him and the manna in front of him.

The demand has a logic, and the verse exposes it by leaving it in the record. A person who says he will not accept anything he cannot see with his own eyes has decided in advance what kind of evidence God is allowed to give. The sūrah has already answered that position twice, once with the challenge to produce a sūrah, and once with the story of Adam and the angels. Here it answers it with a bolt of fire, and then with a resurrection.

**THE SIGHT THEY ASKED FOR**

The verse names it: ***“until we see Allah with our own eyes,””*** Al-Jalālayn reads the phrase as a demand to see God openly, without a barrier. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it the same and explains the word as plainly, in the way that Moses himself had been addressed. Al-Qurṭubī preserves the same reading of the word: they wanted the sight to be public and unmediated, not a dream and not a veil.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the demand is answered in the same passage, though not in the way they proposed. They heard the words of God, and then they asked to see Him, and what came instead was a blast that took their lives. The lesson is not that God is far away. It is that a creature cannot take the presence of his Maker in this state, and the request was never a test of God's willingness. It was a test of what the askers could survive.

**THE BOLT THAT STRUCK THEM**

The verse states: ***“so a thunderbolt struck you”*** Al-Jalālayn identifies the bolt with the shout, and says it took them and they died. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes lightning striking and killing them. Ibn ʿAbbās says the fire burned them. Al-Baghawī records the report that a fire came down from the sky and consumed them, and al-Qurṭubī adds that the men had heard God's words and then made their demand, and that Moses prayed for their return to life afterwards.

tafsir_initial traces the word for the bolt through the Book, and the trail is instructive. The same word is connected to the swoon that struck Moses when he asked to see God ((7:143)). It is used of the swoon that overtakes the heavens and the earth at the blowing of the trumpet ((39:68)). It is also the punishment that seized an earlier people that rejected its prophet ((41:13)). The note records that the word can mean a great calamity, or a great cry, or fire, or an earthquake.

Some of the commentators, Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī among them, identify this episode with the one told later in the sūrah, where Moses takes seventy of the best of the Israelites up the mountain and asks for their revival after they are struck ((7:155)). On that reading the crowd and the crime are the same, and the two passages are describing one afternoon from two angles.

**THEY WATCHED IT COME**

The Book says: ***“while you were looking on”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the closing words as a statement that the men saw the blast come and watched what happened to them. Al-Mukhtaṣar says some of them looked at the others as they died. Ibn ʿAbbās says they were burned while they watched it.

The detail is doing the same work it did at the sea. A punishment that lands while a man watches cannot be explained away afterwards. Nobody in that group could stand up later and say that nothing happened, or that the report had been exaggerated. The Book keeps the witnesses in the sentence, and it keeps them there for the sake of the readers who come after them.

Think of a man who is handed a letter from a king and refuses to read it until the king comes to his house in person and delivers it at his door. The letter is real, the seal is on it and the messenger is standing in front of him. The demand is not a request for better evidence. It is a way of staying exactly where he is.

---
## Verse 2:56

> Then We brought you back to life after your death, so that perhaps you would be grateful

**LIFE RETURNED AFTER DEATH**

The verse names it: ***“Then We brought you back to life after your death”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the verse as a return to life after the death that had just been described. Ibn ʿAbbās spells it out: God brought them back to life after they had been burned to death. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the same in one line.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains why the revival was granted, and the reason is practical. The Israelites had a long history of suspecting Moses of things he had not done. He feared that they would say he had taken the best of their men into the wilderness and had them slaughtered there. So he prayed, and God gave the seventy men their lives back, and the accusation never had to be answered.

The sūrah returns to the theme of the dead coming back to life several times in its course, and this verse is the first of those scenes. Later in the same chapter, a murdered man is brought back when his body is struck with a piece of the cow, and the verse that describes it names the purpose: this is how God brings the dead to life and shows His signs ((2:73)). Still later, a man who wondered how God could revive a ruined town is made to die for a hundred years and then raised ((2:259)). The note in tafsir_initial on the verse before us points out that the demand for a visible God is repeated elsewhere with the same ending ((4:153 — **“They demanded what is even greater than this from Moses, saying, ‘Make Allah visible to us!’ So a thunderbolt struck them for their wrongdoing”**)). The Book treats the request and its answer as a settled matter, and it repeats the incident because the community being addressed in Madinah needed to know what their own scriptures said about it.

tafsir_initial records the alternative reading of the verse, which turns on the range of the Arabic verb for raising up. Its root carries the sense of rousing or stirring, and the Book uses it for the sending of prophets ((2:213)). On that reading the verse describes God raising up prophets among the Israelites rather than returning the dead to life, and the note mentions that one of the Islamic festivals is named from the same root because it marks the day the Prophet was chosen. The first reading is the one the commentators take as primary, and it fits the verses on either side.

**THE GRATITUDE THAT WAS THE POINT**

The verse records: ***“so that perhaps you would be grateful”*** Al-Jalālayn and Ibn ʿAbbās both read the ending as the purpose of the revival: that the people might give thanks for the second life they had been handed. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the same and keeps the sentence directed at the readers in Madinah, who were the descendants of the people brought back.

The passage has now given this community a rescue from a tyrant, a crossing through the sea, a book on a mountain, a pardon after idolatry, and a dead group brought back to life. Each gift ends with the same word, and the word is gratitude. The sūrah is not asking for a compliment. It is asking a people who were given repeated second chances to notice the pattern in their own history and to live as though they had noticed it.

Think of a man who survives a heart attack on a hospital bed and walks out of the ward with instructions in his hand. The doctors saved him once, and the instructions are the second chance. The verse says the seventy men were brought back from the dead, and the last word of the sentence is the one that names what a person does with a life that was handed back to him.

---
## Verse 2:57

> And ˹remember when˺ We shaded you with clouds and sent down to you manna and quails, ˹saying˺, “Eat from the good things We have provided for you.” The evildoers ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves

**SHADE IN THE OPEN DESERT**

Its words are: ***“And ˹remember when˺ We shaded you with clouds”*** Al-Jalālayn describes the shade as fine clouds that sheltered the people from the heat of the sun while they were in the wilderness. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the same in plainer words: God sent clouds to shade them from the sun's heat while they were wandering the earth. Al-Qurṭubī opens his commentary on the word with its root, which means to cover. A cloud is a covering over the sky, and he follows the word into ordinary Arabic, where a man whose mind is covered over is described from the same root, and the moon is described with it when a cloud hides it.

Ibn Kathīr records the report that al-Nasāʾī carries from Ibn ʿAbbās, that God shaded the Israelites with clouds during the years of wandering. He adds that similar reports came from other early authorities. The point of the detail is the setting: this was not a pleasant stop on a journey through farmland. It was a stretch of country with no roof and no harvest, and the roof and the harvest arrived anyway, every day, for a whole generation.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān fills in the reason the people were in that country at all. The Israelites belonged to Syria by ancestry and had settled in Egypt in the time of Joseph. When they were told to march against the people who had taken their homeland, they came near the border, looked at the strength of the enemy and refused the fight. Forty years of wandering was the consequence, and the story of the shade belongs to those forty years.

**FOOD FROM AN UNEXPECTED PLACE**

The verse continues: ***“and sent down to you manna”*** tafsir_initial notes that the Qur'an never describes the manna in detail. It only says that it came down from the sky, and it is always mentioned beside the quails. The commentators filled the gap with what they had from the earlier scriptures and from reports: some said it came from the tamarisk, some described it as a honeylike substance, and some described it as a fine bread that fell like snow. The note points the reader to the description in the book of Exodus, where the taste is compared to wafers made with honey ((Exodus 16:31)).

Ibn ʿAbbās describes the manna as honey and the quails as the familiar bird. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the manna as a sweet drink similar to honey, and it keeps the two gifts together in one sentence, which is how the Book keeps them too.

The two things that fell from the sky are worth naming side by side for what they are. One was sweet and could be gathered by hand in the morning. The other was meat that arrived on a wind in the evening. A people who had lived on slave rations in Egypt were being fed from above at a table that never ran out, and every morning the food was new rather than stored.

**GOOD THINGS AND THE COMMAND WITH THEM**

Then come the words: ***“and quails, ˹saying˺, “Eat from the good things We have provided”*** The instruction attached to the gift is as important as the gift. Al-Jalālayn reads it as permission to eat what God had provided. Ibn ʿAbbās adds the detail that makes the verse an account of a failure rather than a list of blessings: the people were told not to store any of it for the following day, and they stored food anyway. The Book reports the two facts in one verse so that the reader can see the command and the behaviour together.

tafsir_initial explains the term for the good things, which names what is wholesome, beneficial and lawful at the same time. The note adds that the Qur'an often corrects people who try to forbid these things, and that among those corrected in the Book are the Children of Israel themselves ((4:160; 5:87; 7:32)). A community that had been given its food by the sky was in no position to draw up a list of what God should have sent.

Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the practical shape of the favour. The people were told to consume what they had been provided with, and the message came with a warning that the gifts were meant to be used and not banked against the next morning.

**THE HARM THEY DID NOT DO TO GOD**

The verse records: ***“for you.” The evildoers ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us”*** The second half of the verse answers the behaviour described in the first. Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as a statement that the people who stored the food and were ungrateful did not damage God by their conduct. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the same: their ingratitude and their rejection of the blessing touched nothing in God, and they lost only what had been set aside for them.

Ibn Kathīr reads the clause as a rebuke aimed at the behaviour in general, and he places the whole verse inside the passage's pattern. God has spent several verses listing rescues, and now He lists a rescue that happened daily in the form of bread and water. A reader who has followed the list can feel the change in temperature. The Book is no longer describing a sea that opened once. It is describing a household that was fed every morning for decades and still complained about the menu.

The verse also quietly answers a question people ask about sin in general. If no wrong reaches God, why does the Book speak in the language of offence? It does so because the wrong reaches the person who does it, and the sentence that follows says so directly.

**WHOSE LOSS IT REALLY WAS**

As the verse says: ***“but wronged themselves”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the last phrase as the place where the harm landed: the evil consequences fell on the people themselves. Ibn ʿAbbās says they harmed themselves by storing what they had been told to leave, and al-Mukhtaṣar says they cut themselves off from good and exposed themselves to suffering.

This is the third time the sūrah has used this word for wrongdoing in the story of the Israelites. The people wronged themselves by taking the calf. They wronged themselves by the change they will make at the gate of the city in two verses' time. Here they wrong the same selves by treating a daily gift as a private stockpile. The Book is building a pattern the reader can use on his own account: the same word keeps appearing at the point where a person decides to keep something back.

Think of a family whose meals arrive on the doorstep every morning without fail. One member of the household decides to hide half of each delivery in a cupboard in case the arrangement ends, and within a month the cupboard smells of rot and the kitchen has stopped trusting the doorstep. The verse is about the cupboard, and it says plainly whose house it was in.

---
## Verse 2:58

> And ˹remember˺ when We said, “Enter this city and eat freely from wherever you please; enter the gate with humility, saying, ‘Absolve us.’ We will forgive your sins and multiply the reward for the good-doers.”

**THE COMMAND TO ENTER THE CITY**

In the verse's own words: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We said, “Enter this city”*** Al-Jalālayn identifies the city and gives the two candidates the commentators discussed: the Holy House in Jerusalem, or Jericho. Al-Baghawī lists a wider set. Ibn ʿAbbās said it is Jericho, the city of the giants, where there lived a remnant of the people of ʿĀd known as the ʿAmāliqah, whose chief was ʿŪj ibn ʿUnaq. Mujāhid said it is Bayt al-Maqdis. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk named Ramlah, Jordan, Palestine and Tadmor. Muqātil said Iliyā, and Ibn Kaysān said Syria.

tafsir_initial explains why the disagreement exists. The identity of the city is tied to the identity of the leader, because Moses never entered the Holy Land, and this command is given at a gate. If the command came through Moses, the city is likely to be somewhere he could reach. If it came through Joshua, the city is likely to be the one taken at the end of the wandering. Al-Rāzī even raises the possibility that the city is Egypt itself, on the grounds that the punishment in the next verse arrives during the life of Moses. Al-Baghawī's note on the word for city is worth keeping as a small piece of language: the Arabic term comes from a root that means to gather, so a town is a place where people come together.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reports two readings of when the command was given. One places it after the people grew tired of the manna and the quails and asked for the food they used to eat, so the command to enter a city where they could find what they wanted answers their complaint. The other places it at the conquest of the city after the wandering, delivered through Joshua. Either way, the command is the beginning of a settled life after a generation in the open.

**LIFE OF PLENTY WITHIN**

The verse goes on: ***“and eat freely from wherever you please”*** The permission repeats the abundance of the wilderness with a difference. There the food came down; here it grows and is gathered. Al-Jalālayn explains the instruction as permission to eat plentifully and without restriction from anywhere in the city. Al-Saʿdī describes the city as a place that would give the people honour, a homeland and a dwelling, with wide provision inside it.

tafsir_initial notices that this command echoes an earlier one. Adam was told to live in the Garden and eat freely from wherever he pleased ((2:35)), and the Israelites are given the same words at the door of a city. The echo is deliberate, and it puts the reader on notice. The last time these words were spoken, a single tree in the middle of the garden was the test. This time the test is at the gate, and it is about the posture of the people entering.

Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the generosity of the sentence in view: enter and consume abundantly, with ease, from the good things in it, from any place they wished. The command before the test is a banquet.

**THE GATE AND THE WORD**

The text says: ***“enter the gate with humility, saying, ‘Absolve us.’ We will forgive your sins”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the posture and the word. They were to enter bowing, and to say a sentence that asked for their sins to be lifted off them. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the posture as prostration in humility. Ibn ʿAbbās records two readings of the word they were told to say: forgive our sins, or, on another report, the declaration that there is no god but God.

tafsir_initial gives the literal form of the phrase. It is a single word in Arabic, and it means unburden us, or place our burden down. Al-Zamakhsharī read it in the shape of a common Arabic construction: unburden us with an unburdening. The word names a weight being removed, and it was to be said by a people who had spent forty years learning what weight felt like.

Al-Saʿdī draws the whole etiquette of the entry out of the two instructions. The people were to enter with humility in deed, which is the bowing, and in speech, which is the request for pardon. He also notes a detail in the next verse before he reaches it: God says that those who wronged changed the word, and He does not say that they all changed it, because not everyone at the gate took part in the mockery.

Think of a family moving into a new house after a long journey in the open. The instructions at the door are that they walk in with their heads slightly down and that the first sentence out of their mouths is an apology for the past. A household that can do those two things in that order is ready to live somewhere.

**THE REWARD THAT WOULD MULTIPLY**

The sentence continues: ***“and multiply the reward”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as a promise of more for those who do good, through obedience. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the increase as extra reward for the people who did what was right. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the multiplication as the way God rewards the doers of good.

The word for increase stands at the end of a sentence about forgiveness, and the order is worth noticing. Forgiveness clears the record; the increase is what comes after a cleared record, and it is given for doing good rather than for doing penance. The Book closes its description of the entry with an open hand, and the next verse explains what the people did with it.

**WHO THE PROMISE BELONGED TO**

The verse says: ***“for the good-doers.””*** Al-Saʿdī notes that the promise is attached to a quality rather than to a group: those who do good. The word covers the person who does what is right in the matter at hand, which at that gate meant walking in with the humility of a man who had been forgiven for something huge and knew it.

The two ends of the verse now stand in front of the reader. A people with a long record of rescue, provision and pardon are given a city and an instruction about how to enter it. One sentence was asked of them, and one posture, and the door was open. The next verse tells what happened instead, and the reader who has been following the passage already knows what to expect from this community and from himself.

---
## Verse 2:59

> But the wrongdoers changed the words they were commanded to say. So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them for their rebelliousness

**THE SWAP THEY MADE**

The wording runs: ***“But the wrongdoers changed the words they were commanded to say.”*** Al-Jalālayn names the substitution the reports describe. The people were told to say a word asking to be unburdened, and they said instead a phrase about a grain inside a hair, and they entered the town dragging themselves along on their backsides. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the change as mockery of God's law. Ibn ʿAbbās records the simpler version of the joke: the word was turned into the word for wheat, and the people laughed at the command on the way through the gate.

Al-Qurṭubī examines the offence and draws a rule from its size. They added a single letter to a sentence about repentance, and they met with the punishment they met. He then makes the argument that has kept this verse alive in the books of the scholars. If the change of one word brought all that, what should a person expect from changing what is greater than a word?

tafsir_initial raises a doubt that a careful reader will have. The wordplay described by the reports only works in Arabic, and these people did not speak Arabic, so the joke could not have been a pun between two Arabic words. The note also mentions that the traditional accounts add the detail that they entered on their backsides, which is the part of the story that survives in the parallel passage ((7:162)). The exact wording of the mockery is a matter of report, and the crime the verse itself states is clear: they changed what they had been told to say.

**WHAT CAME DOWN ON THEM**

The verse names it: ***“So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them”*** Al-Jalālayn identifies the punishment as a plague, and he records that just under seventy thousand of the people died in a short time. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes it as a torment sent down because of what they had done. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the word as a plague from heaven. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān names the same figure and the same disease, and he adds the observation the scholars made about it: this was a punishment for a people who had turned away, while for a people who obey, the same sort of event is a mercy.

tafsir_initial lists the other places where the word for this punishment appears, so that a reader can see the width of its meaning: (7:134-135), (8:11), (29:34), (34:5). In those verses it covers punishment, wrath, and in one case the calm that God sent down on the believers before a battle. The word names what comes down from the heavens, and what it carries depends on who is standing underneath it.

The sentence also answers a question about the previous favours. The sun was shaded, the bread came down, the sea opened, and now the sky sends something else. The same channel that carried provision for forty years carried a punishment for one mocking word, and the Book places the two facts side by side without explanation. That side-by-side placement is the explanation.

**THE BEHAVIOUR THAT NAMED THEM**

Its words are: ***“for their rebelliousness”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the last word as the name of the behaviour: they deviated from obedience, which is what the word for rebellion means. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the offence as crossing the limits of the law and disobeying the command.

The sūrah's vocabulary for rebellion has appeared before, in the closing line of the parable passage, where God said He leaves none to stray except the rebellious ((2:26)). Here the word is used for a people who had been given more than any other community of their era and who answered a gate command with a joke. The verse does not describe a mistake or a misunderstanding. It names a settled attitude, and it places that attitude at the door of a city the people had been given for free.

Think of a man who is handed the keys to a house, told to walk in with his hat off and to greet the owner of the property once in the doorway, and who puts his hat back on the moment he crosses the threshold and shouts something funny for his friends. The house is still his on paper. Something else in the arrangement has just changed, and the rain that comes through the roof afterwards is not an accident.

---
## Verse 2:60

> And ˹remember˺ when Moses prayed for water for his people, We said, “Strike the rock with your staff.” Then twelve springs gushed out, ˹and˺ each tribe knew its drinking place. ˹We then said,˺ “Eat and drink of Allah’s provisions, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.”

**THE PRAYER FOR WATER**

The verse says: ***“And ˹remember˺ when Moses prayed”*** The scene is the wilderness again, and the need this time is water. Al-Jalālayn says the people were thirsty in the open country and Moses asked God for water for them. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the thirst as severe and the request as a prayer on their behalf. Ibn Kathīr explains the place of the verse in the passage: God is listing favours, and this one answered the prayer of their prophet at a moment when the community had nothing to drink.

The parallel passage in the seventh sūrah carries the same story and the same number of springs ((7:160)). The Book returns to it because it fits the pattern the sūrah is building. A people with no water in a country with no wells are given a supply that follows them. Their job was to drink it and be grateful, and what they did instead fills the next dozen verses.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān places the incident in the wilderness of Tīh, the same stretch of country where the clouds shaded them and the manna fell. One favour after another is being described, and every one of them meets a basic need: shade, food, and now water.

**A SMALL COMMAND FOR A GREAT NEED**

The wording is: ***“for water for his people, We said, “Strike the rock with your staff.””*** The command is oddly small. The people needed water, and Moses was told to hit a rock with the stick in his hand. Al-Jalālayn records the descriptions the commentators gave of the rock: a marble stone shaped like a cube, about the size of a man's head, which travelled with them and was named in the reports. The note in tafsir_initial reports the same tradition and adds the detail that Moses struck its four sides, and each side produced three streams, which makes twelve.

Ibn ʿAbbās describes the rock as one God had given to Moses, with twelve openings on it that looked like teats, and each opening poured out a spring when it was struck. Al-Baghawī and al-Ṭabarī carry the same reports in their long accounts of the wandering.

The staff is worth a moment. Moses had used it before, in front of a king, and it had turned into a living thing. He will use it later to strike the sea. Here it strikes stone and stone gives water. The Book is teaching a lesson that runs through this whole story: the instrument is ordinary and the supply is not.

Think of a plumber who tells a family in a dry street to hit the wall in one particular place with a hammer. The hammer is nothing, and the wall is nothing. The water behind the wall is the whole point, and the family's test is whether they will swing the hammer at the spot they were told rather than at the spot they had in mind.

**TWELVE SPRINGS AND WHAT THEY SHOWED**

The verse goes on: ***“Then twelve springs gushed out, ˹and˺ each tribe knew its drinking place. ˹We then said,˺ “Eat”*** Twelve is not a random number here. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains the tribes: Jacob had twelve sons, and each son's family grew into a large clan with its own organisation and its own head, so the nation was twelve tribes. Al-Jalālayn says each tribe among them came to know its own drinking place, and that none of them shared a fountain with another group. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the clause the same way: each tribe knew its own spring.

Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the reason the division matters. God made clear to each tribe which spring was theirs so that there would be no conflict between them. A single spring in a crowd of thirsty people is a fight waiting to happen, and the Book quietly mentions the arrangement that removed the fight from the situation.

The detail is easy to pass over, and it is one of the most human things in the passage. Hundreds of thousands of people, one rock, twelve outlets, and an allocation that everyone could see. The Book is describing a mercy that arrived with an address on it.

Imagine a compound of twelve houses with one water tap in the yard. The tap is a blessing until the morning queue becomes an argument, and then the landlord digs a line to each door and tells every family which tap is theirs. Nothing about the water changed. Everything about the mornings changed.

**THE COMMAND TO EAT AND DRINK**

The verse carries on: ***“and drink of Allah’s provisions”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the command as covering both supplies at once: eat the manna and the quails, and drink from every spring that has come out of the rock. The two gifts are being named together, food and water, the way a household counts what it has in the kitchen and what it has in the well.

Al-Jalālayn notes that the sentence is a command to eat and drink of what God has provided. Al-Mukhtaṣar points out something about the economy of the arrangement: the food and the water came to the people without any work on their part. There was no field to plough and no well to dig, and the Book names the arrangement a provision rather than a wage.

This is the third verse in a row where the gift arrives while the people are doing nothing to earn it. That pattern is the subject of the whole passage, and it explains the sharpness of what comes next.

**THE ORDER NOT TO SPOIL THE GIFT**

The sentence continues: ***“and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.””*** A command is attached to the gift, and it is about behaviour rather than worship. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as a warning against causing damage and disorder in the earth. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds that the people were told not to spend their energy on ruin and disobedience.

The word for corruption has already appeared twice in this sūrah. When the hypocrites are told not to spread corruption, they answer that they are only setting things right ((2:11-12)), and the Book calls them liars for it. The Israelites in the wilderness are given food, water and shade, and the single instruction that comes with the package is that they should not use their freedom to break things.

The pairing is worth keeping in view as the next verse arrives. A people who are fed from the sky, watered from a stone and shaded by clouds are still free to behave badly, and the provision does not run out because of their behaviour. What changes is the account that is kept.

---
## Verse 2:61

> And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses! We cannot endure the same meal ˹every day˺. So ˹just˺ call upon your Lord on our behalf, He will bring forth for us some of what the earth produces of herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions.” Moses scolded ˹them˺, “Do you exchange what is better for what is worse? ˹You can˺ go down to any village and you will find what you have asked for.” They were stricken with disgrace and misery, and they invited the displeasure of Allah for rejecting Allah’s signs and unjustly killing the prophets. This is ˹a fair reward˺ for their disobedience and violations

**THE COMPLAINT THAT OPENED**

The verse names it: ***“And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses!”*** A new complaint opens with a name and a tone. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the address as the beginning of an ungrateful request. Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Jalālayn both record the sentence that follows, and the commentators treat the moment as a turning point in the wilderness story.

Notice who is speaking and to whom. The people do not address God. They come to Moses with a demand and ask him to carry it upstairs. That habit, taking the prophet as a channel for their preferences, runs through the whole passage.

**TIRED OF ONE MEAL**

The verse says: ***“We cannot endure the same meal ˹every day˺.”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the complaint in plain terms: they could not bear one kind of food, meaning the manna and the quails. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the same thing with the context added, that this was the food God had sent down to them, and that they grew tired of it.

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the words as a refusal to keep eating honey and quails. Ibn Kathīr observes that the food they were tired of was pure, good, beneficial and easy to get, and that the verse is a record of what they did with it.

There is a detail in the way the Book reports the complaint. It says they could not endure one kind of food, as though variety were a right that had been withheld from them. The reader who has followed the passage knows what the alternative to that menu looked like. It was a land of forced labour, where the menu was whatever the overseer allowed.

**THE REQUEST THEY MADE**

The verse puts the matter: ***“So ˹just˺ call upon your Lord on our behalf, He will bring forth”*** Al-Jalālayn records the request almost word for word: pray to your Lord for us, and He will bring out for us something from what the earth grows. Ibn ʿAbbās has the same. Al-Mukhtaṣar notes the revealing shape of the sentence: they asked Moses to ask God for vegetables from the ground, and they did this after God had fed them from the sky.

The command to Moses is put in the imperative, and the commentators read a note of insistence in it. The people are not asking whether there might be another option. They are telling their prophet what to request, and they expect his prayer to work like a counter at a shop.

**THE PRODUCE THEY LISTED**

The verse states: ***“for us some of what the earth produces of herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils”*** The list is specific and everyday. Al-Jalālayn names the items: green herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, onions. Ibn Kathīr gives the same list from the verse. Al-Mukhtaṣar translates them into a modern kitchen: herbs, vegetables, cucumbers, grains, lentils and onions.

tafsir_initial points out the parallel in the earlier scriptures, where the people in the desert long for the fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic they ate in Egypt ((Numbers 11:4-5)), and it notes that the word translated as garlic may also mean wheat. The note adds the sequel in that account, where quails arrive on the wind and the people who craved them are struck down, which is the same warning the Qur'an delivers in its own words.

The detail that lingers is the phrase about the earth. The people ask for food that grows out of the ground, in a place where food had been coming down from above. They wanted to be farmers again, and they asked for it in the one region where farming had been taken off their hands.

**MOSES TURNS THE QUESTION BACK**

The wording continues: ***“and onions.” Moses scolded ˹them˺, “Do you exchange what is better”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the question as a rebuke, and he marks the tone of the Arabic: the form of the verb carries a complaint rather than a request for information. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the sense in a comparison: would you trade what is better and more honourable, the manna and the quails, for what is lower? Ibn Kathīr has the same reading.

Al-Mukhtaṣar spells out the argument Moses made. The food they wanted to trade for was less in value and less in benefit, and the food they were tired of had come to them without effort or work. He also names the attitude behind the request: they had grown tired of the blessing and were no longer grateful for it.

The question is one of the most useful sentences in the whole sūrah for a reader who wants to test his own appetites. It asks what a person is trading away, not what he is asking for. Nobody in the story is being refused vegetables. They are being asked to see the price tag on the shelf.

**THE EXCHANGE THEY PICKED**

The verse poses it: ***“for what is worse?”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the word as a straight comparison: do you substitute what is lowlier for what is better, and the rebuke stands. Ibn Kathīr records the same question from Moses.

The Book does not pretend that lentils are worthless. Bread and vegetables are good things, and the sūrah has already said that the wholesome food of the earth is lawful for people to enjoy. What the verse names is the exchange, the trade of a thing for a lesser thing while believing that nothing is being lost.

Think of a man who is given a free dinner every evening at a good restaurant and who trades it for the right to peel potatoes in the kitchen, because peeling is familiar and free dinners feel like charity. The problem is not the potato. The problem is the swap, and the way he made it while convinced he was improving his position.

**THE DOOR THEY WANTED**

As the verse says: ***“˹You can˺ go down to any village”*** Moses gives them what they asked for and does not pray for a miracle to supply it. Al-Jalālayn renders the answer as an instruction to go down to a city, whichever one it may be, and there they would find what they were demanding. Ibn ʿAbbās records the reading that the city is the one they came from, and also the wider reading: any city at all. Ibn Kathīr keeps the plain sense, that they should go down to any town and find what they wanted.

tafsir_initial makes a language note that removes a wrong picture. The Arabic verb for going down does not have to mean a change in height. It is used the way English uses it when a person goes down to the shops. The command is not a punishment of descent. It is a release from the arrangement they had complained about.

The verse is one of the quietest forms of correction in the Book. God does not send the vegetables. He sends them to a place where vegetables grow and lets them do the work of growing them. The wilderness arrangement of bread from the sky ends here for anyone who wants out.

**WHAT THEY WOULD FIND**

The verse carries on: ***“and you will find what you have asked”*** Al-Jalālayn closes the sentence with the promise that they will get what they demanded. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the same, that any town would have what they asked for.

The gift then comes with a cost that the verse does not itemise but the next phrases make plain. A city, a market and farmland come with rent, tax, neighbours, weather and a bad harvest to worry about. The manna did none of that. The reader is invited to count what came with the freedom to choose a menu.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān says the Israelites were told they could go to a town in the wilderness, work the land there and eat whatever they liked, and that their request was impertinent. The comment has a bite to it: the nation that had watched the sea split was asking for permission to do the kind of work that farmers do everywhere.

**DISGRACE AND MISERY**

Its words are: ***“for.” They were stricken with disgrace”*** The sentence turns. Al-Jalālayn reads the word as a covering laid on them: disgrace was struck onto their faces like a mark. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same, that humiliation was fastened upon them. Ibn Kathīr keeps the sense of a stamping down of humiliation and misery upon the people.

The third sūrah carries the same sentence in nearly the same words, and there it makes the condition general: the Israelites were struck with disgrace wherever they were found unless they took refuge in a covenant with God or a covenant with other people ((3:112)). The Book treats the disgrace as a dwelling place rather than a single event. A community that keeps trading down ends up living somewhere it did not choose.

The word for struck matters, because it makes the punishment passive. The people did not sit down and decide to be a humiliated nation. They asked for vegetables, and a page later they were a people with a reputation.

**THE ANGER THEY DREW ON THEMSELVES**

The next words are: ***“and misery, and they invited the displeasure of Allah”*** Al-Jalālayn adds the second covering: poverty along with disgrace, and anger from God. Ibn ʿAbbās lists misery beside the disgrace. Ibn Kathīr reads the pair as humiliation and poverty together.

The phrase about inviting the displeasure is worth pausing on. The Arabic makes the people the ones who brought it on, which is the same formula the sūrah uses for the wrongdoers who earned a punishment in the parable of the gnat ((2:26)). The Book uses one grammar for this kind of loss everywhere: God does not owe anybody anger; people collect it.

The verse also reads like a small piece of history written from the outside. A people who had been slaves and were freed ended up with a reputation that followed them through centuries and into the scriptures of other nations. Their complaint about food is remembered in three sacred books. Nobody plans that ending from the top of a water line in the desert.

**THE REASON GIVEN**

The text says: ***“for rejecting Allah’s signs”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the reason as their rejection of God's signs and their killing of the prophets without right. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the same reasons in the same order. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the cause as going beyond the limits and refusing to obey, and he places the rejection of the signs of God at the head of the offences.
