The sūrah has already used the word for rejection of faith in its opening description of the disbelievers ((2:6)), and the same word describes the people who broke the covenant over the calf ((2:54)). Here it is used for a nation that had signs in front of it every morning: bread on the ground, water from a stone, clouds for a roof. The word names what a person does with evidence he would rather not have.

The next phrase gives the second reason, and it is one of the heaviest charges in the Qur'an.

**THE KILLING OF THE PROPHETS**

The sentence moves on: ***“and unjustly killing the prophets. This is ˹a fair reward˺”*** Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Jalālayn record the charge of killing the prophets without right. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the same. The scholars of the later books identify the prophets the reports mention: Zakariyyā, Yaḥyā and others who were killed by a community that had been given a book and had been told to obey it.

The word for unjustly carries the point. These were not killings in a war between equals. They were murders of men who had come to the same people with the same message about the same God, and the nation that killed them still counted itself as the nation of the book.

The sentence is worth holding next to the modern reader's own position. Every generation shapes a version of itself that can live with its record, and the Book does not let this community keep one. It names the murders in the same verse it names the lentils.

**THE REBELLION BEHIND IT ALL**

In the verse's own words: ***“for their disobedience and violations”*** Al-Jalālayn ends the verse with the two qualities that produced everything above: they were disobedient, and they went on and on in that disobedience. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same pair. Ibn Kathīr reads the closing phrase as the summary reason for the disgrace, the misery and the anger.

The tense of the second word is the detail to notice. The Book does not say that they disobeyed once. It says they kept going beyond the limits as a settled habit. A nation that kills its own prophets is not having a bad week. It has developed a way of dealing with anyone who tells it something it does not want to hear.

The verse is the last one in the passage about the wilderness gifts, and the shape of the passage is now complete. Shade, bread, water, and a command to behave. Stockpiling, mockery at a gate, and a demand for a better menu. A reader who thinks the story is about a nation that lived long ago has not been paying attention to the way these verses keep using the second person.

---
## Verse 2:62

> Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians—whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**WHO THE VERSE NAMES**

In the verse's own words: ***“Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians”*** Al-Ṭabarī explains who is being named. The believers are the people who accept what the Prophet brought them from God. The ones called Hūd, meaning the Jews, take their name from a verb that means to turn or to repent. Al-Baghawī collects the reports on the name: some say it comes from their own words in the Book, that they turned to God ((7:156)); some say it is because they turned back from the worship of the calf; another report says it is because they turned away from the religion of Moses. Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ gave an image that has stayed in the commentaries, that they used to sway and rock while the Torah was read.

Al-Qurṭubī records a report from Sufyān that the believers named in this verse are the hypocrites, on the grounds that ordinary believers would not have been listed beside Jews, Christians and Sabians. He then explains the structure the verse uses: the groups are named, and the ruling that follows covers whoever among them believes in God and the Last Day.

tafsir_initial points to the companion verse in the fifth sūrah, where the same list appears with the same promise ((5:69)). The Book repeats the sentence because the question it answers keeps coming back: what happens to the people who were born into older communities and lived decently by the light they had.

**THE FAITH THE VERSE REQUIRES**

The verse adds: ***“and Sabians whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah”*** tafsir_initial gives the most careful discussion of the Sabians among the sources in hand. The name is derived by some from a verb that means to leave one religion for another, and the same letters also give a meaning of rising, which is used of stars, and a meaning of coming out or coming upon. Others take it from a word that means to incline, as a person inclines from one religion to another (al-Ṭabarī). The pagan Arabs used the word for the Prophet himself, in the sense that he had left the religion of his fathers (al-Rāzī).

The same note lists the opinions about who the Sabians were: a people with no religion that could be recognised, followers of a prophet, star worshippers, or, in the reading al-Saʿdī prefers, one of the groups of the Christians. The commentators disagreed because the community itself had faded by the time the books were written, and the disagreement is recorded rather than hidden.

What the verse does with all four names is the real point. It takes a mixed list of communities and puts the same condition on every one of them: whoever truly believes in God. The Book treats the condition as the door, and the community as the label on the door.

**THE LAST DAY IN THE CONDITION**

Then the verse says: ***“and the Last Day”*** The second article of the condition is belief in the Last Day, and al-Qurṭubī notes that it is paired with belief in God in several places in the Book. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the pair together in his translation and explains that the promise concerned those communities before the coming of Muhammad.

The pairing is not accidental. A person who believes in God but not in the reckoning has a God without a court, and a person who believes in a reckoning but not in God has a court without a judge. The verse treats the two beliefs as one doorway with two hinges.

**GOOD DEEDS AND THE REWARD**

The wording continues: ***“and does good will have their reward with their Lord.”*** Ibn Kathīr draws the lesson out of the verse in a sentence: faith and doing righteous deeds equal salvation in all times. He reads the passage as a message of hope after the previous verse, which described a nation loaded with disgrace, and he places the earlier nations who were righteous and obedient inside the promise. He also notes that the promise holds until the Day of Judgement, and that whoever follows the final Messenger is included.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains why the verse was needed here. The verses just before it describe a people who drew down anger by habit, and a listener, especially a Jewish listener, might conclude that no repentance from such a community could be accepted. The verse answers that worry with a general principle: a person who submits fully to God in belief and in action is accepted, whatever he was before. Maʿārif then adds the condition that follows the final revelation, that the accepted way of life is the one God has now set out ((3:85)).

Al-Saʿdī places the verse in the same frame and draws the other half of it as well, that whoever among these communities rejects God, His messengers and the Last Day stands on the opposite side of the promise, with fear and grief as his portion.

The phrase about reward with their Lord is placed where it is for a reason. It does not say that they will be given a share of what the others receive, or that their deeds will be counted at a discount. It says the reward is kept with God, which is the way the Book speaks about a wage that cannot be lost, stolen or devalued.

**THE PROMISE WITH NO FEAR**

The sentence moves on: ***“And there will be no fear”*** Ibn ʿAbbās records three readings of the promise among the early commentators: that no fear will come upon them about punishment in the world to come; that they will not grieve over anything they have left behind; and, on another report, that they will have no fear on the day when death itself is slain and the fire is closed.

Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the two halves in plain order: they will not fear what is waiting for them afterwards, and they will not grieve over what happened to them in this world. The Book's standard blessing for the successful keeps appearing in this shape ((2:38, 2:112, 10:62)). Fear faces forward and grief faces back, and the verse closes both directions.

**AND NO GRIEF**

The end of the verse returns the reader to the community standing in front of the Prophet in Madinah. The Book has just described their ancestors at a gate and in a wilderness, and it has told them what a person's own record does and does not decide about his future, provided the belief and the good work are real.

Its words are: ***“for them, nor will they grieve”*** Think of a large office where a new manager arrives and changes the way the place is run. The old staff are not asked which badge they were given years ago. They are asked whether they are doing the work now, under the rules that now apply. That is the shape of the verse, and the next verse returns to the covenant the community had already broken. The Book makes the same promise elsewhere with the same two words of comfort: (10:62 — **“no fear for the close servants of Allah, nor will they grieve”**).

---
## Verse 2:63

> And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from you and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.”

**THE COVENANT THAT WAS TAKEN**

The verse starts with: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from you”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the covenant as the pledge to act on what was in the Torah. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as consent taken from the people. Ibn Kathīr explains the content of the pledge in a wider sentence: they were bound to believe in God alone, without a partner, and to follow His messengers.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān gives the setting. Moses came down from Sinai with the Torah and recited it to the people, and the injunctions in it were heavy because their habits needed heavy discipline. The community that had asked for lentils was being handed a law with a large number of detailed obligations.

The Book uses the word for covenant in this sūrah more than once, and it always carries the same weight: an agreement made with full knowledge, on a mountain, with witnesses. The next phrase explains what the ceremony looked like.

**THE MOUNTAIN LIFTED OVER THEM**

The sentence continues: ***“and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to”*** Al-Jalālayn is blunt about the scene: God lifted the mountain from the earth and held it over the people when they refused to accept the Torah. Ibn ʿAbbās says the mountain was pulled up and fixed high above their heads as the covenant was taken. The seventh sūrah keeps the same picture, where the mountain is lifted as if it were a canopy ((7:171)).

Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the raising of the mountain as a means of inspiring awe and as a warning against breaking the agreement. Ibn Kathīr keeps the reports that describe the mountain held over the assembly while the pledge was taken.

The command that came with it is the one the verse stresses: hold firmly. Al-Saʿdī explains the word: take it with seriousness, with effort, and with patience in carrying out what God has ordered. Ibn ʿAbbās renders it as earnestness and diligence. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the instruction as a warning not to take the book lightly or to be lazy about it.

Think of a young man who is given charge of a family business and is told on the day he takes it over that the accounts are kept in one particular book, that the ledger matters more than his preferences, and that the building will not stay standing if the book is ignored. A shadow over the roof is not the lesson. The book in his hands is the lesson.

**THE BOOK THEY WERE GIVEN**

The verse records: ***“that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you”*** The object of the command is named twice in the passage, and the naming carries a claim. This was not a law that Moses invented in a tent, and it was not a tradition the community had made for itself over generations. It was given. Ibn Kathīr reads the phrase as the covenant to hold fast to what had been handed to them.

The sūrah will return to this claim at several points. Moses will later say that the Book he brought was a light and a guidance ((21:48)), and the Qur'an will describe itself with the same words. The reader in Madinah is being asked to see the pattern: God sends a book, a community is bound to it, and the community's record is measured against the book it was given.

There is a plain fact worth marking in this phrase. The people had a scripture in their possession, in their own language of learning, and they had teachers. The Book still had to be given to them in the sense that mattered, which is the sense of a thing held firmly rather than a thing owned.

**HOLDING TO WHAT THEY HEARD**

The verse goes on: ***“and observe its teachings”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the instruction as: remember what is in it, and act on it. Ibn ʿAbbās expands the clause into its parts: remember the reward and the punishment it contains, and keep in mind what it makes lawful and what it makes unlawful. Al-Saʿdī says the command covers reciting it and learning it.

The phrase rules out the arrangement many communities settle into, where the book is respected, shelved, and never opened in the house. The command is to remember what is inside it, which assumes a person has been inside it recently.

Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the practical direction of the instruction. The people were told to remember and reflect on what was revealed to them, so that they would be careful about what they earned from God.

**THE MINDFULNESS IT ASKED FOR**

The verse puts it: ***“so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.””*** Al-Jalālayn explains the closing phrase as the purpose of the whole arrangement: so that they might protect themselves from the fire and from acts of disobedience. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same, that they might ward off God's anger and torment. Al-Saʿdī gives the two sides of the word: that they might be protected from God's punishment and displeasure, or that they might become people of heedfulness.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān describes the ceremony from the other end. Seventy men had been chosen to go up to the mountain, where they heard God confirm that the Torah was His book, and they came back and told the community what they had witnessed. Their testimony is the reason the covenant had the shape it had, with a mountain above them and a clear command in front of them.

The verse ends on a word that the sūrah will use again and again for the quality it wants from its readers. The whole book is aimed at it, and the next verse records how quickly the people who had the mountain over their heads let it go.

---
## Verse 2:64

> Yet you turned away afterwards. Had it not been for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you, you would have certainly been of the losers

**THE TURNING AWAY THAT FOLLOWED**

The verse has it: ***“Yet you turned away afterwards. Had it not been”*** Al-Ṭabarī examines the verb closely. It comes from a root that describes a person turning his back on another and leaving him behind his shoulder, and it is used for anyone who abandons an obedience he was commanded to carry out. He gives the plain sense: you turned away, you turned your faces aside.

The word afterwards is the part that stings. Al-Saʿdī notes the order of the story: after all that emphasis, after the mountain and the covenant and the witnesses, they turned away. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same sequence, and he notes that the sentence follows the moment of the greatest possible confirmation.

Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the turning away as a failure to keep the contract, with the mountain raised and the warning given. Ibn ʿAbbās says the people turned their backs on the covenant itself.

The turn in this verse is the fourth in a series the sūrah has been building. The calf story added a turn where the covenant had been broken ((2:54)). The gate incident added a turn where a word of repentance was mocked ((2:59)). Now the story of the mountain ends the same way, and the reader is being shown a pattern rather than a series of accidents.

**THE GRACE THAT KEPT THEM**

Its words are: ***“for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you, you would have certainly been of the losers”*** Al-Saʿdī draws the lesson from the sentence: after so much confirmation, the people turned away, and that conduct deserved the heaviest of punishments, but grace and mercy kept them from it. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same reading, that the failure to keep the covenant would have brought the greatest punishment without those two qualities of God.

Ibn ʿAbbās gives the two gifts specific content. The grace was the delay of the punishment that had been earned. The mercy was the sending of Muhammad to them. On that reading, the same community that broke the covenant over the mountain was given centuries and a final messenger, and the verse is an account of what that patience cost God and gained them.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān separates mercy into two kinds. One kind is general and reaches believers and unbelievers alike, and it shows itself in the ordinary goods of worldly life. The other is special to believers and appears in the world to come as salvation and nearness to God. The mercy that kept this community from ruin in this world belongs to the first kind, and the verse leaves the second kind open.

The closing word for losers is a market word. It names a person who has lost his capital, and the loss is not the loss of a business but the loss of the self. The fifth sūrah uses the same description for a nation that had asked for a feast from heaven and then broken its promise: whoever among them rejects the faith afterwards has lost the straight road ((5:12)).

Think of a man who signs a contract in a room full of witnesses, has the penalty clause read aloud to him, and breaks the first term the same afternoon. What saves him from ruin is not that the terms were unclear. It is that the other party chose to be patient, and patience of that kind is not a license to keep signing and keep breaking.

---
## Verse 2:65

> You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath. We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!”

**THE TOWN ON THE SEA**

The sentence opens: ***“You are already aware of those of you”*** Al-Jalālayn places the story in the town called Eilat and dates it to the people of that place who broke the Sabbath by fishing on the day they had been forbidden to fish. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the reader knows the story of the ancestors who prepared to fish on the Sabbath and then did it through trickery. Ibn ʿAbbās dates the incident to the time of David.

Ibn Kathīr opens the verse with the rebuke the Book is delivering: remember that God sent punishment on the village that disobeyed Him, broke its pledge and used deceitful methods to avoid honouring the day it had been ordered to keep. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān fills in the place. These people lived on the sea shore and were very fond of fish, and Saturday had been set apart for worship, so fishing was forbidden on that day.

The seventh sūrah tells the same story at more length, and there the test is described in a way that makes the temptation clear: the fish came to them in shoals on the day they were not allowed to catch them, and were gone on the day they could ((7:163)). Al-Baghawī reports the scene the same way: when the Sabbath came in, no fish was left in the water, and the fisherman watched the sea fill up on the day he was not permitted to touch it.

**THE TRICK AND THE WORD THAT CAME**

The verse declares: ***“who broke the Sabbath. We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!””*** Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the trick plainly: they set up their nets in advance for the Sabbath, so that the fish would be caught without any work being done on the day itself. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān adds the history of the trick from al-Qurṭubī: the people began with clever pretences, then stopped hiding what they were doing. The community split over it. On one side were the ones who fished by whatever method, and on the other were scholars and pious people who warned them.

The verdict arrived as a command, and the Book reports it in four words. Al-Jalālayn reads the word for disgraced as rejected and despise. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the same sense: they were turned into humiliated and base apes. Al-Jalālayn adds the report that they died three days after the transformation. Ibn Kathīr carries the same account, that they became monkeys, rejected and despised, and the note in tafsir_initial records the wider reading of the word, that it can mean lowly, so that the punishment was as much a status as a body.

Al-Baghawī gives a small piece of language that helps the whole passage. The root of the word for the Sabbath means to cut. The day was named for a cutting off, either because God finished and cut off from creating, or because the community was told to cut off its work on it. The people of Eilat found a way to keep working at the exact thing they had been told to cut off, and they kept it by making the day itself look innocent on paper.

Think of a shopkeeper whose licence allows him to trade every day except one. He locks the door on the closed day, leaves the till on the counter, and stands outside telling a friend to take the notes and put the money in his pocket. He will tell anyone who asks that the shop was shut. The inspector's record will say otherwise. The verse is about the space between the two sentences.

---
## Verse 2:66

> So We made their fate an example to present and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing

**A FATE MADE AN EXAMPLE**

The verse puts it: ***“So We made their fate an example to present”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as God making the punishment an exemplary one, a deterrent meant to stop others from doing what the people did. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as God subjecting them to a punishment that stood as an example of what their sins had earned. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the town that went past the limits as a warning to the villages around it.

Al-Qurṭubī pauses over a question of grammar that turns into a question of meaning: what exactly was made an example? He lists the opinions the commentators brought. Some said the punishment itself. Some said the town, because the sentence demands it. Some said the community that was transformed. Some said the fish, though he gives that view less weight. The disagreement is a small window into how carefully these people read, and the practical sense of the verse stays the same in every reading. A whole community's ruin was left standing in front of others as a warning sign.

The word for the example carries an extra shade that matters. It also means a restraint, something that holds a person back from a course of action. The Book is not gloating over a ruined town. It is placing a fence at the edge of a cliff and making the fence visible to the next traveller.

**A LESSON FOR THOSE WHO FEAR**

The sentence moves on: ***“and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the phrase for those in front and those behind as the people of that time and the people who came later. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as the generation that committed the sin and the generations after them. tafsir_initial gives the three readings the commentators recorded: those present and those who would come, the villages around the place, or the sins that had come before and after. The note also explains a subtlety in the promise. The punishment became a lesson for the people who were still there and for the people who would read about it.

The second half of the verse names the audience that learns. Al-Jalālayn explains that the God-fearing are mentioned specifically because, unlike other people, they are the ones who take a warning and use it. Ibn ʿAbbās identifies them as the Prophet and his companions, who received the account and drew the lesson from it.

tafsir_initial adds a note on the Arabic word for lesson, which can carry either a positive meaning such as counsel and advice, or a negative one such as a reprimand. Both senses sit comfortably in the verse. The people who heed the word get advice. The people who ignore it get the same account read out at a trial.

Al-Qurṭubī notes that the Arabic root behind the word for this kind of warning also gives the word for fetters. A warning is named for what it does. It holds a person back the way a chain holds a wrist, and the ruin of one village becomes a restraint on the hand of the next traveller who passes the place.

The closing phrase has a counterpart at the head of the sūrah, where the Book describes itself as guidance for the people who are mindful of God ((2:2)). The warning about the town and the guidance of the Book are aimed at the same reader. For a person who takes God seriously, a story of ruin is instruction. For everyone else the same story is only news.

Think of the burnt car that is left for a week at the side of a road with a sign giving the reason for the crash. Nobody enjoys the sight, and nobody is asked to celebrate it. It stands there because the next driver who wants to take that bend at speed should see it before he decides.

---
## Verse 2:67

> And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow.” They replied, “Are you mocking us?” Moses responded, “I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!”

**THE COMMAND TO SLAUGHTER A COW**

The sentence opens: ***“And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow.” They replied, “Are you mocking us?””*** The sūrah takes the story up from the middle. Al-Jalālayn explains the situation behind the command: a man had been killed among the people and the killer was unknown, so they asked Moses to pray that God would reveal the murderer, and the answer came back as an instruction to sacrifice a cow. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the same and keeps the order of events clear.

Ibn Kathīr identifies the place of the cow in the story of the children of Israel. The command was the beginning of the means by which the killer would be named. He records the report from ʿUbādah al-Salmānī about the family affairs behind the murder, and other reports that name a murder over a marriage.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān gives the account from Maʿālim al-Tanzīl, that a man among the Israelites wanted to marry a girl and was refused by her father, and he killed the father and disappeared. It adds a legal detail that shapes the whole episode: no ruling about the killer had yet been sent down, which suggests the event took place before the Torah was revealed. The community went to Moses for the answer to a crime scene, and they were told to slaughter a cow.

Their answer is the reason the verse is quoted again and again. Al-Jalālayn explains the question as an accusation that Moses was making fun of them when he gave them an answer of that kind. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the words as open mockery. Al-Mukhtaṣar notices that the people did not rush to obey, and that their question was asked in stubbornness rather than in confusion.

The scene has its own dark humour, and the Book leaves it there for the reader. A community brings a murder to their prophet and demands that heaven reveal the killer. Heaven answers with an instruction, and the community's first response to the instruction is to ask the prophet whether he is joking.

**MOSES TAKES REFUGE FROM THEIR MOCKERY**

The verse names it: ***“Moses responded, “I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!””*** Al-Jalālayn reads the reply as Moses a taking refuge with God from being one of the ignorant, which in his rendering means one of those who mock. Al-Mukhtaṣar explains the sense: Moses asked for God's protection from being among the foolish, meaning the people who lie about God and make fun of other people. Ibn ʿAbbās renders it: God forbid that I should be among the foolish; God forbid that I ever mock the believers.

The answer is worth reading slowly, because Moses does not defend himself. He does not say that he has never lied, or that he has a record of forty years of service. He puts the whole question in a different place: if the charge were true, he would be a fool about the most serious thing there is, and he asks God to keep him far from that.

The word he uses for refuge comes from a verb for taking cover, the way a man steps behind a wall when something dangerous passes. The man who is speaking has just carried a message from God to a community, and the first thing he does with their insult is to hide behind God from their accusation.

Think of a man who brings a sick child to a doctor, and when the doctor names a course of treatment, asks the doctor in front of the room whether he is playing games. The doctor has nothing to gain from the joke. The father has just made the illness harder to treat, and the doctor's answer is not an argument. It is a step back behind his own profession.

---
## Verse 2:68

> They said, “Call upon your Lord to clarify for us what type ˹of cow˺ it should be!” He replied, “Allah says, ‘The cow should neither be old nor young but in between. So do as you are commanded!’”

**THE QUESTION ABOUT THE KIND**

The verse names it: ***“They said, “Call upon your Lord to clarify”*** The people move from mockery to a request for information, and al-Jalālayn notes the reason: they realised that Moses was serious. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the words as a request for the details of the cow, whether it was large or small. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the sequence plain: they asked Moses to call on his Lord and explain what sort of cow it was.

Al-Qurṭubī names the behaviour behind the question with a phrase the scholars used: this was a straining of the matter and a lack of willingness to obey. He cites Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū l-ʿĀliyah and others with the rule that has become famous in the commentaries: if the people had obeyed the command and slaughtered any cow at all, their purpose would have been achieved. But they made the matter hard on themselves, so God made it hard on them.

The pattern of these verses is a conversation that grows longer than the task. One command, an answer, a question, a clarification, another question, another clarification, and a description that only becomes narrower with every exchange. The Book lets the reader watch a small task turn into a difficult one.

**WHAT THEY ASKED HIM TO FIND OUT**

The Book says: ***“for us what type ˹of cow˺ it should be!””*** Al-Jalālayn phrases the request as a question about the true nature of the animal. Ibn ʿAbbās has the same, with a note that the people wanted to know whether the cow was large or small.

A reader may ask why the request is a fault at all, since asking about a duty is normal. The commentators answer from the far end of the story rather than the near end. The command was already clear enough to act on: any cow would have done. What the questions produced was not understanding but a longer list of conditions, and each condition was supplied by the same God who had given the first instruction. A person can keep asking for certainty about a duty that is already clear, and the asking itself can become the delay.

**THE DESCRIPTION THAT CAME BACK**

The verse says: ***“He replied, “Allah says, ‘The cow should neither be old nor young”*** Al-Jalālayn gives the description as a cow that is neither old nor a virgin heifer, a middle-aged animal between the two extremes. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the words as neither old nor immature, between the two conditions. Ibn Kathīr has the same: not too old and not too young, but between the two conditions.

The detail is small and the effect is large. The range of acceptable animals has just narrowed from every cow in the country to a band of ages in the middle. The people asked for a specification and received one, and the specification was given in a form that still required them to choose an animal themselves.

There is an old comment on this passage in the books of tafsīr, carried by Maʿārif al-Qurʾān from the Hadith, that if these people had obeyed God's command without raising so many doubts and asking unnecessary questions, the strict conditions would not have been imposed, and the sacrifice of any cow at all would have been accepted. The lesson sits at the level of the reader's habits rather than the history of a nation.

Think of a customer in a bakery who is offered any loaf on the shelf and instead asks which field the wheat came from, which oven baked it and which hands kneaded it, with each answer narrowing the choice, until the only loaf left is the most expensive one in the shop and closing time is near.

**NEITHER YOUNG NOR OLD**

Its words are: ***“but in between. So do”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the middle term as the age between the two extremes, and the command that follows as an instruction to carry it out. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same shape.

The order of the sentence is worth noticing. The information arrives first, and the command comes after it, and the command is short. Do it. Two words in Arabic, and the whole conversation is folded back into a task. The Book is presenting obedience as a thing that resumes after an explanation rather than as a debate that continues.

**THE ORDER TO DO IT**

As the verse says: ***“as you are commanded!’””*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the closing words as an instruction to do what had been ordered and to stop asking further questions. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the plain sense: he told them to do what God had commanded them.

By this point the people have spent a whole exchange on the details of an animal they had not yet bought. The command they were given at the start still stands, and nothing in the conversation has reduced it. The verse ends with a sentence that is almost a sigh: as you were commanded.

The community in Madinah reading this passage knew what the story was about. They had their own clear commands in front of them, and the habit the Book is exposing is not a Jewish habit or an ancient one. It is the ordinary human method of turning a simple duty into a research project.

---
## Verse 2:69

> They said, “Call upon your Lord to specify for us its colour.” He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should be a bright yellow cow—pleasant to see.’”

**THE THIRD QUESTION**

The verse says: ***“They said, “Call upon your Lord to specify”*** The people come back a third time. Al-Jalālayn records the request as a prayer for clarification from Moses's Lord. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the sequence and the tone.

The pattern is now visible enough for the reader to predict it. The command has been given, the mockery has been answered, the first specification has arrived, and the people have found another gap to fill. They have not yet lifted a hand towards the task, and the verse marks the gap between information and action.

**THE COLOUR THAT WAS GIVEN**

Its words are: ***“for us its colour.” He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should be a bright yellow cow”*** Al-Jalālayn gives the answer as a yellow cow, and Ibn Kathīr renders the description as a yellow cow, bright in its colour, pleasing to beholders. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the colour and the effect together.

The colour narrows the field again. A middle-aged cow that is bright yellow is not a rare animal, and it is not a common one on any given morning in a village market. The community that could have sacrificed any cow has now been handed a description specific enough to send men out to search, and they still have not done anything.

The word the sources use for the animal's appearance is about the pleasure it gives to people who look at it. The Book gives a detail that is purely aesthetic, an instruction about beauty, in the middle of a legal errand that began with a murder. There is a gentleness in the detail that sits oddly beside the stubbornness of the people receiving it.

Al-Qurṭubī comments on the shade of colour itself. The word used in the verse describes a bright, strong yellow, the sort of animal that stands out in a herd. In a market where several cows are tied up for sale, this is not a riddle for the people to solve. It is a shopping note with enough detail for anyone willing to walk and look.

The Book also keeps the growth of the command in front of the reader. The duty began as a single word: sacrifice. It is now a search for one animal of a particular age and a particular colour, and a third condition is waiting in the next verse. The description has grown with every question, and the task itself has not yet been started.

Think of a family told to paint a wall before visitors arrive. They ask for the exact shade, then for the brand, then for the finish, and the wall stays bare through all the questions while the visitors are on the road. The instructions were never the problem. The pot of paint by the door was.

**PLEASING TO THE EYE**

The wording runs: ***“pleasant to see.’””*** Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Jalālayn keep the closing phrase as part of the description, and the verse stops there without a further command. The reader waits for the people's next move, and the next verse supplies it.

Notice where the sūrah places this story in its argument. The previous passage ended with a nation that turned its back on a covenant while a mountain hung above it. Now the same nation is given a task with a simple answer and turns it into a long negotiation. The Book is not telling the story to mock a people. It is teaching a reader to see the same instinct in himself when he asks for one more detail instead of doing the thing he already knows how to do.

The floor of the passage sits in a single fact. A cow had to be sacrificed so that a dead man could speak and a murderer could be named. Every question the people asked pushed the animal further away, and every answer they received was a mercy they met with another excuse.

---
## Verse 2:70

> Again they said, “Call upon your Lord so that He may make clear to us which cow, for all cows look the same to us. Then, Allah willing, we will be guided ˹to the right one˺.”

**THE COW THEY SAID WAS LIKE ANY OTHER**

The verse starts with: ***“Again they said, “Call upon your Lord”*** The people come back a third time, and al-Mukhtaṣar names the behaviour plainly: they continued in their stubbornness and told Moses to ask God for a further description of the cow. Al-Jalālayn records the request in the form the reports give it: pray to your Lord for us, that He make clear what she is, whether she grazes freely or is used for work.

By this point the pattern of the story is fixed. The community has a command that any cow would have satisfied. Each round of questions has narrowed the field instead of opening it, and each answer has been met with another question. The Book does not hide the growing cost of the conversation, and the next verse presents the bill.

**THE REQUEST FOR CLARITY**

The wording is: ***“so that He may make clear to us”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the request as a question about work: is the cow one that ploughs the soil or not? Al-Jalālayn puts the same two options in front of the reader, grazing or labouring. The detail has a purpose. A cow that has never been yoked is a cow with no marks from a yoke, and the question is about to be answered with a description that rules out both kinds of work.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān gathers the story up at this point and says what the verses are showing. The Israelites were disposed to disobedience, and that disposition came out in different shapes across the passage: in the demand for vegetables, in the mockery at the gate, and now in a long negotiation over a farm animal.

A note in the Hadith, carried by Maʿārif, states the rule that the passage is teaching: if these people had obeyed God's command without raising so many doubts and asking unnecessary questions, the strict conditions would not have been imposed, and any cow at all would have been accepted.

**WHY ONE COW LOOKED LIKE THE NEXT**

The verse has it: ***“which cow, for all cows look the same to us.”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the complaint behind the words. The described kind of cow is common, and because there are so many of them the people say they have not been able to find the one they are looking for. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same line: to us, cows are much alike, and we cannot tell between them.

The sentence is honest in a way that hurts the community that said it. There are many cows in the country that match the description, and the problem is not the shortage. The problem is that the neighbours of a man who has been murdered are not willing to pick one and start walking. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān says the same thing about the community in general: they were prone to disobedience, and their questions were a form of it.

Think of a man who needs to catch a train that leaves in an hour. He stands at the counter asking whether the seats recline, whether the carriage has a socket, and whether the biscuit trolley takes cards. There are dozens of trains on dozens of platforms, and every one of them would have carried him. The plain fact is that he is not moving, and his questions are the reason.

**A CONDITION ADDED AT THE END**

The verse records: ***“Then, Allah willing, we will be guided ˹to the right one˺.””*** The sentence ends with a condition, and the condition saves the request from being a flat refusal. Al-Jalālayn notes the report in the Hadith that if the people had not said, if God wills, the description would never have been made clear to them. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the last words as a hope that they would be guided to the right animal, and one report adds the shadow of the murder behind the errand.

The Book treats the phrase as a small piece of wisdom. A person who plans anything, and certainly a person who promises anything, holds the future open in his own mouth. The sūrah of the Cave turns the same point into a direct instruction: do not say of anything that you will do it tomorrow without adding, if God wills ((18:23-24)). Here the words come from a community that has been stalling, and they still mark the difference between confidence and arrogance.

A reader may notice where the phrase sits. It arrives at the end of the third request, after two rounds of questioning, and it is the first sign in the whole exchange that the people expect to finish the task. God accepts the sign and narrows the animal one last time.

---
## Verse 2:71

> He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should have been used neither to till the soil nor water the fields; wholesome and without blemish.’” They said, “Now you have come with the truth.” Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly

**NEITHER TILLING NOR WATERING**

The verse puts the matter: ***“He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should have been used neither to till the soil”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the clause as a description of a cow that has not been broken in for work, one that has never ploughed the earth to turn its soil for sowing. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the word for unyoked as unfettered and free, and the clause as the statement that the animal was never forced to plough. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same sense in his account of the verse.

The condition was the third one the community asked for, and it arrived as a direct answer to their own question about grazing and labour. Moses had put the two options in front of them at their request, and the answer came back with both of them excluded. The animal they were told to look for had never done a day of work in its life.

**THE TWO DUTIES IT NEVER DID**

The wording runs: ***“nor water the fields”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the second half of the description as a cow that has never been used to carry water to land being prepared for sowing. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the same reading. The two uses named in the verse are the two ways a working cow earns its keep in a farming village: pulling a plough and hauling water.

The effect of the description is that the animal is set apart from ordinary farm life in a way that can be checked. A man who walked into any village in that country could look at a cow's shoulders and neck and see whether it had worked. The Book has turned a vague command into a search with visible criteria, at the request of the people who wanted more information.

**WITHOUT BLEMISH**

The verse records: ***“wholesome and without blemish.’” They said, “Now you have come with the truth.””*** Al-Jalālayn reads the description as a cow free from faults and the marks of toil, with no blemish of a colour other than its own. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the words as whole, free from any defect, and without spots or flecks of white. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes a cow with no faults and no marks of another colour on her yellow.

The people's answer is the moment the arguing stops. Al-Jalālayn renders the words as: now you have explained it clearly. Ibn ʿAbbās reads them as an admission that the description was right all along. The community that had spent three rounds calling for clarity had received it, and the truth they were praising was the same message they had been given at the start, only now with the scale of a search attached to it.

**THEY SLAUGHTERED IT AT LAST**

The verse has it: ***“Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly”*** Al-Jalālayn records what happened after the search. They looked for the animal, found it with a boy who served his mother well, and bought it for the weight of the cow in gold. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the same account of the price and says the animal was extremely costly. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the closing phrase as a description of a community that finally went through with the sacrifice, having almost failed to do it because of all the arguing.

The verse ends with the cost on the table. The command had been one word and one cow, and any cow in the country would have settled it that morning. The community now had a cow that had cost the price of gold, bought from a family that had not wanted to sell, after a search that took days. Nobody in the story forced them to make the task expensive except the people asking the questions.

Think of a household that needs a bucket of water to put out a small fire in the yard. Instead of filling the bucket, the family spends the evening discussing which shop to buy it from, what colour it should be, whether the handle is strong enough, and what the neighbours will think of the brand. By the time they agree, the one bucket in the country that fits every condition costs the price of a bicycle, and the fire has reached the roof.

---
## Verse 2:72

> ˹This is˺ when a man was killed and you disputed who the killer was, but Allah revealed what you concealed

**THE KILLING THAT BEGAN THE DISPUTE**

The verse opens with the words: ***“˹This is˺ when a man was killed”*** The verse names the event that started the whole errand. Al-Jalālayn reads the words as a plain statement: a life was taken. Ibn ʿAbbās supplies the name the reports give to the murdered man, ʿĀmil. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the person killed was one of their own people, which is what makes the next phrase so heavy.

The order of the sūrah is worth pausing over here. The command to sacrifice a cow was given before the reader is told what the cow was for. Moses was asked for help in a murder case, and the answer that came back was an instruction about slaughter. The connection between the two is only explained when the animal has been bought, the search has been paid for, and the carcass is on the ground.

**THE ARGUMENT OVER THE KILLER**

The sentence continues: ***“and you disputed who the killer was”*** Ibn Kathīr records the discussion among the commentators about the verb in this phrase. Al-Bukhārī explains it as disputing, and the same reading is reported from Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, who all took it as an argument between the people about the crime. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān describes what the argument looked like in practice: the killer had supporters who wanted the matter buried, and they joined in by accusing other people.

Al-Mukhtaṣar says the community accused each other, each person denying the killing and pointing to somebody else, until the argument became a fight.

The verse is a small study in how a cover-up works in a community that has no police to call. Everybody in the village becomes a suspect, everybody has an alibi, and the loudest voices belong to the people with the most to hide. The Book puts the whole scene in a single line and lets the reader see what the community had come to before anyone thought to ask God for the truth.

Think of a group of colleagues in an office where the petty cash has gone missing. Every one of them stands in the kitchen explaining where he was, and each explanation places the blame on someone else. None of them is going to find the money, and one of them is quietly clearing his own drawer.

**WHAT ALLAH BROUGHT TO LIGHT**

The wording is: ***“but Allah revealed what you concealed”*** Al-Jalālayn marks the sentence as a parenthetical statement placed in the middle of the story, and he reads it as God bringing out what the people were hiding. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as the demonstration of what they had concealed about the murder. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the plain sense: God made known what had been concealed about the killing of an innocent person.

The word for concealing is the one the sūrah will use again and again for the people who know a truth and keep the lid on it. The Book says here that the lid came off, and it says so in a way that gives the credit to God. The village could not solve its own crime, its courts had no ruling to apply, and the answer arrived from outside the case file.

Al-Jalālayn's note on the grammar of the phrase is a reminder of how carefully these accounts were kept. The sentence sits inside the story as a comment from the One who is telling it, and it turns a murder inquiry into a lesson about concealment in general. A person can bury a fact in a village, and he cannot bury it from the One who saw it happen.

---
## Verse 2:73

> So We instructed, “Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow.” This is how ˹easily˺ Allah brings the dead to life, showing you His signs so that you may understand

**THE COMMAND TO STRIKE**

The verse says: ***“So We instructed, “Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow.” This is how ˹easily˺ Allah brings the dead to life, showing you His signs”*** Al-Jalālayn describes what happened after the strike. The man came back to life and said who had killed him, and after naming two of his cousins he died again. The report adds that the two killers were denied the inheritance of the dead man and were themselves put to death afterwards. Ibn ʿAbbās records the same sequence and notes the reports that describe which part of the animal was used, its tongue or its tail.

Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the purpose in plain words: the man would be brought back to life to say who the murderer was, and it happened. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the event as a display of God's power over death, and it explains why the Book placed the story where it did. The Qur'an presents this revival as an answer to the people who deny that the dead will be raised for judgement.

The verse then says the reason out loud. This is how God brings the dead to life, and the word chosen for how is a word about ease. Al-Jalālayn draws the argument out: the One who is able to revive a single soul is able to revive a multitude of souls. The Book is using one dead man in one village to teach a lesson about every human being who has ever lived.

The pronoun in the instruction is worth following. The people were told to strike the body with a piece of it, meaning the cow they had argued about for three rounds. The animal that had cost them so much, fetched from a herd and paid for at a dreadful price, became the instrument of the miracle. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the two halves of the story joined in the order they happened: the cow was sacrificed, and then the murdered man was struck with part of it and came back.

**THE UNDERSTANDING IT WAS MEANT TO BRING**

The wording runs: ***“so that you may understand”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the closing phrase as a purpose: so that you may believe in the rising of the dead after death. Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the same sense: the signs were given so that the people would think and understand and hold a true faith.

This is the first of several scenes in the sūrah where the dead are raised, and it is not the last. Later in the chapter a group of people are brought back to life after a punishment ((2:56)). Further on, a man who wondered how God could revive a ruined town is made to die for a hundred years and then raised ((2:259)). The Book uses the murder case at the start of that series because the evidence arrived in the most human way possible: a man who had been mourned and buried walked back into the middle of the argument and ended it.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes how the event ended. The man gave the name of his killer and then died again. He was not handed a second life in the ordinary sense. He was given a few sentences, long enough to settle a case and teach a village, and then he went back to his grave.

Imagine a courtroom where the case has gone nowhere for weeks. The judge has heard the same accusations from the same people, and every one of them has an alibi. Then the door at the back opens and the victim walks in, says the name of his killer in front of everyone, and lies back down. There is no cross-examination after that. The Book says the sign was given to these people so that they would understand what kind of power they were dealing with.

---
## Verse 2:74

> Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers; others split, spilling water; while others are humbled in awe of Allah. And Allah is never unaware of what you do

**THE HEARTS THAT BECAME HARD**

The verse records: ***“Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as a direct address to the community: your hearts grew stiff against the truth after the raising of the murdered man and after all the signs that had come before. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the word for hardened as dry and barren. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes hearts that had stopped changing after lessons and miracles that would change anyone, until they were like rock.

Al-Qurṭubī collects the meanings of the Arabic word into one picture: hardness, severity, dryness, and, most importantly, an emptiness where the turning back to God should have been. He also records the disagreement over whose hearts the verse means. Abū l-ʿĀliyah and Qatādah and others said it means the hearts of the whole community. Ibn ʿAbbās said it means the hearts of the murdered man's heirs, because when he was brought back and named his killer and died again, they denied the whole event and said the man had lied.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the weight of the charge in his comment. These people had watched the greatest signs, including a man returning from death, and their hearts grew harder rather than softer. He points to the warning the Book gives to believers against copying them, in a verse that asks whether the time has not come for the hearts of the faithful to be humble when God and His revelation are mentioned ((57:16)).

**HARDER THAN STONE**

Its words are: ***“or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the comparison as an argument for how far the hearts had fallen: they were like stones, or worse than stones, because stones still do things. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the phrase the same way and then lists the three kinds of stone before him. Al-Mukhtaṣar makes the point about change: the hearts never changed, while the rocks do.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān lays out the three states the verse names. Some stones pour out a large amount of water. Some split and release a smaller amount. Some give no water at all, and they fall from their places out of awe of God. The first two are ordinary facts a person can see in any mountain stream. The third is the part of the verse that makes the heart the harder thing of the two.

The comparison is patient and precise, and it turns the people's own countryside into the witness. Water comes out of stone in that region. Springs come out of rock and feed villages, and the Book uses the fact as a mirror: something with no life in it at all can still give what people need.

**ROCKS THAT SPLIT WITH WATER**

In the verse's own words: ***“others split, spilling water”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads this as stones that break apart so that water flows from them. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same picture and follows the water down to the fields, where it feeds people and animals.

The second state matters because it is the small one. Not every stone is a river mouth. Some give a little, and a little is enough to keep a family alive in a dry country. The verse is saying that even the stones that are stingy with their water are doing something the hardened heart refused to do, which is to release what had been stored inside them.

**ROCKS THAT FALL IN AWE**

As the verse says: ***“while others are humbled in awe of Allah.”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the phrase as stones that come down from on high in fear of God, and he adds the sting: while your hearts were not moved and not humbled. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as stones falling from the top of a mountain to its foot out of awe of God.

The Book repeats this image elsewhere with a different subject. In the sūrah of Exile, the Qur'an says that if it had been sent down on a mountain, the mountain would have been humbled and torn apart in awe of God ((59:21)). The comparison is the same in both places: rock responds to its Maker, and the human heart that has been given a book does not.

This is the shape of the charge the sūrah is making, and it is one of the heaviest in the Qur'an. A stone falling from a cliff is described as doing something the heart of a person with a scripture in his hands would not do. There is no contempt for the people in the image, only a plain measurement.

**THE WARNING THAT CLOSES IT**

The next words are: ***“And Allah is never unaware of what you do”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the closing sentence as a statement that God is not heedless of what they do, and he adds the note that God gives them time until their appointed moment. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as a promise that the wrongdoing will not go unpunished. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the practical face on it: God knows everything a person does, and He will hold him to account.

The sentence is placed after a comparison that a reader might take as pure poetry. The verse has just said that rocks are more responsive than hearts, and a person could be tempted to hear in that a general complaint about humanity. The last line removes the comfort. Nothing about this is abstract, and the Book is not describing an age, a nation, or a mood. It is describing conduct that is being recorded.

Think of a cliff face after a week of rain. Water comes out of cracks and runs down to the fields below, and the farmer at the bottom fills his channels from the drips of a stone he never touched. Now picture the plot next to his, whose owner has a well and a rope and a full week of free time, and who never lowers the bucket once. The rain did its part for both fields. The difference between the two harvests is the point of the verse.

---
## Verse 2:75

> Do you ˹believers still˺ expect them to be true to you, though a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it

**THE EXPECTATION THE VERSE REFUSES**

The wording runs: ***“Do you ˹believers still˺ expect them to be true to you”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the opening question as a rejection rather than a request for information. The sense he gives is: do not be so eager for them to believe you, because they had already rejected the truth before this. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the same in direct address to the believers: do not expect, after knowing their nature and their stubbornness, that they will be truthful with you.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains the situation that produced the verse. The Muslims in Madinah were taking great pains to bring the Jewish community to accept Islam, and they kept hoping for a breakthrough. The Book answers their effort with a piece of history that had been sitting in front of everyone the whole time.

tafsir_initial notes who is being addressed and who is meant. The plural address goes to the Muslim community, and the people referred to are the Children of Israel. The verse is one of a small group that names the practice of altering scripture ((2:59; 3:78; 4:46; 5:13; 5:41)).

Think of a shopkeeper who has caught the same man twice switching the price tags on the shelf. The man comes in again, smiling, and says the price on the box is wrong. The shopkeeper may still hope for a good sale, and the hope has to be built on something. The verse is asking the believers what their hope is built on.

**THE GROUP THAT HEARD AND CHANGED**

The verse puts it: ***“though a group of them would hear the word of Allah”*** Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the group. These were the seventy men who were with Moses, the same seventy who had gone up to the mountain, and they used to hear Moses reciting the word of God. Al-Jalālayn keeps the same identification and describes them as a party of their rabbis who heard God's word in the Torah.

tafsir_initial gives the scene in the words of the reports. When the seventy returned, Moses would tell the people that God commanded such and such, and this group would answer that God commanded something else, which is how the misrepresentation entered the community that had heard the original with its own ears.

The detail matters for the argument. Someone who has never been told the truth can be excused for missing it. Someone who stood in the presence of the revelation and then repeated it in a changed form knows exactly which word he is moving.

**KNOWING WHAT THEY DID**

Then come the words: ***“then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar lays the weight of the charge on the word knowingly. The scholars changed the words and the meanings after they had understood what the text really meant, and they did it with full awareness of how serious the offence was. Al-Jalālayn describes the change as tampering, done after they had grasped the meaning.

The verb for corrupting is the one the Book uses for damage that is done at the back of a good thing. The verse is not describing a copyist's slip or a weak memory. It names an act that requires the actor to know the original first, because only a person who knows the original can work out what to replace it with.

This is why the sūrah spends so much time on this community before it turns to anybody else. The Book is not complaining about people who never received guidance. It is describing a house with a lamp in it, where the people living in the house spent their evenings repainting the lamp and telling the neighbours it came that colour from the factory.

---
## Verse 2:76

> When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But in private they say ˹to each other˺, “Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you, so that they may use it against you before your Lord? Do you not understand?”

**WHAT THEY SAY IN PUBLIC**

The verse begins: ***“When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.””*** Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the believers in the story as Abū Bakr and his companions, and the people speaking as the hypocrites among the people of the Book. Al-Jalālayn says the same group would tell the believers that they accepted Muhammad and that he was the one their own Book had announced.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān describes the political situation. Some Jews watched the growing power of the Muslims in Madinah and around it, pretended to accept Islam, and now and then told the Muslims that the Torah itself carried the good news of the Prophet and mentioned the Qur'an.

tafsir_initial records the careful distinction some commentators drew. The words may have meant only that they acknowledged Muhammad as a prophet, not that they accepted him as a prophet sent to them. A sentence can be true in one sense and false in the sense that matters, and the verse leaves that possibility on the table.

**WHAT THEY SAY IN PRIVATE**

The verse puts it: ***“But in private they say ˹to each other˺, “Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the scene as a conversation among the community itself. The leaders turn on the people who had spoken too freely and ask them whether they intend to tell the believers what God had made known to them about the description of Muhammad in the Torah. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the leaders speaking to the ordinary people in the same way, with Abū Bakr and his companions named as the believers involved.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān adds what happened when the two groups met. The ones who had been doing the pretending admitted to the other Jews that their friendly words were a way of deceiving the Muslims, and they insisted that their loyalty had never moved. The leaders then scolded them for saying too much.

The scene is a small portrait of a community that has decided in advance what it will not do. The evidence in its own book is not treated as evidence. It is treated as a bargaining chip that must not be shown to the other side.

**THE REASON THE LEADERS GAVE**

The verse demands: ***“so that they may use it against you before your Lord?”*** The leaders' reason for the scolding is in this phrase, and it is the most revealing line in the passage. Al-Jalālayn reads it as a fear that the believers would argue with them on the strength of their own admissions, and he notes the reading that the argument would be in front of their Lord.

tafsir_initial reports the range of meanings the commentators gave to what God had disclosed. Al-Ṭabarī listed what God had commanded you, what God had decided for you, and what knowledge God had given you or made easy for you to gain. Al-Rāzī's reading is the knowledge God gave them to hold. The most common understanding is the prophecies that announced the coming of the Prophet.

Whatever was disclosed, the fear is the same. Here is a community with a document in its own possession that says exactly what the Qur'an says about the Prophet, and the leaders are worried that the document might be quoted in public. The verse is not about a lack of information. It is about what a person does when the information is where he can reach it.

**THE QUESTION THAT CLOSES IT**

The verse says: ***“Do you not understand?””*** Al-Jalālayn keeps the closing question as a rebuke aimed at the group that had done the arithmetic. Ibn Kathīr reads the verse the same way, as part of a passage that deals with the hypocrisy of the People of the Book.

The question is aimed at the strategy rather than the morality of the plan. The people hiding the text were worried about being argued against in front of God. Whether the document is produced in the market or kept in a cupboard, the case is already in front of God, and the believers did not need a copy of the Torah to make their position clear.

Think of two employees who praise the new manager to his face in the morning meeting, and then sit in the car park in the evening explaining to each other that the praise was only a tactic. One of them is worried that the others might quote him. Both of them have forgotten that the car park has a window, and that the manager's desk faces it.

---
## Verse 2:77

> Do they not know that Allah is aware of what they conceal and what they reveal

**THE QUESTION THAT IS A REBUKE**

As the verse says: ***“Do they not know”*** Al-Jalālayn notes that the question here works as a statement rather than a question, and Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as a pointed remark about the leaders. The Book is not asking for information about their knowledge. It is telling them that the thing they are counting on cannot happen.

The question arrives directly after the leaders' plan and it aims at the hole in it. The community had built a strategy on secrecy, and the Book points out that the two people who matter in every secret are the one who tells it and the One who already knows it.

**WHAT HE KNOWS THEY HIDE**

The verse states: ***“that Allah is aware of what they conceal”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the phrase as God knowing what the leaders keep hidden among themselves. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the behaviour as a people acting as though they had forgotten that God knows what they hide in what they say and do.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws the practical conclusion that the verse is making: it makes no difference whether the hypocrites hide their rejection from the Muslims, or whether the other group keeps quiet about the verses in the Torah that speak of the Prophet. God has already told the Muslims what is in their hearts and what their book contains.

Al-Baghawī identifies the people meant and the two verbs of the verse: what they hide and what they make known, with the Jews named as the subject. The question in the verse is not about their intelligence. It is about a plan that assumes God is not present in the room.

Al-Mukhtaṣar draws out the result of the verse for the people involved. They behaved as though they had forgotten that God knows what they say and do in private and in public, and the sentence ends with the promise that He will bring it into the open and expose them.

The sūrah has already described a group whose private conversations were not private at all. In the opening verses, the hypocrites are told that they deceive only themselves ((2:9)), and their secret meetings are described in the same passage ((2:14)). This verse joins that set. The Book keeps telling its readers that a hidden position is still a position, and it keeps naming the One who can see it.

A reader can carry the verse away from its first audience without any strain. The person who shapes his public words around what will be agreed with, and keeps his real position for the private conversation, is making the same calculation the leaders in this verse made. The verse is a short and complete answer to that calculation.

**WHAT THEY SHOW AS WELL**

The verse goes on: ***“and what they reveal”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the pair together: God knows what they keep secret and what they make public, in this matter and in every other matter, and the knowledge is stated so that they might stop. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading of the verse.

tafsir_initial notes that this theme runs through the whole Qur'an, and it lists a handful of the places where the same knowledge is stated: (21:110), (24:29), (27:74), (28:69), (33:54), (36:76). The note also observes the link to the passage in hand, since the conduct the previous verse exposed is exactly the kind of thing a person thinks he can keep off the record.

Think of a man who checks the corridor twice before saying something to a colleague in his office. He closes the door, lowers his voice, and finishes with a laugh. What he has done is check for the people who might listen and forget the One who does not need the door to be open.

---
## Verse 2:78

> And among them are the illiterate who know nothing about the Scripture except lies, and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate

**THE PEOPLE WHO COULD NOT READ**

The wording is: ***“And among them are the illiterate”*** Ibn Kathīr explains the word. The term is the plural of a word used for a person who does not write, and this was the reading given by Abū l-ʿĀliyah, al-Rabīʿ, Qatādah and Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī. He notes that the same description was applied to the Prophet, who was unlettered.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws the line between the two verses. The verse before this one dealt with the educated people among the community, and this verse deals with those who had no education at all. The scholars, he says, had not given the ordinary people correct information about their religion, so their minds were filled with superstitions that pleased them and flattered their wishes.

Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the same group from the other side: they did not know how to read or write, they had no idea what was in the Torah or what it said, and they held only lies they had heard from some of their leaders and took to be the Book revealed by God.

Al-Baghawī explains the name behind the translation. The word is the plural of a term traced back to the mother, and it describes a person who stays as he came from her and never learned to write or to read. Al-Qurṭubī gives the same derivation and adds that reading is included in the description along with writing. The word that the Book uses for these people is therefore about what they never had the chance to learn.

The Book does not blame the unlettered people for being unlettered. What it blames is the arrangement in which a community is kept from its own book by the people who are supposed to teach it.

**WHAT THEY SUPPOSED ABOUT THE BOOK**

The verse records: ***“who know nothing about the Scripture except lies”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the phrase as describing people who know nothing of the Torah except the wishes and inventions that their leaders handed down to them and that they leaned on. Ibn Kathīr gives the word as false hopes, and he reads the phrase as a description of a people who trust in them instead of in the book.

The word the verse uses for what they had instead of knowledge is a word for long wishes. It describes the kind of belief a person builds because he wants it to be true, the one that survives in a community because nobody has checked it against the text.

Think of a village with a notice board at the gate. Nobody in the market has walked up to the board and read it, and every trader in the square can tell you exactly what it says. The version in the square is longer than the one on the board, it makes better promises, and it has been repeated so often that the board looks like the copy.

**GUESSES TAKEN FOR KNOWLEDGE**

The verse goes on: ***“and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the closing phrase as a description of a community with nothing but guesswork in the place where knowledge should be, both in its rejection of the Messenger and in the stories it told about other matters. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same sense, that they do nothing but guess.

The verse is a diagnosis of a whole way of holding a religion. A person can have a book, a teacher, and a family tradition, and end up with a set of opinions that feel like knowledge and have never been tested by reading. The scholars in the previous verse had their education and used it to reshape the text. The people in this verse had no education and inherited the reshaping without knowing it had happened.

---
## Verse 2:79

> So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, “This is from Allah”—seeking a fleeting gain! So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they have earned

**THE WOE THAT OPENS THE VERSE**

The verse names it: ***“So woe to those”*** Al-Qurṭubī opens his treatment of the verse with a discussion of this word. He reports from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān a report that it names a mountain of fire, and from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī a report that it names a valley in Hell. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it simply as severe punishment.

tafsir_initial sets out the different readings with care. The word is an ordinary Arabic cry of distress, and it is also read by some as the name of a valley in Hell, on the strength of a report that a disbeliever will fall into it for forty autumns before reaching the bottom, a report Ibn Kathīr disputed. Others said it is a mountain in Hell made of blood and pus, in which case the sentence can be read as a statement that a place called woe will be waiting for them. Others again said it is the cry that the punished themselves will make, the sound of the people in the fire.

The verse opens with this word, and then it names the crime that earned it.

**THE WRITING DONE BY HAND**

The wording runs: ***“who distort the Scripture with their own hands”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the phrase as writing the scripture out themselves and making it up. Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the subject of the charge: they changed the description and the traits of Muhammad in the Book. Al-Jalālayn names the alterations the reports describe, the description of the Prophet in the Torah and the verse about stoning, both rewritten in a form different from the way they came down.

tafsir_initial notes two stories behind the verse. One account describes some Jews who wrote a page of their own and then passed it off to the ignorant Arabs for a small profit. Another links the verse to the alteration of the prophecies that announced the coming of the Prophet ((7:157)), which is the same deed as the one described in the previous verse, only written down and sold.

The phrase about their own hands is precise. It takes the act out of the realm of interpretation and puts it in front of a person's fingers. Somebody sat with a pen and paper and chose the letters, and the letters were not the ones he had been given.

**THE CLAIM THEY MADE**

The verse adds: ***“then say, “This is from Allah””*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the words as the false claim, that what they had written came from God. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes it as saying falsely that it comes from God. Al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense.

The Book treats the claim itself as a second offence, and the verse places it right after the writing. A community can produce a document for its own reasons, and the moment it stamps the document with God's name, the harm travels further than the paper does. The claim is what makes the problem permanent, because the next generation has no way to tell the forgery from the original.

**THE SMALL PRICE THEY WANTED**

The verse states: ***“seeking a fleeting gain!”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar names the price: a small share of this world, whether money or position. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as a small gain in the means of living and in surplus property. Al-Jalālayn adds the detail that the earnings involved bribes, and he gives the Arabic word for a bribe that stands behind the phrase.

The translation calls the gain fleeting, and the word is worth holding on to. The Book is not telling the reader that the price was small in money. It is telling him that the price was small in time. A page of scripture was rewritten to keep a position in a village, and the position lasted as long as a life, and the page stayed.

**THE WOE SAID AGAIN**

Its words are: ***“So woe to them”*** The repetition is part of the verse's structure, and the commentators treat it as two separate charges. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the first one as a severe punishment for what their hands had written, meaning the alterations they had made.

The Book often states a sentence once and moves on. Here it says the same word twice, and each time it names a different part of the crime. The first charge is against the hand that did the work.

**THE WRITING THAT DAMNS THEM**

The act is named again in the same words the verse used the first time, and the repetition gives the reader the image in full. Somebody wrote something, and the writing is still on the page, and the book of deeds has a copy.

The verse declares: ***“for what their hands have written”*** Think of a man who takes a letter from the landlord, adds a clause about a rent increase, and shows the new version to the tenants.
