The tenants pay, because they cannot read the letter well enough to check it, and because the paper has the landlord's name at the bottom. The extra money in the man's pocket is the small gain, and the clause he added is still in the letter when the landlord finally reads it.

**THE SECOND WOE**

The next words are: ***“and woe to them”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the second charge as the punishment for what the people earned through the practice, which he identifies as unlawful gains and bribes. Al-Qurṭubī's discussion of the verse sits in the same frame.

**WHAT THEIR HANDS EARNED**

The two charges cover the whole act. The first covers the thing made, and the second covers the money that comes from making it. A reader who has ever shaped a document to get something he wanted has both halves of the verse aimed at him, and the verse is short enough that there is no room to hide in it.

As the verse says: ***“for what they have earned”*** The passage ends here, and the next verse turns to a claim that this same community made about its own future, which the Book will answer in its own terms. Another passage names the same crime and the same price in one line: (3:187 — **“they cast it behind their backs and traded it for a fleeting gain”**).

---
## Verse 2:80

> ˹Some of˺ the Jews claim, “The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Have you taken a pledge from Allah—for Allah never breaks His word—or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?”

**THE CLAIM ABOUT THE FIRE**

The verse says: ***“˹Some of˺ the Jews claim, “The Fire will not touch us except”*** Al-Jalālayn records the claim and the number the people attached to it: the fire will not touch us, they said, except for a few days, and the reports give the figure as forty, the very number of days their ancestors spent worshipping the calf. Ibn ʿAbbās has the same reading, forty days for forty days.

tafsir_initial notes that the same claim appears in the third sūrah ((3:24)), and it collects the different numbers the commentators recorded. Some said forty nights, matching the calf. Some said forty years. Some said seven days, one day for each thousand years of the world's existence. The purpose behind the numbers was the same in every version, which was to fix a small, known quantity of punishment and then close the account.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān sets out the reasoning the community was leaning on. The laws that came before Islam held that a person with faith who commits sins is punished for a time, in line with what he did, and is then released because his faith is still with him. The step the people took was small and fatal. They moved a general hope into a personal guarantee and attached a fixed timetable to it.

**THE CHALLENGE PUT TO THEM**

In the verse's own words: ***“for a number of days.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Have you taken a pledge from Allah”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the question as a direct challenge: have you received a covenant from God for what you are saying? Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the two options on the table, that the Prophet should ask them whether they had a promise from God about this matter, and whether they were simply saying about God what they did not know.

The Book uses the language of contracts here, and it uses it deliberately. A claim about the future is either backed by a promise from the One who owns the future, or it is a guess dressed as information. The verse offers the community both doors and waits for them to choose one.

**THE WORD ALLAH NEVER BREAKS**

The verse has it: ***“for Allah never breaks His word”*** The clause is stated as a fact in the middle of the challenge. Ibn Kathīr reads the whole verse as a refutation of the claim, arranged in two branches: if there is a covenant, then God honours His covenants, and if there is no covenant, then the claim is an invention. Al-Jalālayn notes that the meaning is that God will not fail in His covenant.

The sentence gives the community a compliment and removes its excuse at the same time. The Book affirms that God keeps His word, which is exactly why the people had to produce the word He had given. If a promise exists, it will be honoured to the letter. If it does not exist, the letter the people were quoting was written by a human hand.

**THE CHARGE BEHIND THE QUESTION**

The verse declares: ***“or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?””*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the closing question as a demand: are you saying about God what you know does not exist in your Book? Al-Jalālayn gives the same force to the sentence, as an alternative to the claim of a covenant.

The offence the verse names is not the hope of mercy. Hope is a duty in this religion. The offence is the sentence that turns a hope into a schedule and then signs God's name under it. The Book is asking the people a question every generation has to answer in its own way: where is the paper that says what you just said?

Think of a tenant who tells the agent that the landlord promised him two years of free rent. The agent asks for the letter. The tenant says the promise was made privately and never written down. The agent's answer is simple and complete: the landlord keeps every promise he makes, and this is exactly why we need to see whether he made this one.

---
## Verse 2:81

> But no! Those who commit evil and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever

**THE DEED THAT BECOMES A HABIT**

The sentence opens: ***“But no! Those who commit evil”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the word for evil in this verse through the reports that treat it as the sin of setting up partners with God. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it the same way: whoever does evil by joining others to God, and Ibn ʿAbbās adds the condition that the person dies in that state. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the group as the people whose rejection of faith reaches its worst and whose disobedience has taken hold of them.

tafsir_initial gathers the options the commentators gave for the word evil. Most of them understood it as idolatry, the setting up of partners beside God, and the note points to the verse that names the same offence as unforgivable when a person dies upon it ((4:48)). The same note explains what it means for sins to surround a person. Al-Ṭabarī recorded three readings: a person who stays in sin, a person who dies in sin before turning back, or a person who commits major sins and dies without regret.

The Book opens the sentence with a word that means no, and it is aimed at the claim of the previous verse. Al-Kathīr reads the passage as a statement that the matter is not as the people had wished it to be. Ibn Kathīr explains the case the verse describes: a person who does an evil deed and stays in his error deliberately, arriving on the Day of Judgement with no good deeds to weigh against it.

Think of a hiker walking down into a narrow valley in the afternoon. He keeps taking the easy path down, and the walls on both sides rise as he goes, and the slope behind him turns into a cliff. Nothing that has happened to him is dramatic. The word the verse uses for the condition is about being surrounded, and a person does not notice the moment it happens.

**THE FIRE THAT BECOMES A HOME**

The sentence continues: ***“and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the state as one in which the person's wrongdoing covers him completely and encircles him, and he says the description fits the person who dies an idolater. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the same picture, and he reads the closing words as a sentence that will hold: they will stay in the fire and will neither die nor leave it.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains the law that the verse is setting out, and it makes the same point the opening word makes: evildoing that a person commits knowingly and deliberately, until the evil takes hold of him and leaves no trace of good behind, ends in the fire and no release. The second verse of the pair then describes the other group.

tafsir_initial notes the theology that later scholars built on the two verses together. The mainstream position across the schools of Islam is that a believer who commits a grave sin is still a believer, and that such a person is not described by the first verse of this pair. What the verse describes is a person whose evildoing is not a lapse he regrets but the state he lives in. The note also keeps an honest limit in front of the reader: we are told that God forgives, and we are not told whose sins are forgiven here and whose are carried further.

---
## Verse 2:82

> And those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever

**WHO THE PROMISE IS FOR**

The Book says: ***“And those who believe”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the group as the people who believe in Muhammad and the Qur'an. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same identification and adds the description of the deeds: acts of obedience carried out between a person and his Lord.

The pairing of belief and action is the same in this verse as it was in the earlier passage about the earlier communities ((2:62)). The sūrah likes to state the formula twice in different company, once when it is describing people from the nations that came before and once when it is describing the readers themselves.

The promise attached to the formula has already appeared in this same sūrah at greater length, where the believers are told about gardens beneath which rivers flow and about a state they will remain in ((2:25)). The verse in front of the reader is the short version of the same promise, and the shortness is part of its force. Two conditions, one reward, and no negotiation. The Book is consistent about the shape of salvation across its pages. A claim of faith without a deed behind it, and a pile of deeds without a faith under it, are both described in this sūrah, and neither of them is given the promise in this verse.

**A HOME THAT NEVER ENDS**

The verse adds: ***“and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever”*** Al-Jalālayn keeps the promise short: they are the people of the Garden, and they remain in it. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the closing words as a state that does not end: they will not die and they will not be taken out.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the two verses as the answer to the claim at the start of the passage. The people who had fixed a small number of days for themselves were told what the actual rule is: the state a person dies in is the state he stays in. The verses do not leave the reader without hope, and they do not leave him with a formula either. Belief and good work are named as the door, and the Book repeats them together everywhere.

The word the Book uses for the people of each destination is a word for companions. It describes a person who lives somewhere long enough to belong to the place, rather than a guest who is passing through. The Book chooses that word for both destinations, which is how the promise and the threat are held in the same sentence.

Think of two queues at a checkpoint. The paper each passenger holds decides which queue he joins, and the officer at the desk has no interest in what the passenger meant to bring. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the contrast sharp in his translation. One group carries the description of evil and receives the fire, and the other carries belief and good deeds and receives the Garden, and both will be told to remain. The sūrah returns to the same formula later in a single sentence, that whoever submits himself to God and does good work will have his reward kept with his Lord ((2:112)), and it is worth noticing how often the Book repeats a thing the reader already agrees with. A reader can see both lines from where he stands, and the Book has made sure he cannot say afterwards that he did not know which line he was in.

---
## Verse 2:83

> And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺, “Worship none but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy; speak kindly to people; establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.” But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away—except for a few of you—and were indifferent

**THE PLEDGE BINDING THE TRIBES**

The sentence reads: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺, “Worship none”*** Al-Jalālayn says the covenant was taken in the Torah. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads it as a promise made between God and the Israelites covering the duties that follow in the verse. Ibn Kathīr places the verse in the sequence the sūrah has been building: God reminded the community of the commandments He had given them and the covenants He had taken from them to keep those commands, and they turned away from all of it knowingly.

tafsir_initial notices the family resemblance between this verse and other passages that list the foundation duties in one place, and it names two of them: (6:151-153) and (17:23-39). The note also mentions a reading of the verse in which the opening is in the third person and the verse then shifts to a direct address, a move that happens in the Qur'an from time to time.

The list in this verse is a summary of what a decent life looks like in any community at any time: one God, parents looked after, the vulnerable provided for, gentle speech, prayer, and organised giving. The Book then records what the people did with the list.

**NO PARTNER WITH GOD**

The verse records: ***“but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as the prohibition of worshipping anything other than God. Ibn ʿAbbās puts the same duty in positive form: declare Him the only true God and do not ascribe any partner to Him. Ibn Kathīr notes that this command was given to every creature and that it is the reason people were created ((51:56)).

The order of the list matters. The duties that follow, kindness, speech, prayer and giving, are given their place in a life that is anchored to one God first. A community that begins with the other items on the list and forgets the first one ends up with a system of ethics that changes with the fashion of the decade.

**KINDNESS THAT STARTS AT HOME**

The verse goes on: ***“and the needy”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the command as covering parents and the near of kin, with kinship attached to parents in the same sentence. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same, dutiful to parents and keeping contact with relatives. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the orphans and the poor in the same breath.

The Book puts the family before the strangers and the strangers before the general public. The order is not accidental. The people closest to a person are the ones he can neglect without anyone noticing, and orphans are the ones nobody is paid to notice at all.

Ibn Kathīr reads the whole list as the covenant the community was bound to keep, and he notes that they turned away from it knowingly. The mercy in the list has a direction. It starts with the people who have a claim on a person by blood and has its outer edge among the poorest people in the village.

**THE POOR AND THE STRANGER**

The verse puts it: ***“speak kindly to people”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the clause as generosity towards the needy, and al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense. The word covers people who have no property to fall back on, in a society where the family was the first bank.

The list places the needy immediately after the orphans because their situation is the same in one respect: neither group has anyone whose duty it is to feed them. The Book is building a picture of a community where no person is left outside an arrangement because he has no relatives with money.

**A GOOD WORD TO PEOPLE**

Its words are: ***“establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.””*** Al-Jalālayn reads the command as speaking well to people, and he explains what that includes: telling people to do what is right and to stop what is wrong, being honest about the position of Muhammad, and treating orphans and the needy with kindness. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as speaking the truth about Muhammad. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the instruction as good words that call people to what is right, without harshness or severity.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws a lesson from this clause that the scholars of the later generations wrote about at length. The verse asks the community to speak to people gently, whatever state they are in, whether good or bad, religious or not, firm or wavering. The note makes the point that harsh speech drives people away from the message and gentle speech brings them near, and it observes that the duty is placed among the duties of a person towards God.

The sentence is one of the smallest commands in the sūrah and it has the widest reach. Everybody in the audience speaks to somebody. No one can claim he lacked the means to carry out this item on the list, and no one can carry it out in secret.

**PRAYER AND ALMS**

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the two duties as the five daily prayers performed and the poor-due paid from a person's wealth to those entitled to it. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the alms as a share given to those who have a right to it, which is a useful reminder that the payment is a right owed and not a favour given.

The two duties come last in the list and they are the pillars of the whole arrangement, one of the body and the other of the wallet. Prayer is a person's private account with God, and the alms-tax is his public account with his community. The Book puts them side by side so that neither can be used to cover for the other.

The verse then reports what happened to this list, and the report is contained in the same sentence. The covenant was accepted by the people, and so the reader waits for the outcome the Book is about to give.

**THE TURNING AWAY THAT FOLLOWED**

The verse states: ***“But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the phrase as the community's refusal to fulfil the obligations they had accepted. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes it in plain terms: all they did after making the promise was to turn away and reject what they had agreed to.

Ibn Kathīr reads the turn as deliberate: they turned away from the whole list knowingly and on purpose, and he links the clause to the many reminders in the sūrah that they had heard the obligations read out to them and had given their word.

The word the verse uses describes a person walking away from something he had been standing in front of. The community in the story had given its pledge over a list of duties that any reasonable person would sign, and the Book records what the signature was worth.

Think of a shop with a list of terms pinned beside the door: pay the fair price, be polite to the staff, queue in order, keep the floor clean. A customer reads the list, nods at the owner, and walks in. An hour later he has bargained the price down, shouted at the boy on the till, pushed past the queue, and left a trail of paper on the floor. When the owner points at the list, the man says he never disagreed with it. The verse is the owner's answer: he did not disagree, and he did not obey either.

**THE FEW WHO KEPT IT**

The verse declares: ***“except for a few of you”*** Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the few as a small group from among the ancestors, and one report names ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and his companions. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains who they were: the people who acted on the law of Moses while it was in force, and who followed the law of the final Messenger when the earlier law was replaced.

The clause is a small door left open in a heavy verdict, and the Book keeps it open in passage after passage. The sūrah has already described a group among them who were true to the covenant ((2:62)), and it will describe more of them later. A reader should notice what the exception does to the sentence around it. The community is condemned as a community, and no individual in it is condemned on the grounds of his community's record.

**WHAT INDIFFERENCE MEANT**

The next words are: ***“and were indifferent”*** Ibn Kathīr reads the last word as the state of people who are backsliders, and al-Jalālayn reads it as a refusal to carry out the obligations they had accepted. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same clause as a denial of the covenant and a setting aside of it. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the sense in a single phrase: they rejected the promise they had made.

The word describes a person who keeps his position and lets the duty slide past him. He does not argue against the list. He does not tear it off the wall or write a letter of complaint about it. He simply stands in the shop and lets the moment for each duty pass, one after another, until the day is over.

The verse ends with the community in that posture, and the next verse returns to the same covenant with a second set of items on it. The list of duties is about to include an item that the people were breaking with weapons in their hands, and the Book is going to remind them of it in the same patient voice.

---
## Verse 2:84

> And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant that you would neither shed each other’s blood nor expel each other from their homes, you gave your pledge and bore witness

**THE OATH ABOUT BLOOD AND HOMES**

The verse starts with: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as part of the same pledge taken from the community, and he marks it as a distinct set of items. Al-Mukhtaṣar names the document: the contract taken from them in the Torah.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that this verse is a supplement to the previous one, and that it carries other articles of the same pledge. The duties in the previous verse dealt with worship and mercy. The duties here deal with the community's own internal peace, which makes them the natural next topic in a passage that is building a picture of a nation's obligations.

**NEITHER BLOOD NOR EVICTION**

The Book says: ***“that you would neither shed each other’s blood”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the item as the prohibition of killing one another, and Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as the command not to kill each other. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the sense plain: the contract forbade them to kill each other.

The wording is worth attention. The Book does not say that you shall not shed blood. It says that you shall not shed your own blood, which turns the community into one body. In this arrangement, a man who kills his neighbour has wounded himself, and the injury is not a metaphor. It is the whole point of calling a scattered crowd one nation.

The clause is also a reminder of scale. The covenant did not begin with duties towards outsiders. It began with the rule that a community cannot have a future if its members are willing to settle their quarrels with weapons.

**THE HOMES THEY WERE NOT TO TAKE**

The wording runs: ***“nor expel each other from their homes, you gave your pledge”*** Ibn ʿAbbās supplies the names behind the command and says the verse speaks about the two tribes, Banū Qurayẓah and Banū l-Naḍīr. tafsir_initial explains the situation in Madinah: there were three Jewish tribes, al-Naḍīr, Qurayẓah and Qaynuqāʿ, and two main Arab tribes, Aws and Khazraj. When war broke out between the two Arab groups, the Jewish tribes fought on both sides, so that Jews were killing Jews, driving each other out of their homes and taking one another prisoner.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān pauses on the strength of the agreement. The community did not simply find the terms acceptable in general. They confirmed the pledge in clear and explicit terms, the way a witness states what he saw. The verse records the confirmation and the witness in the same sentence as the crime, and the reader can already feel the weight of the next verse.

The item on the list is about homes rather than lives, and the Book names it separately because a community can be pushed out of a house and left alive, and that is a kind of killing that takes years. Exile was an ordinary instrument of war in the region, and the covenant closed it as an instrument for use between members of the same nation.

**THE WITNESS THEY GAVE**

The sentence moves on: ***“and bore witness”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the closing words as the people's acceptance of the covenant and their own testimony against themselves. tafsir_initial records the two meanings of bearing witness here: a direct attestation, or simply being present at the event as a group. The note also raises the question of shared responsibility that these verses bring up, that a person can be caught up in the crimes of his community, and that he can also take an active part in them.

The word witness is what makes the rest of the passage bite. A pledge that has been witnessed is not a private opinion that a person can quietly revise. The Book has the whole community on record, and it will quote the record back to them in the following verse.

Think of two brothers who inherit one family business and sign an agreement that neither of them will fight the other in court or lock the other out of the office. Both sign in front of the family. The following year one of them changes the locks, the other hires a lawyer, and both are still telling the family that they honour the agreement. The verse is the page the family keeps in the drawer, and it has both signatures on it.

---
## Verse 2:85

> But here you are, killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin and aggression; and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you as captives, you still ransom them—though expelling them was unlawful for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest? Is there any reward for those who do so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment? For Allah is never unaware of what you do

**THE COVENANT THEY BROKE WITH THEIR OWN HANDS**

The wording is: ***“But here you are, killing each other”*** The verse opens by turning the covenant around and pointing it back at the people who had witnessed it. Ibn Kathīr reads the paragraph as the exposure of a community that had ratified the pledge and then gone out and broken it, and he keeps the two halves of the story in one frame: the promise not to shed each other's blood, and the killing that followed.

The tone is the tone of a man holding up a signed page. The Book has just reminded the community that they gave their word and bore witness. The next sentence begins with the word of a courtroom, here you are, and the evidence is their own recent history in Madinah.

The two halves of the covenant are placed next to each other so that the reader can see how quickly the community crossed from one to the other. The word for killing here is not about war against an outside enemy. It is about members of one nation taking up arms against each other.

**THE EVICTION THEY CARRIED OUT**

Then come the words: ***“and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the phrase as the community helping each other against their own people, and he explains the two words at the end of the clause as disobedience and injustice. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same, that the tribes supported each other against their own kin in sin and transgression.

tafsir_initial gives the historical picture that the commentators carried. In Madinah there were three Jewish tribes, al-Naḍīr, Qurayẓah and Qaynuqāʿ, and two main Arab tribes, Aws and Khazraj. When war broke out between the two Arab groups, the Jewish tribes enlisted on both sides of the field, so that a Jew was fighting a Jew, driving his own people out of their houses and taking prisoners from among them.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān sets out the three injunctions the community had been given: not to kill one another in an internal war, not to force their own people into exile, and to pay the ransom of any of their number who was taken prisoner. The verse in front of the reader deals with the first two, and the next clause deals with the third, which the community continued to honour while breaking the other two.

**THE CAPTIVES THEY BOUGHT BACK**

The verse adds: ***“and aggression; and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as the arrival of their own people in captivity, and Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the captives as people of their own religion. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the scene in the plainest terms: some of them killed others, drove a group out of their homes and helped their enemies do it, and then paid money to rescue their own people from the enemy's hands.

The situation has a dark comedy in it that the Book lets stand without comment. The same people who had expelled a family from its house were willing to pay good money to bring that family home from a prison, because the second act was something a community could be proud of and the first act had already been agreed to in a tribal quarrel.

A reader should notice how ordinary this is. The community in the story did not plan to break its own covenant. It made a series of separate decisions, each of which looked reasonable to the people involved at the time, and the collection of those decisions added up to the sentence the Book is now reading out to them.

**THE RANSOM THEY PAID**

The sentence reads: ***“as captives, you still ransom them”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the ransom as the payment that bought a prisoner's freedom from the enemy. Al-Jalālayn records the same and notes the alternative reading of the word for captives. The duty to ransom their own people was a genuine obligation in their law, and the community kept it.

The verb the verse uses for their action carries a sense of eagerness, and the reader is meant to hear the effort in it. These were people willing to pay, to travel and to bargain for the release of a relative. The Book is not accusing them of being hard-hearted in every direction. It is accusing them of being generous where generosity was comfortable and violent where violence was convenient.

**THE LINE THEY WOULD NOT CROSS**

The verse states: ***“though expelling them was unlawful”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the sentence as a statement that expelling their own people and killing them had been forbidden from the start. Al-Jalālayn keeps the same force: the deportation itself was unlawful for them, and they carried it out anyway.

The Book is pointing out what the community already knew from its own scripture. The prohibition on expelling a member of the nation was not in a footnote. It sat in the same passage as the duty to ransom prisoners, which the same community had read, accepted and acted upon. A person cannot keep half of a paragraph and claim to be following the paragraph.

**THE BOOK THEY SPLIT IN TWO**

The verse records: ***“for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the question as a charge: do you accept one part of the Book and reject another? Al-Mukhtaṣar asks the same question in his translation, whether the community believed in the section of the Torah about ransoming captives while rejecting the section about not killing each other.

The question is one of the sharpest in the sūrah, and it applies far beyond the people it was first asked about. Any reader who keeps the verses he likes and shelves the verses that cost him something is being shown his own face here. The Book does not call the people unbelievers for reading selectively. It asks them whether a book can survive being treated that way and still be called their book.

**WHAT THEY THREW BEHIND THEM**

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān says the community ignored the first two injunctions and acted on the third alone, which they supposed to be the easier of the three. The comment captures the way the arrangement worked in practice: the community kept the duty that cost money and dropped the duties that cost restraint.

Choose the item that is easiest to obey, and you will usually choose the one that is cheapest for you and most expensive for somebody else. Paying a ransom buys a person's freedom and a reputation. Not going to war against a brother costs a tribe its advantage, and the Book had made that the first article of the agreement.

The next words are: ***“and reject the rest?”*** Think of a driver who obeys every traffic sign on the road except the one on the street where he lives. He has a licence, a clean record on the motorway, and a habit of rolling through the junction outside his own gate. If a court asked him whether he believed in the highway code, he would say yes, and the court would ask him which part of it he believed.

**THE QUESTION ABOUT THE REWARD**

The verse has it: ***“Is there any reward”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the question as a rhetorical one leading to the sentence that follows. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same shape, with the answer supplied by the next clause.

The Book often builds its verdicts as questions. The question format makes the reader supply the answer himself, which is why it has lasted in the sūrah from the earliest pages. The reader who has been following the argument about the covenant already knows what is coming.

**WHO THE QUESTION NAMES**

The Book says: ***“for those who do”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the phrase as referring to the people who had done exactly what the passage describes. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same reference.

The clause is short and it carries the weight of everything above: the killing, the deportations, the alliances with enemies, the payment of ransoms, and the choice of which part of the Book to follow. The Book is about to name the price, and the price is stated in two parts, one for this life and one for the next.

**DISGRACE IN THIS WORLD**

The text says: ***“so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the word as humiliation and disgrace, and Ibn Kathīr keeps the same sense of a verdict passed on the community in the present world. The disgrace the Book names is not a punishment postponed to the Day of Judgement. It arrives in the ordinary run of a life: lost standing, broken alliances, and the reputation the community carried among the tribes of the region.

The sūrah has already used the same word for the community in the wilderness, where humiliation was fastened on a nation that had argued about its food ((2:61)). This is the second time the same verdict is pronounced on the same people, and the second time it is attached to conduct rather than to belief alone.

**THE GREATER PUNISHMENT AHEAD**

The verse carries on: ***“and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment?”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as a reference to the most severe of punishments on the Day of Judgement, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same force. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the community preferred what is temporary to what is eternal and will meet the result.

The two-part verdict is one of the sūrah's most frequent patterns, and it is worth naming as a pattern. A community that breaks a covenant over land and blood is told what it will lose here and what it will lose later. The Book is not describing a God who waits for years to collect. It is describing a God who pays some wages in the same currency the person was working in.

**NOTHING IS HIDDEN FROM HIM**

The verse puts the matter: ***“For Allah is never unaware of what you do”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the closing sentence as a warning that nothing the community did was outside God's knowledge. The same sentence closed the parable of the hardened hearts a few verses earlier ((2:74)), and the repetition is deliberate. The sūrah keeps returning to this line whenever it confronts a community, or a reader, with a gap between the words they said and the things they did.

The verse does not end on a threat. It ends on a statement of fact that gives the reader the same information it gave the people in the story. Everything is being recorded, including the small decisions that looked reasonable at the time, and the record is the only document in the case that cannot be edited.

---
## Verse 2:86

> These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world. So their punishment will not be reduced, nor will they be helped

**THE LABEL THEY EARNED**

In the verse's own words: ***“These are the ones”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the opening as a label attached to the people described in the previous verse. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reference, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān says the verse explains why the punishment is so heavy: the community disobeyed God to get what its desires wanted.

The Book uses this phrase in the sūrah when it wants the reader to stop and identify the group it is talking about. It is a pointer, and it stands at the head of a sentence that names the trade the people made.

**WHAT THEY SOLD**

The verse states: ***“who trade the Hereafter”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the trade as a purchase: they bought the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter, by preferring the first to the second. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same, that they chose the lower world in place of the world to come, and rejection in place of belief.

The word the Book uses is a market word, and it deserves to be taken as one. A trade has two sides, and both sides are named here: what the person receives and what the person hands over. The Book never describes the deal as a mistake or an accident. It describes a transaction between a buyer and a seller, with a price agreed and paid.

**WHAT THEY BOUGHT**

The text says: ***“for the life of this world.”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the exchange as trading what lasts for what does not, preferring the temporary to the eternal. The phrase is worth holding for a moment because it is so ordinary. The thing the community wanted, land, standing and an advantage over a rival tribe, is a legitimate thing to want. The Book is not accusing them of wanting a worthless object. It is accusing them of paying for it with something they could not get back.

Think of a man who sells his house to pay for one very good dinner. The dinner is real, the restaurant is excellent, and the bill is settled. When the plates are cleared, the man has a pleasant memory and no house, and the trade cannot be reversed because the deed has been signed.

**THE PUNISHMENT THAT IS NOT LIFTED**

The verse records: ***“So their punishment will not be reduced”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the clause as a statement that the punishment will not be made lighter, and he also gives the alternative reading that it will not be lifted. Al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense: the punishment shall not be lightened on their account.

The sentence marks the end of a hope that runs through the whole passage. The people had been told repeatedly about the mercy of God, and the previous verses described nations that were fed, sheltered and forgiven. The verse here says that the door they assumed would open at some point in the future is one they had already pulled shut with their own hands.

The Book does not usually state such things without naming the reason. The next clause gives it, and it has nothing to do with the size of God's mercy.

**NO HELP ON THAT DAY**

The wording runs: ***“nor will they be helped”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the phrase as a statement that no one will come forward to protect them, and Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as a promise that they will not be kept back from the punishment. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains what the clause rules out: no intercessor will be allowed to speak for them.

The two halves of the verse answer two different hopes. The first says the sentence will not be shortened, and the second says no one will be able to stand in front of it. In the community's own vocabulary, the second half is the heavier one, because the people in the story had built their sense of safety on their lineage, their scholars and their standing. When the Book closes the door on help, it is closing it on all three at once.

---
## Verse 2:87

> Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. Why is it that every time a messenger comes to you ˹Israelites˺ with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some and killing others

**THE BOOK GIVEN TO MOSES**

The verse puts the matter: ***“Indeed, We gave Moses the Book”*** Al-Jalālayn identifies the Book as the Torah. Al-Mukhtaṣar says God gave Moses the Torah and then followed him with other messengers. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān opens its treatment of the verse by naming the theme: the Qur'an is reminding the Israelites how God had forgiven their offences again and again and had given them every means of guidance.

The order of the gifts in the verse is worth noticing. God did not begin with the messengers or with the miracles. God began with a book, which is the most patient of all the gifts, because a book can be opened, argued with and read again by people who were not standing in the room when it was delivered.

**MESSENGERS ONE AFTER ANOTHER**

The verse goes on: ***“and sent after him successive messengers.”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as God sending messengers one after another in a train behind Moses. tafsir_initial names the figures the commentators had in mind from the earlier scriptures: David, Solomon, Elias, John and others, and it explains what they were sent to do. They preached the Oneness of God and called the people to obey, and they worked inside the law of Moses rather than bringing a new religion.

The clause is a picture of steady provision. A community that had broken its covenant, retaken a calf as a god and asked for a change of menu was not left with a single book and no teacher. It was given a line of teachers, one after another, through the following centuries.

The Book will use the same pattern in the next part of the verse to make the charge sharper, because every messenger in that line carried the same fate to the same community, and the community's record with them was the same.

**JESUS AND THE PROOFS HE BROUGHT**

The next words are: ***“And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the clear proofs as the miracles: bringing the dead back to life, healing the blind and healing the leper. Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the same list of signs that showed the truth of what Jesus came with. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the words more widely, as commands, prohibitions, wonders and signs.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes the position of Jesus at the end of this line of messengers, with clear and undeniable proofs of his prophethood, including the Gospel and his miracles, and it describes the appointment as a mercy to the community that received it.

The Book names him here by his mother, which is the way the Qur'an usually introduces him, and it places him within the same chain as Moses and the prophets before him. The passage is being read by a community in Madinah, and it is being read to a group of Jews who had a position on Jesus. The Qur'an gives him a full place in the line and then tells the people what they did with the line.

**THE SPIRIT THAT SUPPORTED HIM**

Then come the words: ***“and supported him with the holy spirit. Why is it”*** Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the holy spirit as Gabriel, the purified, and al-Mukhtaṣar reads the support the same way, that Jesus was strengthened with the angel Gabriel. Al-Jalālayn explains the phrase as a construction in which the noun is joined to its describing adjective, so that the sense is the holy spirit.

The word for support describes help given to somebody who is carrying something heavy. Jesus is identified in the verse as a man given a book's worth of signs and a strength that came from outside himself. The verse is building the case it needs for the question that follows, which is about what a community does with a messenger it has been given, and its answer is going to be ugly.

**THE MESSENGERS THEY TURNED ON**

In the verse's own words: ***“that every time a messenger comes to you ˹Israelites˺ with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some”*** Al-Jalālayn gives the clause its sting: every time a messenger came with what they themselves did not desire, they became proud. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same, that the messengers came with what the people's whims rejected. Ibn Kathīr frames the whole verse as a description of the insolence of the community, their defiance and their arrogance.

The phrase about what they did not like is the key to the whole passage. The community was not rejecting the messengers for a lack of evidence. The verses just before this one list the evidence: a book, a succession of prophets, and a man who raised the dead. The people were rejecting the parts of the message that interfered with their arrangements.

Think of a sick man who calls for a specialist, pays for the best one in the city, and then throws him out of the house because the advice is to give up salt. The next specialist arrives, gives the same advice, and follows the first one into the street. The problem was never the supply of doctors.

**THE PROPHETS THEY KILLED**

The verse continues: ***“and killing others”*** Al-Jalālayn and Ibn ʿAbbās both read the clause as the plain charge that the community killed some of the messengers. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same, that some they rejected and some they killed. tafsir_initial notes that the sūrah has already named this offence in the passage about the wilderness ((2:61)), and that the charge is repeated here after the long account of the gifts God had given.

The verse is a summary of a nation's dealings with the teachers it was sent. It begins with a book given to Moses, moves through a line of messengers, reaches Jesus with his clear proofs, and then arrives at the treatment the people gave to the line. The Book presents the whole history in five lines, and the last two words are the verdict.

---
## Verse 2:88

> They say, “Our hearts are unreceptive!” In fact, Allah has condemned them for their disbelief. They have but little faith

**THE CLAIM ABOUT THEIR HEARTS**

The wording is: ***“They say, “Our hearts are unreceptive!””*** Al-Jalālayn reads the statement as mockery aimed at the Messenger: our hearts are wrapped in covers and cannot take in what you say. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān describes the saying as sarcasm, a way of congratulating themselves on being unshaken, as though their hearts were so well protected that the message could never reach them.

tafsir_initial sets out the range of meanings the word carried. It means covered, and it can mean sheathed, the way a sword sits in its scabbard. The same word also allows a startling opposite reading: our hearts are vessels, full of knowledge already and in no need of anything more. Another reading gives the sense that the hearts are empty vessels, in which nothing that others say resounds as true.

Ibn Kathīr records the commentators behind those readings: Ibn ʿAbbās through Muhammad ibn Isḥāq with the sense of screened; Mujāhid with covered; ʿIkrimah with a stamp on them; Abū l-ʿĀliyah with the sense that they do not understand. One reading from Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAṭāʾ takes the word to mean that the hearts contain every kind of knowledge and have no need of what Muhammad brought.

The last reading is the one that explains the sarcasm best. The people were not claiming to be helpless. They were claiming to be full, and the Book answers the claim in the next sentence.

**THE VERDICT THE VERSE PASSES**

As the verse says: ***“In fact, Allah has condemned them”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as a rebuttal that begins with the word no: the hearts are not covered in the way the people describe, and God has instead removed them far from His mercy and brought them low because of their rejection of the messengers. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same, that God sealed their hearts as a punishment for their rejection.

Al-Mukhtaṣar turns the sentence into a straight correction of the excuse. The people claimed that their stubbornness came from hearts that were wrapped in coverings, so that nothing could reach them. The Book says the actual cause is the judgement that their rejection brought on them.

tafsir_initial raises the question that a modern reader will want to ask, and it does so by putting two verses side by side. The passage here, where God seems to dismiss the community's excuse, sits beside another verse in which the same people say that their hearts are under coverings from what they are being called to ((41:5)). The question the commentators took from the pairing is about responsibility: if the organ of understanding is covered, can the person be blamed? The Book's answer in this verse is that the covering is not the cause of the rejection. It is the result.

**THE CAUSE IT NAMES**

The verse puts the matter: ***“for their disbelief. They have”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the cause as their rejection of the messengers, and he states plainly that the condition of their hearts was not the result of anything defective in the organ itself. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same logic, that the sealing came as a punishment for a rejection that had already happened.

The order of cause and effect is the point of the sentence. A person refuses a message, and the door of his heart stiffens over years of refusing. The Book does not describe God choosing a random group of people and closing their hearts before they had a chance. It describes the natural end of a long series of decisions, and it names the decisions first.

**HOW LITTLE THEY BELIEVED**

In the verse's own words: ***“but little faith”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the closing phrase as an emphatic statement that their belief is very small. Ibn ʿAbbās records two readings: that they believe neither much nor little, and that they do not believe in what the Messenger says at all. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān points out the sense in which a small faith is real and still not enough: the little belief such people had was in the doctrines their religion shared with Islam, such as belief in God and in the Day of Judgement.

That last observation is the one a reader should carry away from the verse. A community can hold true beliefs about God and about the Last Day and still be described in this passage, because the beliefs it holds are the ones nobody is asking it to change. The Book is measuring a heart by what it does with the part of the message that costs something.

Think of a student who tells the teacher that the classroom door is locked. He is standing at the door with the key in his hand, and the lock has been open since the beginning of the lesson.

---
## Verse 2:89

> Although they used to pray for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists, when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺, they rejected it. So may Allah’s condemnation be upon the disbelievers

**THE PRAYER THEY USED TO MAKE**

The verse begins: ***“Although they used to pray”*** Al-Jalālayn opens the verse with the community's own history. Before the coming of the Prophet, they used to pray for victory and assistance against the disbelievers, saying that God should give them the upper hand through the Prophet who was to be sent at the end of time. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the same practice: they used to say that they would be helped against the idolaters and would win when a prophet came, because they would believe in him and follow him.

The verse is one of the most painful histories in the sūrah for the community it describes, and the Book tells it without commentary. A people had been praying for years for a victory that was going to arrive with a messenger, and their prayer was being answered during the very years in which they were refusing the answer.

**THE VICTORY THEY ASKED FOR**

The prayer was specific: victory over the idol worshippers, the people who set up partners with God. The community asking for it was proud of its own monotheism, and its request was rooted in a genuine belief that God would vindicate the people who held to one God.

The verse names it: ***“for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists”*** The detail gives the verse its force. These were not people who had no interest in revelation. They were waiting for it, praying for it, and describing themselves as the party that would receive it. The Book is not describing indifference. It is describing an expectation that was answered in a form the people had not chosen, which is a test that the sūrah returns to again and again.

**THE BOOK THEY HAD WAITED FOR**

Its words are: ***“when there came to them a Book from Allah”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar names what arrived: the Qur'an, coming from God and agreeing with the true principles that were in the Torah and the Gospel. Al-Jalālayn stresses the word of confirmation, that the Book confirmed what was already in the community's hands.

The phrase about a book from God is the hinge of the verse. The community had been asking for help from God against its enemies, and God sent the help in the form of a book. A book does not ride a horse or carry a sword. It requires the people who receive it to read it, to accept it and to change, and it gives them the strength to do the work that victory actually needs.

**THEY RECOGNISED IT AND REFUSED IT**

The wording runs: ***“which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺, they rejected it.”*** Al-Jalālayn gives the reason for the rejection: envy, and the fear of losing leadership. He notes that the Book confirmed what was already with them, that it was the very thing they had been waiting for, and that they recognised it anyway. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the same sequence together in one sentence: the Book came to them according to the description they recognised and the truth they knew, and they disbelieved it.

The verse names recognition as a stage that makes the rejection worse rather than better. The people knew the description of the Prophet from their own scriptures, they had been praying for his arrival, and when he arrived they found a reason not to accept him. The reason the reports give is the fear of losing the position that their book had given them among the tribes of the region.

A reader can carry this verse a long way from the seventh century. Every generation has a class of people whose standing is built on being the ones who know, and the arrival of a truth from an unexpected direction threatens the standing before it threatens anything else. The Book does not describe the community as stupid. It describes them as recognisers, which is the harder word of the two.

**THE CURSE THEY CALLED DOWN**

The verse puts it: ***“So may Allah’s condemnation be upon the disbelievers”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the closing sentence as the judgement on the people who rejected the Book. Al-Mukhtaṣar ends his treatment of the verse the same way, with the curse of God on those who reject Him and His Messenger.

The word for condemnation is the same one used in the previous verse for the sealing of the hearts, and its return here closes the loop between the two passages. The people claimed that their hearts were covered; the Book said that they had been left outside God's mercy for their rejection; and now the sentence is pronounced on the state they chose.

Think of a village that prays all summer for rain, buys new buckets for the season, and then sits indoors with the shutters closed when the storm finally arrives. Nobody in the village denies that the rain came. They simply have reasons of their own to leave the buckets empty.

---
## Verse 2:90

> Miserable is the price they have sold their souls for—denying Allah’s revelation and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants! They have earned wrath upon wrath. And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment

**THE MISERABLE PRICE**

The verse puts the matter: ***“Miserable is the price they have sold their souls”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the opening as a judgement on the bargain itself: what they received in exchange for their share of the reward in the next life is a miserable thing. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the sense that the community sold its own selves, and al-Mukhtaṣar describes the deal as an exchange for a portion of faith in God and His messengers.

tafsir_initial notes that the same sentence returns later in the sūrah as the closing of another passage ((2:102)), which makes it one of the Book's standing verdicts on the choice. The note also explains the belief the commentators said was behind the choice. The community held that prophethood should come only from the Children of Israel. When the honour passed to the Arabs, they bought the comfort of tribal pride with their faith.

The Book uses the language of buying and selling again, as it did two verses earlier ((2:86)). The sūrah is telling the same story twice with different words, and the repetition is a signal to the reader that the choice being described is not a rare one.

**THE REVELATION THEY DENIED**

As the verse says: ***“for denying Allah’s revelation”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the clause as the rejection of the Book and the Messenger. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the community as rejecting what God had revealed, and adds the injustice and envy that came with it.

The verse names the act before it names the motive, which is the pattern the sūrah has been following for several pages. A reader is shown what a community did, and only afterwards is he shown what was going on inside the people who did it. The Book is teaching its readers to look at conduct first, because conduct is visible and motives are usually invented afterwards.

**THE ENVY THEY HELD**

The wording continues: ***“and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants!”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the clause as envy and resentment that God should send His bounty to whomever He chooses. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the community as rejecting the prophet out of injustice and envy because prophethood and the Book were given to Muhammad. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same sense, that they begrudged God's grace to a servant of His choosing.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws the point out in a way that makes the offence clear. Prophethood is not a wage for effort or a prize for ancestry. It is a grace that God gives to whom He wills, and a community that resents the choice is not disputing with the prophet. It is disputing with the One who made the choice.

That is the sentence that turns an argument about a man into an argument about God, and the Book states it without softening it. The community had been given a book, a line of prophets, a rescue at the sea and food from the sky, and its complaint came down to the fact that the next instalment went to somebody else.

**WRATH UPON WRATH**

The wording runs: ***“They have earned wrath upon wrath.”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the phrase as curse upon curse. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains the two layers of anger: the first for rejecting a true prophet, and the second for the envy that produced the rejection. Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the same accounting, with the rejection of Muhammad and the distortion of the Torah before him standing as two separate offences.

The Book is exact in its arithmetic here. A single act, the refusal of one messenger, is traced back to two different failures, and each of them brings its own share of the sentence. A reader who has followed the sūrah from its first page can see the accumulation being described: one generation's mistake carried forward by another, with new mistakes added to the account each time.

Think of a man who is offered a good position in a company and turns it down because the owner's son was given a better one. He has refused the job for a reason, and the reason has now become a second offence. The Book keeps the two charges separate because they are separate, and it lets the reader count them himself.

**THE HUMILIATION THAT FOLLOWS**

The verse goes on: ***“And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the closing clause as a punishment that carries shame with it. The word the Book chooses is aimed precisely at the group it is describing. These were people whose standing in the region rested on being the nation with the book and the ancestry, and the verdict they are given takes that standing away in public.

The sūrah has used the same word for the same community twice before ((2:61), (2:85)), and it uses it again here as the close of the passage. Three times humiliation is named as a punishment for a people who had been warned, fed and forgiven. Each time, the Book attaches the word to a decision the people made rather than to a fate assigned to them.

---
## Verse 2:91

> When it is said to them: “Believe in what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “We only believe in what was sent down to us,” and they deny what came afterwards, though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures! Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Why then did you kill Allah’s prophets before, if you are ˹truly˺ believers?”

**WHAT THEY ARE TOLD TO BELIEVE**

The verse names it: ***“When it is said to them”*** Al-Jalālayn sets the scene as a plain exchange. The community is told to believe in what God has revealed, meaning the Qur'an and the books before it. They answer with a claim about their own book. Al-Mukhtaṣar frames the same exchange and says the instruction was to have faith in the truth that God had revealed to His Prophet.

The verse has the shape of a conversation that has been repeated many times in the streets of Madinah. Somebody makes the invitation, somebody gives the answer, and the reader is shown both halves so that he can see what the answer actually does.

**THE ANSWER THEY GIVE**

The verse says: ***““Believe in what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “We only believe in what was sent down to us,””*** Ibn ʿAbbās records the answer as a claim to believe in the Torah, with the implication that anything else is somebody else's business. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains what the answer gives away. The community refused to believe in any book of God except the Torah. It justified the refusal on the grounds that the Torah alone had been sent down to them.

The reasoning has a crack running through it that the verse does not bother to point out directly, because the next sentence does the job. If a person believes a book because it was sent to his own nation, then his belief is not in the book. It is in the fact that he belongs to the nation, and every message that comes to somebody else is refused before it is read.

The Book has been describing this community's relationship with its own book for several pages. They had distorted it, hidden what was in it, sold pages of it, and kept the parts that suited them. A man who says that he only believes in what was sent down to his people is stating a principle that has nothing to do with what is written on the page.

**THE REVELATION THEY REJECT**

The next words are: ***“and they deny what came afterwards”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the clause with a note of grammar. The denial covers what is other than the Torah, or what came after it. The verse adds that this denial is happening while the later revelation is the truth. tafsir_initial records al-Ṭabarī's two readings of the word beyond: after, or other than.

The clause names the act in the plainest available language. There is no attempt to dress the refusal as caution, as a waiting period, or as a matter that needs more study. The community had the later book in front of it, and it denied the book, and the Book records it in five words.

**THE TRUTH THAT CONFIRMS THEIR BOOK**

In the verse's own words: ***“though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures!”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the clause as a statement that the Qur'an is the truth and that it affirms the Oneness of God that their own book carried. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the same, that the Qur'an is the truth and confirms what God had already revealed to them.

The clause removes the last shelter available to the community. The message they refused was not a rival announcement that contradicted their tradition. It was the same announcement, arriving with the same content and confirming the book in their hands, and the description in their own scriptures had told them who would bring it.

The next sentence drops the question that the reader has been waiting for, and it does so by reaching back into the community's own history.

**THE QUESTION PUT TO THEM**

The Book says: ***“Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Why”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the question as a rebuke aimed at the claim the community had just made. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same shape, and tafsir_initial explains the logic of the question: the prophets the community had killed were themselves Israelites, and they had commanded their people to follow the Torah.

The Book asks a question that the community cannot answer without giving away its position. If a person's loyalty to a book is what drives his conduct, then the murder of the book's own teachers should be impossible for him. The question is not about whether the community respected the Torah. It is about what the community's conduct proves about the reason it gave.

**THE PROPHETS THEY KILLED BEFORE**

Then come the words: ***“then did you kill Allah’s prophets before”*** The charge is the same one the sūrah made in its account of the wilderness ((2:61)) and in the summary of the nation's history ((2:87)). tafsir_initial draws the conclusion the verse wants the reader to draw. Those prophets were Israelites who called the people to their own book. The killing of them shows, then, that the refusal to accept a prophet came from something other than loyalty to the Torah.

The Book has now named this offence three times in one sūrah. The repetition is a form of weighing. A nation's claim to love its scripture is tested by what it does with the people who read it out. The record in this passage puts the community on the wrong side of that test before the reader was born.

**THE CLAIM THEY COULD NOT SUPPORT**

The verse states: ***“if you are ˹truly˺ believers?””*** Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the closing words as the end of the challenge, and al-Jalālayn reads them the same way. The question returns to the claim the community made at the start of the verse, which was that they believed in what had been sent down to them.

The verse ends with the community holding a claim in one hand and a record in the other, and the Book has arranged the two of them so that they cannot both be kept. A reader with a book on his shelf and a dispute he is managing with his neighbours is being handed the same pair of objects. That is why the passage has been returned to so often in the centuries since it was revealed.

Think of a man who says the only doctor he trusts is the one his family has always used. In the last three years he has driven three of those family doctors out of his house for telling him to change his habits. The next time he says he trusts the family doctor, the sentence will carry less weight than he thinks.

---
## Verse 2:92

> Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully

**THE PROOFS THAT CAME WITH MOSES**

Its words are: ***“Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs”*** Al-Jalālayn lists the proofs: the staff, the hand, and the splitting of the sea. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the words widely, as commands, prohibitions and signs. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān observes that these miracles had happened even before the Torah was given: the staff that became a snake, the hand that shone, and the sea that opened into a path. Ibn Kathīr identifies the proofs the same way and adds the manna and the quails.

The verse reaches back into the middle of the sūrah, where the same events were described in detail ((2:49-61)). The community being addressed in Madinah had those stories in its own tradition, told at its own tables, and the Book can refer to them in a single line because the people knew what the line contained.

**THE CALF AND THE WRONG THEY DID**

The sentence moves on: ***“then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as the worship of the calf during the time Moses was away at his appointment, and he says the people were wrongdoers for taking it as a god. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the timing: the calf was taken up after Moses had gone to meet his Lord. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same.

tafsir_initial notes that the sūrah has already told the story in more detail ((2:51)) and points the reader to the fuller version in the seventh sūrah ((7:148-155)). The mention here is compressed, and it is doing a specific job in the argument. The community in Madinah is being reminded that the calf was built within weeks of the sea splitting, by the same generation that had walked through the water.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains what the proofs were for. They were given to affirm the Oneness of God and His power. They were also the evidence on which the message rested, and they had arrived before the Torah was handed down. The community therefore had proof of the messenger before it had the book in its hands. The ninth verse of the same list of favours is worth reading against this one, because the Book gave the community manna and quails and shade in the same wilderness where the calf was built ((2:57)).

tafsir_initial points the reader to the fuller telling of the story in the seventh sūrah ((7:148-155)) and reminds him that this sūrah has already told it once ((2:51)). In that longer account the calf is described as a body made from the ornaments of the people, lowing as though it had a voice, and the account reports the regret the people fell into afterwards. The community in front of the reader had the whole scene in its own memory, with the voice of Aaron warning them while Moses was on the mountain.

The brevity of the verse is deliberate. A community that had watched the sea open and then built a god out of its jewellery does not need a long commentary, and the Book gives it one line. The line is placed here, thirty verses after the same incident was described in detail, because the argument of this passage needs the fact and not the story. The people who claimed an exclusive right to the next life had taken up a calf within living memory of the sea.

Think of an audience that has just watched a man walk out of a burning building alive, and who spend the following week praying to a matchbox. The verse is not accusing the community of forgetting. It is accusing it of remembering the wrong thing, which is the older and more common problem.

---
## Verse 2:93

> And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and obey,” they answered, “We hear and disobey.” The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts because of their disbelief. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “How evil is what your ˹so-called˺ belief prompts you to do, if you ˹actually˺ believe ˹in the Torah˺!”

**THE COVENANT AND THE OATH**

The sūrah opens the sentence: ***“And when We took your covenant”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the covenant as a binding promise to follow Moses and to accept what he brought from God. Al-Jalālayn keeps the pledge tied to acting on what was in the Torah. Ibn Kathīr frames the verse as a reminder of the covenant and the breaking of it.

This is the third time in the sūrah that the Book has described a pledge taken from this community ((2:63), (2:83), (2:84)). Each account has added a detail the previous one did not have. A reader who has followed the sequence can see one scene being drawn from several angles: the mountain, the command, and now the answer the people gave.

**THE MOUNTAIN LIFTED AGAIN**

The verse adds: ***“and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as the mountain lifted over the people, to be dropped on them if they refused to accept. Ibn ʿAbbās describes the mountain as extracted, raised and fixed above their heads, and the command as diligence and earnestness with the book. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the people were left awestruck by the mountain and were told to hold tightly and seriously to what had been sent to them, and to listen and follow.

The scene has an edge to it that the earlier telling kept more gently. Here the Book spells out the alternative the people faced, that refusal would bring the mountain down on them, and it records the command to listen before it records the answer. The next phrase is the answer, and it is one of the bleakest sentences in the whole sūrah.

**THE BOOK THEY WERE TOLD TO HOLD**

The object of the command is named for the third time in the sūrah, and the naming keeps the same emphasis. The book was given, not invented, and the community was bound to it by an agreement taken on a mountain with witnesses present.

The verse has it: ***“that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you”*** The phrase is small and it carries the weight of the passage. A person who is told to hold firmly to something is being told that the something is worth holding and that his grip is the variable in the arrangement. Nothing in the sentence suggests that the book was difficult to find or hard to understand. It was in the people's hands, and the command was about what they would do with it.

**THE ANSWER THEY GAVE**

Then the verse says: ***“and obey,” they answered, “We hear”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the answer as the people saying they heard the words, and Ibn ʿAbbās records the report that the people meant they had heard with their ears. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the answer as hearing with the ears and rebelling in action.

The first half of the answer is the response that a person gives when the question has not left him any room. The mountain was over the assembly and the command had been read out. The community said the only thing left to say, which was that it had heard.

**THE CALF THAT STAYED IN THEIR HEARTS**

The sentence continues: ***“and disobey.” The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the second half of the answer as a statement that the people would have heard and disobeyed even without the mountain hanging over them. He reads the strange image in the next clause as the people being made to drink the love of the calf, so that the golden animal had soaked into their hearts the way a drink soaks into a body. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the worship of the calf taking hold of their hearts. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the clause as the worship of the calf having entered their hearts.

The image is one of the most striking in the sūrah. The calf had been made from melted ornaments and had never said a word to anyone. It had entered the community not as a doctrine but as a taste, and the Book describes a people whose refusal was not a decision they made on the day. It was something they had absorbed, and it was already sitting in the place where the covenant should have been kept.

Think of a man with a bad habit he has never admitted to. He can stand in a room and agree with everything said about the harm it does. The habit is still there when the meeting ends, because it made its way into him long before the meeting was called.

**THE QUESTION ABOUT THEIR FAITH**

The verse records: ***“because of their disbelief. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “How evil is what your ˹so-called˺ belief prompts you to do”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as the cause of the condition: the calf entered the hearts because of the community's rejection. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same link between the state of the heart and the earlier refusal of the message.

The next sentence turns to the claim the community was still making about itself. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the question as a challenge to the community's claim of belief. What their belief was commanding them to do was an evil thing. The Book asks them to look at the instruction and then at the record.

**FAITH THAT CONTRADICTS ITSELF**

The verse says: ***“if you ˹actually˺ believe ˹in the Torah˺!””*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the closing clause as the same challenge the sūrah made a few verses earlier ((2:91)), and al-Jalālayn keeps the sense that the community's own book is the measure being applied. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān observes that the community did hold the Torah to be genuine, and the verse takes them at their word in order to test them by it.

The verse has now done four things in a single passage. It has described the covenant, the mountain and the command. It has recorded the answer the people gave. It has explained where that answer came from. And it has closed by asking the community to read its own claim against its own conduct. The next two verses will test the same claim from a different direction, with a request the people cannot refuse without answering the question.

---
## Verse 2:94

> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively for you ˹Israelites˺ out of all humanity, then wish for death if what you say is true!”

**THE CLAIM PUT TO THE TEST**

In the verse's own words: ***“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the verse as a challenge built on the community's own claim. The claim was that the home of the next life belonged to them alone and not to other people. From that claim there is a consequence they can test. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same construction and says the claim was that the Garden was only for them.

The Book has used this community's sense of exclusivity several times in the sūrah, most recently in the claim about a fixed number of days in the fire ((2:80)). Here it takes the same instinct and turns it into a test with a single question, and the question is designed so that the answer will be visible to everyone standing nearby.

**THE HOME THEY SAID WAS THEIRS ALONE**

The phrase names the claim as it stood: the Garden reserved for one nation, with the rest of humanity outside it. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the challenge as an argument aimed at the claim itself. It notes the principle the sūrah has been stating throughout, that acceptance with God rests on belief and good work rather than on ancestry.

The verse says: ***“for you ˹Israelites˺ out of all humanity”*** A claim of this kind is not rare, and the Book's treatment of it is worth noticing. It does not simply deny the claim. It hands the community a way of testing it, and the test is available to anybody who wants to pick it up.

**THE WISH THEY WERE INVITED TO MAKE**

Then come the words: ***“then wish for death”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the logic carefully. The two conditions are connected, so that the sense is this. If you are telling the truth when you claim that the Garden is yours, you would naturally incline towards what belongs to you. The road to it is death. So wish for it. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the same reasoning in direct address: if the Garden is only for them, they should wish for death and ask for it, to reach the place quickly and rest from the burdens of this world.

The logic is exact and it embarrasses nobody but the person who has to answer it. A man who is certain that he is going home to a house that belongs to him alone, and who knows the road to it, does not linger in a foreign country because he is fond of the weather. The desire for the destination is the proof of the belief in the destination.

**THE CONDITION THAT PROVES IT**

The verse puts the matter: ***“if what you say is true!””*** Al-Jalālayn keeps the closing clause as the condition on which the whole argument rests, and al-Mukhtaṣar reads the verse the same way. The question is not whether the community wanted death. It is whether the community believed what it had said.
