The next verse gives the answer, and the answer is included in the Book so that the reader can see what happened when the claim met its test. The community did not wish for death, and the Book explains why in a phrase about what their hands had sent ahead ((2:95)).

Think of a man who tells everyone at the gate that he holds a first-class ticket to a destination he has wanted all his life. The gate opens, the staff call the flight, and the man is still in the queue an hour later with his bag in his hand. Nobody needs to ask him whether the ticket is in his pocket, because his feet have already answered the question.

---
## Verse 2:95

> But they will never wish for that because of what their hands have done. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers

**THE WISH THEY WILL NEVER MAKE**

As the verse says: ***“But they will never wish”*** The challenge of the previous verse hangs over this one. The community had been told to wish for death if its claim about the next life was true, and the Book now gives the answer before the community can produce it. Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as a statement of what will never happen, and he names the reason in advance: what their own hands have sent ahead of them. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same, that they will never ask for death, and the cause he gives is what they themselves did in the practice of their religion.

Al-Baghawī adds the detail that explains why the Book could speak for them. They knew that they were lying in the claim they had made. A community that knows the size of its own file cannot ask for the court date.

The same challenge appears in the sūrah of the Congregation, where the community is addressed by name: ((62:6 — **“O Jews! If you claim to be Allah's chosen people out of all humanity, then wish for death, if what you say is true”**)). The answer there is the same answer, given in the same words: ((62:7 — *****“But they will never wish for that because of what their hands have done”*****)). The Book repeats the exchange because the claim it answers was not made once. It was the settled position of a community, and it needed to be met in more than one place.

Al-Mukhtaṣar sets out the deeds the Book has in view. The list is short and heavy: rejection of God, refusal of His prophets, and the distortion of His books. Every one of those items has been described in this sūrah during the last thirty verses, and the reader has watched them happen in order.

**THE HANDS THAT HOLD THEM BACK**

The verse puts the matter: ***“for that because of what their hands have done.”*** The phrase about the hands is one of the small pictures the Book uses for a whole life. Al-Baghawī explains why the hand is chosen here. Most of the harm a person does is done with his hands, so the deeds of a lifetime are attached to the hand even when the hand had no share in them. The wording turns a person's record into a parcel that he packed himself and sent on ahead of his own arrival.

A reader in Madinah hearing this verse would have understood the travel image without any help. A caravan sends its loads forward, and the traveller who follows finds his goods waiting at the destination. Nothing in the arrangement is a surprise. The Book is saying that the community knew what was waiting for it, and that the knowledge was the reason for its silence when challenged.

Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the same clause as the summary of a life: the disbelief, the rejection of the prophets and the changes made to the scriptures. The Book never treats those acts as one bad afternoon. It treats them as a stock that a person keeps adding to, and the verse says the stock decides whether he wants to arrive.

Think of a man who tells the whole street that the big house at the end of the road has been left to him in a will. The lawyer's office is open, the paper is on the desk, and the only thing required is for him to walk in and sign. Everyone watches him find one reason after another to stay on his side of the road, and the reasons stop mattering after the third week. What his feet say about the inheritance is more exact than anything he says with his mouth.

**THE KNOWLEDGE THAT SEES IT ALL**

The sentence continues: ***“And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers”*** The closing sentence is the sūrah's standing line, and it has closed several passages already ((2:74), (2:85)). Al-Mukhtaṣar draws the practical meaning out of it: God knows the wrongdoers among this community and among everybody else, and each person will be given exactly what he has earned.

The verse does not need the sentence for its argument, since the argument was settled by the refusal to wish for death. The sentence is there for the reader, and it is doing two things at once. It warns the person who has a record he has kept quiet about, and it comforts the person who has been wronged by somebody whose name nobody could prove.

The next verse turns to the same community and shows what their refusal looks like from the outside. The Book moves from the wish they would not make to the life they were clinging to, and the second picture explains the first.

---
## Verse 2:96

> You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people, even more than polytheists. Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years. But even if they were to live that long, it would not save them from the punishment. And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do

**THE GRIP ON THIS LIFE**

The verse declares: ***“You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people, even more than polytheists. Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years.”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the comparison. The community is the greediest of people for life, and greedier still than the idolaters, who do not accept the rising of the dead. His reason for the difference is sharp: the community knew that its journey ended in the Fire, while the idolaters did not believe in that even as an idea. One group was holding on to a room it feared, and the other was holding on to the only room it had.

Al-Qurṭubī records the line of Arabic poetry that the commentators used to describe the older Arabs, a verse that tells a man to enjoy this world because he is mortal and will not live forever. The lines are not quoted as wisdom. They are quoted as a description of the people who had nothing after death to look towards.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān finds the real force of the verse in the contrast it draws with the community's own beliefs. The Arabs who worshipped stones had no teaching about a judgment and no claim to an inheritance in the next life, and their attachment to this one was easy to explain. The community being addressed believed in the resurrection, and it told itself that the Garden was reserved for it alone. It still loved this life above every other people on earth. The claim and the appetite did not match.

tafsir_initial sets out the possibilities in the grammar. The words one of them may refer to the community described at the start of the verse, or to the idolaters, which would produce the strange reading that the community is greedier than people who want a thousand years because they have no belief in the next life at all. It also records the report that the phrase points to the Persians, and the Persian blessing that wished a person ten thousand years.

The Book is not measuring the community against a standard of courage. It is measuring the claim against the behaviour of the people making it, and the measurement is being taken in public.

**EVEN A THOUSAND YEARS**

The verse records: ***“But even if they were to live”*** The sentence turns from the wish to the arithmetic. Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as a conditional that the wish cannot survive, and al-Mukhtaṣar puts the result plainly: however long a life a person might be given, it would not move him any distance away from the punishment.

A thousand years is an enormous number for a man who has known an ordinary life span, and the Book lets the reader feel how large the wish is before it answers it. The answer does not haggle with the number. It points out that the number is the wrong thing to have chosen, because the matter being decided is not how long a person lives but what happens after the living stops.

The wish itself is interesting for what it leaves out. Nobody in this picture asks for a clean record, a forgiven past or a good end. The wish is for more time in the same condition, which is a wish any prison can grant.

Think of a passenger who is flying to a city where a court case is waiting for him. He hopes for fog on the runway, then for a mechanical delay, then for a longer route. What he wants is not the destination, and no airline can give him a schedule that solves his problem, because his problem was on the departure side.

**THE DELAY THAT SAVES NOBODY**

The verse has it: ***“that long, it would not save them from the punishment.”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar and al-Jalālayn read the clause the same way: the length of a life does not buy a person a centimetre of distance from what is owed. The verse has already said the same thing in the previous sentence with a different word, and the repetition is the Book's way of hammering a nail.

The truth the clause states is one the sūrah has been building since its opening pages. Time is not a currency that can be traded for forgiveness. In the story of the cow, a community spent days of arguing and ended up paying the price of gold for a delay that gained it nothing ((2:71)). Here a community wants a thousand years of the same delay, and the Book tells them what the delay would be worth.

The clause also closes an old door. A person can persuade himself that some future version of himself will sort out the matter, and that a long life is the space he needs for the sorting. The verse answers the persuasion directly: a longer life in the same condition is not a plan. It is only a longer version of the same account.

**THE EYE THAT SEES WHAT THEY DO**

The sentence continues: ***“And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do”*** The verse returns to the ground that the previous verse also stood on. The Book has said that God knows the wrongdoers ((2:95)), and here it says that He sees what they do, which adds the sense of watching rather than of filing. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the sentence as a statement that nothing is hidden from God and that every person will be paid what he earned.

The two closing lines of the two verses are placed close enough that a reader can hear the pair. Knowledge of the people, and sight of the deeds. The Book keeps both sentences because a person can believe that God knows who he is while imagining that the specific act was small enough to be forgotten.

The next verse changes the subject to the excuse the community was offering for its position, and that excuse turns out to be about an angel.

---
## Verse 2:97

> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it—a guide and good news for the believers.”

**THE ANGEL THEY DECLARED WAR ON**

The Book says: ***“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know”*** Al-Ṭabarī opens his treatment of the verse with a report of agreement among the scholars. The verse was sent down in answer to a group of Jews who claimed that Gabriel was their enemy and that Michael was their friend, and the commentators differed only about the occasion that produced the claim.

Al-Qurṭubī records the exchange. The community told the Prophet that every prophet receives his message through an angel, and they asked him who his angel was. He said Gabriel. They answered that this was the one who brings war and fighting, the one who was their enemy, and they added that if he had said Michael, who brings rain and mercy, they would have followed him.

Al-Baghawī names one of the questioners, a learned man of the community called ʿAbdullāh ibn Ṣūriyā, and he has the speaker list the reasons for the grudge: Gabriel brings punishment, war and hardship, and the destruction of their sanctuary stood at the head of the list.

tafsir_initial gives two accounts of the same exchange and a piece of the history behind it. In one, a group tests the Prophet with questions only a true prophet could answer, and the question about the angel who brought the message is among them; when the answer is Gabriel, they say they would have followed him if he had said Michael, who is an agent of mercy in their eyes. In the other account ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb visits the community while it is studying the Torah, and is told that the people believe Muhammad is a prophet and still do not follow him, because they are at peace with some angels and not with others. ʿUmar is astonished that one angel should be a friend and another a foe while both stand near to God, and when he goes back and asks about the matter, he learns that the verse has already come down.

The note adds the older material on Michael: in the earlier scriptures and the later writings of the Jewish tradition he is the great angel, named as the prince of Israel, described as its advocate and as the teacher of Moses, and paired with Gabriel in complementary roles, one being snow and the other fire.

Read together, the reports give the shape of the verse's answer. The community had turned the two angels into two parties, and then decided which party it supported.

**WHAT GABRIEL BROUGHT DOWN**

The verse has it: ***“that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as the plain fact set against the grudge: Gabriel brought the Qur'an down upon the Prophet's heart by the command of God, confirming what came before it of the earlier scriptures. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the same and names the books being confirmed, the Torah and the Gospel.

The little phrase about permission is doing a great deal of work. An angel who brings a message does not decide the message, and a man who carries a letter does not write it. The verse places God at the origin of the revelation and the angel in the role of the carrier, and it does the same for the grudge: whatever the messenger is like, the letter on the page stays what it is.

The other phrase worth holding is the heart. The Book does not say that the revelation reached the Prophet's house, his scroll, or his scribes. It says it reached his heart, which is the one address a person cannot keep clean by sweeping the yard, and the one place where a message has to be accepted before it can be spoken about.

Al-Mukhtaṣar adds that the Book confirms the earlier scriptures, the Torah and the Gospel, which is the point a reader of those books would have wanted. The Qur'an was not arriving as a rival announcement from a different department. It was arriving as confirmation of what the same sender had sent before.

Think of a man who refuses to accept a letter because he does not like the postman's face. The postman may have delivered news of a fine to that man before, and the man may remember it every time he sees the uniform. None of that changes what is written on the paper, and the letter is still from the same office that has been sending him letters for years.

**GUIDANCE AND GOOD NEWS**

The wording is: ***“a guide and good news”*** The verse does not stop at the defence of its carrier. It tells the reader what the Book is for. Al-Jalālayn reads the two words as a guidance away from error into the right way, and as good news of the Garden for the people who believe.

The description is short and it covers the two halves of a person's need. A traveller who has lost his road needs a guide, and a man who is tired of bad news needs good news. The Book presents itself as both, and it attaches the second to a condition: the good news is for the believers.

**WHO THE GOOD NEWS IS FOR**

The sentence reads: ***“for the believers.””*** Al-Mukhtaṣar names the promise that the good news carries: the bliss that God has prepared for those who believe. The clause closes the verse by naming the audience, and the naming is what makes the sentence a test rather than a slogan.

A reader can see the whole passage working in one movement. A community raised an objection about an angel, the Book answered with the identity of the sender, the content of the letter, and the purpose of the message, and then it put both results in front of the reader. The next verse widens the objection from one angel to the whole of God's household, and it answers the larger version in a single sentence.

---
## Verse 2:98

> Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel, and Michael, then ˹let them know that˺ Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers

**THE LIST OF ENEMIES**

The verse opens with the words: ***“Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel”*** Al-Ṭabarī's report on the previous verse applies here as well: the scholars agree that these two verses came down together in answer to the community's claim about Gabriel and Michael. The list in front of the reader begins with God and then widens out through the angels and the messengers.

tafsir_initial pauses over the shape of the list and explains it. Gabriel and Michael are named after the angels in general, and the naming is not a claim that they stand outside the category. The Book does the same thing elsewhere, where fruit is mentioned and then the dates and the pomegranates are named separately ((55:68)). The note adds that angels are also described as messengers in the Book ((11:77)), which is why the word appears in the list before the two names.

Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the sentence as a declaration of where the line is drawn: whoever takes a stand against God, His angels, His prophets, and against Gabriel and Michael, has chosen an impossible position. The community in the story had wanted to negotiate with one part of the arrangement and refuse the rest, and the verse tells it that the arrangement does not work that way.

The order of the list is worth following step by step. It begins with the One who sends, moves to the angels who carry the message, and ends with the human beings who deliver it to their peoples. Enmity towards any part of that chain is enmity towards the whole of it, which is a rule the Book states in another place in the plainest terms: ((4:150 — **“Surely those who deny Allah and His messengers and wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers, saying, ‘We believe in some and disbelieve in others,’ desiring to forge a compromise”**)). The next verse in that passage supplies the verdict, that they are the true disbelievers ((4:151)).

The same sūrah that is doing the accusing here puts the opposite position in the mouth of the believers near its end, where they say that they believe in God, His angels, His books and His messengers, and add that they make no distinction between any of the messengers ((2:285)). The two sentences face each other across the whole chapter, and a reader who has followed the argument from the opening page can see what the Book has been building towards.

A person cannot decide which member of a king's household he is willing to receive. The messenger who comes to the door is not the king, and the message is not his own, and the man who turns him away has turned away the sender and everybody who works for him.

**THE ANSWER GIVEN TO THEM**

Then the verse says: ***“and Michael, then ˹let them know that˺ Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers”*** The second half of the verse states the answer in the Book's plainest terms. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the result in front of the reader: whoever has God as a rival faces certain defeat, since nothing a person can field will stand against that.

The sentence is built as a mirror. The community had announced an enemy, and the Book names the enemy that the announcement produced. A person can dislike an angel and be left alone with his dislike. A person who sets himself against God has picked the one opponent whose side has no exit.

Al-Mukhtaṣar notes one more detail in the wording, that the declaration covers the disbelievers among the community being addressed and among everybody else. The Book never limits a rule to the group that produced it, and this sentence is a case of that habit: the door it closes is closed for every reader who stands in the same position.

Think of a customer who decides that the delivery driver is his enemy, and who then stops dealing with the shop, refuses the manager's calls and turns away the owner at his gate. The quarrel began with one face at the door. By the end of the week the whole company is on the other side of it, and the customer is still standing in his own hallway holding the parcel he needed.

---
## Verse 2:99

> Indeed, We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ clear revelations. ˹But˺ none will deny them except the rebellious

**THE SIGNS THAT WERE SENT DOWN**

The sūrah opens the sentence: ***“Indeed, We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ clear revelations. ˹But˺ none will deny them except the rebellious”*** Al-Jalālayn gives the occasion for the verse. A man of the community had told the Prophet that he had brought them nothing, and this sentence came down as the answer. Al-Qurṭubī records the same report from Ibn ʿAbbās and names the speaker: Ibn Ṣūriyā, who asked what sign had come down with him that they might follow.

Al-Ṭabarī describes the signs the verse is talking about in a way that answers the complaint exactly. The clear signs are those in the Book that was sent to Muhammad, and they include what the Book tells about the hidden knowledge of the Jews, the secrets of their history, the news of their ancestors, and the contents of their own scriptures, which only their scholars knew. God placed those things in the Book sent to His Prophet and opened them for everybody to read.

That is a strong answer to a man who says that nothing recognisable has arrived. The Book was handing his community a mirror. It described their history, their agreements, their alterations of the text and their private reasoning, and any scholar among them could see that the description came from outside the room where the material had been kept.

tafsir_initial reads the clear signs as the marks of the Prophet's prophethood, his qualities and the knowledge he carried, which the commentators say should have been plain to any believing member of that community. The note keeps the focus on recognition, which is the word the passage has been circling since the challenge about the angel.

**THE UNJUST WHO DENY THEM**

The last part of the verse names the people who will reject the signs, and al-Jalālayn gives them their name: the wicked, the ones who have already turned away. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the same word as people who have left the path of God. The choice of word matters, because this sūrah has used it before, at the close of the parable of the gnat, where the Book says that God leaves none to stray except the rebellious ((2:26)). The sentence does not describe a reader who has not yet heard. It describes a person who has heard, who knows the material, and who has decided that the road is not for him.

The address of the verse is worth noticing as well. God says that He has sent the clear revelations down to the Prophet, and the sentence names the person who carries them rather than the crowd who will deny them. The signs were not left at the door of a community to be approved by a committee. They were given to one man, and the community's judgement of them was a judgement of the delivery, not of the contents.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws the practical conclusion that the community's own complaint collapses under. The people said that no clear proof of the prophethood had been given to them. The Book answers that the proofs were plain enough for them to see, and that the refusal did not come from a shortage of evidence. It came from a habit, and a habit of turning away is exactly what the last word of the verse names.

Think of a man who demands a written guarantee before he will move into a house, who is handed the guarantee on the day he asks for it, and who then tells the agent that the page is blank. The second inspection is not about the paper. It is about the man, and the verse says so in the fewest words it can find.

---
## Verse 2:100

> Why is it that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside? In fact, most of them do not believe

**THE COVENANT THEY CAST ASIDE**

The verse begins with the words: ***“Why is it that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside?”*** Al-Jalālayn explains what the covenants were: pledges that the community would accept the Messenger when he appeared, and pledges that it would not help the idolaters against him. The question in the verse is a rebuke rather than a request for information, and it names the pattern the whole sūrah has been documenting. A group takes the agreement, and a group throws it away.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān adds the piece that makes the rebuke heavier. The earlier scriptures carried a pledge about the coming of the final Messenger, and the community had taken it. When the matter was raised with them, they denied that any such pledge existed. The Book answers the denial by pointing at the rest of their record, since a community that keeps the agreements nobody can check is not in a position to have forgotten the one that turned out to be inconvenient.

This sūrah has walked through the same scene four times already. A covenant was taken over a mountain ((2:63)). A covenant covered the family, the orphan and the poor ((2:83)). A covenant forbade the shedding of blood and the expulsion of neighbours ((2:84)), and the community broke it in the following years ((2:85)). Another was taken, and the people answered with words that admitted the fault ((2:93)). The question in front of the reader is the Book's summary of all four scenes, and it is aimed at a habit rather than an incident.

Think of a landlord who has rented the same shop for twenty years and who keeps a drawer of unsigned agreements. Every tenant has promised to pay on the first of the month, and every tenant has explained, in the second week, why this month was different. The landlord stops asking about the reasons after a while and starts looking at the drawer.

**THE UNBELIEF BEHIND IT**

The verse names it: ***“In fact, most of them do not believe”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the closing sentence as a move from the group to the majority: the ones who throw the agreements away are not a minority on the edge of a faithful community. Ibn ʿAbbās goes further and says that the phrase means all of them in fact. The Book is not splitting a good community into a good part and a bad part. It is naming the state of the whole body.

Al-Mukhtaṣar draws the connection between belief and conduct in a single line: faith leads a person to keep his commitments and to honour his promises, so a community with a long record of broken agreements has told the reader something about the faith it claims.

Ibn Kathīr's comment on the same passage is that the community was accused of setting aside the pledges that had been taken from it, and the verses that follow supply the instance that mattered most in Madinah. The Book is not describing a distant chapter of history. It is describing the agreement that the men standing in front of the Messenger had inherited from their fathers and then let fall at the moment it was asked for.

The sentence is a good place to stop and take the test in hand. The Book does not measure belief by what a person says about his own heart. It measures it by what stays standing after the pressure arrives, and the standing agreements of this community are the evidence it was asked to answer for.

---
## Verse 2:101

> Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them—confirming their own Scriptures—some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs as if they did not know

**THE MESSENGER THEY HAD BEEN WAITING FOR**

The verse begins: ***“Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them”*** Al-Jalālayn identifies the messenger as Muhammad and gives the purpose of his coming in the same breath: he came confirming what the community already had. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the sequence clear, that he came with the description the Torah had carried, and that the match was exact.

The verse repeats the word now from the previous passage, which ties the two verses together. The Book has just described a community that threw agreements away, and it moves straight to the largest agreement of all, the one that concerned the arrival of the man standing in front of them.

**THE BOOK THAT CONFIRMED THEIR OWN**

The Book says: ***“confirming their own Scriptures”*** The confirmation is the part of the story that the Book keeps returning to. The community's own book had spoken of a messenger to come, and the messenger arrived with a message that honoured the earlier books instead of replacing their authority with his own opinions. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws the conclusion that the refusal reached further than the community intended. A person who turns away from the final Messenger is turning away from the book that announced him.

The sūrah has made the same point before, in its description of the earlier generations, where the later revelation was said to confirm the book already in their hands ((2:89)). The verse in front of the reader takes the same sentence and applies it to the people standing at the door of the Prophet's city.

**THE BOOK THEY THREW BEHIND THEM**

The verse puts the matter: ***“some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the picture. They did not act on what the scriptures said about belief in the Messenger, and the word for that failure is the casting of the Book behind the back. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as a rejection of what the Torah contained about the description of the coming prophet, and al-Mukhtaṣar describes a group turning away from the scripture that proved the matter.

The gesture is worth a moment, because the Book chooses it carefully. Nobody in this scene burns the book, and nobody rewrites it a second time. The community takes the book that has been with it for centuries, and it puts the book where a traveller puts the bag he does not want to carry: behind him, out of sight, still in his possession. The Book keeps its place on the shelf and loses its place in the argument.

The Book keeps this detail because the covenant was not a private arrangement between a person and his conscience. Ibn Kathīr reads the whole passage as a reminder of the pledges and promises that were taken from the community to believe in God alone and to follow His messengers, and he places the broken pledges of this verse inside that larger account of a nation's record.

A reader who has ever postponed a document he did not want to read will recognise the movement. The paper is not destroyed, and the decision it asks for is not answered. It is simply moved to a place where it cannot be seen while the person gets on with what he had already decided to do.

**AS IF THEY HAD NEVER KNOWN**

The verse declares: ***“as if they did not know”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as the community behaving like people who have no idea what the book contains about the Messenger or about its own origin. Ibn Kathīr has the same sense, that they behaved like fools. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes a group that gains nothing from the truth or the guidance in the book it owns.

The phrase is the Book's way of naming an act of pretending. The community knew the contents of its scripture well enough to argue with them, to hide parts of them and to sell pages of them. What it did not know, in the sense the verse means, was how to let the book speak on the morning when it mattered.

The next verse shows what the community picked up in place of the book it had put down, and the answer is one of the strangest passages in the sūrah.

---
## Verse 2:102

> They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon. Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved. They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon. The two angels never taught anyone without saying, “We are only a test ˹for you˺, so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith.” Yet people learned ˹magic˺ that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband and wife; although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will. They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them—although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter. Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls, if only they knew

**THE MAGIC THEY FOLLOWED INSTEAD**

The verse puts the matter: ***“They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon. Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved. They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût”*** Al-Ṭabarī identifies the people in this sentence as the scholars among the community who had been described in the verses above, the ones who put the Book behind them while knowing what they were doing. He then explains what they picked up instead: the magic that the devils used to recite in the time of Solomon, which the community followed and preferred to the covenant it had been given.

The verse stops in the middle of the accusation to clear a prophet of a charge. The words never did Solomon disbelieve are placed between the community and the devils, and the commentators explain why the denial was needed. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reproduces the first of the four solutions that Maulana Ashraf Thanavi wrote on this passage, and it is the plain one: the community had gone so far as to attribute magic and sorcery to a prophet, so the Qur'an denies the charge as a parenthetical remark in the middle of its own sentence. Solomon did not reject God, and he did not work the harm the community's stories attached to his name.

tafsir_initial notes a reading in which the words are taken as what was recited about, or in, the kingdom of Solomon, so that the phrase describes the time rather than the man, and it reports the opinion of al-Ṭabarī that the sentence means the era of his rule. The note also observes that the accounts of Solomon that this verse produced filled more pages of commentary than almost any other verse in the Qur'an, and that much of that material sits far away from the main body of Islamic commentary. The Book's own sentence is short: the devils rejected, and Solomon did not.

Al-Qurṭubī records al-Suddī's version of how the community came to this point. When the Jews argued with the Prophet, they brought the Torah out for the debate, and the Torah and the Qur'an agreed with each other. Having lost the argument, they threw the Torah aside and picked up the book attributed to Āṣif and the magic of Hārūt and Mārūt. The material they preferred was the material that could not be checked against a covenant.

**THE TWO ANGELS AND THE TEST**

Then come the words: ***“and Mârût, in Babylon. The two angels never taught anyone without saying, “We are only a test ˹for you˺”*** The verse names the two angels and the place. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the pair, Hārūt and Mārūt, and the city of Babylon beside them. The reports about the two differ wildly, and tafsir_initial sets out the range with an honest warning attached. Some accounts have the angels sent down to the earth because they believed themselves better than human beings, and then falling into sin on earth through a woman. The note says plainly that most or all of these legends are rejected by major classical commentators, including Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī, and that the verse can be read well without any recourse to them.

The same note supplies the reading that holds the sentence together. To the extent that the two angels taught people how to read and work with the hidden side of creation, the teaching would have been for the sake of wisdom, healing and good. Knowledge of that kind is a tool with two edges, and what it does depends on the hand holding it. Al-Rāzī is named among the commentators who identified the two with figures already known from the earlier scriptures.

The warning the angels gave is quoted directly in the verse, and it is the most important sentence in the passage. They told every person who came to them that this was a test and that the learner should not abandon his faith. Nobody in the story was handed the skills as a reward or as a right. The skills came with a statement of what they were for, and the people who ignored the statement did so with the words still ringing in their ears.

**THE WARNING THAT CAME WITH THEM**

The text says: ***“so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith.””*** Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the warning as the condition on which the knowledge was available: it was a trial for the learner, and the learner was told in advance not to step outside belief. The Book quotes the angels rather than the people who came to them, which tells the reader where the responsibility was placed and left.

The sentence also settles a question that people have asked about the passage for centuries, which is why the knowledge existed at all. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān gives the fourth of the solutions it reports. Black magic had become popular in the world, and its effects were so startling that people confused them with the miracles of prophets. Some came to treat magicians as holy men, and others took up the practice as though it were a good deed. Two angels were therefore sent to Babylon to teach people what magic actually was, so that they could tell the difference between a trick and a miracle, and so that they would keep away from both the art and the people who sold it.

On that reading, the arrival of two angels in Babylon was a mercy of the same kind as a doctor who shows a village how a poison works. The information is dangerous, and leaving a village in ignorance of it is worse.

**WHAT PEOPLE TOOK FROM THEM**

Its words are: ***“Yet people learned ˹magic˺”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as a return to the community's choice: what they learned from all of this was the magic itself, and the warning was dropped on the way home. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same sense, that the people took up the practice despite what they had been told.

The Book numbers the learners among the people of the Book rather than among a crowd of strangers. These were people with a scripture, a history and a set of teachers. The knowledge they went looking for was the knowledge that offered power without obligation, and the sentence reports that it was found and used.

**THE SPLIT BETWEEN A HUSBAND AND HIS WIFE**

The verse states: ***“that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband”*** The verse names the result the Book wants the reader to see, and it is not wealth or fame. The magic was used to set a husband against his wife. tafsir_initial observes that causing a rift between a man and his wife was one of the ordinary aims of magic in the societies of the region, and it notes that Solomon's God-given powers were never used for anything of that kind.

Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the same description in plain words, that the people learned something that could divide a couple. The Book could have described the harm in grander terms, and it chooses the household instead, which is the smallest unit the reader lives inside.

The detail shows what the practice was for in the community's own market. Somebody paid a practitioner, and the practitioner did a job, and the job was to break a marriage. The verses around this one have described pledges to protect family, orphans and neighbours, and the sentence in front of the reader describes a trade that does the opposite for a fee.

**THE LIMIT SET AROUND MAGIC**

The sentence moves on: ***“and wife; although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will. They learned what harmed them”*** The verse puts a limit around the whole art, and it puts the limit in the middle of the sentence where nobody can skim past it. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads it as a statement that the magic of the practitioners could not harm anybody at all except by the permission of God. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same sense, that nothing of it lands without the will of God.

That clause removes two fears at once. It removes the terror of the reader who imagines that a paid practitioner holds an independent power over his life, and it removes the excuse of the practitioner who tells himself that the harm was caused by forces he only pointed at. Nothing in the universe runs outside the permission of its owner, and the man who sold the spell was selling a service that only worked in a world God was still running.

The same sentence says what the learners got out of it, and the answer is nothing. Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as a direct statement that they learned a thing which harmed them and gave them no benefit. Every field of knowledge in the world returns something to the person who studies it. This one returned the bill.

Think of a man who spends his savings on a device that breaks his own front door while leaving every other house in the street untouched. He has bought a tool with one use, and the use is against the people inside his own gate.

**HARM AND NO GOOD**

The sentence continues: ***“and did not benefit them”*** The verse repeats the uselessness as a separate charge, and the repetition is the Book's way of making the reader feel the weight of the purchase. No health, no wealth, no standing and no security came back to the buyer. The Book lets the empty return stand on its own for a moment before it turns to the thing the buyers already knew. The craft is judged in the same terms elsewhere: (20:69 — **“the magician will not succeed wherever he is”**).

**WHAT THEY ALREADY KNEW**

As the verse says: ***“although they already knew”*** Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains the structure of the next few words with unusual care. The community knew perfectly well that this practice was a sin and that it involved a rejection of God, and it knew that the practice could not help them. So the Book says first that they knew, and then closes the whole passage with the words if only they knew. The note draws the lesson out: a person who does not act on what he knows, and does not use his understanding to look at his own position, has knowledge that is no better than ignorance.

That is one of the sharpest observations in the commentary on this sūrah, and it explains why the Book keeps closing passages with the same phrase. The knowledge being described in the verse is not information about a subject. It is the understanding of a person's own situation, and a person can carry that understanding around for a lifetime without letting it touch a single decision.

**THE PRICE THE BUYER PAYS**

The verse records: ***“that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter. Miserable”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as the thing the community knew and ignored: the buyer of magic has no share in the next life. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the sentence in the same place, inside the knowledge the people already had.

The Book does not say that the practitioner would be punished, which would leave room for the hope of a reduced sentence. It says that the buyer has no share, which is the language of an inheritance denied. The sūrah has used the same word for the community's claim to an exclusive share of the Garden ((2:94)), and it turns the claim around here and applies it to a purchase the community was making in the market.

**THE SALE THEY MADE**

The verse says: ***“indeed was the price”*** The sentence is the same verdict the Book passed on the community's earlier bargain, where their trade of the next life for this one was called a miserable price ((2:90)). The repetition is a signal, and the reader is expected to hear it. The sūrah has shown him two markets in twenty verses, one where the community sold its share for a position and one where it bought a spell with the same share.

**WHAT WAS ON THE COUNTER**

The verse declares: ***“for which they sold their souls”*** The clause names what was on the counter. Al-Jalālayn and Ibn ʿAbbās both read the verse as the sale of the self, and the Book keeps the accounting in the same terms it used for the earlier trade. Nothing in the passage suggests that the buyers were foolish people. They were people who had decided that the thing in front of them was worth what they were paying.

A reader can test the arithmetic in his own life without much effort. Every person has something he would trade a portion of his future for, and the Book's judgement is that the price is always wrong when the seller has not looked at the whole invoice.

**IF THEY HAD UNDERSTOOD**

The wording runs: ***“if only they knew”*** The verse closes with the same words that will close the next verse as well ((2:103)). The phrase is the Book's way of leaving the reader inside the sentence instead of outside it. A community that knew and acted as though it did not is the subject of the verse, and the phrase invites every reader who is holding something he has already understood to take the same seat.

The next verse gives the community the alternative it did not take, and it does so in a sentence that is shorter than the loss it describes.

---
## Verse 2:103

> If only they were faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, there would have been a better reward from Allah, if only they knew

**THE CONDITION THEY MISSED**

The Book says: ***“If only they were faithful”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the conditional as a statement about belief and restraint: if the community had accepted the Messenger and the Book and had feared God enough to leave the practice of sorcery, the outcome would have been different. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the clause the same way, and he names the things the community would have had to put down, which are its inherited position and the trade in magic.

Al-Jalālayn draws attention to a feature of the sentence that a careful reader will want to know about. The answer to the conditional is not written out in the verse, and the reader has to take it from the words that follow, so that the full sense is that a reward from God would have been theirs. The omission is a small piece of style with a large effect, because the sentence ends up putting the reward and the price beside each other without ever naming the punishment.

The verse does not mention the practice by name in its first words. It names the state of the heart first, which is where the sūrah has been directing the reader for several pages. The deeds are the fruit, and the sentence starts at the root.

**THE REWARD THAT WOULD HAVE COME**

Then the verse says: ***“and mindful ˹of Allah˺, there would have been a better reward from Allah”*** Al-Jalālayn notes that the answer to the conditional is left out and has to be supplied from what follows, so that the sense is that a reward from God would have been waiting for them. The clause compares that reward with the thing the community had sold itself for, and the comparison is the whole point of the sentence. Nothing about the alternative required a sacrifice of goods. It required the community to keep the covenant it had already signed.

Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the comparison in plain words: the reward from God would have been far better for them than what they took, if they had only known.

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the pair of conditions as two doors that were open at the same time: faith in the Messenger and the Book, and a turning away from the inherited position and the trade in magic. He adds the note that the community knew all of this from its own scriptures, which is why the closing phrase of the verse stings the way it does.

Think of a man who resigns from a job with a fixed salary to sell a gadget he does not understand, and who does the sums for the first time after the money is spent. The offer he walked away from was never hidden, and the difference between the two incomes was printed on the paper he signed.

**THE UNDERSTANDING THEY LACKED**

In the verse's own words: ***“if only they knew”*** Al-Jalālayn and Ibn ʿAbbās both read the closing phrase as the third and last step of the same argument. The community is told what it would have received, and the sentence ends by naming the thing it lacked, which was not the offer but the understanding of the offer. Ibn ʿAbbās adds the report that they had this knowledge in their own book.

Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the reward in the same simple frame, that a reward from God would have been far better for them, and he keeps the two halves of the sentence in the order the Book gives them. The community's own books had carried the news of the Messenger, and the teaching they had taken up instead was doing harm to the households of the very people who paid for it.

The phrase closes two verses in a row, and its repetition is one of the strongest effects in the sūrah. The Book does not shout at this community. It tells it, three times in a row, that the information was available, and then it lets the reader sit with the gap between what the people knew and how they lived.

---
## Verse 2:104

> O believers! Do not say, “Râ’ina.” [Herd us!] But say, “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!] and listen ˹attentively˺. And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment

**THE WORD THE BELIEVERS WERE TOLD TO DROP**

The verse begins: ***“O believers! Do not say, “Râ’ina.” [Herd us!]”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the word and the reason for the ban. It is an imperative that the community used when addressing the Messenger, and in Hebrew the same sound carried a meaning taken from a root for thoughtlessness, so the community found it funny and used it as a way of insulting him while appearing to be polite. The believers were told to stop using it because the word had been turned into a weapon.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān gives the fuller story. In Arabic the word meant be mindful of us, and it was an ordinary way of asking a speaker to give a listener his attention. In Hebrew it was a curse. The community intended the second meaning, the Arabs could not hear the difference, and some Muslims began using the word in good faith, which gave the community a way to insult the Messenger openly while the believers joined in without knowing.

tafsir_initial reports al-Ṭabarī's careful discussion of the matter, and his conclusion is worth keeping. The phrase came from an idiomatic expression that meant something like lend me your ear, and in the region of Makkah and Madinah that way of speaking to a person was considered demeaning. Al-Ṭabarī considers the wider opinion that the Prophet was in the habit of replacing coarse expressions with finer ones, and he sets aside the theory that the whole matter turned on a Hebrew pun. His reason is plain: the command is addressed to the believers, and a group of believers would not have taken up a phrase whose meaning they could not understand.

The note adds a second reading of the verse, which points to a verse in the sūrah of Light where the believers are told not to treat the Messenger's call to them the way they treat each other's calls ((24:63)). The command in this verse and the command in that one are aimed at the same careless habit, which is the habit of speaking to a prophet as though he were one of the neighbours.

**THE WORD THEY WERE GIVEN INSTEAD**

The wording is: ***“But say, “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!]”*** The Book does not leave the believers without words. It hands them a replacement with the same practical meaning, which asks the speaker to give him attention and to wait for him. Al-Jalālayn glosses the new word as: look at us, and give ear to what you are commanded. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the replacement and its sense side by side.

The method here is worth noticing, because the sūrah uses it more than once. A community finds a way to say something ugly in the clothing of something polite, and the Book takes the word away and gives the believers an honest word for the same request. The door for the insult is closed without a debate about who meant what.

Think of a school where a group of pupils starts using an ordinary word as a code for an insult. The word sounds harmless in the register and the teachers cannot punish it, so the staff stop using it in class and teach the children a different way of asking for help. The mockery has nothing left to stand on.

**LISTEN, AND A WARNING FOR THOSE WHO REJECT**

The command to listen is the second half of the instruction, and it changes the sentence from a rule about vocabulary into a rule about attention. The believers were told to give the Messenger the hearing he had been asking for, using words that were clean and an ear that was open.

Then the verse says: ***“and listen ˹attentively˺. And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the closing line as a statement about the people who had turned the word into a joke, and he identifies the punishment as the Fire. The verse ends by naming the group that had been amusing itself at the Messenger's expense, and the sentence moves the matter from the level of manners to the level of belief.

The next verse stays with the same subject, and it gives the reader the reason the community could not be pleased by any good that came to the believers.

---
## Verse 2:105

> The disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord, but Allah selects whoever He wills for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty

**THE TWO GROUPS WHO WISHED IT AWAY**

The verse begins with the words: ***“The disbelievers from the People of the Book”*** The verse opens by naming the two groups that shared the attitude, the disbelievers among the People of the Book and the polytheists. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains the situation the verse answers. Some of the community had been assuring the believers of their goodwill and telling them that they would have welcomed a better teaching for the Muslims if one had arrived. The verse answers the claim by describing the actual feeling.

The Book has spent twenty verses on the community's agreements, its distortion of scripture, its appetite for magic and its mockery of the Messenger's name. The sentence now takes the mask off the goodwill and names what was underneath it, without any need for argument.

**WHAT THEY WANTED TO END**

The verse adds: ***“and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the clause as a statement about the wish rather than the act: neither group would want any good to come to the believers, and the Book describes the resentment as a settled condition of the heart. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws out the point that the jealousy is not about a particular gift. It is about the idea that the blessing should arrive at all, and it does not care which blessing it is.

tafsir_initial explains what the blessing means in this sentence. The commentators read it as the revelation and the wisdom that came with the prophethood of Muhammad, and the note lists the places where the Book states that the choice of a messenger belongs to God ((3:179), (16:2), (40:15)). The envy of the two groups was not directed at a message they had read and rejected. It was directed at the fact that the message had gone to that household instead of another.

**THE CHOICE THAT BELONGS TO GOD**

The verse states: ***“but Allah selects whoever He wills”*** The sentence is the answer the sūrah has given twice already, once when the community resented the grace given to a servant of God's choosing ((2:90)), and again when the claim of an exclusive hereafter was met with a test ((2:94)). The choice belongs to the One who owns the mercy, and the resentment is aimed past the messenger at the sender.

Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the clause short in his rendering, and the shortness is what makes it effective. The whole objection of two communities is answered in four words, and nothing about the answer invites a negotiation.

**MERCY AND THE LORD OF BOUNTY**

The verse declares: ***“for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty”*** The verse ends with the widest word in its sentence. The bounty the Book names is not a fixed quantity that one group can take away from another, and the mercy of God is not a pie that has to be divided. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the closing phrase as a description of the size of what God gives.

The passage that began with a community throwing a book behind its back now ends with a statement about the supply of mercy. A reader who has followed the sūrah to this point has watched the Book answer broken covenants with patience, distortion with a broader revelation, and envy with a sentence about the giver. The next few verses turn to a question that the same two communities put to the Prophet about the verses themselves.

Think of two neighbours who stand in the street complaining about a will they have read, because a third family has been left something they wanted. Neither of them has spoken to the person who wrote the will, and the sum waiting to be shared out has not become smaller because it went to somebody else's door.

---
## Verse 2:106

> If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything

**THE VERSE THAT IS REPLACED**

The Book says: ***“If We ever abrogate a verse”*** Al-Jalālayn gives the occasion. The disbelievers had begun to mock the whole matter of abrogation, saying that one day Muhammad orders his companions to do a thing and the next day he forbids it. Ibn ʿAbbās puts the same complaint in the mouth of the Quraysh: why do you command us to do something and then forbid it?

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān sets out the change that gave the complaint its material. The Muslims at first prayed facing the Sacred House in Jerusalem, and later they were commanded to turn towards the Kaʿbah. Other rulings were also replaced or set aside. The community's enemies took the changes as evidence that the Book was being edited by a man, and their purpose was to plant a doubt in the minds of the believers.

Al-Jalālayn explains the two ways a verse can be dealt with. In one case the ruling is removed while the words stay in the Book, so that the verse continues to be recited after it stops being acted upon. In the other case the words themselves are set aside. The verse covers both, and it answers them with one sentence about the replacement.

Ibn Kathīr devotes a section to the term and reports the explanation given by Ibn ʿAbbās through Ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, which is the plain one: whatever verse is abrogated, its replacement arrives from the same source as the original. Nothing in the arrangement passes out of the owner's hand.

**WHAT COMES IN ITS PLACE**

The wording is: ***“or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar explains the replacement in terms of benefit. When God removes a ruling or causes people to forget it, He brings something better for the situation it addresses, either for the moment or for what comes later, or He brings something similar. The change is attributed to wisdom and knowledge rather than to a second thought.

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the word better in the same practical direction, as something easier to carry out and more profitable for the people who have to live with it. That is worth holding on to, because the objection in the mouths of the community assumed that a change must be a loss. The verse answers the assumption before it answers the objection.

The Book makes the same point in the sūrah of the Bee, where the replacement of one verse by another is reported along with the accusation it produced ((16:101 — **“When We replace a verse with another—and Allah knows best what He reveals—they say, ‘You are just a fabricator.’ In fact, most of them do not know”**)). The final clause is the diagnosis the sūrah gives for the whole complaint. The people were watching the changes without holding the picture of the One who was making them.

Think of a doctor who adjusts a patient's prescription as the treatment moves from week to week. The doses change, the tablets change, and the doctor's diagnosis never changes. A man who stood outside the clinic and counted the prescriptions would see nothing but contradictions. A man who sat inside the consultation would see one plan being carried out.

**THE QUESTION THAT FOLLOWS**

The verse does not only promise a better replacement. It allows for one that is similar, which closes a second door. A person might accept a change when the replacement is plainly an improvement and object when it is not, and the sentence takes that objection away in advance. The owner of the law may replace a ruling with something equal to it, and the arrangement is no less his for that.

The verse declares: ***“or similar one. Do you not know”*** The question form is worth noticing. The Book does not lecture the objectors about the mechanics of revelation. It asks them whether they know who they are dealing with, and the question is aimed at the root of the complaint, which was never about the rulings themselves.

**POWER OVER EVERYTHING**

The verse puts it: ***“that Allah is Most Capable of everything”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the closing sentence as the ground of the whole answer: God has power over everything, He does as He wills, and He rules as He wishes. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same sense in his comment on the verse.

The sentence is short and it removes the frame the objectors had been using. The community had been treating the law as a document that a person writes once and cannot revise, and it treated every revision as proof that a human hand was holding the pen. The Book answers by naming the owner of the universe, for whom the first ruling and the replacement are both part of a single plan.

The next verse continues the same question and widens it from a specific ruling to the whole of what God owns.

---
## Verse 2:107

> Do you not know that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah, and you have no guardian or helper besides Allah

**THE QUESTION THAT OPENS THE ARGUMENT**

In the verse's own words: ***“Do you not know”*** The verse repeats the question that opened the previous sentence, and the repetition ties the two verses together as one argument. Al-Jalālayn reads the sequence as a single movement: the first question establishes the power, and the second establishes the ownership that goes with it.

A reader who has been following the sūrah will recognise the method. The Book has asked this community a set of questions across the last fifty verses, and each one has been designed so that the answer would settle the matter being disputed without any further debate.

**THE KINGDOM THAT BELONGS TO HIM**

The wording is: ***“that the kingdom of the heavens”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as a statement that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs to God, and that He acts within it as He pleases. Al-Mukhtaṣar spells out the consequence for the complaint that started this passage: God instructs His servants as He wills, forbids what He wills, establishes the law as He wishes, and removes what He wishes from it.

tafsir_initial notes a reading of the same passage in which the question is addressed to the Jewish community and not to the Prophet. On that reading, the clause about having no friend or helper besides God answers the assumption that the people had an ally in heaven who would speak for them on the day of judgement.

The ownership of the heavens and the earth is the widest claim the Book makes about God, and it is placed here to answer a question about the wording of a few rulings. The Book does not scale its answers to the size of the objection. It scales them to the size of the truth the objection has forgotten.

**THE EARTH INCLUDED**

The sentence continues: ***“and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah, and you have no guardian”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the two closing nouns as the help a person needs in two directions: a friend who can bring him benefit, and a helper who can hold back punishment. Al-Jalālayn gives the same pair, a protector to keep a person safe and a helper to keep the chastisement away when it arrives.

The sentence removes the last piece of ground the objectors could stand on. A person may complain about how another man runs his business, and the complaint is at least imaginable if he has some claim on the business or a friend inside it. The verse tells the reader that neither claim exists. The property is God's alone, and the whole population of the earth has no standing to bring to the counter.

Think of a tenant who objects to the colour the owner has chosen for the front door of the building. The objection can be reasonable, and the tenant can make it with respect. What he cannot do is inform the owner that the doorway belongs to the tenant's family, because the deeds were signed before the tenant arrived, and the address of the owner is in the register.

**NO PROTECTOR BESIDE HIM**

The verse puts the matter: ***“or helper besides Allah”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar closes the verse by naming the practical comfort the sentence carries for the reader as well as the rebuke it carries for the objector. God is the guardian who takes care of His servants, and no other guardian can defend a person from harm. The verse has now answered the complaint about the replaced rulings and has given the believer a place to stand when a ruling he was used to is lifted.

The next verse turns from the question of the verses to a question of the questions themselves, and it reaches back to the community of Moses for its example.

---
## Verse 2:108

> Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger as Moses was asked before? But whoever trades belief for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way

**THE REQUEST LIKE AN OLDER ONE**

The wording runs: ***“Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger”*** Al-Jalālayn gives the occasion from one side: the people of Makkah asked the Prophet to enlarge the boundaries of the city and to fill its valley with gold, and the verse came down in answer. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the verse as a warning against demands of that kind, including the demand to see God and to hear His speech. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān gives another request that was made to him: that he should bring the whole Qur'an down at once, in the way the Torah had come to Moses in one delivery.

Al-Saʿdī makes the distinction that a careful reader needs here, and it is one of the most useful sentences in the commentaries on this passage. The questions the verse forbids are the questions of resistance and argument, asked to test a prophet and to score a point against him. The questions of a person who wants to learn and be guided are praised in the Book, and the servants of God are told to ask the people of knowledge when they do not know ((16:43)). The Quran itself answers such people in passage after passage. The line the verse draws is not between questions and silence. It is between a student and a litigant.

Ibn Kathīr places the verse beside an instruction in the fifth sūrah, where the believers are told not to ask about matters that would trouble them if they were disclosed ((5:101)). He reads both passages as a restraint on curiosity that has nothing to do with the love of learning.

**THE DEMAND MADE IN AN EARLIER AGE**

The verse puts the question: ***“as Moses was asked before?”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar names the request that stands as the example: the demand of the people of Moses to see God openly ((4:153)). Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same, that the community asked to see their Lord and to hear Him speak. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān adds the observation that these demands were not made in the spirit of enquiry, since the intention behind them was never to accept an answer.

The sūrah has already told this story twice. It told how the demand to see God was met with a thunderbolt ((2:55)), and how the request was repeated elsewhere in the Book with the same result ((4:153)). A community that had read those accounts in the same book was now standing in front of a prophet and making the same request with new wording, and the verse asks whether the believers want to walk into the same corridor.

Think of a family that hires an architect to draw a house. The drawings arrive, the plans are sound, and one member of the family spends every meeting demanding that the architect prove he exists by lifting the foundations with his hands. Nothing about the house is being discussed after the first week, and the family is still paying rent while the meeting goes on.

**THE TRADE BETWEEN BELIEF AND DENIAL**

As the verse says: ***“But whoever trades belief”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as the consequence for the person who takes disbelief in place of faith, and he describes the trade as the failure to look at the clear proofs while asking for something else instead. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sense of a person who chooses one thing in place of another.

The sūrah has used the language of buying and selling for this community twice already ((2:90), (2:102)), and it uses it a third time here. A reader who has watched the accounting through the chapter can see the pattern the Book is building. The community in each scene has something valuable in its hands, and in each scene it hands the thing over for something it wanted more.

**THE ROAD THEY LEFT**

The verse records: ***“for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way”*** Al-Jalālayn supplies the picture behind the word for the right way, which comes from a root meaning the middle. The road is not the edge. It is the centre line, and a person who leaves the middle has left it in one of two directions.

Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the verdict plain, that a person who exchanges faith for disbelief has lost the balanced road. The sentence closes a passage that opened with a community mocking the revision of rulings, and it ends by naming the price of the mockery. The next verse returns to the community's envy and gives the believers an instruction about how to live beside it.

---
## Verse 2:109

> Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them. Pardon and bear with them until Allah delivers His decision. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything

**WHAT THEY WISH FOR YOU**

The verse declares: ***“Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the wish in its plainest form: many of the People of the Book would like to see the believers return to the worship of idols, as they had before their faith arrived. Ibn ʿAbbās names some of the people involved and identifies the believers the verse addresses.

The sentence does not describe an argument. It describes a wish, and the Book is precise about the difference. These people were not writing books of refutation or studying the claims of the new community. They were hoping for its collapse, and the Book reports the hope as the thing it is.

**THE ENVY BEHIND IT**

Its words are: ***“because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them. Pardon”*** Al-Jalālayn names the motive and its source in a way that leaves no room for confusion: the envy came from their own souls, and it arrived after the truth about the Messenger had become clear to them in their own book. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the same, that the truth had become plain to them.

That clause is the one that turns a disagreement into a charge. Two people can differ about a matter in good faith, and the Book allows for that. What it does not allow is the pretence of ignorance in a community that has read its own scriptures on the subject. The verse tells the readers that the envy is not produced by the evidence, because the evidence is already settled.

The instruction that follows is the answer the Book gives to being wished off your feet. Al-Jalālayn reads the command as an instruction to leave them alone and to make no move against them. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the same instruction and adds the reason: forgive them and pardon them for their ignorance, until the command of God arrives about them.

Think of a man who takes a job at a company where two senior colleagues had expected one of themselves to get the post. Both of them had seen his record and had spoken to the interview panel. The new man is told to get on with his work and to leave their attitude alone for the time being, not because their envy is harmless, but because the matter has an owner who will settle it on his own timetable.

**BEAR WITH THEM**

The wording continues: ***“and bear with them”*** The second command carries a stronger sense than the first. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the pair as an instruction to forgive them what they do and to pass over their misconduct without retaliation. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same in the same order, that the believers were told to leave them and to overlook their behaviour.

The instruction is one of the most demanding in the sūrah, because it is given to a community that had been reading, for a hundred verses, about what the other community had done to its own prophets. The believers are told what the record contains, and then they are told to be patient beside the people who carry that record, which is a much harder position than ignorance would have been.

**UNTIL THE DECISION COMES**

The text says: ***“until Allah delivers His decision. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as a waiting period that ends when God brings His command about them, and he identifies that command as concerning the fighting that would follow. Al-Mukhtaṣar sets out the three shapes the matte took when the command arrived: acceptance of Islam, payment of the protection tax, or the use of force.

Those words describe the end of the waiting period, and the Book has already shown the reader what the waiting period was for. The community that wished the believers off their road was given time, and some of its members used that time to accept the message and join the community they had been envying.

The verse closes with the sentence that ended the previous two verses in this passage, that God is capable of everything. The Book repeats it because the reader needs it in a scene where he is being asked to wait without knowing how the matter will turn out.

---
## Verse 2:110

> Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**TWO DUTIES AND A PROMISE**

The community has just been told to bear with its enemies while the matter is decided. The next sentence tells it what to do with the years of waiting. The answer is the two duties that have stood at the end of every list in this sūrah: prayer and the alms-tax.

In the verse's own words: ***“Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth”*** Al-Ṭabarī opens his treatment of the verse by pointing back to his earlier discussion of both duties. The sūrah had already explained them, one as a duty performed with all its conditions and the other as a payment given willingly to those entitled to receive it. He does not repeat that work here, which tells the reader that the duties being named are old knowledge in this community, and that the verse is arranging them to be used.

Al-Baghawī gives the sense of the good that a person sends forward: it is obedience and good work. He records a second reading of the word, in which the good means wealth given out in the alms-tax. He adds the detail that the return on such a gift reaches even a single date given away, and a single morsel of food.

tafsir_initial observes that the phrase about sending good forward is joined to prayer and to charity here, and again in the sūrah of the Enshrouded One ((73:20)). It explains the meaning of finding it with God: the fruit of a person's deeds is met on the Day of Judgement. The Book is talking about a deposit account whose statement arrives on a day when the account cannot be reopened.

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the two duties in the plain terms they were given to the community. Prayer means the five daily prayers performed properly, and the alms-tax means the portion of a person's wealth that belongs to the poor. He then reads the good that is sent forward as the good deeds and the charity a person puts away for himself, and he reads the closing sentence as God's knowledge of the intention behind the gift rather than only the gift. On that reading, the smallest coin given in the right spirit is a deposit with a witness attached to it.

**WHAT YOU SEND AHEAD**

The clause about the future is the answer the reader needs to the instruction about patience. While the waiting lasts, the person who has been wished harm can keep busy with something that cannot be taken from him. The Book then names the place where the deposit is held, and the naming is the comfort in the sentence.

The sentence reads: ***“for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do”*** Ibn Kathīr reads the verse as a promise in the form of a description, and he records the practice of one of the companions who heard the Prophet recite these words. After this verse, the recitation would end with the statement that God sees all things. The companion's report adds that the Prophet often paused in the middle of his recitation to pray in line with what the verse he was reciting had said.

That single report is worth keeping in mind while reading the passage. A person does not only read the command to send good forward. He stops at the sentence about God seeing what he does and answers it, and the man who heard the pause wrote it down for the people who would come to the verse later.

Think of a worker who spends two years at a company where a senior colleague is quietly working for his removal. He cannot solve the colleague, and he has been told to leave the matter to the owner. What he can do in the meantime is fill his own box in the company's pension scheme, which is the one part of his position that the colleague cannot reach.

---
## Verse 2:111

> The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof if what you say is true.”

**THE CLAIM EACH GROUP MAKES**

In the verse's own words: ***“The Jews and Christians each claim”*** Al-Qurṭubī sets out the claim in the form the two communities made it: the Jews said that nobody would enter the Garden except a Jew, and the Christians said that nobody would enter it except a Christian. Al-Baghawī reports the same two claims with the wording the reports give them, and he records the grammatical discussion among the early scholars about the word used for the Jewish claim.

tafsir_initial lists the places where the Qur'an meets the same claim again. The next verse shows each community saying that the other stands on nothing ((2:113)). Another passage has right guidance described as following only their own religion ((2:135)). A third has the two communities calling themselves the children of God and His beloved ((5:18)). The sūrah of the Congregation puts the claim to be God's chosen people to the test of wishing for death ((62:6)).
