The note adds the reminder that the Book deals with the same claim in the fourth sūrah ((4:123-124)).

A reader should notice how often this claim appears in the Book, and how the Book keeps answering it. The community making the claim was not asking a question about the next life. It was describing the arrangement it had grown up inside, and the answer it received in every place was the same.

**THE ANSWER THE VERSE GIVES**

The verse says: ***“that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof”*** The sentence that stands in the middle of the verse is the Book's verdict on the claim, and it names it as a wish. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the word in his rendering, that these are the desires of the two communities and nothing more. The claim had been dressed as information about the next world, and the Book takes the clothing off it.

Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the instruction that follows: the Prophet is told to ask them for their proof, the evidence on which they are standing. tafsir_initial explains the word for proof, which means a demonstration or an evidence. The note adds that the Book uses the same word in the sūrahs of the Prophets and the Ant when a claim needs to be brought to the table ((21:24), (23:117), (27:64), (28:75)).

The request is one of the fairest sentences in the Book, and it is worth noticing what it does not say. It does not tell the two communities that they are wrong about the next life, and it does not claim that the Garden is reserved for somebody else. It asks for the document. A person may believe anything he likes about the arrangements of the world to come, and if his belief rests on a promise then the promise can be produced and examined.

Think of two men in a corridor arguing about whose name is on a will. One of them has heard the news from his father, and the other has heard a version from his uncle. Neither of them has been to the lawyer's office, and the door is open. The Book's question is short: show me the paper, and then the two of them can stop arguing about what they have heard.

**THE PROOF THEY WERE ASKED FOR**

The wording runs: ***“if what you say is true.””*** Al-Jalālayn reads the closing clause as the condition attached to the challenge, that the claim stands only if the people have something to stand on. The verse ends without an answer because the answer arrives in the next verse, where the Book sets out what the actual arrangement is: whoever submits himself to God and does good work has his reward kept with his Lord ((2:112)).

The passage that began with a community mocking the revision of verses now ends with the same community asked to produce its evidence about the next life. The next verses will show that the two communities level the same claim against each other, and the Book will answer both of them in one sentence.

---
## Verse 2:112

> But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**THE WORD THAT CLOSES THE CLAIM**

The verse has it: ***“But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah”*** The verse opens with the word that closes the claim made by the two communities. Al-Jalālayn reads the answer as a statement about who enters the Garden: whoever submits his purpose to God and holds to His commands. He explains why the Book uses the word for the face or the self in this sentence. The face is the noblest part of a person, and if the whole purpose has surrendered, the rest of a person follows.

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the phrase as sincerity of religion and work done for God. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads it as sincerity in turning back to God, serving Him, and following what the final Messenger brought, whatever group a person came into the world inside. The clause about the group is the part that answers the claim of the previous verse. The Book does not say that the Garden belongs to one community and its neighbours. It says that it belongs to the person who submits himself, and it leaves the person's family tree out of the sentence entirely.

Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the condition that a reader of the final revelation needs to hear. The promise belongs to those who follow the Messenger, and after his coming the path that is accepted is the one he brought. The earlier communities were told the same thing in their own time and in their own books, which is what makes the claim of exclusive entry in the verse before this one so strange.

**THE CONDITION THE VERSE SETS**

The verse continues: ***“and does good will have their reward with their Lord.”*** The first condition is about the direction a person's life faces, and the second is about what he does while facing it. Al-Jalālayn reads the clause about doing good as a description of a person who affirms the Oneness of God and behaves accordingly. Ibn Kathīr reads the phrase as following the religion of God and doing it well. The Book keeps the pair together everywhere it states the promise, and it has stated it in this sūrah twice before ((2:62), (2:82)).

The promise attached to the pair is that the reward is kept with God. The Book uses the same phrasing it used in the earlier passage about the People of the Book and the Sabians ((2:62)). A reader who has followed the sūrah will notice that the sentence is not new. The Book has been offering the same arrangement to everyone who would take it since its early pages, and it returns to the sentence at the end of a long argument about privilege.

**AND WHAT IT BRINGS**

Then come the words: ***“And there will be no fear”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the two clauses as the two halves of the promise: no fear of punishment in the world to come, and no grief over what has been left behind. Ibn ʿAbbās draws the pair out in the same direction, with fear attaching to the outcome and grief attaching to loss.

This is the third time the sentence has appeared in the sūrah, and the reader is expected to hear it each time in the company of a different audience ((2:38), (2:62)). The Book keeps the same comfort for the believer from any community who does the work, which is a steadiness of promise that the sūrah has been demonstrating in every passage since its opening.

**FEAR AND GRIEF LIFTED**

The verse puts the matter: ***“for them, nor will they grieve”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the two clauses in the plain modern sense: no fear about what is waiting for a person after death, and no sorrow about what he has left behind in this life. The verse then stops, and it has answered the entire claim of the previous verse in four short clauses and without a single mention of ancestry.

Think of two families arguing for a month about which one has the right to a seat in a stadium that neither of them has ever bought a ticket for. A third man walks past both families to the gate, holds up his ticket and goes in. The argument does not need the referee, and the gate does not know the families' names.

---
## Verse 2:113

> The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on” and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,” although both recite the Scriptures. And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺. Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute

**THE ACCUSATION THE JEWS MAKE**

The verse records: ***“The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on””*** Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as a mutual accusation: the Jewish community said that the Christians had nothing to stand on, and in saying so it rejected Jesus. Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the two groups in the conversation, the Jews of Madinah and the Christians of Najran, and says that each of them claimed that no religion was true except its own.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws the wider observation out of the pair of sentences. The two communities were hostile to each other as much as to the new Muslims. They had come to identify their religion with an affiliation, rather than with the doctrines it taught and the deeds it required. The verse shows the result of that shift, which is a community that can recite a book it no longer listens to.

The pair of accusations has an obvious hole in it, and the Book lets the reader find the hole before the next clause names it. Each community said that the other had nothing to stand on. Each community said this about people who held the same core teaching of the One God and who had received a scripture from Him.

**THE ACCUSATION THE CHRISTIANS MAKE**

The sentence moves on: ***“and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,””*** Al-Jalālayn notes the symmetry of the charge: the Christians rejected Moses in the same way the Jews rejected Jesus, and each side threw away the part of the story that did not belong to it. That is the shape of the argument as the verse reports it, and the Book keeps the two halves identical on purpose.

Ibn Kathīr reads the same mutual denial in the passage, and he places it between the challenge of the previous verse and the answer of the one before it. The reader is shown a community claiming the Garden, then denying its neighbours a standing place, and then being told what the actual arrangement is.

**THE BOOK THEY BOTH RECITE**

The verse says: ***“although both recite the Scriptures.”*** The clause in the middle of the verse is the Book's whole verdict, and it is delivered as a fact rather than as an argument. Al-Jalālayn observes that the two communities recite the scripture that was sent to them, and that the Jewish book carries the confirmation of Jesus while the Christian book carries the confirmation of Moses.

Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the clause the same way, and he points out what the scriptures they read commanded, which was to believe in all the prophets without drawing a line between them. The two communities were reading the command every week in the books that defined their communities, and each of them was using the book to reject the prophet named in the other book.

Think of two brothers who inherited a letter from their father and who both quote it at every family meeting. Each of them has read the paragraph naming the other son and the share that was left to him, and each of them skips that paragraph whenever the letter comes out of the drawer.

**THE IGNORANT WHO SAID THE SAME**

The wording continues: ***“And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺. Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute”*** The verse then adds the third group and the sharper comparison. Al-Mukhtasar explains that in this behaviour the two communities are like people who know nothing at all, since the idolaters reject every prophet and every scripture. The doctors who read the chart are behaving like the patients who never opened the file.

Al-Jalālayn closes the verse by naming the court where the dispute will be settled, and the Book does not give the verdict in this world at all. That restraint is worth noticing. The verse reports the accusation, names the fact that both sides read the books, and then hands the matter to the Day of Judgement.

The next verse turns from the argument about the books to a far heavier charge, and the subject is a house of worship and the people who try to close it.

---
## Verse 2:114

> Who does more wrong than those who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship and strive to destroy them? Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear. For them is disgrace in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter

**THE WORST WRONGDOERS NAMED**

The verse has it: ***“Who does more wrong than those”*** The question is one of the Book's strongest forms of condemnation, and Al-Jalālayn reads it as a statement that nobody does greater evil than the person described in the sentence that follows. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the occasion from the side of the earlier history. He names the ruler he understands the verse to be describing, the king who destroyed Jerusalem and whose soldiers filled the sanctuary with the dead.

tafsir_initial sets out the candidates the commentators named. Some understood the mosques in the verse to be the Temple in Jerusalem, called the farthest mosque in the sūrah of the Night Journey ((17:1)), together with the Kaʿbah in Makkah. They gave differing accounts of who destroyed the Temple. Others connected the verse with the year when the people of Makkah stopped the Prophet from entering the city to pray at the Kaʿbah ((6/628)). The note also explains the word for mosques, which comes from the verb for prostrating.

The two readings leave the sentence with the same force. A person who keeps other people out of a place of worship, or who pulls the place down around them, has attacked the arrangement between people and their Lord. The attack happens in the one spot where the two sides were free to meet.

**THE NAME PREVENTED FROM BEING MENTIONED**

The text says: ***“who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the offence in the plainest available terms. The people in the sentence stop the name of God from being said in His houses, and they prevent prayer, remembrance and the reading of the Book inside them. They also try to ruin those houses, either by pulling them down or by keeping worshippers away from them.

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the prevention as the blocking of the declaration of God's Oneness and the call to prayer in the sanctuary. He describes the destruction in the reports as the filling of the place with the bodies of the dead. The picture that comes out of the reports is not a debate about buildings. It is a campaign to make a house of God unusable as a house of God.

The Book has spent a hundred verses on a community that broke covenants, distorted books and argued about angels. The charge in this verse is of a different order, and the Book marks the difference with the question that opens it. A person can argue about the address of a house of worship. The people in this scene are locking the door.

**THE EFFORT TO DESTROY**

The verse goes on: ***“and strive to destroy them?”*** The verb carries effort, and the effort is the part that fixes the responsibility. A building can be damaged in a war or by an earthquake, and nobody is asked to account for the weather. The verse describes people who work at the ruin of the place, which means they have planned it, paid for it and returned to the task more than once.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws the rulings out of the verse for the community that would come after it. Every mosque in the world is owed the same respect, and the desecration of any one of them is as grave as the desecration of the three that carry the highest rank. The note adds the ranks and the rewards attached to prayer in them, and then the practical point that the verse is the foundation of the rule.

A reader should notice that the verse does not restrict its protection to one building or one community. The protection belongs to places of worship as such, which is why the commentators could build a general law about mosques on a verse that first described events in Jerusalem and Makkah.

**THE HOUSES THEY MAY NOT ENTER**

The verse records: ***“Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear.”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as both a statement and an order. The people who did this have no right to enter the sanctuaries except in fear, and the words also command the believers to strike that fear into them. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same clause as a statement about the rulers who destroyed the sanctuary, who would not enter it again except in hiding and in fear of the believers.

Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the practical shape of the sentence. The people who try to ruin the houses of God should not enter them except in fear and with trembling hearts, after the harm they have done.

The sentence is one of the few in the sūrah that describes a punishment carried out inside this world rather than at the end of it. The Book has told the community about a hereafter for several pages. Here it tells the reader that a person who attacks a place of worship will not walk into one comfortably again. The place he ruined will be a room full of people who know what he did.

Think of a man who breaks into a school at night and tears down the notice board, smashes the water tanks and scatters the books. The building can be repaired in a month. What does not repair is the walk he has to make past the gate every morning, because the parents standing there all know what he did, and he knows that they know.

**SHAME THAT ARRIVES HERE FIRST**

The Book says: ***“For them is disgrace in this world”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the sentence as shame and humiliation in this life at the hands of the believers. The word the Book uses is the same one it has used twice already for the community that broke its covenants ((2:61), (2:85)). The repetition ties the fate of the people who close the doors of worship to the record of the people who broke their agreements.

The Book is not describing a punishment that the readers have to wait for. A person who pulls down a place of prayer in a town where people pray will live the rest of his life among neighbours who watched him do it.

**THE PUNISHMENT THAT FOLLOWS**

Then come the words: ***“and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter”*** The second half of the verdict covers what this world cannot reach. Al-Jalālayn keeps the sentence as the punishment of the next life, and the verse ends by joining the two judgements the Book keeps separate elsewhere. Some harm is paid for in a courtroom, and some harm has to wait for the court that owns the whole file.

The next verse moves from the doors of the sanctuaries to the four directions of the earth, and it answers the argument that had grown up around the direction of prayer.

---
## Verse 2:115

> To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah. Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing

**BOTH DIRECTIONS BELONG TO HIM**

The verse begins: ***“To Allah belong the east”*** Al-Jalālayn gives the two occasions the commentators supplied for the verse. It came down either when the Jewish community criticised the change of the direction of prayer, or when the believers wanted to know about the extra prayers they offered on a journey. A traveller may pray facing any direction he can manage. The verse answers both questions with one fact: the east and the west belong to God, and the two of them stand for the whole earth.

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the verse as a provision for the person who does not know the correct direction of prayer. He reports the group of companions it was revealed about, who had done their best to work out the direction while travelling, had prayed facing the wrong way, and were relieved by the verse. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the other practical case, of a person who makes a mistake or is unsure. To God belongs every direction, and a person cannot face a direction that is outside the property of its owner.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān sets out the three groups that had been troubling the community about the direction of prayer and about the houses of worship. It then shows how the verse answers the argument about the old direction without conceding the point. The change of the direction was not the surrender of one piece of land to another. It was the owner of the land telling His servants where to stand.

**WHEREVER YOU TURN**

The wording continues: ***“and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah. Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as a promise with two halves. A person who turns in prayer as he has been commanded is turning towards the direction with which God is pleased. A person who cannot determine the direction is still inside the ownership of the One he is addressing. The closing pair of names, the All-Encompassing and the All-Knowing, carries the same two ideas. The first is the wide mercy that covers a person's difficulty, and the second is the knowledge that sees the intention behind the direction.

tafsir_initial collects the other places where the Book describes God as the owner of the horizons. The sūrah of the Enshrouded One calls Him the Lord of the east and the west ((73:9)). The sūrah of the Most Merciful names Him the Lord of the two easts and the two wests ((55:17)). Another sūrah uses the plural, the Lord of the easts and the wests ((70:40)). The note also points at the famous verse of light, where the olive tree that fuels the lamp is described as belonging neither to the east nor to the west ((24:35)). The whole family of verses makes the same point: no patch of the earth is closer to God than another, and no compass can point a person out of His reach.

Think of a man who lives in a country where the government owns every road, and who spends a week arguing about which highway he must take to the capital. He is not being asked which road he prefers. He is being told that whichever road he takes, he is driving on the same government's land, and the offices at the other end are open in both directions.

---
## Verse 2:116

> They say, “Allah has offspring.” Glory be to Him! In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth—all are subject to His Will

**THE CLAIM ABOUT OFFSPRING**

The verse begins with the words: ***“They say, “Allah has offspring.” Glory be to Him!”*** Al-Jalālayn names the groups behind the claim: the Jewish and Christian communities and those who said that the angels were the daughters of God. Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the two names the claims attached to, Ezra among the Jews and the Messiah among the Christians. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān adds the third group, the idolaters of Makkah, who called the angels the daughters of God.

tafsir_initial sets the verse in a wider family of passages that deny the claim. The Arab pagan belief that the angels were God's daughters is answered in several places ((16:57), (37:149), (43:16), (52:39)). The denials attached to Jesus appear in others ((5:17), (5:72), (9:30), (19:35)). The note explains the foundation the Book reasons from, which is the conception of God as one, transcendent, absolute and unlike anything in creation, and therefore in need of nothing at all.

The glory clause in the middle of the sentence is the Book's standard answer to any statement that lowers God, and it takes the claim out of the realm of debate before the argument begins.

**WHAT BELONGS TO HIM**

The verse names it: ***“In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens”*** The Book answers the claim with an inventory. Everything in the heavens is His, and the sentence is the first half of the answer, since a person owns what he has made and what he sustains. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the clause as the statement that all creation is God's servants, belonging to Him, and that every one of them stands in relation to Him as a servant to his Lord.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān sets out the reasoning the scholars drew from these two verses. If God had offspring, the offspring would have to be one of two things. It would be a creature like every other creature, in which case it is His servant and not His child. Or it would be a partner in His divinity, which destroys the whole meaning of a God who is one. The Book takes the second possibility away with the clause in front of the reader, and it takes the first away with the word that ends the verse.

**THE EARTH IN THE SAME SENTENCE**

The verse carries on: ***“and the earth”*** The clause completes the ownership claim and leaves nothing outside it. The Book has used the same sentence in the previous verses about the kingdom of the heavens and the earth ((2:107)). It repeats the formula here because the claim it is answering is the largest one a human being can make about God.

Nothing that exists can be used to fill out a family relation with God, because everything that exists is on the other side of the divide. A reader can hold the sentence up against every version of the claim he meets, including the versions that arrive with softer words and modern clothing, and the answer is the same inventory.

**EVERYTHING BOWS BEFORE HIM**

The Book says: ***“all are subject to His Will”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the closing clause as the statement that every creature is devoted to God and submits to what is required of it. He notes that the emphasis of the sentence falls on the beings who can understand and choose. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same phrase as the bond of servitude and the declaration of God's Oneness.

The English word will in the translation is the part to hold on to. The creatures the Book is describing are not volunteers in a partnership with their maker. They are servants, and their standing depends on His decision. The whole population of the heavens and the earth is covered by the sentence, and no member of it is exempt.

Think of a man who walks into a workshop he has never entered before and introduces the owner's son to the customers. Everyone in the room knows the owner, and everyone knows that the owner has one apprentice and no children. The claim does not need a debate about the apprentice's qualities. It needs somebody to ask the owner, and the verse does that asking for the reader in the sentence that follows.

The next verse gives the reader the act that no servant can imitate and the sentence that settles the whole argument.

---
## Verse 2:117

> ˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and the earth! When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!” And it is

**THE ONE WHO CREATED WITHOUT A MODEL**

Its words are: ***“˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the word for the originator as the One who created the heavens and the earth without any prior model. The Book does not describe a craftsman working from a design that existed before him. It describes a maker who brought the design and the material into being at the same time.

The same phrase stands at the head of the sūrah of the Cattle, where it answers the same claim about a child. The verse there adds a detail the Book leaves the reader to supply here: how could He have children when He has no mate, and He created all things and knows everything ((6:101)). The sentence in front of the reader supplies the other half of the answer, which is the manner of the creating.

**BOTH REALMS UNDER ONE HAND**

The verse continues: ***“and the earth!”*** Ibn Kathīr reads the pair as the standard description of God in the Book. The sūrah has already used it near its own beginning, when it described the creation of the earth and the sky ((2:29)). The verse now returns to the subject with the argument about offspring still in view.

The Book keeps the two together because the claim it is answering was usually made by people who looked at the world and assigned parts of it to a family. The answer is that the whole thing was made, and the maker of a thing does not become the father of it.

**WHEN HE WILLS A THING**

The Book says: ***“When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!””*** Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as the description of how God's decisions are carried out: He says to a thing, be, and it comes to be. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same sense. The Book uses the phrase here for the act of creation. It uses the same words in the sūrah of Mary for the argument about the Messiah, where the claim about a son is answered in the same way ((19:35)).

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the words of this verse as the direct answer to the claim of the previous one. The matter God decrees here, he says, is the creation of a child without a father, like Jesus. The command that makes him is the same command that made Adam, who had neither father nor mother. Al-Baghawī reads the word for originator as the One who brought the heavens and the earth into being from no prior model. He explains the word for decreeing as the act of measuring a matter and completing it, so that it is finished in the plan before it begins in time.

The Book uses that example itself in the sūrah of the Family of ʿImrān, where the case of Jesus is placed beside the case of Adam in a single sentence ((3:59 — **“Indeed, the example of Jesus in the sight of Allah is like that of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, ‘Be!’ And he was”**)). The two men had no ordinary beginning, and neither of them is a relation of God, and the Book treats the matter as a piece of arithmetic that anybody with the two facts can work out.

The sentence removes the last piece of scaffolding that a claim about a divine child could stand on. A son arrives through a process, and the Book has just told the reader that the processes which fill the world were each started by a word. There is no queue of natural causes in front of God, and there is no arrangement of the world that He has to work around.

**AND IT IS**

The verse adds: ***“And it is”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the closing word as the completion of the sentence: the thing comes to be, at once, with nothing left to add. The verse ends on two words that close the argument, and the sūrah then turns to the direction the community was facing in prayer and the community's own claims about it.

Think of a builder who is asked for the plans of the house and who answers by putting the house down in front of them. There is no sketch that came first and no workshop where the materials were cut. The question about who else lives in the family is answered by the fact that the builder has no family, and the question about how the house was made is answered by the house standing there.

---
## Verse 2:118

> Those who have no knowledge say, “If only Allah would speak to us or a sign would come to us!” The same was said by those who came before. Their hearts are all alike. Indeed, We have made the signs clear for people of sure faith

**THE DEMAND FOR A SIGN**

The text says: ***“Those who have no knowledge say, “If only Allah would speak to us”*** Al-Jalālayn identifies the speakers as the disbelievers of Makkah who had no knowledge of God's Oneness. He gives their demand in the form the verse reports: why does God not speak to us and confirm that you are His Messenger? Ibn ʿAbbās places the same demand in the mouths of the People of the Book, who wanted God to address them directly.

Al-Mukhtaṣar widens the description to both groups, the people of the earlier scriptures and the idolaters. He names the thing that ran through their request, which was stubbornness against the truth rather than a search for it. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains the shape of the demand and its logic. They wanted God to speak to them either directly, as He speaks to the angels, or through an angel, as He speaks to the prophets, and they wanted Him to announce the rulings to them in person.

Ibn Kathīr records the exchange in a report from Ibn Isḥāq. One of the questioners tells the Messenger that if he were truly a messenger, he should ask God to speak to them so that they could hear the words themselves. The demand has an obvious answer that the Book supplies later in the passage, and it also has an obvious problem, which is that a person who hears God speak directly has no further room to negotiate.

**A SIGN OF THEIR OWN ORDER**

The verse says: ***“or a sign would come to us!””*** The second demand is the one the sūrah has been meeting since its early pages. The community wanted a sign of the kind it would choose, and the Book has already pointed out the signs that were standing in front of them ((2:99)), including the Book itself ((2:106)).

Al-Jalālayn keeps the two demands together, one about speech and one about a sign. He reads the whole request as a demand for proof of the Messenger's honesty according to the terms of the people asking. The Book treats the request as a form of argument rather than as a search for knowledge. The same people had a book in their hands whose predictions were being fulfilled in front of them, and their request for a personal miracle tells the reader what kind of evidence they wanted.

**THE SAME DEMAND IN EARLIER TIMES**

The wording is: ***“The same was said by those”*** The verse answers the demand by placing it in history. Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as a statement that the communities of the past spoke to their prophets in the same way, in the same stubbornness and with the same appetite for signs. Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the same reading and adds the conclusion the Book draws from it, that the hearts of these communities were alike.

The Book has used this method throughout the sūrah. It takes the reader who thinks he is arguing with a man standing in front of him, and it lifts him up so that he can see a queue of identically worded requests stretching back through the centuries. The objection loses the freshness that made it feel like his own thought.

**HEARTS THAT RESEMBLE EACH OTHER**

The Book says: ***“who came before. Their hearts are all alike.”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the closing clause as a statement that the words and the hearts of the objectors are the same as those of their predecessors. Al-Mukhtaṣar draws the point out in plain language: the disbelievers of every time and place are alike, whether they are separated by centuries or by continents.

This is one of the most useful sentences in the sūrah for a reader who has ever felt that his objections are original. The Book states that the objections are a family, and that the family is large, and that the members of it are recognisable by the shape of what they ask for. The next clause then says what the signs were for.

Think of a man who has just discovered that the tap in his kitchen drips and who announces the problem to his family as though he were the first person in the building to notice. His wife points out that the same tap has been dripping in every apartment for thirty years, and that there is a plumber's number on the wall beside it. The drip is real. The discovery is not new, and neither is the fixture.

**THE SIGNS ALREADY GIVEN**

The verse records: ***“Indeed, We have made the signs clear”*** The Book turns from the request to the supply. Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as the statement that the signs have been made clear. Ibn ʿAbbās identifies what they include: the commands and prohibitions, and the descriptions of the Messenger that stood in the earlier scriptures. Ibn Kathīr reads the same clause as the plain statement that the proofs have been set out.

The sentence does not say that the signs are hidden or that they are reserved for experts. The Book's position is that the evidence is present and readable, and that a person who has received it is responsible for what he does with it. The verse that follows the demand for private miracles therefore answers with a statement about public ones.

**FOR WHOM THE SIGNS ARE CLEAR**

The verse names it: ***“for people of sure faith”*** The last clause names the audience the signs were aimed at, and it is not the audience that made the demand. Al-Mukhtaṣar explains the condition in the word: the signs are made clear for people who are certain of the truth when it appears to them, without doubt and without argument. Al-Jalālayn keeps the same sense.

The sentence is careful not to say that the signs fail. It says that the signs are clear, and it names the people who read them as clear, which puts the difference on the side of the reader. A person who has decided in advance what he will accept can stand in front of a mountain of evidence with his arms folded, and the next verse tells the Messenger what his responsibility in that situation actually is.

---
## Verse 2:119

> We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺ as a deliverer of good news and a warner. And you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire

**THE MESSENGER SENT WITH THE TRUTH**

Its words are: ***“We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺”*** The verse opens as a word of consolation to the Messenger, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains why it was needed. The previous verse showed a group of people persisting in denial out of malice and ignorance, and a man sent as a mercy to the worlds might well grieve over people who could not be expected to reform. The sentence tells him what he was actually sent with.

Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the truth as the Qur'an and the declaration of God's Oneness. Al-Jalālayn reads the phrase as the guidance that was placed in his hands. The verse does not tell him that everybody will accept the message, and it does not promise a change in the people who had been asking him for private signs. It tells him what he is carrying, which is a thing that keeps its value whether or not a particular door opens.

**THE GOOD NEWS HE CARRIES**

The verse has it: ***“as a deliverer of good news”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the first half of the assignment as good news of the Garden for the people who respond. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the same reading, that the glad tidings belong to the believers. The Book places the messenger's two duties in a fixed order, and this one comes first.

The order matters for a reader who has spent the last few pages reading about broken covenants, magic, and a community that wanted God to speak to it in person. The Book has been describing the worst behaviour in the whole chapter, and it introduces the man who was sent to those people as a bringer of good news before it introduces him as a warner.

**THE WARNING AND THE RESPONSIBILITY**

Then come the words: ***“and a warner. And you will not be accountable”*** The second half of the assignment is the warning, and Al-Jalālayn reads it as the warning of the Fire for those who do not respond. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the whole task as the clear delivery of the message, and he reads the clause that follows as the limit on the Messenger's responsibility.

That limit is the burden the verse lifts, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān reads the verse as a consolation on exactly that point. The messenger's work is to deliver the message in full. The response belongs to the people who hear it, and the Book tells him that he will not be questioned about the choices of people who rejected what they were given.

A reader can take the limit and apply it to every person who has ever explained something true to somebody who did not want it. The work is the explanation. The result is not the work, and the Book says so here to a man who had every reason to take every rejection personally.

Think of a postman with a bag of letters and a street of houses. He delivers every letter to the correct door and gets a signature for the ones that need one. What he cannot do is open the door for the man who refuses to read his own post, and his employer does not ask him to account for the letters that were never opened.

**WHO THE WARNING CONCERNS**

The wording runs: ***“for the residents of the Hellfire”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the closing phrase in two ways, and both of them are worth keeping. In the first reading, it is not fitting for the Messenger to be questioned about the people of the Fire. In the second, he is told not to ask God for their forgiveness, because the matter has been decided.

Al-Jalālayn notes a variant reading of the sentence in which the verb is read as a prohibition, so that the sense is that the Prophet should not ask on their behalf. The two readings come to the same place. The Messenger was not sent as a guarantor for people who had heard the message and turned away from it, and the Book closes the verse by releasing him from a duty he had never been given.

---
## Verse 2:120

> Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith. Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.” And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against Allah

**THE PLEASURE THEY WILL NEVER GIVE**

In the verse's own words: ***“Never will the Jews”*** The verse opens with a statement about the future that the reader is expected to test against everything he has just read. Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as the announcement that neither community will ever be satisfied with the Messenger until he adopts their religion. Al-Baghawī reports the occasion from another direction: the two communities were asking for a truce and holding out the hope that they would follow him if he gave them time, and the verse answered the hope.

Al-Qurṭubī states the meaning plainly. Their object was not the signs they kept requesting, since they would not be satisfied even if every demand were met. What would satisfy them was the abandonment of what the Messenger stood on.

tafsir_initial observes that for several commentators this verse confirms what the previous demand for signs really was, since the question at the start of the passage was not an honest request for information. The note also explains the word translated as faith here. It can mean a community, a way of life, or the religious law that defines a community, and it lists the places in the Book where the word carries that sense ((2:130), (2:135), (3:95), (4:125), (6:161), (12:37), (16:123), (22:78)).

**WHY THE TWO GROUPS ARE NAMED**

The two communities are named separately because the sentence has to cover both sets of expectations. A man who is willing to satisfy one set of requests discovers that a second set is waiting behind it, and the Book tells the Messenger in advance that the queue does not end.

A reader who has watched the sūrah deal with this community for a hundred verses knows why the sentence is put in this form. The Book has described the covenants broken, the pages rewritten, the signs denied and the magic bought. It now tells the man who had been working on this community for years that he can stop measuring his success by how pleased they are with him.

The sentence reads: ***“or Christians be pleased with you”*** Think of a craftsman who is asked to build a table. The customer asks for a different wood, then for a different height, then for the legs to be changed, and then for the table to be turned into a chair. Somewhere around the fourth request the craftsman understands that he was never building a table, and that the point of every request was to keep him sanding.

**THE FAITH THEY WANT YOU TO FOLLOW**

The verse declares: ***“until you follow their faith. Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.” And”*** The Book gives the Messenger one sentence to say in return, and it is a statement rather than an argument. Al-Jalālayn reads it as the declaration that the guidance which came from God is the guidance, whatever else a person may call by that name.

Al-Saʿdī draws the whole logic of the passage out of this clause. The two communities were inviting people to the way they followed, and they believed it to be guidance. The answer tells them what the actual guidance is, and it names what they were following in its place, which is their own desires. He also notes that the address, though it goes to the Messenger, includes the whole community, since rules in the Book are applied by the meaning of the sentence rather than by the identity of the person addressed.

The word the Book uses for their religion can mean a way of life as well as a set of beliefs, and the sentence sets the two paths side by side without spending a paragraph on the comparison. One is guidance from God, and the other is what a group of people have decided to want.

**THE SENTENCE THE MESSENGER IS GIVEN**

The verse states: ***“if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge”*** The sentence turns to the Messenger with a warning that is stated in the strongest terms the sūrah has used. Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as the statement that if he followed their wishes after the knowledge that had come to him, there would be no protector and no helper for him against God.

tafsir_initial notes that a similar message appears later in the same sūrah ((2:145)), where the same word is used for the preferences of the two communities. The note also explains what the word for desires means in this context, which is a person's own wishes dressed up as a principle. The Book is not describing the search for truth that ends in a different opinion. It is describing a decision to prefer a wanted outcome over a known one.

The warning has a detail that readers of the entire chapter will recognise. It is addressed to the Messenger, and the Book has just spent a hundred verses describing what happened to a community that did exactly what the sentence forbids. The verses are placed so that nobody can read the warning and think the subject is theoretical.

**THE WARNING ABOUT DESIRES**

The verse puts the matter: ***“that has come to you, there would be none to protect”*** The Book names the two things a person loses when he makes that trade. The first is the protector who would have stood between him and harm, and the second is the helper who could have brought him what he needed. Al-Jalālayn keeps both in the sentence, and he places the whole danger in the clause about God, since the help being described is help against the One who has been left.

A reader can hold the sentence up against the earlier passage where the same loss was described for the community that broke its covenants ((2:107)). The Book has been telling its readers that certain kinds of help exist and that certain roads lead away from them, and it says the same thing here about the man who delivers the message.

The next verse describes the people who were given the Book and handled it correctly. That description is the answer the passage has been waiting for since it first raised the question of the reader and his book.

**NO PROTECTOR AND NO HELP**

The text says: ***“or help you against Allah”*** The clause closes the warning and completes the pair. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the whole sentence as a prohibition of the greatest weight, since the Book addresses the Messenger in order to forbid something to the community that follows him.

Al-Saʿdī makes the application explicit in his comment on the verse. The warning is directed at the Messenger and it covers his community, because the Book judges by the general meaning of a sentence and not by the particular person it addresses. A reader who has been taught by this chapter to look for the pattern can see the pattern here as well. The Book keeps speaking to the people in front of it, and the sentences keep arriving at the reader's own door.

---
## Verse 2:121

> Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed. It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it. As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers

**READING IT THE WAY IT DESERVES**

The verse puts it: ***“Those We have given the Book follow it”*** The verse answers the question the sūrah has been asking for a hundred verses: what does a community look like when it handles its book properly? Al-Ṭabarī records the two readings of the subject, that the recipients of the Book are the Muslim believers, or the learned among the Jewish community who read the Torah sincerely.

tafsir_initial explains the two senses of the word translated as follow here, which can also mean to recite. On the second reading, the sentence describes people who recite the Book in the way it should be recited, and the note reports that many of the exegetes preferred the sense of following it as it should be followed. The note adds that reciting it properly means, among other things, reciting it with humility, and that following it properly means abstaining from what it forbids and taking what it permits.

The Book returns to the theme elsewhere, where the People of the Book are commanded through the Qur'an to uphold the Torah and the Gospel ((5:47), (5:66-68)). The command is worth holding, because it settles a question the sūrah has been circling since the beginning. The earlier scriptures were not the problem. The way they were handled was.

**THE CLAUSE THAT CARRIES THE CONDITION**

The clause that carries the condition is short and it does all the work of the verse. The Book does not say that the people who have the scripture are the believers. It says that the people who follow it as it should be followed are the believers, and the phrase as it should be is the whole test of a community's life with a sacred text.

The verse states: ***“as it should be followed. It is they”*** A reader should notice that the sentence leaves no room for a community to pass the test by owning the book, printing it, binding it in leather or quoting from it in an argument. The measure is use. The Book has described a community that hid parts of its scripture, sold pages of it and rewrote its prophecies. The sentence in front of the reader describes the opposite behaviour without naming a single one of the offences.

**WHO BELIEVES IN IT**

The sentence reads: ***“who ˹truly˺ believe in it.”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as the identification of the believers: the people who follow the Book properly are the ones who believe in it. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same order, with the belief attached to the practice rather than standing in front of it.

The sūrah has placed the two groups of people side by side throughout the chapter. The ones who threw the book behind their backs are described in one passage ((2:101)), and the ones who follow it as it should be followed are described here. Both groups had the same document, and the difference between them is what they did with it on an ordinary week.

**THE GROUP THAT TURNS AWAY**

The verse has it: ***“As for those who reject it, it is they”*** The verse then names the other group, and it does so with the same brevity. The rejection in this sentence is not only the refusal of the new revelation. The Book has already made the case that a person who turns away from the Messenger is turning away from the book that announced him ((2:101)), and the sentence sits at the end of that argument.

The two clauses of the verse answer two questions at once. The first tells the reader what belief looks like when it is real, and the second tells him what the opposite looks like. Neither answer mentions a family, a nation, or a teacher.

**WHAT THE LOSS MEANS**

The text says: ***“who are the losers”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the final word as the description of the people who rejected the Book, and the word is one the sūrah has used twice before for the losing side ((2:27), (2:64)). The Book's word for loss is a market word, and it has kept the market language running through the chapter: credit and debt, buying and selling, price and gain.

Think of two men who inherit the same ledger from their father. One of them sits down with it every month, checks the columns, collects what is owed and pays what is due. The other keeps it on a shelf and tells visitors about the fine handwriting on the cover. Years later, the two of them have inherited exactly the same document, and only one of them has inherited the estate.

---
## Verse 2:122

> O Children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you and how I honoured you above the others

**A THIRD ADDRESS TO THE SAME PEOPLE**

The verse starts with: ***“O Children of Israel!”*** The verse is the beginning of a second address to the same community, and the Book has used the same words at an earlier point in the sūrah ((2:40)). Al-Mukhtaṣar reads it as a fresh reminder to the community of the favours it had been given. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān treats the repetition as deliberate, since the two passages bracket a long section of the sūrah, and the community is addressed again with the same words after a hundred verses of evidence.

The repetition is one of the structural markers of the sūrah. When the Book returns to a phrase it used earlier, the reader is expected to look back and see what has been built in the space between the two uses. What stands between the two addresses is the entire record of the community's dealings with its covenants, its book and its prophets.

**THE FAVOURS THEY WERE TOLD TO REMEMBER**

The verse says: ***“Remember My favours upon you”*** The instruction is to remember, and it is placed at the head of the passage rather than at its end. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the sentence as a call to bring the favours of God to mind: the rescue from slavery, the sea, the shade, the manna, the water from the rock and the books.

The Book has spent the last eighty verses describing what the community did with those favours. It now asks the community to hold the favours themselves in view, which is the only way to measure the distance between what was given and what was done with it.

**THE HONOUR THAT SET THEM APART**

The sentence continues: ***“and how I honoured you above the others”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the closing clause as the reminder of the preference that was given to the community above the other nations of its time. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sense. The preference was real, and it is why the community was given prophets, books and signs that other nations did not receive.

Al-Ṭabarī describes what the whole address is doing, and his description names the audience. The verse is an admonition from God to the Jewish community living in the very city to which the Messenger had migrated, and it is a reminder of the favours that had been given to their ancestors. He lists the favours the Book is pointing back to. They include the rescue from the hand of their enemy Pharaoh and his people, the sending down of the manna and the quails in the wilderness, and the establishment of the community in the land. The purpose of the reminder is stated as well, that the community might be drawn towards the religion of God and towards belief in the Messenger standing in its streets.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the same three parts in his comment on the sentence. Al-Jalālayn notes in a single line that a similar verse has been mentioned before in this sūrah, which is the point the repetition is making.

The sūrah has already explained the terms of that preference in an earlier passage ((2:47)), and the two mentions frame the same lesson. The honour was a responsibility, and it was given to a community that had been fed and sheltered by the sky. The verses that follow this one will describe the day on which every claim to honour is settled by a different ledger, and the sentence about preference is placed in front of that description for a reason.

Think of a family that is given the only scholarship in the village for its eldest son, on the understanding that he comes back and teaches the other children. Twenty years later the family is proud of the scholarship and the village still has no school, and the letter from the foundation is on the wall in a frame.

---
## Verse 2:123

> And guard yourselves against the Day when no soul will be of any help to another. No ransom will be taken, no intercession accepted, and no help will be given

**THE WARNING ABOUT THE DAY TO COME**

The verse has it: ***“And guard yourselves against the Day”*** The verse opens with an instruction to protect the self, and the thing the reader is told to guard against is a day rather than an enemy. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the sentence as a warning to prepare for the day when every person will be paid what he has earned.

The sūrah has used the same instruction, with almost the same words, in its earlier passage about the same community ((2:48)). The repetition of the sentence at this point in the chapter is one of its strongest structural features. The community was addressed with the warning at the beginning of the sūrah's treatment of its history. It is addressed with the same warning again at the end of it, after the evidence has been laid out.

**WHEN NO ONE ANSWERS FOR ANOTHER**

The verse says: ***“when no soul will be of any help to another. No ransom will be taken, no intercession accepted”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the three clauses one after the other. On that day, no person can render any help to another person. No compensation will be accepted from anyone, and no intercession will be taken, meaning that nobody will be able to speak for another person. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the clauses in the same order and with the same force.

The Book has been describing a community that leaned on its ancestry, its book and its standing in the region. The verse takes those three supports away in a single sentence, and it takes them away by naming the mechanisms the community had been counting on for its own dealings in this world. A person can pay a debt with money, and a person can be saved by a friend with influence, and the verse says that both instruments are out of service on that day.

The same three refusals appear in the earlier passage in nearly the same words, and the Note on the earlier verse records the same list ((2:48)). The sūrah closes its treatment of the community by repeating the warning it opened with. A reader who has followed the whole chapter has now read the same sentence twice, with the entire record standing between the two readings.

Think of a man who arrives at an airport with three cards in his wallet: a credit card, a membership card from a club, and a letter from a friend who works at the airline. The airline has gone out of business, and the only document anyone at the gate is checking is the passport in his hand.

**NO HELP FROM ANY QUARTER**

The final clause covers the possibility that has not been ruled out by the first three. Nothing of value can be offered, no advocate can speak, and the sentence ends by closing the door on the idea that help might simply arrive from somewhere unrequested.

The next words are: ***“and no help will be given”*** Al-Jalālayn keeps the clause as a plain statement that no help will be given on that day. The verse has now removed four avenues of rescue, and it has done so in a passage addressed to a community that had been offered a fifth one repeatedly. The Book has told this community what would save it, and the next verses turn to the man the whole sūrah has been preparing its readers to receive.

---
## Verse 2:124

> ˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments, which he fulfilled. Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model for the people.” Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?” Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.”

**THE TESTS ABRAHAM PASSED**

The verse begins: ***“˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments”*** Maʿārif al-Qurʾān opens its treatment of this section by naming the argument the Book is about to settle. The community addressed in the previous passage took pride in being the descendants of Jacob and of Abraham, and it believed itself to hold the exclusive right to lead humanity, so that prophethood could not be given to anyone outside its line. The Book leaves the family of Jacob and begins the story of Abraham, and the answer to the whole claim is contained in the order in which the story happened.

Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the opening sentence as a statement about testing: God instructed Abraham to carry out commands and obligations, and Abraham fulfilled the orders completely. Al-Saʿdī explains the purpose that runs through all such testing in the Book. God tries His servants with commands and prohibitions the way a refiner works on metal. The person who cannot hold firm is separated from the person who can, and the true one comes out with his rank raised and his work purified.

The testing in the sentence had a shape that readers of the earlier books knew well. tafsir_initial notes that the passage gives no list of the commands, and the commentators differed widely on what they were. Some said they were duties of cleanliness and bodily grooming and purification. Some said they were the rituals of the pilgrimage, which Muslims trace back to Abraham, including the walking around the House, the running between the two hills, and the throwing of the stones. Others said the tests were trials of hardship, such as the command to sacrifice his son.

The report al-Ḥasan gives in the collection of occasions of revelation sets them out in a line. Abraham was tried with the stars, the moon and the sun, and he answered well in each case, because he knew that his Lord stays and never sets. He was tried with the sacrifice of his son, and he was patient and did not fall short. The note that follows the report is the useful part. The point of the testing was not to inform God, who already knew the outcome. It was to show Abraham himself what he was made of and how he walked the road of a servant.

Think of a man who is handed a certificate for a skill he has never been asked to use. The certificate says nothing until the day the workshop catches fire and he is the only person standing in it. The verse is describing a life that had already been tested many times, and the certificate was issued after the fire.

**THE PROMISE MADE TO HIM**

The sentence reads: ***“which he fulfilled. Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model”*** The clause about fulfilment is the hinge of the whole passage, and it is three words long. Al-Saʿdī reads it as the completion of everything God had tested him with, done in full and paid in full, and he adds that God then thanked him for it, since God is always ready to acknowledge a servant's work.

The reward that followed is described in the verse as a role model for people, and Ibn Kathīr reads the sentence as the statement that Abraham was made a leader to be followed. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the appointment as one of behaviour as well as of position, that his manners and his conduct were made an example for people. Ibn ʿAbbās records the additional sense of the word as a successor or a leader in the affairs of the community.

The order of the two sentences is the answer to a claim. The community in Madinah traced its standing to a man of its own blood. The Book says that the standing was granted to that man because of something he did, after he had been tried, and that the granting was an award rather than an inheritance. The next words show what happened when Abraham asked about his children.

**THE QUESTION ABOUT HIS FAMILY**

The verse has it: ***“for the people.” Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?””*** The question in the sentence is the question of every father who receives an honour for himself. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads it as the request that his descendants should also be made leaders whom people would follow by. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the same request.

The Book records the question with approval rather than with a correction. Abraham had spent his life building a family in a barren valley, and the prayer for his children runs through every stage of his story ((14:35), (14:37)). The answer he receives is the one the reader needs, and it arrives in the next clause in a form that leaves no room for a claim of blood.

**THE ANSWER THAT LIMITED IT**

The verse says: ***“Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.””*** Al-Mukhtaṣar states the answer plainly: the promise of sacred leadership would not be given to the wrongdoers among Abraham's descendants. Ibn Kathīr reads the whole verse as the honour given to Abraham and the limit that came with it, and he identifies the covenant in the sentence as the covenant of prophethood.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws the conclusion the section exists to deliver. The community that had been resting on its descent from Abraham was told that the promise of leadership does not pass through blood alone. A descendant who does wrong is not covered by the agreement made with his ancestor, and the sentence leaves the community to work out where that places the people who had rewritten their book and rejected their prophets.

The Book uses this pattern elsewhere, where the claim of a nation to Abraham is settled by conduct rather than by descent ((3:68)). A reader who has followed the sūrah from the beginning can see the whole argument being assembled from the first verse about the believers and the last verse about the wrongdoers.

---
## Verse 2:125

> And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer.” And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺

**THE HOUSE MADE A CENTRE**

The verse starts with: ***“And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the word for the House and the two qualities granted to it. It was made a place of visitation to which people come from every direction. It was also made a sanctuary in which a person could meet his father's killer and not raise a hand, which was a protection no other place in the region offered.

Ibn ʿAbbās reads the first quality as a place of return, a destination that people long for and come back to. Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the reason the meaning matters: the House connects the hearts of people to God, so that when they travel away from it they come back. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān sets the verse in the argument of the passage. The two communities scoffed at the Muslims for turning towards the Kaʿbah in prayer, and the section that follows gives the history of the House and shows whose house it was and who built it.

The Book describes the House as an institution established for people, and it says so in a chapter that has spent most of its length examining the records of two communities. The House is placed in front of the reader as the one address on earth that belongs to every direction at once.

**A PLACE OF SAFETY**

The verse goes on: ***“and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham”*** The second quality is safety, and the verse names its practical effect before it names the station of the man who built the place. Al-Jalālayn gives the picture of a person who could come across the killer of his own father inside that boundary and would leave him alone.

The instruction that follows is addressed to the community reading the verse. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as the command to the community of Muhammad to take the stone where Abraham stood as a place of prayer. The Book is not describing a museum of the earlier prophets. It is telling the new community to use the place, and the command turns the history into an instruction.

**THE SITE OF PRAYER**

In the verse's own words: ***“as a site of prayer.””*** Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the command in the same place, that people were told to make the stone Abraham stood on while building the House into a place of prayer. The Book attaches the instruction to the memory of the builder rather than to the stone itself, which is the way the sūrah has handled every object it has mentioned.

The sentence is part of the answer to the two communities. Both of them respected Abraham, and both of them had turned against the community that had followed his prayer. The verse gives the readers the standing place of the man they all admired and tells them to pray there, which is a way of settling the argument about which community belongs to him.

**THE CHARGE GIVEN TO ABRAHAM**

The verse carries on: ***“And We entrusted Abraham”*** The verse moves from the founding of the House to its maintenance, and the maintenance was assigned to two men. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the charge as an instruction to purify the sanctuary from filth and from idols. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same, that the House was to be cleaned of the objects of worship that had been brought into it.

The command is given to a man who had already been tested in other ways, and the work it assigns is not heroic. Somebody had to keep the courtyard clean and the shrine free of the idols that the surrounding tribes kept bringing in. The Book treats that labour as an honour, and it names it in the same sentence as the founding of the House.

**ISHMAEL JOINS THE WORK**

The next words are: ***“and Ishmael to purify My House”*** The second name in the charge is the son, and his inclusion matters for the audience the sūrah is addressing. Ibn Kathīr reads the command as the instruction given to Abraham and Ishmael to purify the House for the worship of God. The two of them are named together because the House was built by the two of them together ((2:127)).

The Book has just said that the promise of leadership does not extend to the wrongdoers among Abraham's descendants ((2:124)). The next verse names one of those descendants, the son of Abraham through whom the community of the final Messenger traces its line. It shows him standing beside his father with a broom in his hand, carrying out the duty that the House required.

The picture answers several arguments at once. The community in Madinah had been told that prophethood could not come from outside a particular family, and here is the family's own ancestor working on the building with the son that the claim had overlooked.

**THOSE WHO WALK AROUND IT**

The wording is: ***“for those who circle it”*** The purpose of the purification is spelled out in a list of the people who would use the House, and the list begins with the pilgrims who walk around it. Al-Jalālayn keeps the sense of the circuit, and the verse has already told the reader that the House was made a destination that people come back to.

The purification is not for the sake of the building. It is for the sake of the worshippers, and the Book names three kinds of them in the next two clauses. A reader can see the shape of the arrangement from the list. The House was kept clean because specific people were going to stand in specific places to pray, and the cleaning was part of the welcome.

**THOSE WHO STAY THERE**

The text says: ***“who meditate in it”*** The second group is the people who stay in the House, and the word describes a person who remains in a place rather than passing through it. The Book keeps this group separate from the pilgrims who circle the building, and the two kinds of visitor have different needs. One needs a circuit that works, and the other needs a corner that stays quiet.

Ibn Kathīr reads the three groups in the list as the people who walk around the House, the people who stay in it, and the people who bow and prostrate in prayer. The word of God accommodates them all in a single sentence, which is the way the Book has been treating its readers since the beginning of the sūrah.

**THE ONES WHO KNEEL AND BOW**

The verse adds: ***“and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺”*** The third group is the one that prays in the two postures the sūrah described near its beginning when it described the people of the Book ((2:43)). The list closes with the worshippers in their physical positions, and the whole sentence is a picture of the House in use.

The verse has now given the reader the founding of the House, its safety, its direction of prayer, and its cleaning, and it has named the people for whom all of that was done. The next verse returns to Abraham and puts a prayer in his mouth, which is the prayer the sūrah has been setting up since the first mention of the community that followed him.

---
## Verse 2:126

> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure and provide fruits to its people—those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day.” He answered, “As for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves for a little while, then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire. What an evil destination!”

**THE PRAYER FOR SAFETY**

As the verse says: ***“And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the answer to the prayer before explaining the prayer itself. God granted the request and made the place a sanctuary in which no blood is shed, no injustice is done to anybody, no animal is hunted and no part of it is ever left deserted. The Book says in another place that the prayer was made when Abraham settled his family in a barren valley near the House ((14:37)), and the sūrah of Abraham preserves the same words.

The sūrah of Abraham records the earlier form of the same prayer, where Abraham asks for the city to be made secure and asks to be kept, along with his children, away from the worship of idols ((14:35)). The two prayers sit in the same story. One asks for the place, and the other asks for the family that would live in it.

**FRUIT FOR THE PEOPLE**

The verse carries on: ***“and provide fruits to its people”*** Al-Jalālayn records that this request was also granted in the way it was asked: supply came in from as far away as Syria to a valley that had no vegetation of its own. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the prayer as a request for every kind of crop for the people who lived there.

The request is the second half of the same thought. A man who has built a house in a valley with no water and no soil asks for two things, safety and food, and the Book answers the request in the sentences that follow. The prayer has an honesty to it that a modern reader can measure. Abraham is not asking for wealth or for influence. He is asking for the two things that keep a household alive.

**THE PRAYER NARROWED**

Its words are: ***“those among them who believe in Allah”*** The prayer is narrowed in the sentence that follows, and the narrowing is Abraham's own doing. He asks for provision for the people of the city who believe in God, which is the standard he had in mind when he made the request. Ibn Kathīr keeps the reading in the same shape.

The sūrah has already shown the reader what Abraham did at the door of the city in another passage ((2:58)), where a community was told to enter a town and eat freely of what it contained. The prayer in front of the reader is the other side of the same gesture. A man who has been given a place asks that the place be fed, and he specifies who he had in mind.

**THE ANSWER THAT WIDENED IT**

The next words are: ***“and the Last Day.” He answered, “As”*** The sentence that follows is the answer to a prayer that was narrower than the mercy of God. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the reply as a statement from God that the provision would reach beyond the people Abraham had named, and Ibn Kathīr records the same reading.

The answer has a shape that the reader should notice. The good that was requested for the believers was granted to them, and then it was extended to the people who had not been mentioned in the prayer. The Book has shown the same pattern in the story of the community that was given manna in the wilderness, since the gifts arrived every morning whether or not the people receiving them were grateful.

**THE ENJOYMENT GIVEN TO THE DENIER**

The sentence reads: ***“for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the sentence as the statement that the disbelievers would also be given provision in this life, along with the warning that follows. The verse has been describing a prayer made for a specific group, and the answer then opens the supply to everyone standing in the city.

The reader has seen the same arrangement in operation for several pages. The sūrah has described a community that was fed from the sky, shaded by clouds and watered from a rock while it was busy breaking its agreements, and none of those supplies were cut off as a punishment. The Book is consistent about this in both directions, and the verse confirms it inside a prayer.

**FOR A SHORT TIME ONLY**

The clause names the size of the enjoyment, and the size is the whole point of the sentence. A person who is given provision in this world has been given something real and something measured, and the Book describes the measure as short.

In the verse's own words: ***“for a little while”*** Al-Jalālayn keeps the sense of the sentence as it stands, and the words for a little while are placed between the enjoyment and the destination for a reason. A reader who has followed the previous hundred verses has watched a community being given favour after favour, and the verse tells him how long the arrangement runs.

**THE DESTINATION THAT FOLLOWS**

The verse continues: ***“then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire. What an evil destination!””*** The verse closes with the destination, and Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the sentence as the final end of the people who were given provision and did not use it for anything. The clause about the evil destination is the Book's standard verdict on the road that ends there, and it has used the same phrase about the people who earned a different home ((2:90)).

The prayer has now been answered twice, once as it was asked and once more widely than it was asked. The next verse returns to the two builders at the wall and shows the reader what they were doing while they worked.

Think of a father who builds a house in a valley with no road and plants a small orchard beside it. He prays for two things before he prays for anything else, that the road will stay safe and that the trees will bear. The family that inherits the house may later argue about who owns which room. The man who dug the foundations would have told them what he actually asked for, and the verse records the words he used.

---
## Verse 2:127

> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael, ˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord! Accept ˹this˺ from us. You are indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**THE FOUNDATIONS RAISED TOGETHER**

The Book says: ***“And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael, ˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord!”*** The verse describes the work as a joint effort: two men lifting the foundations of the House together. Al-Saʿdī draws the picture out of the sentence with care. Abraham and Ishmael are standing over the foundations of the House, working at the greatest task of their lives. The condition of their hearts is fear and hope at the same time, because the first thing they do with the work is ask God to accept it.

Ibn Kathīr reads the sentence as the raising of the base of the House at Makkah. He links it to the command in the previous verse, where the two of them were charged with purifying the House for the worshippers ((2:125)). The Book shows the reader the building going up and the prayer going up beside it.

The detail about their hands is worth holding on to. The Book could have described the founding of the House as a decree, and instead it describes two men lifting stones on a foundation in a valley with no water. The greatest building in the story of the Book begins as a piece of manual labour shared by a father and a son.

tafsir_initial relates the verse to two other passages. In one of them God assigns the site of the House to Abraham and tells him to purify it ((22:26)), and in the other the House at Bakkah is called the first house of worship established for humanity ((3:96)). It also records the older traditions that the commentators attached to this verse. In those accounts the House had an origin long before Abraham, and it was raised again out of the ground at his hand. The note adds the report in which the stones taken from the building during a later repair were recognised as the foundations Abraham had lifted. The Book does not spend its words on the legends, and it keeps the reader's attention on the two builders and their prayer.

Al-Qurṭubī explains the word for the foundations and reports the view of the early authorities that it means the base of the building rather than the walls. He also records the discussion among the scholars about how much of the House the two of them built, and whether the site had been lost and was shown to them again.
