**THE PRAYER THAT ROSE WITH THE WORK**

The verse records: ***“Accept ˹this˺ from us. You are”*** The first sentence the two of them say is not about the building. Al-Saʿdī reads it as the request that the work be accepted, and he says the prayer came with the hope that the work would carry benefit for others. The Book has recorded the words of many prayers in this sūrah, and this one asks for the least and the most at the same time.

A reader who has watched the sūrah deal with a community that offered its worship alongside a rewritten book can see what the prayer is guarding against. The two men did not ask for the building to be famous or for the family to be honoured. They asked for the work to be received, which is the one thing a person cannot check for himself.

**THE TWO NAMES THAT CLOSE IT**

The verse states: ***“indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing”*** The two names that close the sentence carry the reasons behind the request. God hears the prayer and knows the intention behind the work, and Ibn Kathīr keeps both senses in his comment. The names also answer the fear that a sincere person feels about his own effort, since the One being addressed knows what the work was worth even when the worker does not.

The next verse continues the prayer in the same voice, and the two verses together are the longest prayer by a prophet in the sūrah. A reader who has been following the chapter can see the contrast the Book is building. The community that inherited this House argued about its own privileges, and the men who built it were asking whether their work would be accepted.

---
## Verse 2:128

> Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You and from our descendants a nation that will submit to you. Show us our rituals, and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

**THE PRAYER TO BE MUSLIMS**

The Book says: ***“Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You”*** The second request in the prayer is for the two of them, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān marks what is surprising about it. Abraham had spent his whole life in obedience, and he still asks to be made obedient, because the more a person knows of God's majesty, the more he understands how far short his own service falls.

tafsir_initial explains the word that the translation renders as submit. It is the participle of a verb meaning to submit oneself to God, and the note ties it to the mention of submission in the next passage ((2:132)). Here is a word that describes the state of Abraham and his son. The two of them are asking God to make that state a reality in them, which is the same request a believer makes every time he asks to be guided.

Al-Saʿdī reads the sentence as a request for the submission of the heart, which is the surrender of a person's will to his Lord and which carries the surrender of his limbs along with it. The two builders were not asking for information about how to obey. They were asking for the thing itself to be given to them.

**THE NATION THAT WOULD COME**

The sentence moves on: ***“and from our descendants a nation”*** The prayer widens from the two men to their descendants, and the Book records it because the answer to that part of the prayer is standing in front of the community reading the sūrah. Ibn Kathīr keeps the sense of a nation that would submit to God.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān observes what the request shows about Abraham. He had been willing to sacrifice his own son when he was commanded to, and he still asked that his descendants be included in the mercy. The note draws the lesson that a person who is prepared to give everything for God does not stop caring about his family, because the two loves are not in competition.

The Book has already told the reader that the promise of leadership would not extend to the wrongdoers among the descendants ((2:124)). The prayer in front of the reader is the other half of that arrangement. The honour is not inherited, and the descendants are still prayed for, and both things are true at once.

**A TEACHER AND THE RITES OF WORSHIP**

In the verse's own words: ***“that will submit to you. Show us our rituals”*** The third request asks for instruction in the rites, and the phrasing asks for something seen rather than something explained. Al-Saʿdī notes that the form of the request suggests a teaching that comes with demonstration, so that the meaning lands with more force. tafsir_initial explains the word for rites, which is often taken as the rituals of the pilgrimage, or as sacrifice, or as worship in general. The note points to the places where the Book uses the same word for the practices given to other communities ((22:34), (22:67)).

The request is made by a man who had been tested with commands he could not read in advance. He and his son had built a house of worship and were asking to be shown how to use it, which is the proper order for both halves of the arrangement. The Book keeps the two questions together in the same sentence: the place and the practice.

**THE GRACE THAT ANSWERS THEM**

The wording continues: ***“and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”*** The prayer ends where the sūrah's argument has been pointing for a hundred verses. Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as the request that God relent towards them, and the two names at the end carry the reasons. One of them names the One who accepts a person's return, and the other names the mercy that follows it.

The sūrah has spent most of its length on a community that was offered forgiveness repeatedly and took it up in the wrong currency, arguing about days of punishment and rewriting the pages that promised it. The man who built the House in front of the reader asks for the same door to be kept open for himself and for his children. The Book quotes him asking, so that the reader can hear how a person speaks when he knows the size of his own account.

Think of a master craftsman who has finished a piece of work and who hands it to the client without a word about the hours it took. What he says instead is a request that the work be accepted and that he be told what the next job requires. The prayer in this verse is the same sentence, made by the men who built the most famous building in the Book.

---
## Verse 2:129

> Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, All-Wise.”

**THE PRAYER FOR A MESSENGER**

The text says: ***“Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger”*** The last request in the prayer is the one the sūrah has been moving towards since its opening, and the community reading the passage was the answer to it. Ibn Kathīr reads the sentence as the prayer that a messenger should come from among Abraham's descendants.

The Book has used the same pattern in the story of Adam, where the names of all things were taught and then displayed ((2:31)). In both cases the honour runs in the direction of knowledge and teaching, and in both cases the Book places the arrangement in front of a community that had been arguing about who had the right to lead.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān treats the rest of the prayer as a description of the work the messenger would do. The Book then fulfils that description in the verses near the end of this sūrah, where the sending of the Messenger from among the believers is described ((2:151)). The prayer and its answer are separated by seventy verses and by fifteen centuries of history, and the Book puts them in the same sūrah so that the reader can see both ends.

**WHAT THE MESSENGER WOULD DO**

The verse puts it: ***“who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book”*** The description of the messenger's work begins with recitation, and the order is worth noticing. The words of the revelation are spoken first, and the teaching of the Book comes after the words are in the air. Ibn Kathīr keeps the sequence, and he reads the whole clause as the work of a teacher who gives his students the text before he explains it.

The Book uses the same list in the closing verses of the sūrah, where the sending of the messenger is described as recitation, purification, and teaching the Book and wisdom, together with what the people never knew ((2:151)). The prayer in front of the reader is the request, and the later verse is the receipt.

**WISDOM AND PURITY**

The verse carries on: ***“and wisdom, and purify them.”*** The second half of the list names wisdom and purification. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the whole clause as the complete education of a community: the words recited, the book taught, the understanding of it given, and the character of the people cleaned.

The order of the last item is the part that deserves a moment. The Book does not stop at information. A community can be taught the words of a revelation and remain exactly as it was, and the sūrah has described one such community in detail across a hundred verses. The prayer asks for the cleaning as well as the teaching, which is the request of a man who knew what his own descendants would do with a book they had inherited.

**THE NAMES THAT CLOSE THE PRAYER**

The prayer closes with two names, and the two of them answer the doubts a person has about a request of this size. The first names the power that can bring such a community into being, and the second names the wisdom that decides how and when it will happen.

The sentence reads: ***“Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, All-Wise.””*** Al-Saʿdī reads the whole passage as the model of a person who works with his hands and asks with his heart, and he notes that the two builders left nothing out of the prayer they made over the foundations. The next verses turn to the community that the prayer produced and to the man who had been sent to it, and the reader is asked to hold the whole span in view at once.

Think of a grandfather who plants a row of trees and asks, while he is still holding the spade, that the children who climb them will be honest people. He will not live to see the harvest, and the prayer is not for him. The Book puts the request in front of a community that was living inside its answer and arguing about the paperwork.

---
## Verse 2:130

> And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool! We certainly chose him in this life, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous

**THE QUESTION ABOUT ABRAHAM'S FAITH**

The verse puts the matter: ***“And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool!”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the question as a statement rather than a request for names: nobody turns away from the way of Abraham except a person who has made a fool of himself. He gives two explanations of what that means. The person may have ignored the fact that he was created for God and obliged to worship Him, or he may have treated his own self with contempt and lowered it.

Ibn ʿAbbās gives the same verdict in the same two directions, that the person rejecting the way of Abraham has ruined himself or lost his judgment. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the matter in the plainest words available: nobody turns away from the way of Abraham to another way of life except people who do not know their own worth, and who are content with humiliation.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains what the question is doing at this point in the sūrah. The verses before it set out the religion of Abraham and called people to follow it, and they also answered the claims of the two communities that traced themselves to him. The question in front of the reader is the closing of that case. The community in Madinah had a direct line to the man whose way was on the table. The verse asks what a person is doing when he walks away from the clear way of his own ancestor.

Think of a man who inherits the only well in the village and who, when the water is tested and found clean, announces that he will drink from the puddle behind the market instead. Nobody needs to insult him. The sentence that describes what he did is already on the table, and the verse is that sentence.

**THE CHOICE MADE IN THIS LIFE**

The verse declares: ***“We certainly chose him in this life”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the choosing with the honours that were given to Abraham in the world: prophethood and the rank of a close friend of God. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the selection as covering prophethood, submission, and goodly descendants. The Book elsewhere describes the choice directly, where the believers are told to follow the way of Abraham the upright, who was not one of the polytheists ((3:95)).

The word chosen is the same one the sūrah used when it answered the community's resentment about grace given to a servant of God's own choosing ((2:90), (2:105)). The Book has been telling its readers for eighty verses that the honours of God are distributed by the One who owns them, and it now names the man who received the largest share of them.

**AND IN THE LIFE TO COME**

The verse goes on: ***“and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the second half of the sentence as the statement that Abraham will be among the people whose record stands. Al-Mukhtaṣar expands the word to its practical sense: the righteous are the people who carried out what God required of them and reached the highest ranks.

The Book gives the same description to Abraham in the sūrah of the Women. The believers there are told to follow the way of the man of pure faith, and God says that He took Abraham as a close friend ((4:125)). The two halves of the verse in front of the reader cover the whole of a life, and the Book places the verdict on Abraham immediately before it quotes the sentence that produced the verdict.

---
## Verse 2:131

> When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.”

**THE COMMAND THAT CAME FIRST**

The verse has it: ***“When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.””*** The verse gives the reader the moment that decided everything. Al-Jalālayn reads the command as the instruction to submit and to devote the religion purely to God, and he reads the answer as Abraham's immediate acceptance. Ibn ʿAbbās adds the report that connects the moment to the fire, since Abraham's answer is placed by some accounts at the point where he came out of the furnace his people had built for him.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān pauses over the word of command itself. It comes from the same root as the word for submission. The note observes how hard it is to find an exact equivalent for it in another language, since the word carries the sense of handing over the whole self rather than agreeing with a proposition. The verse is short for that reason. It contains one instruction and one acceptance, and both are made of the same root.

Ibn Kathīr reads the exchange as the moment the religion of Abraham is defined, and the two verses that follow treat the whole tradition as the carrying of that answer from one generation to the next. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the answer as Abraham's swift surrender, and he explains the words Lord of all worlds, which describe the One who created His servants, provides for them and manages their affairs.

Al-Qurṭubī draws out the connection between this verse and the one before it. The choosing described in the earlier sentence happened at the very moment when God said to Abraham, submit, and he submitted. The note reports the view of Ibn Kaysān and al-Kalbī that the command meant: make your religion pure for God alone, in the declaration of His Oneness. Others read it as an instruction to be humble and to lower the heart. Ibn ʿAbbās places the moment at the point where Abraham came out of the hollow in the ground into which his people had thrown him.

**THE ANSWER HE GAVE AT ONCE**

The Book gives the reader the same answer in other places, spoken with the same voice. In the sūrah of the Cattle, Abraham says that he has turned his face towards the One who originated the heavens and the earth, and that he is not one of the polytheists ((6:79)). In the sūrah of the Family of ʿImrān, the Book states the verdict on him in one sentence: Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, and he submitted in all uprightness ((3:67)). The verse in front of the reader is the moment that produced both sentences.

Al-Baghawī records the occasion the commentators attached to the preceding verse, which belongs to the same argument. ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām called his two nephews to Islam. He told them that their own book had announced a prophet from the descendants of Ishmael, and that whoever believed in him was guided while whoever refused him was rejected. One of the two accepted and the other refused, and the verse about turning away from the religion of Abraham came down about the refusal.

The Book has set this verse immediately after the sentence about the choosing, and the order is the Book's argument. A reader who wants to know why Abraham was chosen is given the answer in a single reply. He was asked to hand over his whole self, and he did it in the space of one sentence. The Book then recorded the words he used, and it has kept them in front of readers for the fifteen centuries since.

Think of a man who is offered a place in a house he has admired all his life, and who is asked one question at the door: will he live under the household's rules? The man's answer takes four words, and the whole arrangement turns on it. The Book gives Abraham four words in the same position, and the answer he gave is the reason his name stands at the head of the family that the reader is now being invited to join.

---
## Verse 2:132

> This was the advice of Abraham—as well as Jacob—to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this faith; so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.”

**THE ADVICE ABRAHAM LEFT**

The Book says: ***“This was the advice of Abraham”*** The verse turns from Abraham's own answer to the instruction he left behind, and it calls that instruction advice. Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as Abraham's charge to his sons, and he notes that the same creed was passed on by Jacob to his sons in the same words.

The Book uses the word advice here rather than command, and the choice matters for the audience. The community in Madinah had made leadership into a matter of descent. The verse shows the ancestor of the line doing the one thing a father can do with a legacy that has to be chosen by his children. He tells them what he wants for them, and he leaves the choice in their hands.

**JACOB AT HIS SIDE**

In the verse's own words: ***“as well as Jacob”*** Jacob's name is added to the sentence, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws the lesson out of the pairing. Both prophets gave this counsel to their sons. The note says the two examples show that love for one's children and constant care for their future does not contradict the station of prophethood, or even the rank of the close friend of God.

tafsir_initial explains who Jacob is and where his story is told at length, since the Book gives his family a whole sūrah in the story of his son Joseph. The note also observes that this verse belongs to the general argument that the patriarchs cannot be claimed by any group in an exclusive way. They followed the pure religion of Abraham, which the Book identifies with submission to God.

The name matters for the argument. Jacob is the ancestor that the community in Madinah traced its line to, and the Book has just quoted his own father-in-faith passing the creed on, and it now shows Jacob doing the same thing with the same words.

**THE REASON GIVEN TO THE CHILDREN**

As the verse says: ***“to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen”*** The advice has a reason attached to it, and the reason is a choice that had already been made. Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as the statement that God selected this religion for the children of Abraham. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the sense of a gift already given, which turns the advice into a reminder rather than a proposal.

A reader can see the difference the wording makes. A father who tells his children to be good is giving them an opinion. A father who tells them that the way of life they have been given was selected for them by God is handing them something they already hold, and the sentence tells them what it cost to receive it.

**THE FAITH THAT WAS CHOSEN FOR YOU**

The verse names it: ***“for you this faith”*** The Book has used the noun for this way of life in every passage of the sūrah that dealt with the two communities ((2:120), (2:130)). The sentence here names it as a gift that was chosen for the family, which is the opposite of the exclusive arrangement the two communities had built around descent.

The faith was chosen for the children of Abraham, and the next clauses make clear that the choice is not a guarantee. The father tells them what was selected, and he tells them what he wants for the last hour of their lives.

**THE DEATH THEY WERE TOLD TO AVOID**

The text says: ***“so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.””*** Al-Jalālayn reads the closing instruction as a prohibition on abandoning submission and a command to hold to it until death arrives. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same sense, that Abraham's charge was that his children should not leave this world in any state other than submission.

The sentence is one of the most practical pieces of advice in the Book, and its practicality is in the direction it faces. It does not tell a person to promise anything about the future. It tells him to make sure of the state he will be in when the future is cut off, and the way to be in that state at the end is to stay in it now.

Think of a captain who hands the ship to his sons and tells them the one thing that matters: the vessel must not be flying another flag on the day the inspection comes. He is not asking them to promise that they will never be tempted to change it. He is telling them that the inspection has no fixed date, and that the flag is the state they must be found in.

---
## Verse 2:133

> Or did you witness when death came to Jacob? He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?” They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers—Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac—the One God. And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.”

**THE QUESTION PUT AT DEATH**

The sentence opens: ***“Or did you witness”*** Al-Jalālayn gives the occasion for the verse. The Jewish community told the Messenger that Jacob, on the day of his death, had charged his sons with the practice of Judaism, and the verse came down in answer. The question that opens it asks whether the people making the claim were present at the deathbed.

Al-Qurṭubī reads the address as directed to the two communities that attached to Abraham things he had never instructed his children to do. He says the Book answered them and declared them wrong, with the question put in the form of a rebuke.

This is the same method the sūrah has used in other passages, where claimants are asked from what position they are speaking about events they did not attend. The Book does not forbid a person to have an opinion about history. It asks him to say what his evidence is, which is the same request it made of the two communities when they claimed the Garden ((2:111)).

**THE HOUR OF JACOB'S DEATH**

The verse presses the question: ***“when death came to Jacob?”*** The verse sets the scene at the hour when a man's account is closed, and the question Jacob asks his children is the question that the whole sūrah has been preparing its readers to be asked. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the sentence as the plain account of the moment, when Jacob asked his sons what they would worship after he had gone.

A reader who has followed the chapter will notice what the dying man does with his last conversation. He does not divide the property or name his heir or leave instructions about the family name. He asks his children who will be their God when he is no longer standing over them, which is the one connection he cannot maintain for them from a grave.

**WHAT THEY WOULD WORSHIP AFTER HIM**

The sentence reads: ***“He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?””*** The question is put in the future tense and it is addressed to people who were about to be left without their teacher. Al-Jalālayn reads the words after me as Jacob's own awareness that the question would be answered when he could no longer check the answer.

The Book records both the question and the answer, which is why the verse closes the door on the claim that was made about the deathbed. The community in Madinah was quoting Jacob's final instruction as evidence for its own position, and the Book produces the actual conversation. The answer of the children was not the practice the community claimed to inherit.

**THE ANSWER THEY GAVE**

The wording runs: ***“They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers”*** The answer begins with an act of worship and it reaches back through the family to the line of fathers. Al-Jalālayn reads the words as the promise to worship the God of Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac. He records the grammatical point the commentators raised about Ishmael, who is an uncle of Jacob's children and is included among the fathers because an uncle stands in the place of a father.

tafsir_initial notes a linguistic detail that a careful reader of the Book will find useful. The name of God in this verse is the ordinary noun for a god, and not the proper name used elsewhere in the sūrah. The note explains that the noun is what is being used to describe the object of the family's worship. The children are naming the God of their fathers by the only word that covered Him in their language.

The answer also shows what a family legacy looks like when it works. The children were listing the men who had taught them the way, and the list begins with Abraham, who had been dead for generations by the time Jacob was dying.

**THE ANCESTORS NAMED**

The verse puts the matter: ***“Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac”*** The three names in the answer include the two communities that were arguing in Madinah, since Ishmael is the ancestor of the Arab line and Isaac of the line that the People of the Book trace. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the three names in the answer, and tafsir_initial lists other places in the Book where the same group of prophets is named together ((2:136), (4:163), (12:38)).

The sentence is a small answer to a large argument. The community that claimed Abraham for itself through Isaac is shown the dying man's children naming both branches of the family in the same breath, which leaves the claim of exclusivity with nothing to stand on.

**ONE GOD AND SUBMISSION TO HIM**

As the verse says: ***“the One God. And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.””*** The children's answer closes with the same word that closed Abraham's answer to the command ((2:131)) and the same word the sūrah will use for the whole community of believers ((2:132)). Al-Jalālayn reads the phrase as the declaration of the one God and the acknowledgment of submission to Him.

The word the family used at the deathbed is the word the reader has been given as the name of his own religion. The verse puts it in the mouth of children watching their father die, which is the sūrah's way of showing where the tradition came from and who was keeping it.

Think of a family business that has been passed down for four generations and whose founders are all in the photographs on the wall. On the day the current owner retires, he asks his sons which name will be on the door next year, and they give him the founders' names and the old sign. The next verse tells the reader what happens to the argument over the inheritance when the founders themselves have been gone for years.

---
## Verse 2:134

> That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done

**A COMMUNITY THAT HAS GONE**

The wording runs: ***“That was a community”*** The verse takes the reader away from the deathbed and puts the whole family in the past tense. Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as a statement that the community in question has already gone by, and he keeps the verse in the same words the sūrah uses later when it returns to the same subject ((2:141)).

Ibn Kathīr reads the sentence as the Book's criticism of the claim the two communities had built around the patriarchs, and he places the verse in the sequence of the argument. The Book has just quoted a deathbed conversation from a generation that had passed away, and it now tells the reader what that generation's past means for him.

**WHAT HAPPENED TO THEM**

The clause names what has happened to the men whose names had been used as arguments for a hundred verses. They finished their work, and they were paid for it, and the account is closed. The Book states the fact without any ceremony and lets it land on the reader's own position.

The wording is: ***“that had already gone before.”*** A reader should notice how much of the sūrah's argument rests on this sentence. The community in Madinah had been told about the favours of Abraham, the building of the House, and the covenant taken from the descendants of Israel, and the Book keeps every one of those accounts in the past tense. What remains in the present is the reader's own life and the choices in front of him.

**WHAT THEY EARNED**

The verse records: ***“For them is what they earned”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as the statement that each generation keeps what it earned. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same sense in his comment on the verse and its repeat, and the Book uses the same words for the same purpose in the passage that closes this section ((2:141)).

The word for earning is the same market word the sūrah has used throughout its accounting passages. The Book has shown the reader a community that sold its soul for a spell ((2:102)) and a community that traded the next life for a position in this one ((2:86)). The sentence in front of him uses the language of the same ledger for the whole human family.

**WHAT YOU EARN**

The next words are: ***“and for you is what you have earned.”*** The second half of the sentence turns the ledger to face the reader. The Book stops discussing the ancestors and states the arrangement that applies to the person holding the Book. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the two halves side by side, one for them and one for you.

The sentence is one of the clearest statements of individual responsibility in the sūrah, and it arrives at the end of a long section about ancestry. A reader can carry the verse away with him and apply it to any matter where a person's standing in this world has been turned into a claim about his standing before God.

**NO ONE CARRIES ANOTHER'S DEEDS**

The last clause removes the second half of the burden that a lineage can place on a person. A man is not asked to answer for the deeds of his grandfather, and the sentence closes the door on the pride that comes from the other direction as well.

The wording continues: ***“And you will not be accountable”*** The Book states the principle twice in this sūrah, once here and once at the end of the passage that repeats the address to the community ((2:141)). The sūrah has been conducting an inquiry into the record of a nation and its ancestors for a hundred and twenty verses, and it ends the inquiry by telling each reader which part of the file belongs to him. The same idea is stated at the end of the chapter in different words. There the Book says that no soul is required to carry more than it can bear, and that each person keeps the good he has earned and the harm he has earned ((2:286)).

Think of a family that has spent two years in a court case about an inheritance from a grandfather none of them met. One of the cousins arrives at the hearing and says that what matters is what her own father built, and that she is willing to be judged by her own books. The case does not stop being about the grandfather. The woman simply chooses which set of columns belongs to her, and the verse tells every reader to make the same choice.

**WHAT THEY DID IS THEIR OWN**

The sentence ends with the deeds of the previous generation, and the Book leaves them where they are. The people being addressed were not present at the deathbed of Jacob and were not consulted about the covenant taken at the mountain, and the verse says that neither the credit nor the blame is transferred by blood.

The verse has it: ***“for what they have done”*** The next verses turn back to the same family and give the reader the one sentence that unites them all. The rule is stated plainly elsewhere: (53:38 — **“no soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another”**). The section then closes with an instruction that applies the whole argument to the community standing in front of the Messenger.

---
## Verse 2:135

> The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No! We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright—who was not a polytheist.”

**THEY CALL YOU TO THEIR WAY**

As the verse says: ***“The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No!”*** Al-Jalālayn treats the two halves of the sentence as the words of two different groups. The small word joining them marks a division, so that the first claim belongs to the Jewish community of Madinah and the second belongs to the Christians of Najrān. Each group offered guidance to the Muslims on the condition that they join it.

Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same division. Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the offer in ordinary words: the Jews told the Muslims that they would only be guided if they became Jews, and the Christians told them that they would only be guided if they became Christians.

Ibn Kathīr records the report of Ibn Isḥāq, in which ʿAbdullāh ibn Suriyā al-Aʿwar said to the Messenger that guidance was only what his own people followed. The report shows the shape of the argument. The offer was not an invitation to examine a case. It was a claim to own the meaning of the word guidance.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān places the sentence in the sequence of the sūrah. The verses just before it had set out the religion of Abraham and shown that neither community was following it. Instead of accepting that conclusion, each group asked the Muslims to enter its own religion, and the verse records the answer they were given.

The sūrah has met this instinct twice already. A group had claimed the Garden on the strength of its identity ((2:111)), and the Book answered the claim and gave the Garden to whoever submitted to God and did good ((2:112)). The sentence in front of the reader applies the same answer to the word guidance, and the word no at its centre is the whole correction.

Think of two shopkeepers on the same street, each of whom tells every passer-by that the only honest scale in the market is the one behind his own counter. Neither man has offered to weigh anything for the customer. The verse puts the two offers side by side, refuses both, and points the reader to the merchant who owned the market before either shop was built.

**THE WAY OF ABRAHAM**

The verse has it: ***“We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the word upright as the description of a person who turns away from every other religion and faces the truth. The answer given to the Messenger is not a new claim on the reader's attention. It is the oldest one available, and both communities had spent the previous verses claiming it.

Al-Mukhtaṣar reads Abraham as the man who turned away from false ways of life to the way of truth, and it notes that he never associated anything with God. The Book states the same verdict in the Family of ʿImrān. Abraham is declared there to be neither a Jew nor a Christian, and he is described as one who submitted in all uprightness and was not a polytheist ((3:67)).

The Book gives the community the same instruction in two other places, and both of them use the same word for the way. In one place the Messenger himself is told to follow the way of Abraham, the man of pure faith ((3:95)). In the other the same command is given with the words: surely my Lord has guided me to the Straight Path, the faith of Abraham the upright ((6:161)).

A reader can see what the answer does with the word faith. The two communities had turned it into the name of a building with one door, and the verse takes it back to the man who walked the road before either building existed.

**NOT A POLYTHEIST**

The closing clause is the test that both offers fail. A religion that sets up partners alongside God cannot be the way of Abraham, and the clause states the fact about Abraham in the plainest terms.

The verse declares: ***“who was not a polytheist.””*** Ibn Kathīr reads the sentence as the description of Abraham's religion as pure monotheism, free of anyone or anything worshipped beside God. Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the same sense, and the Book repeats the phrase as a fixed description of the man every time it mentions his way ((3:67), (3:95), (6:161)).

The sentence is short and the argument it closes is long. The two communities had used the ancestry of Abraham as a claim on God, and the Book answers by describing what the man actually believed. The description leaves no room for the claim either community had built on his name.

---
## Verse 2:136

> Say, ˹O believers,˺ “We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us; and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants; and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and other prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them. And to Allah we all submit.”

**WHAT THE BELIEVERS DECLARE**

The verse states: ***“Say, ˹O believers,˺ “We believe in Allah”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the address as directed to the believers, and Ibn ʿAbbās explains the purpose of the sentence. The Book was teaching the believers the way of the Oneness of God, so that the two communities arguing about Abraham would have in front of them a clear statement of what the faith of Abraham actually contains.

Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the verse as the answer the Muslims were told to give to the claims in the previous verses. A community that had just been offered two rival religions was given a declaration to make instead, and the declaration begins with God.

The sūrah has put a statement of faith in front of its readers before, at the beginning of the chapter. It described the people who believe in what was sent down to the Messenger and what was sent down before him ((2:4)). The verse in front of the reader is the expanded form of the same statement.

**THE REVELATION GIVEN TO US**

The sentence moves on: ***“and what has been revealed to us”*** The Book begins the list with the revelation that the community itself had received. Ibn Kathīr reads the clause as the Qurʾān, and he marks the order of the sentence, which places the community's own revelation first and then reaches back through the line of the prophets.

The Book uses the same beginning in the Family of ʿImrān, where the declaration opens with belief in God and in what has been revealed to the Messenger and to the prophets who came before him ((3:84)). The words are almost identical, and the community reading them is given the same place in the family line.

**THE PROPHETS NAMED BEFORE**

The sentence continues: ***“and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as belief in the revelation given to Abraham, which the commentators describe as a set of written pages, and then in the prophets named after him. The verse names the two branches of the family in one breath, the Arab line through Ishmael and the line of Israel through Isaac and Jacob.

The sūrah has already used this list in the dispute about the patriarchs ((2:133)). The verse in front of the reader turns the list into an article of faith, and a reader can see how much difference the change of function makes. The two communities argued about which family the prophets belonged to, and the believers are told to believe in all of them.

**THE DESCENDANTS IN THE LIST**

The wording continues: ***“and his descendants”*** The word in the sentence refers to the tribes that came from the sons of Jacob, and Al-Jalālayn keeps the sense of his sons and their lines. The Book uses the same word elsewhere for the same group ((2:136), (4:163)).

The clause matters for the argument of the sūrah, since the descendants of Jacob are the ancestors of the community arguing in Madinah. The declaration in front of the reader names them all as recipients of revelation, which settles the question of who is entitled to claim the prophets. A believer is told to accept all of them without exception.

**MOSES, JESUS AND THE OTHERS**

The verse goes on: ***“and what was given to Moses, Jesus”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the clause as the Torah given to Moses and the Gospel given to Jesus, and it treats the two books as objects of belief for the Muslim community. The verse names the two books after the two prophets, which is the order of the revelation and not the rank of the recipients.

The Book gives the same list in the sūrah of the Women. The verse there names the revelation sent to the Messenger, the revelation sent to Noah and the prophets after him, and then the same line of patriarchs, before it names Moses, Jesus and the prophets after them ((4:163)). The reader of the sūrah has now seen three versions of one declaration, and all three hold the family together.

**NO DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THEM**

The verse adds: ***“and other prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them.”*** The sentence that closes the list states the principle the whole passage rests on. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads it as the refusal to draw a line between the prophets by accepting some and rejecting others, which is the practice the Book has been describing in the two communities for a hundred verses.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains the purpose of the declaration and calls it comprehensive, since it contains the whole content of faith in a single sentence. A person who says it has accepted every messenger God sent, along with everything they brought, and he has no need to argue about which of them belonged to which nation.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the phrase in the same sense, that the believers do not separate the prophets by believing some and disbelieving others. The Book states the same principle with the same words in the Family of ʿImrān ((3:84)), and the reader can hear the community being taught to answer a claim about ownership with a statement about belief.

**SUBMISSION TO HIM ALONE**

The verse carries on: ***“And to Allah we all submit.””*** The declaration ends with the word that has been the subject of the passage since the mention of Abraham's answer ((2:131)), and the word is the same one that gave the religion its name. Al-Jalālayn keeps the sentence as the statement of submission to God alone.

Think of a man who buys a house and finds a locked room inside it. The previous owner's papers, letters and diaries are in there. A person with a suspicious mind could break the lock and pick out the two letters he likes and burn the rest. The community in this verse is told to open the door and accept every page in the room, because the whole library came from the same hand.

The verse has now given the reader the content of the faith of Abraham in a form that a person can carry in his mouth, and it has done so in the middle of a dispute about ancestry. A reader who has followed the argument can see what the Book has done with the family the two communities were fighting over. It has taken the whole line of prophets and placed them inside the creed of the community that followed the last of them.

---
## Verse 2:137

> So if they believe in what you believe, then they will indeed be ˹rightly˺ guided. But if they turn away, they are simply opposed ˹to the truth˺. But Allah will spare you their evil. For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**IF THEY BELIEVE AS YOU BELIEVE**

The verse puts it: ***“So if they believe in what you believe”*** Al-Jalālayn notes a grammatical point that changes nothing in the meaning and is worth mentioning for the reader of a translation. The Arabic sentence says in the like of what you believe, and the word for like is regarded by the grammarians as extra, so that the sense is simply: if they believe in what you believe.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān treats the verse as the point where the sūrah defines faith. The verses before it had explained the nature of faith in detail, and the sentence in front of the reader gives the definition in a short phrase. A person's faith is measured against what the believing community believes, and the community had just had its creed set out in the previous verse.

The condition in the sentence is not a demand for an exact copy of an opinion. It is the statement that there is one faith, and that the two communities had been arguing about which of them held it while the believers were stating it in plain words.

**GUIDANCE PROMISED**

The verse goes on: ***“then they will indeed be ˹rightly˺ guided.”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the clause as the promise that the two communities would be guided away from their error if they followed the religion of the Messenger and the religion of Abraham. The Book has used the word guidance since its first verses, where it described the Book itself as a guide for the people who guard themselves ((2:2)).

Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the sense of guidance as the way of life that God is satisfied with. The verse holds two things together that a reader might separate. The creed is short enough to state, and the road it opens is the whole purpose of the revelation.

**WHEN THEY TURN THEIR BACKS**

The sentence reads: ***“But if they turn away, they are simply opposed ˹to the truth˺.”*** The second half of the sentence describes the people who refuse the answer, and Al-Jalālayn reads the word for opposition as the state of a group that has separated itself in conflict. Ibn ʿAbbās gives the same sense, that the people who turn away are in conflict with the true religion.

Al-Mukhtaṣar explains what the refusal means in practice: rejecting all the prophets, or rejecting some of them. The distinction is useful, because the Book has been dealing with a community that accepted Moses and refused the Messenger who came after him. The sentence puts that position in the same category as refusing the whole line.

Think of two men who are given a road to walk to a city. They may argue about what stands beside the road, and they may describe the fields on either side differently. The verse is not describing a disagreement of that kind. It is describing men who have left the road and who are walking away from the city they were asked to reach.

**THE HARM THEY CANNOT REACH YOU WITH**

The verse names it: ***“But Allah will spare you their evil.”*** The clause is addressed to the Messenger, and Al-Jalālayn reads it as the promise that God would be enough for him against the two communities and their divisions. The Book has already consoled him in this sūrah for the stubbornness of the people he was sent to, and it does so again here.

The clause follows a statement about opposition, and its position is the comfort the sentence is built to deliver. A man who has been told that the people he is teaching will not accept the road he is on is then told that he does not have to carry the quarrel on his own account.

**THE TWO NAMES THAT CLOSE IT**

The verse has it: ***“For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the two names as the hearing of what the two communities said and the knowledge of their circumstances. Ibn Kathīr keeps the same reading, and the names answer both halves of the verse in front of the reader.

A reader can see how the two names work with the promises of the passage. God hears the offer that was made to the Muslims, and He knows the condition of the people making it. That is why the guidance can be promised to the ones who believe, and why the opposition can be answered without the Messenger having to win the argument himself.

---
## Verse 2:138

> This is the ˹natural˺ Way of Allah. And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way? And we worship ˹none but˺ Him

**THE WAY GOD MADE**

The verse puts the matter: ***“This is the ˹natural˺ Way of Allah.”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the word that the translation renders as natural Way. It is formed from the word for dye, and it is used here for the religion of God. The verse is describing the way of life as something that leaves a colour on the person who takes it up.

Al-Baghawī reports the explanation the early authorities gave of the word. Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah and al-Ḥasan said it means the religion of God, and it was called a dye because the effect of religion shows on the person who practises it the way a dye shows on a cloth. Others gave the reason from the other direction: the dye stays with the cloth, and religion stays with its owner and does not leave him.

Mujāhid read the word as the natural constitution God gave people, and al-Baghawī notes that the two explanations are close to each other. The Book states the same idea in another sūrah, where it tells the Messenger to stand firm in the natural Way of God which He instilled in all people ((30:30)).

Think of a fabric that has been dyed at the mill before it was ever cut into clothes. Every thread carries the colour, so that the shirt does not fade into something else when it is washed. The verse is telling the reader that his religion is not a coat he can hang up at the door, because the Book describes it as the colour of the cloth itself.

**THE QUESTION ABOUT A BETTER WAY**

The sentence continues: ***“And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way?”*** The question is rhetorical, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the sense in the plainest form, asking who could be better than God in laying down the religion a person follows. The Book has used the same question in the same passage about the way of Abraham, where it asked who could be better than God in ordaining a way.

The clause is the second half of the answer to the two communities. Each of them had offered the Muslims a way of life, and the verse asks the reader to compare the source of the two offers. One was put together by a group of people, and the other was sent down by the One who made them.

Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the whole verse as the instruction to hold tightly to the religion of God, which it describes as the natural way of life for a human being, on the inside and on the outside. The two directions matter in a passage about people who wanted the community to change the way it stood in public.

**WORSHIP FOR HIM ALONE**

The sentence moves on: ***“And we worship ˹none but˺ Him”*** The verse closes with a statement of worship, which is the practical form of everything the previous sentences have claimed. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the clause as the declaration of pure monotheism, that the community worships God alone and acknowledges no other god beside Him.

The reader of the sūrah has seen the same words used to describe the religion of Jacob's children at his deathbed ((2:133)). The sentence in front of him is the same sentence, spoken by the community that followed the last Messenger, and the Book places the two of them within a few verses of each other so that the continuity is clear.

---
## Verse 2:139

> Say, “Would you dispute with us about Allah, while He is our Lord and your Lord? We are accountable for our deeds and you for yours. And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺

**THE DISPUTE PUT TO THEM**

The wording runs: ***“Say, “Would you dispute with us about Allah”*** The Book puts the question in the Messenger's mouth and sets it against the argument that had been running for several pages. Al-Jalālayn reads the dispute as the objection of the two communities to the fact that God chose a prophet from among the Arabs.

Al-Qurṭubī records the explanation al-Ḥasan gave of the quarrel. The two communities said they were nearer to God than the Muslims, because they were the sons of God and the ones He loved. Others said their claim rested on the age of their fathers and their books, and on the fact that they had never worshipped idols.

tafsir_initial shows how much wider the dispute was. The argument about a prophet from outside the family of Israel is one version of it, and the objection of the idolatrous Arabs to the social standing of the Messenger is another. The note points to the places where the Book answers that instinct directly, including the passage that states that God gives His kingdom to whoever He wills ((3:26), (43:31)).

The sūrah has answered the same argument in several forms, and the reader can now recognize the shape of it. A group takes something it has been given, turns it into a title, and then argues that the title settles the question of who may speak for God.

Imagine a family that was once trusted with the key to the town granary and that now tells its neighbours that the key has always belonged to their blood. The verse answers the claim with a question about who owns the grain, and the question is addressed to both families standing in the street.

**THE LORD OF BOTH SIDES**

The text says: ***“while He is our Lord”*** The clause gives the reason the dispute cannot stand. Al-Mukhtaṣar explains the argument being made against the Muslims: the two communities said they had more right to God and to His religion because their way of life was older and their books came first.

The answer begins with a fact about ownership. God is the Lord of the Muslims, and the verse does not stop there, because the next clause completes the sentence with the other party in it.

**TWO CLAUSES THAT END THE ARGUMENT**

Then the verse says: ***“and your Lord?”*** The two short clauses together dismantle the claim. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the question in the same form: the argument was about the religion of God, and the One they were arguing about was the Lord of both sides.

The Book makes the same point in other places where a community treats its own history as a claim on God. A Lord who belongs to one nation and not to another is not the Lord the Book has been describing since its first page, and the sentence in front of the reader leaves both communities standing under the same owner.

**WHAT EACH SIDE CARRIES**

The verse states: ***“We are accountable for our deeds”*** The verse moves from the question of ownership to the question of accounting. Al-Jalālayn reads the clause as the statement that the deeds of the community belong to it and that it will be repaid for them.

The sentence has a close relative a few verses back, where the Book told the readers that each community keeps what it earned, and that no one is asked about what another generation did ((2:134)). The Book returns to the same ledger here, and it puts the words in the mouth of the believers as their answer to a dispute about rank.

**WHAT YOU CARRY**

The sentence moves on: ***“and you for yours.”*** The second half of the sentence hands the other ledger back to the people who were arguing. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the two clauses as the division of responsibility: our religion belongs to us and your religion belongs to you.

The sentence is the reason the believers are told not to worry about the outcome of the argument. A person's standing before God is not decided by the age of his community or the size of its library, and the verse states the arrangement in the form of two closed accounts.

**DEVOTION THAT SETTLES IT**

The wording continues: ***“And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺”*** The verse closes where the creed of the previous verses closed, with the direction of worship. Ibn Kathīr reads the clause as sincerity to God, which he explains as worshipping Him alone and obeying His orders.

The same word is used elsewhere in the sūrah for the people the Book accepts, and the reader has now seen the argument made in three stages ((2:112)). The first is a claim to a place in the next life, the second is a claim to the meaning of guidance, and the third is a claim to a closer relationship with God. The Book answers each of them with the same sentence about work and worship.

---
## Verse 2:140

> Do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants were all Jews or Christians?” Say, “Who is more knowledgeable: you or Allah?” Who does more wrong than those who hide the testimony they received from Allah? And Allah is never unaware of what you do

**THE CLAIM ABOUT THE ANCESTORS**

The verse states: ***“Do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob”*** The verse returns to the claim the sūrah has been answering since the story of Abraham began. Al-Jalālayn notes that the Arabic sentence may be read in two ways, as a question addressed to the people making the claim or as a report of what they say, and that both readings leave the meaning the same.

The names in the sentence include both sides of the family that the two communities were arguing over. A Jew could claim Isaac and Jacob by descent, and a Christian could claim them by scripture, and Ishmael stood in the middle of the list as the ancestor of the community they were both dismissing.

**NAMES PUT INTO LATER LABELS**

The verse carries on: ***“and his descendants were all Jews”*** The claim being quoted is an act of backdating. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the sentence in the form of the claim, that the patriarchs and their descendants were followers of the religion that later took its name from the tribe of Judah.

The Book has already given the reader the materials to answer the claim, because it described the deathbed of Jacob and quoted the words his children used there ((2:133)). The religion they named was submission to the one God of their fathers, and no part of the conversation contained the name the claim was built on.

**THE SECOND HALF OF THE CLAIM**

As the verse says: ***“or Christians?” Say, “Who is more knowledgeable”*** The second half of the claim is the Christian version of the same move, and the Book answers both by turning the question around. Al-Jalālayn reads the reply as the assignment of knowledge to God, who has already given His verdict on the matter.

The sentence is a short and complete answer to any historical claim about religion. A person who says what a prophet believed is describing a fact about the past, and the question the verse asks is whether he has more information than the One who sent the prophet.

**THE QUESTION OF WHO KNOWS BETTER**

The Book says: ***“you or Allah?””*** Al-Jalālayn supplies the verdict in the words the Book uses elsewhere, where Abraham is declared to be neither a Jew nor a Christian ((3:67)). tafsir_initial points to the same argument in the Family of ʿImrān. There the People of the Book are asked why they dispute about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not sent down until long after him ((3:65)).

The question in the verse is rhetorical, and its answer is the order of history. The man the two communities were claiming lived centuries before the books they were claiming him for, and the Book leaves the reader to draw the conclusion from the dates.

**THE WRONGDOERS WHO HIDE**

The verse records: ***“Who does more wrong than those”*** The verse turns from the claim to the people making it, and the sentence it uses is the strongest form of the question the Book asks about conduct. The Book has used the same form elsewhere for the people who prevent others from reaching the houses of worship ((2:114)).

A reader should notice that the wrong being described in the next clause is not the act of making the claim. The claim had been made in public and could be examined. The wrong the verse names is the hiding of evidence by people who know what it says.

**THE TESTIMONY THEY BURIED**

The verse puts the question: ***“who hide the testimony they received from Allah?”*** Ibn Kathīr explains the testimony as the truth that the People of the Book had received in their own books, and he reads the verse as the charge of concealing the description of the coming Messenger that their scriptures contained. Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the same sense, that the testimony was hidden after it had been received from God.

tafsir_initial sets out the two directions the word testimony has been given by the commentators. It can mean the religion brought by the Messenger, which testifies to the truths the People of the Book already held, and which their own books describe according to the belief of the Muslim community. It can also mean the testimony God Himself gave that these prophets were not Jews or Christians, which their own histories confirm.

The Book states the same charge in a later verse. It says there that the people who were given the Scripture recognize the Messenger as they recognize their own children, and that a group of them hides the truth knowingly ((2:146)). The verse in front of the reader names the crime that the later verse describes in action.

Think of a land registry in which a clerk holds the original deed to a house that is being sold. He knows the name on the document, and he takes the paper out of the file and says nothing while the neighbours argue about who owns the property. The verse names the withholding of a document as a wrong of its own kind, and it places that wrong at the centre of the dispute about the patriarchs.

**WHAT THEY DO IS SEEN**

The verse closes with the warning the sūrah has used at other points in its argument, and the sentence covers both halves of the passage. The claim had been made in the open, and the hiding had been done in private.

The verse continues: ***“And Allah is never unaware of what you do”*** Al-Jalālayn keeps the clause as the statement that no part of the conduct described in the verse escapes the knowledge of God. The next verse returns to the sentence that closed the previous movement of the sūrah and states the arrangement that applies to every generation reading the Book.

---

> That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done

## Verse 2:142

> The foolish among the people will ask, “Why did they turn away from the direction of prayer they used to face?” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “The east and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah. He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.”

**A QUESTION THE VERSE ANSWERS BEFORE IT IS ASKED**

The verse tells the Prophet ﷺ what is about to be said, and it names the speakers before their words arrive: ***“The foolish among the people will ask, “Why did they turn away from the direction of prayer they used to face?””*** Al-Jalālayn notes that the opening word is in the future tense, so the sentence reports what has not happened yet, and the direction they had faced was the Holy House in Jerusalem. Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the foolish as the ignorant among the Jews and the idolaters, and al-Mukhtaṣar adds the hypocrites to the list. The question was pointed at the Muslims, and it was meant to embarrass them in front of their neighbours.

The story behind the question is reported from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib. When the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah he prayed towards Jerusalem for sixteen or seventeen months, and he wished that his direction of prayer could be the Kaʿbah. Al-Bukhārī recorded the report, and Muslim recorded it by another chain, as Ibn Kathīr notes. The first prayer the Prophet ﷺ offered facing the Kaʿbah was the afternoon prayer, and one of the men who had prayed with him passed a mosque whose people were bowing. He told them what he had just seen, and the whole row turned while still bowing. The change reached the community in the middle of a prayer, and it reached it as news.

**WHAT THE WORD FOOLISH EXPOSES**

Al-Qushairī explains that the eyes of the disbelievers were weak, so the right way of seeing the affairs of the believers was not open to them. They looked with an eye that hunted for ugliness, they let their tongues loose against everything the believers did, and they never saw a new matter without inventing a new objection to it. Kashānī takes the word further: they are called foolish because their minds failed to reach the truth of the religion they were rejecting. Their argument was never about evidence. It was about the fact that the believers had changed a practice the onlookers had come to treat as fixed.

tafsir_initial draws a quieter point from the tense of the verb. The future form does not exclude the past, because the sentence describes a trait that the group carried, not only a single event that would happen once. The same note presses the deeper lesson: what makes a place a direction of prayer is not the place itself, but the command of God. Jerusalem was never invested with power to answer prayers, and the Kaʿbah was not given such power either. Imagine a teacher who tells a class to face the board. He is not claiming that the board is holy; the class faces it because the teacher said so. That is the whole of the answer, and it removes the sting from the question.

**EVERY DIRECTION BELONGS TO HIM**

The verse then supplies the correction in the words of its own answer: ***“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “The east”*** ***“and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah. He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.””*** Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as a statement that every direction belongs to God, so He may command His servants to face whichever of them He chooses and no one has grounds to object. Ibn ʿAbbās says the same in plainer words: prayer towards the Kaʿbah and prayer towards Jerusalem were both by the command of God, so the servant is not the one who decides.

The Book states the same truth where it answers the traveller who cannot fix his direction: (2:115 — **“so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah”**). Tazkirul Qur'an explains the wisdom of having a direction at all. The qiblah belongs to the form of worship and not to its reality, and it was appointed so that prayer would take an ordered pattern among people who pray together. God can change it whenever He pleases, because in every direction a person faces Him. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān adds the social reason for one shared direction: worship that is performed in public gathers the community, and a single direction is what makes a gathered body look like one body rather than a crowd of separate worshippers.

Kashānī reads the phrase about guidance as the answer to the whole dispute. The people who objected were attached to one direction and could accept nothing else, because they had not understood the Oneness that contains all directions. The servant who knows that God is not contained by a place can face east or west and still be facing the One he worships. The verse closes with the gift, not the place: guidance is given, and it is given to whoever God wills, so the wise reader asks for it instead of arguing about it.

---
## Verse 2:143

> And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community so that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you. We assigned your former direction of prayer only to distinguish those who would remain faithful to the Messenger from those who would lose faith. It was certainly a difficult test except for those ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah. And Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith. Surely Allah is Ever Gracious and Most Merciful to humanity

**A COMMUNITY PLACED IN THE MIDDLE**

The verse joins the new gift to the new duty with one word: ***“And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the word as midmost, and explains it as excellent and upright. Ibn ʿAbbās calls the community middlemost. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān records the report of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī in al-Tirmidhī, where the Prophet ﷺ explained the middle as justice, and the best of a thing is often its middle. tafsir_initial gathers the same discussion: the middle of a people is its most esteemed part, and the balanced position is the one that avoids the two extremes, so courage sits between recklessness and cowardice and generosity sits between waste and stinginess. The community is praised for a quality it is expected to practise.

The purpose of the honour is attached to it at once: ***“so that you may be witnesses over humanity”***. Al-Jalālayn explains the witness as testimony on the Day of Resurrection, when this community testifies that the messengers delivered the message to their peoples. Tazkirul Qur'an draws the duty into the present: the chain of prophethood ended with the Prophet ﷺ, and the work of carrying the message to people did not end with it, so the community now stands in the place the prophets used to hold. That is a task and not a badge. Think of a relay race: the honour of the last runner is that the baton is in his hand, and the moment he holds it up as a trophy the race is lost.

**THE MESSENGER WHO TESTIFIES FOR THEM**

The sentence then names the second witness: ***“and that the Messenger may be a witness over you.”*** Al-Jalālayn explains that he testifies that he delivered the message to them, and Ibn ʿAbbās adds that the testimony covers the community's own uprightness and its keeping to the straight path. So the witness stands on both sides of the community: the community answers for what was passed on to others, and the Messenger answers for what was passed down to it. No one in the arrangement is left without an account to give.

**THE OLD DIRECTION AND THE TEST IT MADE**

The verse then tells the reader why the earlier direction of prayer was given at all: ***“We assigned your former direction of prayer only to distinguish those”*** ***“who would remain faithful to the Messenger from those”*** ***“who would lose faith. It was certainly a difficult test except”*** ***“for those ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah.”*** Al-Jalālayn explains that to know here means to make the matter known and visible. Ibn ʿAbbās puts it as a test that sifts one man from another: the one who follows the Messenger in the change, and the one who turns back on his heels. Ibn Kathīr reports from the Companions that the first change of direction was heavy on the hearts, and that it was light only for those whose faith God had settled. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the same: the change showed who was content with God's decree and who followed his own desires.

A test of this kind works on the surface of a habit and reaches the root of a heart. The person who prays because he was raised in a place, or because his neighbours do, discovers at the moment of change what his prayer was attached to. A passenger who has been sitting in the same seat for hours may not know how fond of it he has grown until the conductor asks him to move. The change of direction asked the community one question: is your worship tied to a wall, or to the One who commanded the wall? The answer to that question was worth more than the argument about the two cities.

**THE PRAYERS THAT WERE NOT WASTED**

The verse closes with a word for the people who had already died facing the old direction, and for the living who had prayed that way for months: ***“And Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith. Surely Allah is Ever Gracious”*** ***“and Most Merciful to humanity”***. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as a promise that God will not thwart the faith his servants held before the ruling changed. Ibn Kathīr records the report that the Muslims asked what should be said about those who had died praying towards Jerusalem, and this sentence came down as the answer. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the promise in plain words: they will lose neither their faith nor their good actions, and the prayers they offered before the change keep their reward. Al-Jalālayn reads the two names at the end as the ground of the promise: the Lord is kind with people and does not ask of them more than they can carry.

For a believer this is a small window into how God treats what is past. An employer who changes the way the work is done does not dock the wages of the years already worked, and the Lord of the worlds is more generous than any employer. The verse does not treat the change as a loss to be explained away. It treats obedience offered in good faith as something God refuses to waste.

---
## Verse 2:144

> Indeed, We see you ˹O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven. Now We will make you turn towards a direction ˹of prayer˺ that will please you. So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque ˹in Mecca˺—wherever you are, turn your faces towards it. Those who were given the Scripture certainly know this to be the truth from their Lord. And Allah is never unaware of what they do

**THE FACE THAT KEPT RISING TO THE SKY**

The verse answers a longing that the Prophet ﷺ had carried without putting it into words: ***“Indeed, We see you ˹O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven. Now We will make you turn towards a direction ˹of prayer˺”*** ***“that will please you.”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the turning as the Prophet ﷺ looking up and waiting for the revelation, because he wished for the command that would turn him towards the Kaʿbah. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it the same way: he was waiting for Gabriel to come down with the news. Al-Mukhtaṣar says God saw him gazing at the sky, anticipating the change towards the place he loved.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains why the wish sat so naturally in his heart. The House in Makkah was the direction of Abraham, and the Prophet's way was the way of Abraham, so the longing came out of the shape of the religion itself and not out of a preference for one city over another. Al-Tustarī, in the report Asbāb al-Nuzūl preserves, adds a gentle detail: he kept the wish inside his heart and did not ask for it in words, and God gave him what he had not asked for. Think of a guest who does not mention that he is cold, and the host who quietly brings him a blanket. The verse honours a servant whose request was made of silence and patience.

**THE COMMAND THAT FINISHED THE WAITING**

Then the waiting ends with an order in the plainest form: ***“So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque ˹in Mecca˺”*** ***“wherever you are, turn your faces towards it. Those”***. Al-Jalālayn notes that the address is widened at once from the Prophet ﷺ to the whole community, so that no believer in any land is left without a direction. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the two halves of the command side by side: he is to turn towards the Sacred House, and they are to do the same wherever they may be. The House is one, and the community spread across the earth turns to it as one body.

Tazkirul Qur'an draws out why the change mattered for the message rather than for the map. The faith had to be seen in a pure and distinct form, separated from the traditions that had grown around the earlier communities, and the direction of prayer was the visible sign of that separation. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān makes a related point about congregational worship: a single direction gives a scattered community a shared shape, so a stranger walking into any Muslim town recognises the same prayer by the way the people stand. Imagine a family scattered across many cities that agrees to eat its evening meal at the same hour facing the same table. The table is not the meal and the hour is not the prayer, but the arrangement is what makes the family one.

**THEY KNEW IT AND STILL TURNED AWAY**

The verse ends by naming the knowledge that stood against the objection: ***“who were given the Scripture certainly know this to be the truth from their Lord.”*** and ***“And Allah is never unaware of what they do”***. Ibn ʿAbbās says the People of the Book knew that the Sacred Precinct was the direction of Abraham, and that they concealed that fact. Al-Jalālayn adds the detail their own book supplied: the description of the Prophet ﷺ and the way he would face the House. Al-Mukhtaṣar says they knew the change was truth revealed from their Creator.

So the record closes the argument at its root. This was never a matter of missing evidence. The objection came from people who held the evidence in their hands, and the last sentence puts the whole dispute under the eye of God: what they do is seen, whether they state it plainly or keep it in a drawer. A shopkeeper who hides the fault in a second-hand machine knows what he has done, and no argument he makes to the buyer changes the fact that he knew. The verse leaves that knowledge with them and moves on.

---
## Verse 2:145

> Even if you were to bring every proof to the People of the Book, they would not accept your direction ˹of prayer˺, nor would you accept theirs; nor would any of them accept the direction ˹of prayer˺ of another. And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, then you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers

**PROOF WOULD NOT MOVE THEM**

The verse takes the argument to its end and removes the last hope of settling it by evidence: ***“Even if you were to bring every proof to the People of the Book, they would not accept your direction ˹of prayer˺”***. Ibn Kathīr reads the sentence as a description of stubbornness rather than a lack of proof, and he sets beside it the Qur'anic line that a people against whom the word of the Lord has come due will not believe even if every sign reaches them (10:96 — **“will not believe, even if every sign should come to them”**). Al-Jalālayn calls the refusal obduracy. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān states the matter sharply: it is not that they ask for firm arguments; they have decided, and no proof in the world will satisfy a decision of that kind.

This is a hard lesson for anyone who argues for the truth with the tool of proof alone. A man can win every exchange and lose the room, because the resistance was never in the mind alone. Think of a traveller who refuses to read a road sign because he has already decided which way he is going. The sign is not the problem, and more signs will not help him.

**NEITHER SIDE FOLLOWS THE OTHER**

The sentence then covers the whole field of agreement: ***“nor would you accept theirs”*** ***“nor would any of them accept the direction ˹of prayer˺ of another.”*** Ibn ʿAbbās explains that the Prophet ﷺ will not follow their direction and they will not follow his, and that the two communities among the People of the Book do not follow each other's direction either. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān names the practical shape of this: the Jews prayed towards the Temple and the Christians towards the east, and each group rejected the other's choice. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the reason: each of the two groups calls the other disbelievers.

The verse therefore closes a door that has been kept open through several arguments. Here is a dispute in which the parties will not meet, and the Muslim is told not to spend himself trying to please them into agreement. Tazkirul Qur'an observes that the direction of the Muslims was fixed by a command that would not be abrogated, so no compromise over it was ever available. Two neighbours who each insist that only their own gate leads into the garden can talk for years; what neither of them can do is walk through the other's gate and call it his own.

**THE WARNING SPOKEN TO THE MESSENGER**

The verse ends with a warning that would be unbearable if it were not clear about its purpose: ***“And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge”*** ***“that has come to you”*** ***“then you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers”***.
