Al-Jalālayn explains that the following of whims here is the hypothetical opposite of the guidance that had arrived with proof. Al-Mukhtaṣar states cleanly that God has protected His Prophet ﷺ from ever doing such a thing, and that the sentence stands as a warning to those who come after him. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the wrongdoers as those who harm their own selves.

This is how the Book teaches by addressing the best of its servants. A teacher who corrects the class by naming the brightest student in the room is not suspecting that student; he is making sure that nobody in the room treats the warning as someone else's business. The more knowledge a person carries, the less room he has to bend towards what people want instead of what God has said, and the verse presses that point into one sentence.

---
## Verse 2:146

> Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children. Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly

**RECOGNISED AS A MAN KNOWS HIS OWN CHILD**

The verse turns to the people who had the evidence in their own books: ***“Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺”*** ***“as they recognize their own children.”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the comparison as the descriptions of the Prophet ﷺ that were written in their Scripture, and Ibn ʿAbbās says they knew him by his features and his mission the way a father knows his son among a group of boys. Ibn Kathīr notes that this was a proverb among the Arabs for something utterly plain, used of anything that is beyond doubt. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains how a simile of this kind works: the comparison is not meant to cover every detail of the two things placed side by side, only the single quality they share, so the point here is recognition without hesitation. The Book asks the reader to notice that the evidence for the Prophet ﷺ had reached the level of that plainness. One of the earlier prophets spoke of the same thing when he announced a messenger still to come: (61:6 — **“a messenger who will come after me, whose name will be Aḥmad”**).

Asbāb al-Nuzūl supplies the scene with the scholars who accepted him. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions among the believers of the People of the Book knew the Prophet ﷺ by his description and his mission. He said of himself that he had recognised the Messenger of God as soon as he saw him, more certainly than he knew his own son, and when ʿUmar asked him how that could be, he answered that he could testify with certainty about the Messenger, while no man can be certain about what happens behind his own household door. ʿUmar prayed that God grant him success. The recognition in the verse is not a faint impression; it is certainty of that quality.

**THE TRUTH THEY HID WHILE THEY KNEW IT**

The verse then names the second half of the matter: ***“Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the truth as the description of the Prophet ﷺ that they concealed. Ibn ʿAbbās says they knew it was present in their Book and buried it anyway. Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the motive plainly: envy, with full awareness that the truth had come to them. So the verse separates the two things that a reader might confuse. Ignorance is one condition, and this is another: knowing a thing and covering it over because it costs something to say it out loud.

Tazkirul Qur'an makes the general point that whenever God sends a truth into the world he supports it with clear arguments, so a person who fails to make the truth his own has shown what his heart was really attached to. The reader who has ever stayed silent about a fact that would have helped another person, because admitting it would have cost him standing, has touched the edge of this verse. What the Book holds against the group is not a mistake of reasoning. It is the management of a fact they knew.

Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the two conditions together in one line: they recognise him as fully as a man knows his own children, and a group of them hides the truth out of envy while knowing exactly what it is. The verse therefore does not leave the reader with a puzzle about evidence. It leaves him with a portrait of a heart that had the answer already and chose a different use for it.

The next verse carries the same subject one step further and speaks to the people who had accepted the message: the truth has come from their Lord, and they are told not to be among those who doubt. Readers who have watched a relative refuse a document he himself had asked to see will recognise the shape of this passage. The concealment described here is not the doubt of a searching mind; it is the silence of a settled one.

---
## Verse 2:147

> ˹This is˺ the truth from your Lord, so do not ever be one of those who doubt

**THE TRUTH THAT CAME FROM HIM**

The verse takes the whole dispute and sets it on one side: ***“˹This is˺ the truth from your Lord”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as a confirmation of what the Prophet ﷺ had received, standing against the objections of the people who denied it. Ibn ʿAbbās explains what the truth is: that Muhammad ﷺ is a Prophet sent by God. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same plain sense, that this is the truth from his Lord and there is nothing doubtful in it. The verse does not argue the case again. The case has been argued across the verses before it, with the knowledge of the People of the Book as its witness, and the sentence now states the conclusion.

Ibn Kathīr connects the sentence to the verse before it: the scholars of the People of the Scripture knew the truth of what the Messenger ﷺ was sent with, and a group of them hid that knowledge while they knew it. The truth is therefore described from two sides at once, from the side of the One who sent it and from the side of the people who buried it. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān puts the two verses together in the same way, and says plainly that the Torah and the Gospel had foretold the coming of the Prophet ﷺ and set down the signs by which he would be known, and that many of the People of the Book refused to acknowledge him out of obstinacy rather than uncertainty.

**THE DOUBT THAT IS PUT ASIDE**

The second half of the verse turns from the claim to the heart that receives it: ***“so do not ever be one of those who doubt”***. Al-Jalālayn draws attention to the way the Arabic puts it. The verse does not say "do not waver"; it says, in effect, be not of the sort of people who doubt, which is a stronger and more lasting instruction, because it asks the reader to keep away from the very disposition. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the doubters as the people who waver over whether they know a thing or not, and al-Mukhtaṣar reads the command as being certain of the truth.

Tazkirul Qur'an makes the general point that whenever God sends a truth into the world he supports it with clear arguments, so a person who cannot make the truth his own has shown what his heart was attached to. The arguments that people gather against such a truth look firm to them for a while, and they turn out to be props they built for themselves. Imagine a man who receives a letter signed by a judge and stamped with the seal of the court, and then spends his nights wondering whether the paper is really addressed to him. His doubt is not a shortage of evidence; it is a state he has chosen to live in. The verse speaks to that state and tells the believer to stand away from it, because a messenger does not carry his message in order to doubt it.

The Book uses the same word about itself in the verse that opens this sūrah, where it describes the guidance it brings as (2:2 — **“no doubt about it”**). The reader is asked to hold the same ground in both places. What came from the Lord is set on a different footing from what people gather and scatter in argument, and the believer is to plant his feet on the first and leave the second to the people who enjoy it.

---
## Verse 2:148

> Everyone turns to their own direction ˹of prayer˺. So compete with one another in doing good. Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together ˹for judgment˺. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything

**EVERY COMMUNITY HAS ITS DIRECTION**

The verse widens the view from two houses of prayer to the whole history of worship: ***“Everyone turns to their own direction ˹of prayer˺.”*** Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that this speaks of the followers of the various religions, each nation and tribe choosing a direction for itself, while the direction God appointed is the one the believers face. Abū al-ʿĀliyah made the same point in Ibn Kathīr's report: the Jew has a direction he faces and so does the Christian, and God has guided this community to a direction that is the true one. Al-Jalālayn notes that the Arabic word can be read in two ways, either that each person turns to his own direction or that he is made to turn to it, and either reading leaves the meaning intact.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān builds the argument from ordinary observation. Every traditional community has had an orientation of its own, whether God appointed it or the community chose it for itself, so nobody should be surprised that God has appointed for the Muslims a direction that belongs to them. Ibn ʿAbbās presses the same reasoning in another form: the honour is not in the wall, and the difference between the communities in this matter is not a scandal. Tazkirul Qur'an sees more in the change than a new bearing. The appointing of the House was a sign that the last stage of the religion had arrived, in answer to the prayer Abraham and Ishmael had made when they raised the foundations of that very House: (2:129 — **“Raise from among them a messenger”**).

**COMPETE IN WHAT REMAINS**

The verse then turns the whole discussion into an instruction: ***“So compete with one another in doing good. Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together ˹for judgment˺. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the competition as striving with acts of obedience, and Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as a call to this community to hasten to good deeds more than any other nation has done. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the reason the two halves of the verse belong together: there is nothing wrong in people facing different directions when God has commanded it, so the energy that might have gone into arguing about the direction should go into the obedience they were given.

The promise attached to the instruction is the gathering. Wherever the believers are scattered, whether in different lands or in different centuries, God will bring them together and requite each one for what he did. Al-Jalālayn reads the gathering as the Day of Resurrection, and the closing words as the ground of the promise, since the One who made the heavens and the earth has no difficulty in collecting the people he made. Ibn Kathīr reports the same reading of the phrase about power, that God is able to do all things, including raising the dead and bringing everyone to one place.

The picture the verse gives is of runners on separate roads who all arrive at one finishing line. Two schools in different cities may keep different timetables and face different walls, and it costs nothing, because the examination at the end is the same examination for both. What the verse forbids is letting the difference of directions consume the energy that the race itself requires.

---
## Verse 2:149

> Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. This is certainly the truth from your Lord. And Allah is never unaware of what you ˹all˺ do

**THE DIRECTION NAMED FOR THE THIRD TIME**

The verse repeats the command once more, and the repetition has its own purpose: ***“Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. This is certainly the truth from your Lord.”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the opening as covering the traveller and the resident alike: from whatever place you set out, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque, and the repetition makes it clear that the ruling does not change with the road. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the phrase about the House as the qiblah of Abraham, so that the command restores the community to the direction of its father in faith. Ibn Kathīr counts this as the third command in the passage to face the Sacred Mosque from every part of the world, and notes that the repetition was needed because the matter was new and the change had disturbed people.

Al-Mukhtaṣar states the practical shape of it: wherever the Prophet ﷺ and his followers may be, when they want to pray they face the Sacred House in Makkah. Imagine a ship whose captain must set the same bearing every time it leaves a different port. The ports change and the cargo changes, and the bearing does not, because the destination is one. The verse gives the community that fixed bearing for all the scattered places it would pray in, and it calls the bearing the truth from its Lord rather than a preference of the Messenger ﷺ.

**NOTHING OF WHAT YOU DO IS MISSED**

The verse closes with the sentence that the previous verse about the qiblah also carried: ***“And Allah is never unaware of what you ˹all˺ do”***. Al-Jalālayn notes that the Arabic verb may be read as addressing the believers directly or as speaking about the people who deny, and that either reading fits, since God's knowledge covers both the obedience of the one group and the concealment of the other. Ibn ʿAbbās reads it as covering what the People of the Book were hiding about the qiblah of Abraham and other matters. Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the promise that stands inside the warning: God is aware of everything his servants do, and each of them will be rewarded accordingly.

This short sentence does a quiet kind of work in the passage. It removes the audience from the argument and brings it before the One who sees. The people who argued about the direction had made the change into a public matter; the verse turns it into a matter between each person and his Lord. A worker who finds out that his supervisor checks every part of the job, not only the parts on display, begins to work differently. The Book ends its discussion of the qiblah by reminding every side that the work is supervised, whether the world is watching or not, and that nothing done in obedience is lost.

The House that the community was told to face keeps its place in the religion until the end of time. Tazkirul Qur'an describes the Kaʿbah as the rallying point for the call of the religion, a centre for every believer in God, and it reads that standing in the light of the prayer Abraham made when he built it: (2:125 — **“a centre and a sanctuary for the people”**). A direction that will be used by every generation of a community until the last day is worth more than the noise made about its change in one season of that community's life.

---
## Verse 2:150

> Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. And wherever you ˹believers˺ are, face towards it, so that people will have no argument against you, except the wrongdoers among them. Do not fear them; fear Me, so that I may ˹continue to˺ perfect My favour upon you and so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided

**THE COMMAND GIVEN TO BOTH THE LEADER AND THE PEOPLE**

The verse returns to the direction of prayer one more time, and it divides the command between the Messenger ﷺ and the community: ***“Wherever you are ˹O Prophet˺, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque.”*** ***“And wherever you ˹believers˺ are, face towards it”***. Al-Jalālayn notes that the repetition is there for emphasis: the same instruction is laid on the one who leads and on every believer in every land. Al-Mukhtaṣar phrases the two halves as one practice: wherever the Prophet ﷺ comes from and wherever the believers may be, the face turns towards the Sacred House when the prayer begins. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same breadth into the words, covering the believer on land and the believer at sea, so that no one in any situation is left outside the command.

Ibn Kathīr counts this as the third time in the passage that the command is given, and he notes that the repetition was needed because the ruling was new and had stirred the community. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān observes that every community before this one had been given an orientation of its own, so there is nothing strange in the last community receiving one too. Imagine a family that has moved house a few times and finally puts its table in a fixed place. Nobody asks why the table is there rather than by the window; the household has been told where to sit, and the meal is served.

**THE ARGUMENT THAT IS CLOSED**

The next clause explains one of the purposes behind the command: ***“so that people will have no argument against you, except the wrongdoers among them. Do not fear them”***. Ibn ʿAbbās names the people whose objection would be answered: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions among the People of the Book, who knew from their own Scripture that the Sacred Precinct was the direction of Abraham. Once the community faced that House, the ground of the objection disappeared. Al-Jalālayn spells out the two complaints that this step removed: the Jews could no longer say that the Prophet ﷺ rejected their religion while praying towards their direction, and the idolaters could no longer say that he claimed the way of Abraham while turning away from Abraham's House.

What remains after that, the verse says, is the noise of the wrongdoers, who argue even when the argument is gone. Ibn ʿAbbās identifies them by name in his report, and al-Mukhtaṣar describes them as people who stay in their stubbornness and argue with the weakest of arguments. The command that follows is aimed at the hearts of the believers: do not fear them. A judge who has already read the document does not tremble when the losing party shouts from the back of the court. The Book tells its community that the verdict on this dispute has been given, and that the shouting that follows should not move them.

**THE TWO GIFTS THAT FOLLOW**

The verse then names what the obedience was leading to: ***“fear Me, so that I may ˹continue to˺ perfect My favour upon you”*** ***“and so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided”***. Al-Mukhtaṣar explains the completion of the favour as the distinction God gave this community from all the others and the guidance He gave it to the noblest of all directions. Al-Jalālayn reads the two clauses as the fruit of holding to the command: the blessing is completed and the road stays clear. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same two ends in view, with the guidance standing for the straight way that the community walks in.

The order of the clauses repays a second look. Fear of God is placed first, and the gifts follow it, which tells the reader that the completion of the favour is not a prize handed out before the obedience. A student who is told to follow the syllabus exactly may find the last chapter easier than the first, and the reason is that he trusted the teacher early. The verse closes the long discussion of the qiblah by turning it back into a matter of the heart, where every command from God finally lands.

---
## Verse 2:151

> Since We have sent you a messenger from among yourselves—reciting to you Our revelations, purifying you, teaching you the Book and wisdom, and teaching you what you never knew—

**ONE OF THEIR OWN SENT TO THEM**

The verse names the greatest of the blessings that the sūrah has been counting: ***“Since We have sent you a messenger from among yourselves”***. Al-Jalālayn connects the sentence to the verse before it: just as the direction of prayer was perfected, so the favour is perfected by sending Muhammad ﷺ from the people themselves. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads it as one more blessing added to the account, that God sent them a messenger of their own stock. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān places the verse where it belongs in the flow of the sūrah: the passage began with the prayer of Abraham and Ishmael at the foundations of the House, and this verse announces that the second half of that prayer has been answered. The messenger did not come from a distant land with a foreign book; he came from the same streets and spoke the same tongue.

Ibn ʿAbbās adds a detail that reaches the same point from the other side: the Messenger ﷺ was of their own lineage, which is why the community could bring its questions to him directly. Imagine a village that has been sending letters to a distant city for generations and finally has a man of its own trained in the work. The letter writing does not stop; the distance does. The verse treats the nearness of the messenger as part of the gift itself. Al-Mukhtaṣar draws the same gift into the language of the whole community, and the sūrah states it again elsewhere, where the sending of such a messenger is described as the raising of a mercy among an unlettered people: (62:2 — **“a messenger from among themselves—reciting to them His revelations, purifying them”**). The four things the messenger does in this verse are the four things named there, which tells the reader that the work described belongs to the message itself and not to one community's history.

**WHAT THE MESSENGER DOES AMONG THEM**

The verse then lists his work: ***“reciting to you Our revelations, purifying you, teaching you the Book”*** ***“and wisdom, and teaching you what you never knew”***. Al-Jalālayn takes the recitation as the Qur'an, the purification as cleansing from idolatry, the Book as the Qur'an again, and wisdom as the rulings it contains. Ibn ʿAbbās adds that the purification clears people of sin through the oneness of God, the poor-due and alms, and that the wisdom covers the lawful and the prohibited along with the stories of the nations that came before. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the same in the language of ordinary life: the messenger recites the verses, directs people towards virtue, forbids them from evil and wrong, and teaches them both worldly and sacred knowledge.

The order of the four verbs is worth noticing. The recitation comes first, because hearing the words of God is where the change begins. Purification follows, and then instruction in the Book and in wisdom. The last of the four is the widest of all, since it covers everything the community did not know before: how to pray, how to trade, how to bury the dead, and how to live with one another. A teacher who only hands over a textbook leaves his class where he found it. The messenger recited, cleaned, taught and kept teaching, and the community came out of the process knowing what it had never known. It is worth thinking about how much of ordinary life was included in that last verb. The community learned how to wash for prayer, how to divide an inheritance, how to weigh a debt, how to fast, how to bury its dead and how to settle a quarrel. The Qur'an calls all of it wisdom, and the teaching of it a favour from God that matches the gift of the Book itself.

---
## Verse 2:152

> remember Me; I will remember you. And thank Me, and never be ungrateful

**THE EXCHANGE THE VERSE OFFERS**

The verse gives the community a practice to match its gifts: ***“remember Me; I will remember you.”*** Al-Jalālayn reads the remembering on the human side as prayer, glorification and the other forms of worship, and the remembering on God's side as reward. He also records the divine saying that carries the same promise: whoever remembers God within himself, God remembers him within Himself, and whoever remembers Him in a gathering, God remembers him in a gathering better than it. The words Al-Jalālayn quotes are recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim in the report of Abū Hurayrah, which places the promise on the firmest ground a report can stand on. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the exchange in a way that reaches the difficult days as well: remember God in the time of ease, and He will remember you in the time of hardship. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the whole matter of the heart and body together, that a person remembers God with his heart and with his whole being.

This is the sort of promise that reads differently depending on the mood of the reader. A man who has been ignored by someone he needed may find the idea of being remembered by God almost too large to take in. Yet the verse puts the transaction in the plainest terms: the servant turns his attention to his Lord, and the Lord turns His attention to the servant. It is the pattern of every relationship that has ever worked, raised to the highest level it can reach. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps both commands in their plain sense: remember God with the heart and with the whole being, and He will remember you with approval and protection, since a person is rewarded according to what he does. The Book states the same bargain in a single line elsewhere, where gratitude is tied to increase: (14:7 — **“If you are grateful, I will certainly give you more”**). A person who keeps a small record of what he has asked for and what he has received begins to see the pattern the verse describes, and the record itself becomes a form of remembering.

**THANKFULNESS WITH A WARNING ATTACHED**

The second half of the verse pairs gratitude with a warning: ***“And thank Me, and never be ungrateful”***. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the thanks as gratitude for the blessings God has given, and the warning as an instruction not to stop giving thanks for them. Al-Jalālayn explains what the warning rules out in practice: thankfulness shown by obedience, and ingratitude shown by disobedience. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds that a person becomes ungrateful when he denies the blessing or uses it in ways God has forbidden.

The pairing of the two commands is a lesson in itself. Remembrance without gratitude is easy to say and hard to live, because the tongue can repeat a name while the hands use a gift for something the giver would not approve. Think of a son who keeps a photograph of his father on the wall and sells the family workshop to pay for a holiday. The photograph is not the problem; the rest of his life is. The verse asks for both halves: the name on the tongue and the blessing used in the way it was given.

---
## Verse 2:153

> O believers! Seek comfort in patience and prayer. Allah is truly with those who are patient

**TWO TOOLS FOR EVERY HARDSHIP**

The verse turns to the community with an instruction that answers the troubles the passage has just described: ***“O believers! Seek comfort in patience”*** ***“and prayer. Allah is truly with those”*** ***“who are patient”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the instruction as a command to seek God's help in everything through patience and prayer, and notes that prayer is singled out for mention because of its standing and how often it returns. Ibn ʿAbbās reads patience as steady obedience to what God has ordered and staying away from what he has forbidden, and prayer as including the many voluntary prayers of the night and the day. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts it simply: ask God for help in everything, through patience and by establishing the prayer as he instructed.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains why these two tools are named here rather than somewhere else. The hostility and the objections described in the verses before were likely to weigh on the Muslims, so the verse prescribes the remedy for a discouraged heart. Patience keeps a person steady while the trouble lasts, and prayer keeps him connected to the One who can end it. Think of a farmer in a dry season who keeps watering the single tree he has and keeps walking to the well. Neither action brings rain by itself, and together they are the whole of what a farmer can do while he waits. The same pair of tools was named earlier in the sūrah, where the instruction is given to people who need help before the trouble arrives: (2:45 — **“And seek help through patience and prayer”**). The repetition shows that the community is given a habit rather than a remedy for one emergency. Ibn Kathīr draws the wider rule out of the two commands when he says that a servant is always either enjoying a blessing he should thank God for or suffering a trial he should meet with patience.

**WITH THOSE WHO HOLD ON**

The verse closes with a promise rather than a command: ***“Allah is truly with those”*** ***“who are patient”***. Al-Jalālayn and Ibn ʿAbbās both explain the presence as help and protection, so that the patient person is kept from the acts he might have fallen into without it. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads it as success and support given to those who hold on. The sūrah uses the same expression about a community under pressure, and it does not mean that the patient are spared the difficulty. It means they are not left alone inside it. Al-Mukhtaṣar states the same promise as success and support for those who hold on, so that the community's strength is never placed in its numbers. A believer who prays before the difficulty arrives finds the difficulty lighter when it comes.

That distinction matters to anyone who has waited through a long illness, a debt or a loss of work. The verse does not promise that the pain will be short, and it promises that the person who bears it patiently is not walking through it by himself. A traveller on a hard road may find that the company he keeps matters more than the state of the road. The Book offers its community the company of their Lord as its answer to the pressure of the world.

---
## Verse 2:154

> Never say that those martyred in the cause of Allah are dead—in fact, they are alive! But you do not perceive it

**A SENTENCE THE COMMUNITY WAS TOLD NOT TO SAY**

The verse forbids a way of speaking about the dead: ***“Never say that those martyred in the cause of Allah are dead”***. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the situation behind it: the hypocrites used to say of the men who fell at Badr and Uḥud and in the other battles that such a person had died and lost every comfort, and they said it to trouble the believers. The verse answers that talk directly, and it addresses the believers because they were the ones likely to repeat it in grief. Al-Mukhtaṣar states the prohibition plainly: do not say of those killed while striving in God's path that they are dead the way others are dead. He adds that the talk came from people who wanted to trouble the believers, and that the answer to them is the sentence that follows.

The correction is not only about the words. A community that describes its dead as people who lost everything has already decided what the sacrifice was worth, and the verse refuses that conclusion. It does not deny that the body has gone, and it addresses the manner of speaking because the manner of speaking carries a belief inside it. A family that speaks of a lost father as someone finally free of trouble is not comforting the children the way they think they are.

**THE LIFE THAT IS NOT SEEN**

The verse then supplies the fact: ***“in fact, they are alive!”*** ***“But you do not perceive it”***. Al-Jalālayn reports The Qur'an makes the same statement in another place with a detail that answers the curiosity of the reader: (3:169 — **“they are alive with their Lord, well provided for”**). Al-Jalālayn reports that their spirits are, according to a hadith, in green birds that fly wherever they wish in Paradise, and that people do not know the state they are in. Ibn ʿAbbās describes them as living in Paradise and given comfort and bounty, and says the people left behind are unaware of the honour they have been given. Al-Mukhtaṣar draws the boundaries of the knowledge in the same place: they are alive with their Lord, and the way of that life can only be learned from revelation.

This is where the verse asks the reader to trust the report more than the evidence of his own eyes. A man who stands at a window cannot see what happens behind the wall of the next house,This is where the verse asks the reader to trust the report more than the evidence of his own eyes. Imagine a man who stands at a window and cannot see what happens behind the wall of the next house, and he does not conclude from his blindness that nothing is happening there. The condition of the martyrs is real and hidden at the same time, and the Book tells the community what it needs to know in order to speak about them truthfully. There is a small lesson here about grief itself. The verse does not ask the mourners to stop missing the people they buried; it forbids them to bury the living with the dead in their speech. The difference between the two is the difference between sorrow and despair, and the community is asked to keep the first and let go of the second.

---
## Verse 2:155

> We will certainly test you with a touch of fear and famine and loss of property, life, and crops. Give good news to those who patiently endure—

**THE TRIALS NAMED ONE BY ONE**

The next verse sets out the cost of the road the community has entered: ***“We will certainly test you with a touch of fear”*** ***“and famine and loss of property, life”*** ***“and crops. Give good news to those”*** ***“who patiently endure”***. Ibn ʿAbbās explains each item from the experience of the first community: fear of the enemy, hunger in the years of drought, loss of wealth through its destruction, loss of lives through killing, death and disease, and the loss of crops. Al-Jalālayn reads the testing as a means of showing whether people practise patience, and al-Mukhtaṣar lists the same trials and adds that the loss of life includes death from sickness, from accidents and in God's cause.

The list is arranged from the fear that comes before the event to the crop damage that leaves a family with nothing on the table. Ibn Kathīr reports the hadith that the believer is wonderful in his affairs: no decree of God comes to him without being good for him, since if ease reaches him he gives thanks and it is good for him, and if hardship reaches him he bears it patiently and it is good for him. Tazkirul Qur'an adds the frame that makes the list bearable: this world was not created as a place of reward but as a place of testing, where the serious are distinguished from the indifferent. Al-Mukhtaṣar lists the same trials in the language of daily life: fear of those who are against them, hunger for lack of food, loss of money, death from disease and tragedy, and a failure of what the earth gives. Each of the trials in this verse is named as a touch rather than as a crushing weight, which is why the promise of good news sits inside the same sentence.

**GOOD NEWS IN THE MIDDLE OF THE BAD**

The verse does not finish the list of trials before it changes tone: ***“Give good news to those”*** ***“who patiently endure”***. Al-Mukhtaṣar explains the good news as what will make them happy in this world and in the next. Al-Jalālayn reads it as the promise of Paradise for the people who hold themselves steady when calamity strikes. The sentence is placed inside the announcement of the hardship on purpose, so that the reader hears the promise before the trouble has finished arriving.

A doctor who tells a patient about a painful treatment and then tells him what the treatment is for has not softened the pain, and he has changed the way the patient will experience it. The verse works the same way. The believers are told that fear, hunger, loss and death are coming, and in the same breath they are told that the people who hold on are the ones to whom good news is owed. The next verses say what that news is, and what the patient say when the loss actually reaches them. The Book also fixes the limit of what can be asked of any soul, so that the reader does not measure the trials here against an impossible standard: (2:286 — **“Allah does not require of any soul more than what it can afford”**). Imagine a doctor who tells a patient about a painful treatment and then tells him what the treatment is for. He has not softened the pain, and he has changed the way the patient will live through it.

---
## Verse 2:156

> who, when faced with a disaster, say, “Surely to Allah we belong and to Him we will ˹all˺ return.”

**WHAT THE PATIENT SAY WHEN THE LOSS ARRIVES**

The verse describes the people who earned the good news of the verse before it: ***“who, when faced with a disaster, say, “Surely to Allah we belong”*** ***“and to Him we will ˹all˺ return.””*** Al-Jalālayn explains the two clauses as one act of submission. The first says that the person and everything he owns are God's possession, and that the Owner may do with His property whatever He pleases. The second says that the road ends with God, that the one who lost something is himself on the way back to the One who took it. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same words as an admission of servitude, and adds the sharp edge of it: if a person is not pleased with what God has decreed, then God will not be pleased with his deeds.

Al-Mukhtaṣar joins the two halves into a single sentence of faith. The patient say that all power belongs to God, that He deals with them as He wills, and that they are returning to Him on the Day of Judgement, since it is He who created them and showered them with blessings. The formula is short, and it covers everything a person needs to say when the news is bad: who owns, who decides, and where everyone is going. Imagine a traveller who remembers that he is a guest in the house; he does not shout at the host when the meal is small.

**THE WORDS THAT CARRY A PROMISE**

Al-Jalālayn records the promise that is attached to the formula. Whoever pronounces these words when an affliction reaches him, God rewards him and compensates him with something better. He also records that the Prophet ﷺ used to say these words over small matters, once when a lamp went out, and that ʿĀʾisha asked him about it. The report shows that the sentence is not reserved for funerals. It belongs to the family of everyday losses, the broken vessel, the missed appointment, the money that did not arrive. A person who trains himself to say the words over small things will have them ready when something large arrives, because the sentence is a habit before it is a rescue.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains why the sūrah teaches the words before the hardship and not after it. Accidents are unnerving, and a person who has been told in advance what he will say when the accident comes finds the moment easier to bear. The whole community is addressed here, so every believer is meant to know what he will say before he is asked to say it. A passenger who has been shown where the exit is walks calmly to it when the lights go out, not because the darkness is smaller, but because he already knows the way.

Tazkirul Qur'an draws the reflection that death itself is the disaster the words were made for. A death in the family pulls a person out of his ordinary distractions and puts him in front of the question of where he is going himself. The verse hands him a sentence that answers the question while his hands are still shaking. The Book gives the words as a gift to the living, so that a loss does not close a conversation with God but opens one. The same formula is a reminder of where a person came from and where he is going, and a man who keeps both ends of that road in view carries his losses differently. Imagine a family that has been told in advance that the winter will be hard and that the storehouse has already been filled for them: the cold still bites, and the man who knows about the storehouse carries the season differently from his neighbour.

---
## Verse 2:157

> They are the ones who will receive Allah’s blessings and mercy. And it is they who are ˹rightly˺ guided

**THE LORD'S OWN COMMENDATION**

The verse names the reward of the people who said those words: ***“They are the ones”*** ***“who will receive Allah’s blessings”*** ***“and mercy. And it is they”*** ***“who are ˹rightly˺ guided”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the blessings as forgiveness and the mercy as grace from their Lord. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the first as forgiveness in this world and the second as safety from punishment in the next. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the blessings in a way that lifts the whole scene: these people are praised by God in the highest gathering of the angels, and mercy comes down upon them.

Ibn Kathīr keeps the word for blessings in its place among the names of God's care, so that the sentence reads as a statement that God himself has noticed the patience of these servants and spoken well of them. The word carries the sense of praise that travels, as when a man of standing mentions a good worker in a gathering of his peers. The community that lost its property, its children or its health is told that the loss was seen, and that the One who saw it has spoken about it in a place better than any court of opinion. The reward is described in words that belong to speech rather than to wealth, which is why the verse does not name a sum, a garden or a rank here. The patient are told that God has spoken well of them, and the assurance of the Qur'an is that a word from their Lord does not pass away. Elsewhere the same promise is stated in terms of measure, that the patient will be given their reward without limit: (39:10 — **“only those who endure patiently will be given their reward without measure”**). Imagine a runner who is met at the finish line not with a stopwatch but with a welcome; the praise in this sentence does not add anything to the deed, it tells the reader whose account the deed is being written in.

**THE GUIDANCE THAT SURVIVES THE LOSS**

The last clause of the verse names the third gift: ***“who are ˹rightly˺ guided”***. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the guidance as the ability to keep saying that we belong to God and that we are returning to Him, which is to say that the guidance is in the words themselves. Al-Jalālayn calls them the ones guided to what is right. The three gifts are listed in the order of their reach: forgiveness covers what is past, mercy covers what is coming, and guidance covers the road the person is walking on now. So the verse does not only console the patient; it identifies them as people who have kept their footing while others around them lost theirs.

That is the quiet promise of the verse. Hardship is the test that shows what a person's faith was standing on, and the three gifts named here are the marks of a faith that held. Imagine a bridge that carries traffic every day without comment, and then one flood arrives and shows which of its arches were built properly. The patience of a believer under loss is that arch, and the verse is the report of the inspection. A man may carry a heavy load for years and never learn how much he was being held up, until one day he is thanked in public by someone who saw the whole road. The verse says that this thanking has already happened for the patient, and that the guidance they kept is a possession nobody can take from them.

---
## Verse 2:158

> Indeed, ˹the hills of˺ Ṣafa and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever performs the pilgrimage or minor pilgrimage, let them walk between ˹the two hills˺. And whoever does good willingly, Allah is truly Appreciative, All-Knowing

**THE TWO HILLS MADE SIGNS OF THE RELIGION**

The verse turns to two small hills near the Sacred House: ***“Indeed, ˹the hills of˺ Ṣafa”*** ***“and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah.”*** Al-Jalālayn explains the word for symbols as the waymarks of the religion, the rites God has appointed, and he notes that the walking between the two hills is part of the pilgrimage. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the sentence the same way, that the two hills are among the rites of the pilgrimage that God has commanded. Al-Mukhtaṣar calls them landmarks of the clear sacred law.

Tazkirul Qur'an tells the story that gave the place its meaning. Abraham brought Hagar and the infant Ishmael to the valley at God's command, at a time when there was no settlement there and no water. Thirst drove Hagar to search, and she ran back and forth between Ṣafa and Marwah, looking for help, until she returned to her child and found the spring that is known as Zamzam coming out of the ground. The walking that pilgrims perform is the re-enactment of a mother's search. A man who walks that path is walking in the footsteps of someone who did everything she could and was saved by what she could not do for herself. Think of a family that keeps a worn chair in the corner of a room because that is where the grandfather sat; the chair is not worshipped, and the family would be startled to hear anyone suggest that it was, but the place still carries a memory.

**THE FEAR THAT KEPT PEOPLE AWAY**

The verse then states a permission in the form of a removal of blame: ***“So whoever performs the pilgrimage”*** ***“or minor pilgrimage, let them walk between ˹the two hills˺.”*** Al-Mukhtaṣar explains why the sentence was needed. Some Muslims were avoiding the walk between the hills because idols had stood there in the days of ignorance, and they were afraid of doing something that belonged to the old worship rather than to the religion. The verse comforted them and made clear that the walk was an acceptable act of pilgrimage. Ibn ʿAbbās records the same hesitation and the same answer. A custom that a pagan age has touched is not made unclean if God has appointed it, and the verse says so plainly.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān places this verse at the end of the long passage about the House. The sūrah began with Abraham being tested, then told of the House made a centre and a sanctuary, then recorded his prayer that he and his descendants be taught the rites of worship, and now the rites are named for the community that inherited them. The passage is answering Abraham's prayer in front of the reader's eyes. A builder who finishes a house his father began, and finds the old drawings still on the table, understands what this verse is doing. Imagine a family that keeps a route its grandparents walked to reach a well. The route has no beauty in itself, and the family keeps it because of who walked it, and because the water at the end of it is real. The two hills stand in that position in this religion: small places, heavy with the memory of a mother's search and of the answer God sent her.

**THE GOOD DONE FREELY**

The verse closes with a promise that leaves room for more than the obligation: ***“And whoever does good willingly, Allah is truly Appreciative, All-Knowing”***. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the phrase as covering the voluntary works that a person adds beyond what was required of him. Al-Mukhtaṣar draws the same distinction, that the walking between the hills is what the pilgrimage requires and that anything offered beyond it is received with the two names at the end of the sentence. The Appreciative sees the effort, and the All-Knowing knows the intention behind it.

The two names together answer a question that every quiet believer asks at some point: does anyone notice what I do when nobody is watching? The verse answers with a name rather than with a promise of reward. God is Appreciative, which means the smallest genuine service is registered, and He is All-Knowing, which means the heart behind the service is part of the accounting as well. Imagine a shop that gives an unexpected discount to a customer who never asked for one; it is not paying a debt, it is showing the customer what kind of shop it is.

---
## Verse 2:159

> Those who hide the clear proofs and guidance that We have revealed—after We made it clear for humanity in the Book—will be condemned by Allah and ˹all˺ those who condemn

**THE COVERING OF WHAT WAS SHOWN**

The verse names the people whose silence was the subject of the earlier passage and states its cost: ***“Those who hide the clear proofs”*** ***“and guidance that We have revealed”*** ***“after We made it clear”*** ***“for humanity in the Book”***. Al-Jalālayn identifies the people as those who concealed what their own Scripture contained, including the description of the Prophet ﷺ, after God had shown it to them plainly in the Torah. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the hidden proofs as the commands and prohibitions and the guidance as the description of the Prophet ﷺ and his features, all of it revealed and explained to the Children of Israel in their Book. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the cover wide enough to include both communities of the Book.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān ties the verse to the one that came before it, where the People of the Book were said to recognise the Prophet ﷺ as they recognise their own sons while a group of them hid the truth knowingly. This verse states the consequence of that concealment. The two verses are a pair: the first names the act, and the second names what it costs the people who commit it. The Book returns to the same offence later in the sūrah with a harder picture: (2:174 — **“those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain consume nothing but fire into their bellies”**). Imagine a man who finds a leaking pipe in the wall of a shared building and says nothing because the repair would interrupt his afternoon; the water does not stay on his side of the wall.

**THE CURSE THAT FOLLOWS THEM**

Then the verse gives the verdict in two parts: ***“will be condemned by Allah”*** ***“and ˹all˺ those who condemn”***. Al-Jalālayn explains the curse as being driven far from God's mercy, and reads the second half as covering the angels, the believers, and every created thing that asks that they be cursed. Ibn ʿAbbās describes created beings of every kind joining in the curse, and he reads the first half as a punishment that reaches them even in the grave. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the plain sense: God removes them from His mercy, and the angels, the prophets and people call for the same.

The picture is of a verdict that spreads. A man might bury a fact and think that he has silenced it, and the book that records the deed has more witnesses than he counted on. The concealment was never a private act either, because the thing hidden belonged to a book that had been given to a whole people. The verse does not describe a private penalty; it describes a judgment that every side of creation agrees with, because the thing concealed was not a personal opinion but a guidance sent for all of humanity. Al-Mukhtaṣar widens the group from the Jewish scholars to the Christians as well, so the verse is not about one community. What is condemned is a pattern: people who were given a book, understood what it said, and then managed the information to protect their standing. The cost begins in this life, where concealment of that kind destroys the trust of everyone who later discovers it, and it continues in the curse that the verse names. The verse places the concealment inside a community that had been trusted with a book, which is what makes the offence so heavy. The same covenant is described in another place, in words that name both the duty and the motive: (3:187 — **“to make it known to people and not hide it”**). The people there are said to have cast the book behind their backs once the price offered for their silence was high enough.

---
## Verse 2:160

> As for those who repent, mend their ways, and let the truth be known, they are the ones to whom I will turn ˹in forgiveness˺, for I am the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful

**THE THREE STEPS BACK**

The next verse opens a door in the middle of that verdict: ***“As for those who repent, mend their ways”*** ***“and let the truth be known, they are the ones to”*** ***“whom I will turn ˹in forgiveness˺”***. Al-Jalālayn counts the three steps clearly: turning back from the deed, putting the behaviour right, and making known what was being hidden. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the third step as the public statement of the description of the Prophet ﷺ that had been buried. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the same sequence into the language of ordinary repentance, which involves regret, correction inside and outside, and the return of what was withheld.

The order of the three steps is instructive. Regret alone does not repair a harm; the person has to change what he does and then give back the knowledge he was holding. A man who took a neighbour's only copy of a document and burnt it cannot make it right by feeling sorry in private. He has to say what he knows and help rebuild what his silence cost. The verse asks for the whole of that work and attaches the promise to it. Ibn Kathīr reads the exception as the Book's steady habit of opening a door before it states a penalty. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the concealment meant here is the same offence described a few verses earlier, where a group of the People of the Book hid what they knew about the Prophet ﷺ. The rule the verse gives is therefore general: a person who has held back a truth that was owed to someone else can still put it right, and the promise is attached to the whole repair rather than to the regret alone. The same three steps are promised in another sūrah in almost the same words: (20:82 — **“But I am truly Most Forgiving to whoever repents, believes, and does good, then persists on ˹true˺ guidance”**). Think of a tailor who spoiled a customer's cloth and then offered to make the whole garment again at his own cost; the offer is not a description of the damage, it is a statement about the tailor.

**THE NAME THAT CLOSES THE EXCEPTION**

The sentence ends with the two names that make the promise believable: ***“for I am the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the first name as God's acceptance of the one who turns back, and Ibn ʿAbbās reads the second as mercy for whoever dies in that state. Al-Mukhtaṣar explains the first name in a way that describes the motion of both parties: God turns to those who turn to Him, asking forgiveness and regretting what they did.

The verse was revealed about people whose crime was not a slip of temper but the deliberate concealment of a truth that had been entrusted to them, and the door is still open to them. That is the shape of mercy in this Book. It does not call the offence small, and it does not lock the door behind the offender. A workshop that ruins a customer's order may not expect to keep the customer, and if the owner puts the work right and hands over the record of what went wrong, the customer may decide to stay. The verse holds that possibility out to a much heavier debt. The Book states the same promise in the story of Adam, where the first repentance in human history is accepted with the same two names that close this verse: (2:37 — **“He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”**). Imagine a man who buried a document that would have saved a neighbour from a false charge, and then dug it up and handed it over. The harm he caused is real, and the moment the paper changes hands the sentence of the verse applies to him: the door that his silence closed is open to him again.

---
## Verse 2:161

> Surely those who disbelieve and die as disbelievers are condemned by Allah, the angels, and all of humanity

**THE STATE THAT ENDS THE ARGUMENT**

The verse then returns to the people who do not come back: ***“Surely those who disbelieve”*** ***“and die as disbelievers are condemned by Allah, the angels”*** ***“and all of humanity”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the sentence as a curse that belongs to them in this life and the next, and notes that the word for humanity can mean people in general or the believers in particular. Ibn ʿAbbās explains that the curses which people aim at one another in this world end up landing on those who die in denial of God and His Messenger. Al-Mukhtaṣar states the same in plain words: God removes them from His mercy, and the angels and people ask for the same.

The condition that the verse attaches is the key to the whole sentence: they die in that state. The Book does not say that a person who denied in his youth is outside the door of mercy. It says that the door closes on the condition in which a person leaves this world. Every living denier is a person who may still turn, and every believer who reads this verse knows that his own last day is the only one that matters. Imagine a door that stays open until a fixed hour; the door is not cruel, it simply tells the truth about the time, and the person who walked past it all day has no complaint to make at closing.

**THE RULING THAT GUARDS THE TONGUE**

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws a ruling out of the wording that is worth carrying away. Commentators such as al-Jaṣṣāṣ and al-Qurṭubī took the phrase about dying in disbelief to mean that it is not permissible to curse an individual denier whose end is not known, since no one can be certain about how another person will leave the world. He notes that the Prophet ﷺ cursed some people by name, and explains that this was because their death in disbelief had been made known to him.

The ruling protects the community from two mistakes at once. It keeps the tongue from handing out verdicts that belong to God alone, and it keeps the heart from treating a living person as a closed case. A doctor who has lost many patients to the same disease does not stop treating the one in front of him. The verse names three witnesses in a single line, and the order moves from the highest to the widest: God first, then the angels, then the whole of humanity. The verse describes a condition that is settled only at death, and the ruling tells the reader where the boundary of his speech lies. The Book makes the same point in another place, where it names the exact hour at which the offer ends: (4:18 — **“repentance is not accepted from those who … die as disbelievers”**). Imagine a shopkeeper who keeps his shutters open until sunset. He is not deceiving anybody; he is telling the customer how long the shop works. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the curse in two movements: God removes them from His mercy, and the created order asks for the same removal. Ibn ʿAbbās adds that the curses people direct at one another in this world end up settling on those who leave the world in denial, which is a way of saying that the harm a person aims at others returns to its owner. The community in front of the Prophet ﷺ had heard this verse read aloud, and its first effect was to keep the believers from cursing one another over the disputes of the day, since every curse they sent out was going to settle somewhere.

---
## Verse 2:162

> They will be in Hell forever. Their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be delayed ˹from it˺

**THE PUNISHMENT THAT IS NOT LIFTED**

The verse describes the duration and the weight of what waits: ***“They will be in Hell forever. Their punishment will not be lightened”*** ***“nor will they be delayed ˹from it˺”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the abiding as lasting in the curse and in the Fire, and explains the two clauses that follow as a refusal of any relief and any delay. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same, that the punishment is neither lifted nor postponed. Al-Mukhtaṣar says that their punishment is not made lighter for a single day and that they are given no extra time to repent or to excuse themselves.

The two clauses are the mirror image of the mercy described in the verse before them. There, God accepts those who come back and put the matter right. Here, the time for repairing anything has ended, and the verse names both halves of that ending: nothing is lifted, and nothing is postponed. The sentence mentions no term that might end and no reduction that might come later, which is what makes it the exact opposite of the mercy described one verse earlier. A court may reduce a sentence or grant a deferral; the verse says that neither of those doors opens in the next life. The Qur'an describes the same state with the detail that a person would long for the opposite of the relief he is refused: (35:36 — **“they will not be ˹allowed to be˺ finished by death, nor will its torment be lightened for them”**).

**WHY THE PASSAGE ENDS SO HARD**

Readers sometimes wonder why the sūrah leaves this subject on such a note, when the verses before it were full of gates left open. The order is the answer. The door was opened first, in the verse about repentance, and the passage turns to the closed condition only after the reader has been told what gets a person through it. Imagine a school that posts a warning on the gate. It is not being cruel if it has also printed the way in. The Qur'an repeats this description of the Fire in several places, and the repetition belongs to the same patience: (43:74 — **“Indeed, the wicked will be in the torment of Hell forever”**). A doctor who says the same thing at every visit is not enjoying the sound of his own voice; he is making sure that a patient who has stopped listening still has the sentence in his ears.

The warning also does a service to the community that carries the message. A teacher who is afraid to mention the cost of refusal will not warn anyone in time, and the Book prefers to be plain. Behind the sentence stands the same generous invitation that has run through this whole sūrah: the reader is still alive, the door is still open, and the verses that follow return to a subject the whole passage has been building towards, the oneness of the One who is being worshipped. The warning was never meant to be read by the dead, who cannot act on it. It is read by people who are still in the middle of their working day, with time on the clock and choices in front of them, and the hard sentence exists so that nobody arrives at the end of that day without having been told. The Book states the same permanence elsewhere in a single line: (35:36 — **“they will not be ˹allowed to be˺ finished by death, nor will its torment be lightened for them”**).

---
## Verse 2:163

> Your God is ˹only˺ One God. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful

**THE ONE GOD THEY ASKED ABOUT**

The verse states the answer to a question that had been put to the Prophet ﷺ about the God he was calling people to: ***“Your God is ˹only˺ One God. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him”***. Al-Jalālayn places the verse in the setting of that request and explains the answer as a declaration that God is one, with no equal in His being or in His attributes. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the sentence as a statement made directly against the denial of the polytheists: your God is one God, without a son and without a partner in His rule. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same sense in the language of ordinary address, that the God of this community is the true God, one in Himself and in His attributes.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān records what happened when the people of Makkah heard the sentence read out. The men who joined other beings to the worship of God were puzzled, and they asked how one God could be the object of worship for the whole world. The answer to that puzzle is the passage that follows this verse. The sūrah does not answer the question with a definition; it answers it by pointing at the world, because the same One who cannot be seen has left a workshop full of evidence behind Him. A man who is asked whether a house has a builder does not need a diagram of the builder; he needs to walk through the building. The same sentence was spoken to another audience, and the Book records what it did to them: (16:22 — **“Your God is ˹only˺ One God. As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are in denial, and they are too proud”**). Imagine a man who has lived his whole life in a house and never once looked at the name on the deeds; the verse is the moment somebody puts the paper into his hand.

**THE TWO NAMES THAT CLOSE THE VERSE**

The verse does not end with the unity of God alone. It ends with two names: ***“the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful”***. Ibn Kathīr notes that the meaning of these two names was explained at the beginning of the sūrah of al-Fātiḥah, and that the sūrah opens and closes with them because they are how the One God approaches His creation. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the mercy as vast, with God surrounding His creation with blessing after blessing. So the unity of God is not announced as a cold fact; the verse pairs the One with the Compassionate, and the reader is left with a Lord who is single and generous at the same time.

Tazkirul Qur'an draws the human side of the matter out of the verse. A person owes his existence and everything he enjoys to the One who made him, and if he becomes conscious of that, his Lord will mean everything to him, the way a mother means everything to her infant. The Qur'an repeats the doctrine of God's unity in its shortest sūrah in the same spirit: (112:1 — **“He is Allah—One ˹and Indivisible˺”**). What the verse asks of a reader is not a conclusion to memorise but an attachment to be formed, and it gives him two names to hold on to while  Ibn Kathīr keeps the verse among the passages that describe God by His names rather than by a picture, and the two names here are the ones this sūrah has used since its first lines. A reader who has only the sentence that God is one knows the shape of the doctrine; a reader who has the two names as well knows the manner of the One he is dealing with.

---
## Verse 2:164

> Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth; the alternation of the day and the night; the ships that sail the sea for the benefit of humanity; the rain sent down by Allah from the skies, reviving the earth after its death; the scattering of all kinds of creatures throughout; the shifting of the winds; and the clouds drifting between the heavens and the earth—˹in all of this˺ are surely signs for people of understanding

**THE SKY ABOVE AND THE GROUND BELOW**

The verse answers the demand for proof with a walk through the created world: ***“Indeed, in the creation of the heavens”*** ***“and the earth”***. Al-Jalālayn reports that the people had asked for a sign to prove the claim of the previous verse, and that this passage came down as that sign. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the opening as pointing to the making of the heavens and the earth, or to what has been made inside them. Ibn Kathīr says the same, that the creation of the heavens and the earth is among the greatest witnesses to the One who made them. Tazkirul Qur'an describes the universe as a magnificent introduction to God: the existence of a limitless world in the form of the earth and the heavens shows that there must be a Creator behind it, and the fact that things so different work together in harmony shows that the maker is one.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān points out that the signs in this verse are simple enough for the learned and the ordinary person to grasp together. Nobody needs a laboratory to notice that the sky is above him and that the ground is under him. The most complicated equipment a man needs for this verse is his own attention. Think of a letter that arrives with no signature on it; the paper still tells the reader that somebody wrote it, and the size of the handwriting changes nothing.

**DAY AND NIGHT, SHIPS AND RAIN**

The list then moves from the largest things to the things that carry human life: ***“the alternation of the day”*** ***“and the night”*** ***“the ships that sail the sea”*** ***“for the benefit of humanity”*** ***“the rain sent down by Allah from the skies, reviving the earth after its death”***. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the alternation as the passing back and forth of night and day along with the lengthening and shortening of their hours. Al-Jalālayn describes the ships as the vessels that travel the sea without splitting or sinking, carrying the trade and merchandise that people live on. The rain revives the ground after it has dried out.

The sequence in the verse is worth noticing. After the sky and the earth come time, then travel, then water, which is to say that the evidence is not only in the distance but in the fittings of ordinary existence. Ibn Kathīr keeps the phrase about the benefit of humanity in view, so that the ships are named by what they do for people rather than by their size. Something made for human profit and left in working order for century after century is a hard thing to explain without a maker who intended it. Imagine a household where water arrives at the tap and the bins are collected on time; the children who grow up there may never once think about the system that keeps those two things running.

**CREATURES, WINDS AND CLOUDS**

The signs then spread across everything that moves and everything that blows: ***“the scattering of all kinds of creatures throughout”*** ***“the shifting of the winds”*** ***“and the clouds drifting between the heavens”*** ***“and the earth”***. Ibn Kathīr reads the scattering of living things as the variety of creatures distributed over the earth, and the shifting of the winds as the change of their direction and force by which the clouds are driven and the rain is carried to the places where it is needed. Al-Jalālayn keeps the whole list in the same function, that each item works for the benefit of men. Tazkirul Qur'an adds the observation that each of these things also serves the rest of creation, which shows a designing will and not a random arrangement.

Imagine a workshop where every tool is useful to the other tools, where the lathe supplies the parts that the bench needs and the fan keeps the air fit to work in. A visitor would not ask whether somebody planned the shop; he would ask who the planner was. The verse walks its reader through the workshop of the world and lets the question form on its own.

**WHAT THE SIGNS ASK OF A READER**

The list closes by naming its audience: ***“˹in all of this˺ are surely signs”*** ***“for people of understanding”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the phrase as proof and evidence for those who can work it out, and Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sense, that the signs are there for people with minds. Ibn Kathīr reads the closing words as the marks of a particular kind of person, someone who brings his understanding to what he sees and lets it lead him somewhere. The verse does not say that the signs are hidden from the rest of humanity. It says that they are read by those who are willing to read them.

The verse also teaches something about the way the Book argues. It does not demand of its reader a leap away from the world, and it asks him to use the world in front of him. A child who has watched a kettle boil and a farmer who has watched a field greened by rain have both seen the material this verse is made of. The Book sends the reader back to what he already knows and asks him what he thinks it means. Imagine a man who reads every warning label on a machine but never asks who built it; he has done half of the work this verse is asking for.

---
## Verse 2:165

> Still there are some who take others as Allah’s equal—they love them as they should love Allah—but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more. If only the wrongdoers could see the ˹horrible˺ punishment ˹awaiting them˺, they would certainly realize that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is indeed severe in punishment

**RIVALS TAKEN BESIDE HIM**

After the evidence of the creation, the sūrah turns to the people who read none of it: ***“Still there are some”*** ***“who take others as Allah’s equal”*** ***“they love them as they should love Allah”***. Al-Jalālayn explains the rivals as idols and other created beings who were set beside God and loved with the same devotion that belongs to Him, receiving the service and the reverence that should have gone to their Maker. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the verse as a description of the attachment the polytheists had for their objects of worship. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the sense plain: people take others besides God as gods, treating them as equals and loving them as God is loved.

Tazkirul Qur'an explains why such a thing could happen to human beings at all. A person looks by his nature for support outside himself, for a being who can make up for his helplessness and give him confidence, and when that longing attaches itself to something other than God the result is exactly what this verse describes. The Book is not surprised at the instinct; it names the mistake. The man who leans on a post that can hold nothing has not stopped leaning, and he has chosen the wrong post. Think of a man who fixes a charm above his door and then, when the roof starts leaking, telephones the builder he had stopped speaking to.

**THE LOVE THAT DOES NOT LET GO**

The verse then sets the believers beside that picture: ***“but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more.”*** Ibn ʿAbbās reads the comparison as being about firmness and endurance, that the love of the believers for God lasts longer than the love of the idolaters for their idols. Al-Jalālayn sees the same contrast in the hour of difficulty: the people attached to rivals abandon them when hardship comes and call on God alone, while the believers keep their love for God in ease and in need. Al-Mukhtaṣar says it in one line, that the believers love God in hardship and in ease, and that the others love their gods only while things go well.

A friendship that survives a difficult season is worth more than a friendship that only appears at parties, and the verse is making that comparison on the highest level where it can be made. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the attachment of the polytheist bends as soon as his invented god fails him, while the love of the believer has somewhere to stand when the world goes dark. Imagine a house built on rock and a tent pitched on sand; the storm does not create the difference, it reveals it.

**IF THEY COULD SEE WHAT WAITS**

The verse ends with a sentence that is left incomplete on purpose: ***“If only the wrongdoers could see the ˹horrible˺ punishment ˹awaiting them˺, they would certainly”*** ***“that all power belongs to Allah”*** ***“and that Allah is”*** ***“indeed severe in punishment”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the broken sentence as the Book's way of leaving the reader to fill in the sight for himself, since the wrongdoers will see the punishment and will see at that moment that power belongs to God alone. Ibn Kathīr reads the same scene, that the wrongdoers will see the torment and will know that all authority is God's and that His punishment is severe.

The grammar performs the meaning. A person who says the first half of a sentence and then falls silent has made his point by what he left out, and this verse leaves the reader standing where the wrongdoers will stand on that day, seeing what they will see and unable to say anything useful about it. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the same moment, that if the wrongdoers could see with their own eyes what waits for those who worship others besides God, the sight would change everything they do. Imagine a debtor who has been sent three letters and has opened none of them; the debt knows nothing about his unopened mail.

---
## Verse 2:166

> ˹Consider the Day˺ when those who misled others will disown their followers—when they face the torment—and the bonds that united them will be cut off

**THE DAY THE LEADERS STEP BACK**

The next verse opens a scene: ***“˹Consider the Day˺ when those”*** ***“who misled others will disown their followers”***. Al-Jalālayn identifies the ones who were followed as the leaders, and explains the disowning as a denial that they ever misled anyone. Al-Mukhtaṣar sets the cause of the break in the terrors of that Day: the leaders who were followed in disbelief reject the weak people who followed them once they see what is in front of them. Ibn ʿAbbās calls the followers the lowly among the people, the ones who had no standing of their own to lean on.

The scene is a familiar one in human affairs, performed on the last day without the possibility of a cover story. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān compares it to what already happens in this world when a plan collapses and the men who drew it up are suddenly unable to recognise the people who carried it out. A crowd that follows a leader into a ruin usually discovers, at the moment the ruin becomes visible, that  The verse is also a warning about the people a man chooses to follow. The leaders in this scene were not strangers; they were the ones their followers trusted with the shape of their lives. The Book does not say that following a teacher is wrong in itself; it says that every follower should ask where the road ends and who will still be standing with him when it does. The question costs nothing to ask today, when the answer can still change a decision, and it cannot be asked at all on the day this verse describes. Think of a company whose director denies, before the cameras, that he ever gave the instructions that are written in his own handwriting.

**THE BONDS THAT ARE CUT**

The verse then names what happens to the links between them: ***“when they face the torment”*** ***“and the bonds that united them will be cut off”***. Al-Jalālayn explains the bonds as the ties of affection and kinship that held the two groups together on earth, and reads the cutting as a supplement to the disowning, so that the scene shows both the denial and the severing at once. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the sentence as the collapse of the pledges and the goodwill that had connected them in this life. Al-Mukhtaṣar says that every means of escape is cut off from them together.

This is the part of the scene that touches ordinary life most closely. Every group of people that follows a leader for the sake of gain, whether in business, in politics or in a bad habit, holds its loyalty together with bonds that were made in this world.  Ibn Kathīr reads this verse as the continuation of the warning that closed the one before it, where the severity of the punishment was stated. It is one thing to be told that the punishment is severe, and another thing to watch a crowd of people who trusted each other discover what their trust was worth. Imagine a rope bridge over a ravine where the planks are tied with string. The crossing looks fine until the weight of the whole crowd is on it. The two groups discover in that moment what they were to each other once the advantage that held them together was gone, and the verse reports the discovery without softening it.

---
## Verse 2:167

> The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, “If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us.” And so Allah will make them remorseful of their misdeeds. And they will never ˹be able to˺ leave the Fire

**THE WISH FOR A SECOND CHANCE**

The followers speak last, and what they say is the sentence of every person who has followed a bad example: ***“The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, “If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them”*** ***“as they disowned us.””*** Al-Jalālayn reads the wish as a longing to return to the world and to do exactly what the leaders did, that is to say to declare themselves free of the very people they once obeyed. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the symmetry of the sentence, that the followers would disown their leaders as the leaders have already disowned them. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the whole exchange in the plainest words: if only we could go back, we would reject our leaders just as they reject us now.

The sentence is the sound of a whole life being reopened too late. It is not a statement of repentance in the ordinary sense, because there is nothing left to repair and no time left to repair it in. It is the discovery of what the two groups were to each other once the advantage that held them together was gone. Anyone who has watched a partnership end badly will recognise the tone of it. Imagine a passenger who jumps from a moving bus and then, from the roadside, shouts instructions at the driver.

**REGRET AND A DOOR THAT STAYS SHUT**

The verse then gives the verdict on the scene: ***“And so Allah will make them remorseful of their misdeeds.”*** ***“And they will never ˹be able to˺ leave the Fire”***. Al-Jalālayn explains the regret as something God shows them along with the severity of the punishment, so that they see their own deeds in the shape of a loss they cannot undo.
