Ibn ʿAbbās reads the phrase the same way, that their deeds are shown to them as anguish, and that neither the leaders nor the followers come out of the Fire. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds that the punishment is shown to them together with the consequence of having followed leaders into falsehood.

The order of the two sentences carries its own lesson. The regret comes first, and then the locked door: the sorrow of the verse is not a step in a process of release, it is a description of a state without an exit. That is why the Book tells the story while its readers are still on the road.  Al-Mukhtaṣar notes that the sight of the punishment is what produces the regret, since the followers are shown the consequence of following their leaders into falsehood. Imagine a man who joins a business on the promise of a partner he admired and signs papers he never read because the partner seemed certain. When the business fails, the partner's lawyer is very clear about who signed what, and the man's regret is not a plan but a sentence he repeats to himself. The followers in this verse do not get to send the letter they are composing in their grief, because the moment for writing has passed and the record is closed. The Book tells this story twice in a row, once from the side of the leaders and once from the side of the followers, so that the reader cannot say he was shown only half of the scene. The sentence of the followers is repeated by the Book so that a reader may hear it while there is still time to act on what it says.

---
## Verse 2:168

> O humanity! Eat from what is lawful and good on the earth and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy

**THE TABLE SET FOR THE WHOLE OF HUMANITY**

The passage turns from the story of the previous verses and speaks to every person on the earth: ***“O humanity! Eat from what is lawful”***. Al-Jalālayn reports the occasion that brought the words down. Some people had declared certain animals unlawful for themselves, the camel left to graze at liberty and others of the same kind, and the verse answered them by handing the question of food back to its Owner. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the address in the same setting: the words speak of the lawfulness of cultivating the land and of raising cattle, of eating what grows in the fields and the meat of the herds.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān opens the meaning of the word at the centre of the sentence. The root of ḥalāl carries the sense of opening a knot, so that what has been made lawful is what has had its knot opened and its restriction removed. The picture is worth holding on to, because it turns the permission into an act of kindness rather than a licence. A father who unties the rope from his son's hands has not merely stopped forbidding him; he has freed him, and the freeing is the gift.

**WHAT LAWFUL AND GOOD TOGETHER MEAN**

The order carries two words where one might have done: ***“and good on the earth”***. Al-Jalālayn explains the second word as an emphatic description, so that the food is not merely permitted but good to the taste. Al-Mukhtaṣar spells the range out as the meat, the vegetables and the fruits of the earth that are lawful and good and do not harm the person who eats them. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same two conditions and applies them to the crops of the field and the cattle of the household.

The Book states the same rule twice more, which shows how much it mattered to the first readers: (2:172 — **“O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided for you. And give thanks to Allah”**) and (5:88 — **“Eat of the good, lawful things provided to you by Allah. And be mindful of Allah in Whom you believe”**). Maʿārif al-Qurʾān carries a saying of the early teacher Sahl ibn ʿAbdullāh that ties the subject to the whole of religion: salvation depends on three things, and eating what is lawful stands first among them, with fulfilling the divine obligations and following the practice of the Prophet ﷺ beside it. Imagine a man who reads the label on every tin in his kitchen and never reads the label on his income; the verse is asking him to read both, because a meal that comes from a wrong source cannot be cleaned by the plate it is served on.

**THE ENEMY WHO WHISPERS ABOUT FOOD**

The verse closes with a warning: ***“and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy”***. Al-Jalālayn explains the footsteps as the ways of Satan, and then describes what those ways look like in practice: the suggestions he makes attractive to a person. Ibn ʿAbbās narrows the warning to the subject of the passage, the whisperings that told people to treat the fruits of the field and the cattle of the herd as forbidden. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the reason plainly, that an enemy who wants to harm and mislead his victim is not a companion any sensible person would follow.

The Qur'an repeats the same caution against the same enemy: (24:21 — **“O believers! Do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Whoever follows Satan’s footsteps, then ˹let them know that˺ he surely bids ˹all to˺ immorality and wickedness.”**). The verse before the reader is one of the places where that warning touches the kitchen and the market. Another verse names the habit that the footsteps produce: (16:116 — **“Do not falsely declare with your tongues, “This is lawful, and that is unlawful,” ˹only˺ fabricating lies against Allah”**). Adding to the list of forbidden things may feel like extra caution, but the verse hands the pen back to its owner and asks who gave permission to write with it. Think of a man who lets his enemy tell him which of his own cupboards are locked.

---
## Verse 2:169

> He only incites you to commit evil and indecency, and to claim against Allah what you do not know

**WHAT THE VOICE ACTUALLY ASKS FOR**

The next verse opens the whisper and shows the reader what is inside it: ***“He only incites you to commit evil”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the word translated as evil as sin itself, and pairs it with the second word in the same sentence, the indecency that the Law turns away from. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the pair as evil works and the transgressions that follow them. The command is not an open invitation to something monstrous, and that is exactly the point of the verse. The whisper never announces the end of the road; it describes the first step of it.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān pauses on the Arabic word for the first item and explains it as something that bothers a good and reasonable person when he meets it. The second word, it reports, has been described by some commentators as covering what is immodest, while the first word has been read as sin at large. Al-Mukhtaṣar sets the same pair in the language of harm, that what the voice commands is the action that will bring hardship on the one who does it. So the reader is told two things at once: the thing is ugly, and the ugliness comes home. Imagine a road that begins smooth and pleasant to look at, and a whisperer who says nothing at all about where it ends.

**THE THIRD THING THE VOICE ASKS**

The sentence then names something larger than a bad deed: ***“and indecency, and to claim against Allah what you do not know”***. Al-Jalālayn gives the example that makes the phrase concrete, that the person ends up speaking about God what he does not know, as when he forbids what God has not forbidden. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the last part as lies told about God, statements made without knowledge. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the Arabic form of the opening words describes a suggestion placed in the heart rather than an order shouted from outside, and that the surprise of the verse is that the suggestion arrives carrying the authority of a rule.

The Book puts the same threat beside the same promise: (2:268 — **“The Devil threatens you with ˹the prospect of˺ poverty and bids you to the shameful deed ˹of stinginess˺, while Allah promises you forgiveness and ˹great˺ bounties from Him.”**). Two speeches, then, are on offer, and the verse is written so that the reader may weigh them before he acts on either. Imagine a man who is told by a stranger that the bridge ahead is closed and that he should take the dark lane instead. He asks the stranger one question: have you been there? The third thing the voice asks of a person is that he repeat confident claims about God without ever having stood on the ground of them. The Book names the two directions this whispering takes: (6:112 — **“And so We have made for every prophet enemies—devilish humans and jinn—whispering to one another with elegant words of deception”**) and (17:64 — **“And incite whoever you can of them with your voice”**). The suggestions arrive in attractive language, which is why the verse pairs a bad deed with a confident statement about God; the second makes the first look respectable, and both arrive as help.

---
## Verse 2:170

> When it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.” ˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance

**FOLLOW WHAT ALLAH REVEALED**

The scene shifts to a conversation: ***“When it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “No!”***. Al-Jalālayn explains that the people being addressed are the disbelievers, and that what they were asked to follow was the revelation concerning the oneness of God and the good things He had made lawful. Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the group as the idolaters of the Arabs, and reads the command as the invitation to accept the lawfulness that God had set out in the matter of the fields and the herds. The verse gives one instruction and lets the answer stand for itself.

The same answer appears in the Book wherever this argument is made: (43:22 — **“In fact, they say, “We found our forefathers following a ˹particular˺ way, and we are following in their footsteps.””**). A custom that has been inherited is not a proof of anything, and the Qur'an treats the appeal to it as a blank space where an argument should be. The next sentence of this verse shows what happens when the blank is examined. Think of a man who inherits a heavy set of keys and never asks which doors they open, and who grows angry at anyone who suggests that the locks may have been changed.

**THE ANSWER OF INHERITANCE**

The refusal is spoken, and it gives its reason: ***“We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.” ˹Would they still do so,˺ even”***. Ibn Kathīr titles this passage the imitation of one generation of polytheists by the next, since the answer is not a statement about God at all but a statement about the ancestors. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains the assumption underneath the refusal, that these people took their forefathers to be guided in a way that made the question unnecessary. The Book then asks a question in the middle of their sentence, which is why the words “**˹Would they still do so,˺ even**” arrive before the answer is finished.

Tazkirul Qur'an describes the process that produces this kind of loyalty. Once an object other than God is accepted as divine through superstition, a train of other beliefs follows it, and in the next generation those beliefs root themselves in the heart and are defended with zeal as sacred possessions. The reader can watch the mechanism in ordinary life. Imagine a family that has kept the same recipe for a medicine for four generations. Every member of the family can tell you how well it works, and none of them can tell you what is in it. The verse is asking the children of a custom to open the bottle and read the label.

**THE QUESTION THAT ENDS THE ARGUMENT**

The verse finishes the sentence it began: ***“if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance”***. Al-Jalālayn notes that the Arabic word opening this question carries a tone of protest, as if the Book is refusing to accept what has just been said. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the phrase as a description of people who understood nothing of religion and had no guidance from any prophet, and then draws the conclusion as a question no one can answer in the affirmative. How can a person take the road of blind ancestors as the road of God?

Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the same question in ordinary words: they understood nothing of guidance and no light had reached them, so what exactly is being followed? The Qur'an raises the challenge again: (31:21 — **“When it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.” ˹Would they still do so˺ even if Satan is inviting them to the torment of the Blaze?”**), and (5:104 — **“What we found our forefathers practicing is good enough for us”**), where the last clause stands beside it. Respect for parents is a duty in this religion, and the verse does not ask anyone to despise his family. It asks a narrower and harder question: when the elders themselves had no guidance, what is there to inherit?

---
## Verse 2:171

> The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger’s warning˺ is like a flock not comprehending the calls and cries of the shepherd. ˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb and blind so they have no understanding

**A VOICE THAT CARRIES NO MEANING**

The verse offers a picture of the people who have just spoken: ***“The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger’s warning˺ is like a flock not comprehending the calls”***. Al-Jalālayn explains that the likeness covers both the disbelievers and the one who calls them, so that the caller is like a shepherd raising his voice and the called are like animals that hear a sound without a meaning. Ibn ʿAbbās fills in the scene: camels and sheep and a shepherd, whose words are unintelligible to them when he tells them to eat or to drink. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the point sharp, that they hear the voice but do not understand what it says.

The simile is exact in a way that is easy to miss. A shepherd does not hate his flock, and what he says to the animals is genuinely for their good. The problem lies entirely on the receiving side. Imagine a man standing in front of a machine that has no receiver; he may shout as clearly and as kindly as he likes, and the machine will register nothing but noise. The verse does not accuse the messenger of a fault, and it does not pretend the message was unclear. It says the receiving part is what has stopped working. The Book describes the same condition in a single line elsewhere: (2:18 — **“They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will never return ˹to the Right Path”**). Imagine a man standing in front of a machine whose receiver has been switched off; he may shout as kindly and as clearly as he likes, and the machine registers nothing but noise.

**THREE DOORS THAT SHUT ONE BY ONE**

The verse then names the three faculties that have failed: ***“and cries of the shepherd. ˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb”***, ***“and blind so they have no understanding”***. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads each of the three as a closed door: deaf to the truth so that it cannot benefit them, dumb in the sense that they cannot speak the truth, and blind to seeing it. Ibn ʿAbbās notes that the failure is deliberate, something the people do to themselves rather than something done to them, so that they behave as if they were deaf and dumb and blind in the matters that count.

The Book repeats the description in two other places: (7:179 — **“They have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with, and ears they do not hear with. They are like cattle. In fact, they are even less guided!”**) and (25:44 — **“Or do you think that most of them listen or understand? They are only like cattle—no, more than that, they are astray from the ˹Right˺ Way”**). The closing words of the verse give the reason for the whole picture: “since they have no understanding”. A man who cannot be reached by argument is worse off than an animal, because the animal at least follows the hand that feeds it. The comparison is not an insult thrown at the reader; it is a warning placed in front of him, since the same three doors can be closed slowly, one compromise at a time. Imagine a window that is closed in the morning because the room is cold, and by evening the people in the room have forgotten that there was ever a view.

---
## Verse 2:172

> O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided for you. And give thanks to Allah if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺

**AN ADDRESS TO THE BELIEVERS ABOUT THE TABLE**

The next verse turns the same subject toward the believers, and it addresses them by their faith: ***“O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the good things as the lawful things that have been provided, and the thanks as the response due for them. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sense and adds a note that the verse corrects a serious misunderstanding, because a person who thinks that declaring the good things unlawful is a form of worship has the matter back to front. Al-Mukhtaṣar expands the instruction to the meat, the drink and the produce that God has allowed, and asks for gratitude in the open and in the heart.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains why this verse follows the one about the idolaters. The earlier passage corrected people who had made unlawful what God had made lawful, and this verse warns the believers against copying the same error from the other direction, by eating without asking where the food came from and by treating the limits God set as though they did not exist. The two verses hold the reader in the middle of a narrow path: no adding on the right, no removing on the left. The same instruction was given to the messengers who came before this community: (23:51 — **“O messengers! Eat from what is good and lawful, and act righteously”**). The verse treats the table as part of the mission, since a person who is careless about what he consumes and confident about what he teaches is living in two directions at once. The Book repeats the same point in the Table where the orders stand together: (5:88). The reader is left with an instruction that is wider than a meal and narrower than a licence.

**THANKS AS PART OF THE MEAL**

The verse closes with a condition that gathers the whole instruction: ***“for you. And give thanks to Allah”***, ***“if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺”***. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads thankfulness as covering the tongue and the heart together, and notes that one part of it is to give oneself completely to God and to go against Him in nothing. Al-Jalālayn keeps the promise of the closing words in view: the one who receives a gift and thanks the giver acknowledges that the gift came from a hand, not from the world at large.

Tazkirul Qur'an draws the human picture out of this instruction. A person should feel thankful and obedient to God while he eats and drinks, and should say to himself that he is eating and drinking what God has provided; that attitude builds devotion in the heart. In the same chapter Tazkirul notes where the attitude breaks: when self-made beliefs take over, the blessing that should have produced gratitude instead produces reverence for the food or the object itself. The same verses are read again to the same effect: (16:114 — **“So eat from the good, lawful things which Allah has provided for you, and be grateful for Allah’s favours, if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺”**). Imagine a guest who enjoys dinner at a friend's table and then thanks the chef and never the host, and you have the picture of a person who treats the gift as if it had no giver.

---
## Verse 2:173

> He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—they will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**THE SHORT LIST OF FORBIDDEN THINGS**

The verse then states the other half of the rule in the narrowest terms: ***“He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine”***, ***“and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah.”***. Al-Jalālayn explains the first item as an animal that has not been slaughtered according to the Law, which the practice of the Prophet ﷺ extends to whatever has been severed from a living creature, with fish and locusts excepted. The flesh of swine is named by the part people mostly seek, and the rest of the animal is understood with it. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the last item as whatever has been offered purposefully to something other than God, such as an idol.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes the force of the Arabic words opening the verse, which restrict the prohibition to the items about to be named and leave everything else in the clear. The same short list is given in the sūrah of Cattle: (6:145 — **“I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to eat except carrion, running blood, swine—which is impure—or a sinful offering in the name of any other than Allah.”**), and it is given once more in the sūrah of the Table: (16:115 — **“He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah.”**). Three lists, the same items, in a Book that had to answer generations of people who kept adding to the list. Imagine a doctor who lists four things his patient must avoid and adds nothing else, because the rest of the pharmacy is open to him.

**NECESSITY HAS A NARROW GATE**

The verse then opens the door that mercy opens: ***“But if someone is compelled by necessity”***, ***“neither driven by desire”***, ***“nor exceeding immediate need”***, ***“they will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”***. Al-Jalālayn explains the two conditions as a person who is neither rebelling nor going beyond what the situation requires. Ibn ʿAbbās draws the same limits in more detail: the one who eats under compulsion is not someone who craves the forbidden thing, nor one who declares it lawful, nor one who takes it by force, nor one who eats it by choice while nothing is forcing him. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the sentence simple, that a person pressed by need who does not go past the limit of what necessity requires has done nothing wrong.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān adds the warning that belongs with the concession, that the forbidden stays forbidden and must never be reclassified as lawful, which is what the idolaters of the age of ignorance had done when they ate carrion and animals slaughtered in a name other than God's. The door of necessity is a small door, and it opens only for the person standing at the edge of harm. Imagine a man whose car stops on a mountain road at night; he may take shelter in a stranger's shed, but the shelter is given to the traveller who is stranded, not to the driver who has decided that the shed is a more comfortable place to live. The verse closes with the two names that fit the moment, the Forgiving and the Merciful, because the One who set the limit is the same One who knows how narrow the road can become.

---
## Verse 2:174

> Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain consume nothing but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment, nor will He purify them. And they will suffer a painful punishment

**THE GAIN THAT COSTS THE GAINER**

The verse names a trade that looks profitable and ends in ruin: ***“Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them”***, ***“for a fleeting gain consume nothing”***. Al-Jalālayn explains what was being hidden, that the Scripture contained the descriptions of the Prophet ﷺ, and that the group meant here were the Jews. They concealed what they knew and took a small payment in its place, because making the matter known would have cost them the standing they had among their own people.

Ibn ʿAbbās gives the names of some of the people the verse was revealed about, Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab and his brother, and the setting fits the names: men who argued with the Prophet ﷺ in public while their own books held what they were arguing against. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān places the passage in the flow of the sūrah. The verses before it dealt with unlawful things that can be touched, such as food; this passage turns to unlawful deeds that cannot be touched, beginning with the scholar who sells a verdict and bends a text for a bribe.

**THE FIRE IN THE BELLY**

The sentence that follows is one of the hardest in the sūrah: ***“but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the picture literally and keeps the trade in view, that the price they took becomes the fire they swallow, and that the end of such a road is the Fire itself. Ibn ʿAbbās records two readings of the phrase, one that the money they earned was unlawful, and one that everything they swallowed will become fire for them on the Day of Judgement. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the same end: a person who fills his stomach with what he hid will suffer in the fire of Hell for it.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān draws the warning closer to home. The primary addressees were scholars of an earlier community, and the lesson carries a veiled warning to the religious scholars of this community, that they should keep away from the same practice and never fall short in disclosing what people need to know. The Book stated the offence once more, in the strongest words it has for it: (2:79 — **“So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, “This is from Allah”—seeking a fleeting gain! So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they have earned”**). Imagine a chemist who waters down a medicine because the full dose costs him money; the customer pays the same price and receives less than he came for, and the harm is not in the price but in the promise.

**THE WORD THAT WILL NOT BE SPOKEN**

The verse ends with three losses at once: ***“nor will He purify them.”***, ***“And they will suffer a painful punishment”***. Al-Mukhtaṣar explains the silence of that Day as the absence of anything joyful to hear: the words that would please them will not be said, and no praise will reach them. The purification that is withheld is the cleansing from the filth of sin, so that the person arrives at the end of the road with what he traded for.

The covenant that these people broke is stated plainly in another sūrah: (3:187 — **“when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture to make it known to people and not hide it, yet they cast it behind their backs and traded it for a fleeting gain. What a miserable profit”**). The Book treats the concealment of knowledge as a breach of a promise made to God, and the promise here was not about money at all. Imagine a man who is given a lamp to carry up a dark staircase for a group of people behind him, and who sells the wick at the bottom of the stairs for a handful of coins; the coin is real, and the darkness is real too, and the people behind him are the ones who will stumble in it.

---
## Verse 2:175

> They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment. How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire

**A BAD BARGAIN, NAMED TWICE**

The next verse states the trade in its plainest form: ***“They are the ones”*** ***“who trade guidance for misguidance”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the words as a purchase, that they took error in place of guidance and received it as a buyer receives goods, and Ibn ʿAbbās fills the two sides of the exchange with the choice between disbelief and faith. The language of buying and selling runs through the whole passage, because the people described had a reason for what they did, and the reason is stated in the currency they accepted.

The Book says exactly the same thing about the same kind of person earlier in the sūrah: (2:16 — **“They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance. But this trade is profitless”**). The trade is called profitless because the goods are worthless, and the buyer discovers the value of what he holds only when the market closes.

**THE PRICE PAID FOR PARDON**

The second half of the sentence names the other side of the loss: ***“and forgiveness for punishment. How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire”***. Al-Jalālayn explains the pardon in view as the forgiveness that had been prepared for them in the Hereafter if they had declared what they knew instead of hiding it. Al-Mukhtaṣar says the same in one movement: they exchanged the guidance for misguidance and the forgiveness of God for His punishment, so that both of their hands are empty at once.

The verse therefore measures the price against the thing sold. The scholars in the passage did not lose a doctrine they never had; they lost something that was already theirs and handed over a substitute for it. Imagine a farmer who sells the only water he has for the season and buys a sack of salt with the money; the sack is heavy, and it cannot be drunk. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān keeps the two sides of the exchange in view and adds the detail that makes the loss bitter: the thing that was sold had been entrusted to these people for the benefit of others, so the seller did not even own the goods outright. The Book calls the same trade profitless, and the word is exact, because the loss is measured against the gain rather than beside it. Think of a man who is paid to guard a warehouse and sells the inventory to a passing trader for a night's lodging; the lodging is real, the inventory is gone, and the owner will come back for it.

**THE QUESTION THAT PROVOKES WONDER**

The sentence closes with a question that is meant to stop a reader in his steps: ***“How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire”***. Al-Jalālayn explains that the question is not asking for information; it is a way of expressing amazement at how much patience these people have for the punishment ahead of them. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same line as a question about boldness, how far these men will walk towards the Fire and how calmly they do it.

The wonder in the question belongs to the reader of the verse, not to God. It is written so that a person who is walking in the same direction wakes up while the road is still open. Think of a man who carries a heavy parcel up a hill every morning for a client who never pays him, and who says, when asked, that he has always done it this way. The Arabic form of the question is worth a note, because it carries the tone of astonishment rather than a request for information: a speaker uses it when he wants his hearers to feel the strangeness of what he is describing. The verse is asking the reader to look at the road these men have chosen and to be surprised by it while there is still time to step off it.

---
## Verse 2:176

> That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth. And surely those who differ regarding it are totally engrossed in opposition

**WHY THE SENTENCE IS SO HARD**

The verse supplies the reason for everything the passage has just described: ***“That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth.”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the words as a statement about the Book itself, that God revealed it with the truth, while this group took it in parts, believing one piece and disbelieving another and hiding what they did not accept. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the reason beside the offence, that the scriptures were sent down to be made clear and not hidden, and that the punishment follows the hiding.

Ibn ʿAbbās names the messenger who brought the revelation and the double content of what was revealed, the exposition of truth and falsehood in both the Qur'an and the Torah, and the point is that the people being addressed had the means of knowing. The Book describes its own arrival in the same terms in another sūrah: (3:3 — **“He has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book in truth, confirming what came before it, as He revealed the Torah and the Gospel”**). The Book states the same reason for the sending of revelation in another passage, where the scriptures are described as the means by which disputes are judged: (2:213 — **“revealed to them the Scriptures in truth to judge among people regarding their disputes”**). A revealed book is not a collection of opinions to be sorted according to taste; it is a standard that judges the reader, and the people in this verse had turned the relationship around by keeping the parts that suited them and burying the rest.

**THE BOOK THEY TORE IN TWO**

The second sentence names the behaviour that produced the ruin: ***“And surely those who differ regarding it are totally engrossed in opposition”***. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the opposition as a stance taken by people who accepted some of the scripture and hid some of it, so that their position became distant from the truth they were holding. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same reading and ties it back to the description of the Prophet ﷺ that they had been taught to expect and then found in front of them.

The Book invites a different response to the same verses: (4:82 — **“Do they not then reflect on the Quran? Had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would have certainly found in it many inconsistencies”**). A message that survives an honest reader's questions is worth the reading. Imagine a witness who is handed a document and signs it after reading one page, then insists, when the rest is read out, that the parts he skipped cannot bind him. The document does not depend on the reader's attention to remain what it is, and the Book says the same of itself. Ibn Kathīr reads the closing words as a description of people who have set themselves against the truth so thoroughly that no argument can reach them, and Maʿārif al-Qurʾān adds that the phrase pictures a person stuck in a quarrel at a great distance from the matter at issue. The Arabic describes a distance rather than a difference of opinion, which is why the verse does not invite further debate with the people in question. It sets the Book down in front of the reader and leaves him to decide which side of the distance he is standing on.

---
## Verse 2:177

> Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets; who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives; who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and keep the pledges they make; and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity, and in ˹the heat of˺ battle. It is they who are true ˹in faith˺, and it is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺

**WHAT RIGHTEOUSNESS IS NOT**

The verse opens by clearing away a dispute that had grown loud: ***“Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east”***, ***“or the west. Rather, the righteous are those”***. Al-Jalālayn reports that the words came down in answer to claims made by the Jews and the Christians about the direction of prayer, and the answer does not choose between the two directions. It says that the whole question is beside the point, because a direction is a thing a person turns towards, not a thing a person becomes.

Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the same thought in the language of a person rather than a place: doing good that pleases God is not a matter of turning east or west or arguing about which is right, but of what lives in the heart and shows in the hands. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes where the sūrah stands at this point, past its halfway mark, with the argument for the truth of the Book and the oneness of God already made, and the message now ready to describe the shape of a life. Imagine two men walking to the same mosque from opposite sides of the street; the one who arrives late and stays long is not the lesser worshipper because of which way he faced on the way.

**THE FIRST ARTICLE OF A BUILT LIFE**

The verse then lays the foundation: ***“who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books”***, ***“and the prophets”***. Al-Jalālayn lists the objects of belief in order, God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book and the prophets, so that the reader sees a single structure rather than a set of separate claims. Al-Mukhtaṣar widens the Book to the scriptures as a whole and the prophets as a body, and notes that the faith meant here does not distinguish between one messenger and another.

The narrowest of the words in that list is the smallest and the hardest to say with a straight face: the belief that a person has an account to give. A person who believes in a day of accounting reads his own actions differently, since every unrecorded kindness and every hidden wrong is on a page somebody is keeping. Think of a shopkeeper whose till only balances if he counts the small coins too.

**THE WEALTH THAT LEAVES THE HAND**

The middle of the verse is a list of people, and it reads like the route of a man through his own neighbourhood: ***“who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars”***, ***“and for freeing captives”***. Al-Jalālayn unpacks the items one by one: relatives who are close by right, orphans who have lost a provider, the poor, the traveller far from his home, the one who has been forced to ask, and captives who need to be ransomed out of slavery or prison. The order moves from the nearest circle outward to the people nobody owns a duty to.

The verse states the condition under which the spending counts, that it is given out of wealth the giver cherishes and would rather keep. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same emphasis, that this charity is offered in spite of love for the money. The Book makes the rule explicit in another sūrah: (3:92 — **“You will never achieve righteousness until you donate some of what you cherish. And whatever you give is certainly well known to Allah”**). Imagine a man who gives away the coat he keeps for winter rather than the one that no longer fits him.

**THE PRACTICE THAT FOLLOWS THE CLAIM**

The list then turns from money to habit: ***“who establish prayer, pay alms-tax”***, ***“and keep the pledges they make”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the two acts as the established prayer and the obligatory alms, and the third as the keeping of every promise a person has made, whether with God or with people. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same three, so that worship, giving and honesty stand in one sentence as parts of one description.

The Book counts promise-keeping among the marks of faith, and it does not restrict the promise to a written one. The words a man says in a market, the appointment he makes with a student, the arrangement he strikes with a neighbour, all fall under the sentence. Imagine a man who promises to collect a parcel for his sister and then does not, and who wonders why nobody asks him to carry anything important anymore. The verse treats that small failure as part of the same account as the great acts.

**THE PATIENCE THAT PROVES THE BUILDING**

The last quality named in the list is the one that keeps the others standing: ***“and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity”***, ***“and in ˹the heat of˺ battle. It is they”***. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads the three settings as poverty and illness, hard times of every kind, and the hour of battle, so that patience is asked of a person in the hospital, in the market and on the field at once. Al-Jalālayn keeps the same three circles and reads them as the places where a claim about faith is finally tested by cost.

The closing words then name the people described: ***“who are true ˹in faith˺”***, ***“and it is they”***, ***“who are mindful ˹of Allah˺”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the first phrase as those whose faith is genuine and the second as those who are mindful of their duty to God. Imagine a bridge that has been load-tested in wind and rain; the builders do not speak of what it believes, they point to what it carried. The verse is written the same way, since it lets the reader identify the righteous by what they spend, keep and endure.

---
## Verse 2:178

> O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set for you in cases of murder—a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female. But if the offender is pardoned by the victim’s guardian, then blood-money should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously. This is a concession and a mercy from your Lord. But whoever transgresses after that will suffer a painful punishment

**A LAW SET WHERE REVENGE ONCE RULED**

The verse opens with an address to the believers and a rule that is set over them: ***“O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set”***, ***“for you in cases of murder”***. Al-Jalālayn explains the Arabic words as a prescription that has been made obligatory, and the subject as the killed person and the act that killed him. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same frame, that the verse speaks of retaliation for murder on equal terms.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān sets the rule against the streets it came down in. An Arab tribe whose man was killed did not ask what the killer had done; it asked who he was, and the price of a life varied with the standing of the family, so that a strong tribe took a free man for a slave and a chief for a labourer. The verse ended the bargaining with a sentence that gave the same value to every life it named.

**THE EQUALITY THAT REPLACED PRIDE**

The rule is then spelled out item by item: ***“a free man for a free man, a slave”***, ***“for a slave, and a female”***, ***“for a female. But”***. Al-Jalālayn notes that the practice of the Prophet ﷺ clarified the details of the list, so that a man may be held to account for the life of a woman, and the community's standing before God does not raise the worth of a person above another. Al-Mukhtaṣar states the purpose plainly, that the punishment for a deliberate killing should be the same as the crime.

The same principle is written into the law given to an earlier community: (5:45 — **“We ordained for them in the Torah, “A life for a life, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, a tooth for a tooth—and for wounds equal retaliation”**). The verse in front of the reader is not a licence for a private settling of scores, and the Book keeps the whole matter in the hands of those who can judge it. Imagine a market where every trader invented his own weights; the rule of equal weights is not an insult to the traders, it is the only reason a market can work.

**THE DOOR OF PARDON AND THE BLOOD MONEY**

The verse then opens a second door: ***“if the offender is pardoned by the victim’s guardian”***, ***“then blood-money should be decided fairly”***, ***“and payment should be made courteously. This is a concession”***, ***“and a mercy from your Lord.”***. Al-Mukhtaṣar explains the two stages, that the family of the killed person may waive the retaliation or accept the agreed payment instead, and that the payment must be arranged fairly and handed over courteously so that neither side is shamed by it. Al-Jalālayn reads the concession as the opening to pardon and the closing words as the mercy that accompanies it.

The Book treats the matter of life with the same seriousness in another place: (17:33 — **“Do not take a ˹human˺ life—made sacred by Allah—except with ˹legal˺ right. If anyone is killed unjustly, We have given their heirs the authority, but do not let them exceed limits in retaliation”**). The instruction to the heir is to keep his claim inside the law, and the opening for forgiveness is not a hole in the law; it is a door built into the wall. Think of a family that holds a debt against a neighbour and decides to write it off after a conversation on the doorstep; the debt was real, and the writing-off is a choice the law allowed them to make.

**THE LINE THAT CANNOT BE CROSSED**

The verse ends with a warning to the party who has already been treated generously: ***“But whoever transgresses after”***, ***“that will suffer a painful punishment”***. Al-Mukhtaṣar reads it as a statement about the person who goes back on the agreement and takes the matter past the limits he accepted, so that the punishment becomes his own to answer for. Al-Jalālayn keeps the same edge in the words, that the one who returns to violence after the settlement has put himself outside the protection of what he agreed.

The warning is necessary because the moment a community is given the right to take a life in return, it is also given the power to abuse it. The verse closes the gap by making the settlement binding on both sides. Imagine a court that orders a debt to be paid in monthly instalments and a creditor who takes the whole amount by force anyway; the force is the very thing the court was asked to replace.

---
## Verse 2:179

> There is ˹security of˺ life for you in ˹the law of˺ retaliation, O people of reason, so that you may become mindful ˹of Allah˺

**THE LIFE HIDDEN INSIDE THE LAW**

The verse draws the conclusion that a reader might not expect from a law of punishment: ***“There is ˹security of˺ life”***, ***“for you in ˹the law of˺ retaliation, O people of reason”***. Al-Jalālayn explains the paradox in the plainest terms. A person who intends to kill knows that his own life will be taken in return, and so he holds his hand back; the law that takes a life therefore saves two lives, the life of the man he was about to kill and the life he would have thrown away with it. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the phrase as a continuation of existence for the community, a lesson that keeps its members alive.

Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the same sense and names the result, that the law spares blood and stops the chain of attacks between people. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes where the passage stands: the sūrah has finished describing the shape of righteousness and now turns to the subsidiary rulings that belong with it, beginning with retaliation, so that the reader sees the law as part of the same moral life rather than as a separate subject.

**WHY THE BOOK ADDRESSES PEOPLE OF REASON**

The verse does not address everyone with the same words; it calls out to ***“for you in ˹the law of˺ retaliation, O people of reason”*** and closes with ***“so that you may become mindful ˹of Allah˺”***. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the address as a call to people of sound minds, the ones who can see the connection between a rule and its consequence. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān explains that the injunction is asked to be understood by everyone, and this verse marks the ones who will actually take the lesson: the people who can trace a cause to its result and choose the harder answer now because of what it prevents later.

The Book measures the value of a life in another place with a sentence that has been quoted across the world: (5:32 — **“whoever takes a life—unless as a punishment for murder or mischief in the land—it will be as if they killed all of humanity; and whoever saves a life, it will be as if they saved all of humanity”**). The verse before the reader is the practical consequence of that valuation, because a society that lets every family settle a killing by violence ends up burying its own children. Imagine a town where the only brake on a reckless driver is the knowledge that his own licence will be taken; the rule is not written to punish him, and it is not written out of sympathy for the street either. It is written because the street and the driver cannot both go free. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān points out that the rule falls on the person who committed the crime and not on his family or his tribe, which is the whole difference between a law and a feud. A rule that punishes a clan for the act of one of its members is not justice; it is a licence for the next round of killings, and the Book closes that door before it opens anything else. Imagine a village that burns down the house of a thief's cousin because the thief has run away; the second house is on fire, and the theft is still unsolved.

---
## Verse 2:180

> It is prescribed that when death approaches any of you—if they leave something of value—a will should be made in favour of parents and immediate family with fairness. ˹This is˺ an obligation on those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺

**A COMMAND THAT ARRIVES BEFORE THE END**

The next verse turns to what a person leaves behind: ***“It is prescribed that”***, ***“when death approaches any of you”***, ***“if they leave something of value”***. Al-Jalālayn explains the Arabic opening as an obligation laid on the dying person, and the word translated as something of value as material wealth, so that the instruction applies to those who have something to leave. The command is given while the person is still able to give it, which is the whole point of mentioning the approach of death rather than the death itself.

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān opens the meaning of the word for a will. It literally means an order given about something, whether the order takes effect in the lifetime of the person giving it or after his death, and the common usage of the word settled on what must be done after death. The verse therefore places the making of a will among the religious duties, and it does so with a time limit attached, since a man cannot bequeath anything after his voice has stopped.

**PARENTS, RELATIVES AND FAIRNESS**

The people named first are the nearest: ***“a will should be made in favour of parents”***, ***“and immediate family with fairness. ˹This is˺ an obligation on those”***. Al-Jalālayn notes that the bequest to parents and to the nearest relatives is to be made in kindness, that is with generosity and without strain, and Ibn ʿAbbās adds that the nearer the relative, the greater the claim. Al-Mukhtaṣar supplies the limit that the practice of the Prophet ﷺ gave the rule, that the bequest may not exceed one third of the estate, and that the rest is distributed among the heirs according to the shares the Book sets for them.

The limit is what makes the command a mercy rather than a burden. A dying man has a duty to his parents and his relatives, and he has duties to the children who will live in the same house after him, and the rule keeps him from resolving one duty by ruining the other. The Book later gives the shares of inheritance in detail: (4:11 — **“Allah commands you regarding your children: the share of the male will be twice that of the female. If you leave only two ˹or more˺ females, their share is two-thirds of the estate”**). Imagine a man who gives away the family shop in his last week and leaves his four children with a bare room; the gift may have been generous, and the fairness the verse asks for includes the people he did not ask.

**THE OBLIGATION THAT FALLS ON THE MINDFUL**

The sentence closes by naming who carries this duty: ***“who are mindful ˹of Allah˺”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the words as a description of the people who keep their duty to God, so that the last phrase of the verse is not a comment but a definition: the person who fears his Lord is the person who arranges his affairs before he is called to give an account of them. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps the same sense and notes that the verse was later completed by the laws of inheritance, which settled the shares in detail.

The Book treats the death of a person as a public matter and not only a family one, because a disordered estate leaves debts unpaid and relatives in dispute for years. In another place the Book names that duty of doing right by the one who has died as a companion of the remembrance of God: (4:29 — **“Do not devour one another’s wealth illegally, but rather trade by mutual consent”**). Imagine an old man who has written his instructions on a page in his own hand and reads them to his sons while he is still sitting at the table with them; the conversation is difficult, and the dispute it prevents is worse.

---
## Verse 2:181

> But whoever changes the will after hearing it, the blame will only be on those who made the change. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**THE PERSON WHO CHANGES THE WORDS**

The next verse guards what the previous one ordered: ***“But whoever changes the will after hearing it, the blame will only be on those”***, ***“who made the change.”***. Al-Jalālayn explains that the person meant is either a witness or a trustee who alters the terms of the will after he has heard them and knows what they say, and that the sin of the alteration settles on him and not on the person who dictated the words. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the same, adding that the testator carries nothing of the blame for what was done to his will after his death.

Al-Mukhtaṣar spells out what changing the will looks like in practice: adding to it, taking from it, or withholding something that was meant to be paid, in each case with full knowledge of what the document says. The verse therefore draws a line between a mistake made by a reader who is trying to understand and a decision made by a man who has understood perfectly and prefers a different article. Imagine a man entrusted with delivering a sealed envelope to a widow and who opens it, rewrites the sum, and reseals it in a different room; the envelope arrives, and it does not carry the sender's words. The ruling also tells a reader what to do when he suspects that a document has already been altered, since the work of restoring a trust belongs to the community and not only to the person who wrote it: (4:58 — **“Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners; and when you judge between people, judge with fairness”**).

**THE TWO NAMES THAT WATCH THE TRUST**

The verse closes with two names that explain why such a deed cannot be hidden: ***“Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing”***. Al-Jalālayn reads the first name as God's hearing of the testator's words and the second as His knowledge of what the trustee did with them. Ibn ʿAbbās keeps all three parties in view at once, the one who dictated, the one who changed the text, and the One who heard both conversations.

The Book puts the same warning beside the duties of testimony elsewhere in the sūrah: (2:283), where the concealment of a witness's knowledge is described as a stain on the heart. The point of these two verses is that a will is a piece of testimony spoken by someone who can no longer explain what he meant. A dead man cannot answer a question in court. Imagine a builder who is told to finish a house according to a plan whose author has since died; the plan is the only voice left in the room, and the man who alters the measurements has silenced the owner. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the trustee and the witness now sit in a seat the dying man can no longer occupy: his voice is finished, and theirs has taken its place, so that whatever they do with his words is done in his name. The Book names the same offence in the language of property, that a person's wealth is not to be taken from him by a trick: (2:188 — **“Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly, nor deliberately bribe authorities in order to devour a portion of others’ property, knowing that it is a sin”**). Imagine a nurse who is left alone with a patient's chart and writes a different dose in the margin; the chart is the patient's only voice on the ward, and the nurse has spoken for him without his permission.

---
## Verse 2:182

> Whoever suspects an error or an injustice in the will and brings about a ˹fair˺ settlement among the parties will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**THE OFFICE OF PUTTING THINGS RIGHT**

The passage ends with a door for the person who finds the text already damaged: ***“Whoever suspects an error”***, ***“or an injustice in the will”***, ***“and brings about a ˹fair˺ settlement among the parties will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”***. Al-Jalālayn explains the two possibilities the verse has in view, either an honest error in the way the will was written or a deliberate injustice, as when a dying man pushes a share past the legal limit or names someone who has no claim on the estate. The person who suspects either of these and works to bring the parties back to a fair settlement is not a meddler, and the verse declares that he carries no sin.

Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the work of that person in three movements, that he advises whoever made the will, corrects what can be corrected, and reconciles the people who have fallen into dispute, and adds that he is rewarded rather than blamed for it. The Book names the same work as one of the few good things that can be said behind a closed door: The verse sets a limit on the correction as well: the person named is one who works for a fair settlement rather than a better position for himself, so that the difference between the trespasser of the previous verse and the reconciler of this one is the direction in which the money moves. The Book praises the man who repairs the document, and it does not praise the man who improves his own share in the process. (4:114 — **“There is no good in most of their secret talks—except those encouraging charity, kindness, or reconciliation between people. And whoever does this seeking Allah’s pleasure, We will grant them a great reward”**).

**WHY THE RECONCILER IS NOT A BUSYBODY**

The permission is narrow and worth stating clearly, because the previous verse condemned the person who alters a will, and this verse praises the person who repairs one. The difference is not what he does to the paper but what he does to the dispute. The one acts to take a share, and the other acts to give a share back to the person who was owed it. Imagine a man who notices that a shopkeeper has undercharged his customer by a large sum; correcting the till is not theft, and the accountant who refuses to look at the error because the rule says not to interfere has not served the rule.

The Book repeats the value of this work in a sentence about the community itself: (49:10 — **“The believers are but one brotherhood, so make peace between your brothers. And be mindful of Allah so you may be shown mercy”**). The verse before the reader applies that brotherhood to the hour when it is hardest to practise, the hour when a family is dividing the property of a person they have just buried. Whoever stands between them and their quarrel, and holds both sides to what is fair, has done the work of the book he is reading. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān notes that the reconciler is described as one who acts in good faith and is rewarded for it, and the Book gives the general rule that a person is judged by what he intended rather than by what he touched. The three movements of the verse, advising, correcting and reconciling, are the same three movements the earlier passage asked of the people who had hidden a truth, and the door stands open in both places for the same reason. Imagine a builder who notices that the surveyor's line was stretched wrong and who calls the whole crew together before the concrete is poured; the delay is one afternoon, and the wall is straight for a hundred years.

## Verse 2:231

> Or ˹are you not aware of˺ the one who passed by a city which was in ruins. Just look at your food and drink—they have not spoiled. ˹But now˺ look at ˹the remains of˺ your donkey! And ˹so˺ We have made you into a sign for humanity. And look at the bones ˹of the donkey˺, how We bring them together then clothe them with flesh!” When this was made clear to him, he declared, “˹Now˺ I know that Allah is Most Capable of everything.”

## Verse 2:282

> O believers! When you contract a loan for a fixed period of time, commit it to writing. Let the scribe maintain justice between the parties. The scribe should not refuse to write as Allah has taught them to write. They will write what the debtor dictates, bearing Allah in mind and not defrauding the debt. If the debtor is incompetent, weak, or unable to dictate, let their guardian dictate for them with justice. Call upon two of your men to witness. If two men cannot be found, then one man and two women of your choice will witness—so if one of the women forgets the other may remind her. The witnesses must not refuse when they are summoned. You must not be against writing ˹contracts˺ for a fixed period—whether the sum is small or great. This is more just ˹for you˺ in the sight of Allah, and more convenient to establish evidence and remove doubts. However, if you conduct an immediate transaction among yourselves, then there is no need for you to record it, but call upon witnesses when a deal is finalized. Let no harm come to the scribe or witnesses. If you do, then you have gravely exceeded ˹your limits˺. Be mindful of Allah, for Allah ˹is the One Who˺ teaches you. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things
